TI Psychometric network of the online learning strategies questionnaire in
   Peruvian university students
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE online learning; online learning strategies; educational technology;
   network analysis; psychometrics; university students
AB Online learning strategies refer to the methods and approaches students use to organize study activities, manage course content, and regulate participation in virtual learning environments. These strategies are relevant to educational technology because they provide measurable indicators that can inform instructional design, learning analytics, adaptive learning systems, and student support in online and blended courses. This study examined the psychometric properties of the online learning strategies scale (OLSS) using a psychometric network analysis approach in Peruvian university students. The sample included 520 university students (389 women = 74.8%; 131 men = 25.2%) aged 18 to 40 years. Descriptive analyses were conducted to evaluate item distributions. The psychometric network structure of the OLSS was then estimated using exploratory graph analysis with bootstrap procedures, followed by assessment of community stability and structural consistency. The results identified a four-community structure corresponding to motivation, self-control, Internet literacy, and Internet anxiety. The network showed high structural stability, with bootstrap replication values close to 1.00 for most items and high structural consistency across communities. These findings support the internal structure and reliability of the OLSS in the studied population. From an educational technology perspective, the OLSS may help instructors and instructional designers identify students requiring motivational, self-regulatory, digital literacy, or affective support in technologyenhanced learning environments.

TI Feasibility and cost of partnering with social media influencers to
   promote colorectal cancer screening
SO HEALTH EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID FEAR APPEALS; METAANALYSIS
AB There is considerable interest in collaborating with social media influencers to promote health messages, but little evidence demonstrating how this might be done in organizations with few resources or experience. We tested the feasibility and cost of partnering with social media nano- and micro-influencers to promote colorectal cancer (CRC) screening messages. We identified 16 US influencers through an online influencer marketing campaign platform. To test if influencers would create theory-consistent content, we provided them with recommended CRC screening information and guidelines for including one of four message strategies (threat, efficacy, threat and efficacy, information only). Influencers created and posted one video promoting CRC screening on their Instagram Reels and Stories, June-July, 2025. Engagement metrics were collected 1 month after posting. The videos were viewed 89 764 times (M = 5610, SD = 5545), and cost $0.13 per view. They did not elicit resistance; comments were 96% positive, 4% neutral, 0% negative, and engagement rates were high (mean = 7.9%). Influencers were largely able to follow written guidance for including theory-based content in their posts. In light of the rise in social media use, including among middle-aged and older adults, partnerships between public health organizations and social media influencers could expand health message reach.

TI Project-Based Learning for Resilient Engineering Education: Insights
   from Two Online Cohorts in Mechanics of Materials under Crisis
   Conditions
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Project-based learning; Engineering education; Educational resilience;
   Remote supervision; Low-resource settings; COVID-19; Armed conflict
AB This study examined the implementation of project-based learning (PjBL) in the second-year Mechanics of Materials courses at the University of Khartoum, delivered to two online cohorts during national crises: the COVID-19 pandemic (2019-2020), and the ongoing armed conflict (2022-2023). Both cohorts completed applied design miniprojects involving geometry definition, load estimation, element sizing, and sketching, conducted entirely through text-based asynchronous supervision. Three surveys were administered: a retrospective evaluation of the COVID-19 cohort (n=123), a post-course survey for the War-23 cohort (n=50), and feedback from 16 supervisors. Supervisors reported notable gains in mentoring and instructional skills. Institutional data indicated over a 20% increase in exam averages and pass rates compared with pre-PjBL cohorts, and sustained academic improvements were observed in subsequent structural analysis and design modules. These results affirm PjBL's effectiveness as a low-cost, mentor-supported strategy for preserving learning quality and promoting educational resilience in engineering education under crisis conditions.

   Industry
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Workforce development; Construction industry; Competency framework;
   Sensing technologies; Delphi method
ID PROJECT; SAFETY; BIM; PERCEPTIONS; BENEFITS; DELPHI
AB Data sensing technologies, such as laser scanners and global positioning systems, offer significant potential to enhance safety, productivity, and quality in construction. However, their adoption is often hindered by a lack of clearly defined workforce competencies tailored to these technologies. This study addresses this gap by developing domain-specific competencies grounded in empirical research and industry practice. A comprehensive literature review identified preliminary knowledge, skills, and abilities, which were refined through a Delphi study with experienced construction professionals. To assess the perceived importance and degree of consensus surrounding these competencies, statistical methods such as the median absolute deviation and relative importance index were employed. Nineteen knowledge areas reached consensus, with high priority given to "types of sensing technologies," "applications of sensing technologies," and "safety management." Among the eight skills evaluated, "technical skills," "collaborative skills," and "mapping and visualization skills" ranked highest. For abilities, "problem-solving," "decision-making," and "critical thinking" were top-rated. A focus group further contextualized these findings, validating the relevance of all identified competencies and proposing revisions to their prioritization. Participants ranked "cost-benefit analysis," "data security," and "client-centric knowledge" significantly higher, citing real-world decision-making and client engagement challenges. Similarly, "communication skills" and "data analytics" were elevated among skills, and "analytical thinking" and "safety awareness" gained prominence among abilities. These insights highlight the distinction between theoretical importance and practical impact, emphasizing the need for curricula and training that reflect field-based priorities. The combined Delphi and focus-group results produced a validated set of competencies to guide sensing technology implementation in construction. These outcomes provide guidance for aligning construction education and training programs with the evolving demands of digital construction, as well as offering strategic insights for curriculum design, workforce training, and policy development aimed at closing the technology-competency gap.

TI Enhancing Active Learning in Large Core Engineering Courses: Strategies,
   Evidence-Based Insights, and Challenges
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
AB This article explores the integration of active learning strategies within large, required core courses in undergraduate engineering education, drawing on a case study of a faculty member teaching a Statics and Strength of Materials course to more than 200 students each semester. The focus is placed on pedagogical adaptations, logistical complexities, student participation, and institutional support systems required to make active learning successful on a scale. The study discusses the design and implementation of various techniques such as group hands-on challenges, discipline-specific problems, model demonstration, in-class exercises, and recitation sessions, while critically assessing their impact on student engagement and academic performance. It also highlights barriers including classroom space constraints, time limitations, resistance to change, and the need for ongoing faculty development. Practical recommendations are provided for scaling these approaches and building a sustainable support structure for educators, with the aim of fostering deeper learning and greater student engagement in large engineering courses.

TI Conceptual Understanding of Performance-Based Seismic Design through
   Project-Based Learning during a Five-Week Graduate Course
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID STUDENTS
AB Performance-based seismic design (PBSD) represents a paradigm shift in structural engineering, emphasizing stakeholder-defined objectives and nonlinear evaluation over prescriptive code-based methods. Teaching PBSD at the graduate level is challenging due to its conceptual complexity and students' reliance on conventional design approaches. This paper presents a case study on the effectiveness of project-based learning (PBL) for teaching PBSD in a five-week graduate course within the structural engineering specialization program at Universidad Industrial de Santander. Students designed a four-story residential building using both code-based and performance-based methods, supported by real seismic hazard data and nonlinear analysis tools. Learning outcomes were assessed at three stages with peer-reviewed rubrics and validated through inferential statistical analysis. Results show substantial improvement, with average conceptual understanding scores rising from 1.39 +/- 0.49 to 3.84 +/- 1.05, a mean improvement of 2.45 with a 95% confidence interval of [2.05, 2.85]. Analysis through Bloom's taxonomy, SOLO taxonomy, and experiential learning frameworks indicates that PBL enabled students to progress from routine application of design codes to higher-order skills needed for PBSD. These findings suggest that PBL is an effective strategy for teaching high-complexity engineering paradigms at the graduate level within intensive and time-compressed formats, thereby contributing to the body of evidence on PBL and its application in accelerated professional education.

TI Civil Engineering Competency Map: A Text-Mining Analysis of Job
   Advertisements for the Turkish Construction Industry
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Construction industry; Job advertisements; Text mining; Latent Dirichlet
   allocation; <italic>k</italic>-means clustering
ID K-MEANS; MANAGEMENT; EDUCATION; SIGNALS
AB In response to the evolving demands of the globalized construction industry and the recognized gap between academic training and real-world requirements, this study investigates the contemporary competency landscape for modern civil engineers. Utilizing the Turkish construction industry, which is a prominent global player in international contracting, as a representative case study, the research employs a quantitative text-mining approach. The study analyzed 154 job advertisements from a major professional job portal using term frequency-inverse document frequency for skill importance, latent Dirichlet allocation for thematic modeling, and k-means clustering for role segmentation. The results revealed that the modern civil engineer requires a multifaceted profile combining core technical skills such as project management and the high-impact financial competencies of quantity takeoff and progress payment, with essential soft skills and vital cognitive abilities. Furthermore, distinct skill clusters emerged for different roles, showing an increasing emphasis on leadership as career paths progress. The findings provide a scalable methodological framework and an empirical baseline for international stakeholders. This research offers guidance for educational institutions worldwide to restructure program content to address the dual requirement for foundational breadth and specialized depth, thereby aligning graduate competencies with the evolving demands of global professional practice.

TI Assessing Changes in Innovation Self-Efficacy and Interest among
   Environmental Engineering Students Engaged through Inquiry-Based
   Learning
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Innovation self-efficacy; Environmental Engineering; Inquiry-based
   learning; Innovation interest; Gender differences
ID CREATIVITY; WOMEN
AB This study examined changes in students' innovation-related self-efficacy, interests, and perceived importance of innovation in future careers over the course of a junior-level environmental engineering class. The course incorporated an inquiry-based, open-ended project supported by external mentors and scaffolded with structured reflections based on Dyer's innovation model. A previously validated Likert-scale survey based on expectancy-value theory (EVT) was administered at the beginning and end of the project, with five to six items creating composite scores for self-efficacy, interest, and future work importance. Paired presurvey and postsurvey responses were available from 35 students. Results showed statistically significant gains in students' innovation self-efficacy (presurvey mean 4.0 and postsurvey mean 4.8), including questioning, observing, experimenting, idea networking, and associational thinking skills. However, students' interest in innovation-related tasks and importance in future work remained largely unchanged. The lack of correlation of innovation self-efficacy with future importance of innovative work in this study contrasted with expectations based on EVT and earlier research. Innovation self-efficacy was not correlated with innovation interests in the presurvey but the correlation was significant on the postsurvey, indicating that the intervention may have better aligned these attitudes. Female students initially reported lower innovation self-efficacy than male students (mean of 3.7 versus 4.3, respectively) but by the end of the semester the difference was not statistically significant (mean of 4.6 versus 4.9). Female and male students did not differ significantly in their innovation interests or importance in future work. These findings illustrate how an inquiry-based project can effectively enhance engineering students' confidence in the core skills that drive innovation.

TI EduCase: A Systematic Framework for Developing Educational Case Studies
   in Construction and Engineering Education
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
AB Despite the critical role of educational case studies in construction and engineering education (CEE), there is a lack of systematic frameworks for developing effective educational case studies. This study introduces the educational case study development (EduCase) framework, a structured, multiphase approach for developing educational case studies through iterative, multicohort testing and refinement. The framework guides instructors through four integrated phases: case study creation, pilot implementation, assessment, and systematic refinement cycles. When a case study is created and pilot tested, student assessment data from each implementation cycle inform targeted refinements, enabling continuous improvement until the case study consistently achieves intended learning objectives (LOs). To test the framework, a case study was developed on the topic of target value design through iterative testing with 207 students across multiple cohorts and disciplines. Results demonstrated that the framework produces case studies that significantly improve cognitive engagement, enhance student perceptions including curiosity and confidence, and achieve strong learning outcomes. This study provides a framework for developing pedagogically sound case studies in CEE, offering a structured approach to integrating theory and practice in engineering education.

   Worker Safety

   industry
ID EDUCATION; STUDENTS
AB Construction workers face disproportionately high safety risks, yet the role of empathy-a critical driver of worker-centric safety practices-remains underexplored in civil engineering education. This study examines the level of empathy among civil engineering students in India toward the safety of construction workers. TI Teaching Collaborative BIM in Higher Education: A New Pedagogical
   Framework
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Building information modeling; Building information modeling (BIM)
   education; Functional trefoil; Collaborative work
ID DESIGN; CONSTRUCTION
AB Collaborative building information modeling (BIM) plays a critical role in the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry, yet BIM education still predominantly focuses on technical software skills, often neglecting the collaborative competencies required for interdisciplinary teamwork. This study proposes and validates a pedagogical framework for collaborative BIM education grounded in the Functional Trefoil model, which emphasizes communication, coordination, and production. A hands-on BIM clash detection assignment was designed to replicate professional workflows using industry-standard tools, including Newforma Konekt, Navisworks, Revit, and Tekla Structures, allowing students to engage in model federation, conflict resolution, and structured team collaboration. The assignment was implemented in the BIM830 course at & Eacute;cole de technologie sup & eacute;rieure (& Eacute;TS) and evaluated through student surveys. Responses from 42 participants revealed increased engagement, satisfaction, and confidence in collaborative BIM practices, with over 85% reporting clear instructions, 90% valuing the collaborative effectiveness of the tools, and more than 80% indicating improved confidence in team-based BIM environments. The results demonstrate that integrating collaborative technologies and structured workflows into BIM education can effectively bridge the gap between theory and practice. The proposed approach offers a scalable and adaptable model for institutions seeking to modernize BIM curricula while highlighting the importance of equipping educators with digital and active learning competencies aligned with industry needs.

TI Improving Data-Sensing Technology Training in Construction through
   Immersive Embodied Interaction
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Construction education; Immersive learning; Sensing technologies;
   Knowledge and skills
ID MIXED REALITY; VIRTUAL-REALITY; VISUALIZATION; EDUCATION; MOTION
AB The construction industry increasingly relies on data-sensing technologies, such as drones and quadrupedal robots, for inspection, safety management, and decision-making, but effective training lags due to cost, limited expertise, and a lack of immersive, hands-on practice. Immersive embodied interaction (IEI) can increase effective training by coupling bodily movement to virtual actions, but its application in construction is underexplored. Grounded in embodied cognition theory, this study proposes a process for integrating IEI into data-sensing training and experimentally compared enhanced IEI with traditional virtual reality (VR). A total of 41 participants were assigned to 2 conditions: (1) enhanced embodied interaction using a programmed game controller, and (2) traditional VR interaction using standard controllers. Participants completed two VR-based construction tasks simulating real jobsites: a drone inspection and a quadrupedal robodog operation. Outcomes included task completion time, collision frequency, collision and recovery duration, and subjective ratings. Relative to traditional VR, enhanced IEI reduced completion time by 30% in the drone task (p=0.036) and 37% in the robodog task (p<0.001). In the drone task, collision frequency increased, but collision duration was significantly shorter (p=0.004), indicating faster recovery. In the robodog task, collision frequency was statistically unchanged (p=0.056), and recovery time decreased. Participants reported a higher sense of accomplishment with IEI. These findings suggest that IEI can improve the efficiency and intuitiveness of VR-based training for data-sensing technologies in construction, with potential benefits for learning, skill acquisition, and safety-related behaviors. The study advances knowledge by providing a framework for enhancing data-sensing education in the construction industry.

TI BIM Integration in Civil Engineering Curricula: Maturity Assessment,
   Pilot Testing, and Roadmap Design
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Building information modeling (BIM); Engineering education; Curriculum
   integration; Blended learning; Digital pedagogy; Digital technologies
ID INFORMATION MODELING BIM; IMPLEMENTATION
AB The growing digitalization of the architecture, engineering, and construction (AEC) industry has increased the demand for graduates with strong BIM-related competencies, yet many undergraduate programs-particularly in emerging economies-still approach BIM in a fragmented and software-centered way. This study reports the development and implementation of a structured educational strategy for integrating building information modeling (BIM) into the civil engineering curriculum of a Brazilian public university. The intervention followed a four-phase process: (1) assessment of institutional BIM maturity using a customized 16-indicator matrix, which classified the program at the initial level (MI=37.5%); (2) curriculum mapping across 66 courses, revealing that 56.1% had potential for BIM integration; (3) pilot implementation in four core courses using project-based and team-based learning; and (4) creation of a long-term institutional roadmap aligned with national policies such as the Brazilian BIM Strategy. Survey results from 43 students indicated moderate to high satisfaction with the learning experience (mean scores between 3.84 and 4.35 on a 1-5 scale) and modest perceived gains in BIM conceptual understanding. Iterative refinements addressed gaps in digital literacy, assessment design, and faculty alignment. The proposed roadmap offers a replicable, evidence-based, and context-sensitive approach for institutions-particularly those in emerging-economy contexts, including but not limited to Latin America-seeking to scale BIM integration in engineering education.

TI Analysis of Student Reflections from Civil and Environmental Engineering
   Capstone Courses to Evaluate Service-Learning Experiences and Their
   Effectiveness
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Service-learning; Civil engineering; Environmental engineering; Capstone
   course; Written student reflection
ID PROJECTS
AB Student reflections offer an opportunity to evaluate the effectiveness of service-learning (SL) in engineering courses. This paper explains the approach, analysis, and conclusions of students' written reflections (n=246) from 62 different team-based SL projects in a combined civil engineering and environmental engineering (CEE) capstone course over five consecutive years. The analysis addressed five broad research questions. The reflections were coded for 10 attributes. Anonymous exit surveys taken by the same set of students supplemented the reflections data in addition to instructors' assessment of five attributes-the quality of the deliverables, team dynamics, project scope, and community partners' background and level of project engagement. The analysis showed that the student reflections provided an authentic and reliable set of data to assess student experience. The students' overall satisfaction with their SL experience was largely independent of their gender, major, residency, prior academic record, and affinity toward service. However, student satisfaction did correlate with the student's perception of achieving the three tenets of SL-academic enhancement, personal growth, and civic engagement. The study reinforces the effectiveness of SL as a strong teaching and learning approach for capstone CEE courses. Despite challenges such as team dynamics and community partner interactions, this study showed that most students (almost 90%) had a positive overall experience in their SL capstone projects.

TI Impact of Full-Scale Experiential Learning Modules on Students'
   Understanding of Concepts in Steel Design
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Experiential learning; Structural engineering; Steel design; Steel
   behavior; Failure mechanisms; Active learning
AB The objective of this study was to determine the effect of full-scale experiential learning modules (ELMs) on student understanding of steel behavior in an undergraduate steel design course. Instructors at two universities taught an introductory steel design course with traditional teaching methods for 2 years. The following 2 years, the instructors taught the same course using the same methods with the addition of the full-scale ELMs to better visualize steel behavior and failure mechanisms. Three exam questions on the topics related to the ELMs were given at both universities. The responses to these problems were scored based on the number of correct statements made, awarding a point for each correct statement. On one question, students were also scored based on the inclusion of sketches of the correct steel behavior. Although the differences were not statistically significant, the mean scores for both universities were higher on the Tension Connections question and the Failure Mechanisms of Beams question and lower on the Buckling Modes of Columns question. The number of students including sketches in their responses was also not significant, but the mean number of students using sketches correctly was higher from the control to intervention group. End-of-course surveys were given to test student understanding of topics covered in the ELMs and gauge student satisfaction with the ELMs. Based on the survey responses, students were typically able to describe the steel behavior relating to concepts covered in the ELMs and felt the ELMs was a positive experience for the course. The test scores and end-of-course surveys appear to show the ELMs helped students gain a better understanding of steel behavior and failure mechanisms.

TI Fostering Computational Thinking for an Adaptive Construction Workforce:
   Experimental Study of VR-Based Human-Robot Interaction
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Virtual reality (VR); Construction education; Computational thinking
   (CT); Immersive learning; Human-robot interaction (HRI)
ID VIRTUAL-REALITY; SKILLS; FRAMEWORK; GAME
AB Construction work is becoming increasingly technology-intensive, requiring transferable skills that enable effective human-robot interaction (HRI). We designed and evaluated a virtual-reality (VR) training environment that pedagogically integrates computational thinking (CT) elements (i.e., decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, and algorithm design) within HRI tasks relevant to construction. In this study, CT is conceptualized as a structured problem-solving competency that supports task formulation, decision-making, and interaction with automated systems in construction environments. Participants completed a progression of pick-and-place missions using a six-axis robotic arm on a Mecanum mobility platform across three settings: a warehouse (training), along with realistic construction and unfamiliar extraterrestrial construction (testing) environments. In a proof-of-concept, exploratory study with 14 undergraduate construction students, the CT-integrated training environment was compared with a baseline configuration featuring similar HRI tasks without explicit pedagogical CT integration. Outcomes included knowledge-skill-attitude measures and task performance indexed by accuracy-speed-energy-safety metrics. Relative to the control group, the experimental group (trained in the CT-integrated environment) demonstrated larger gains in CT knowledge and attitudes and achieved superior post-training performance in the realistic construction site scenario, with significant multivariate group differences favoring CT integration. Group differences were insignificant in the extraterrestrial construction site scenario, suggesting that near-term transfer is constrained by contextual factors under unfamiliar conditions. Across groups, pattern recognition and algorithm design were the most consistent predictors of efficient and safe task execution. These findings provide preliminary evidence that integrating CT within immersive VR-based HRI training can strengthen computational competencies and structured task performance in construction-relevant environments, while highlighting the need for expanded instructional designs to better support transfer to unfamiliar, high-complexity contexts.

TI Utilizing Handmade Physical Models in Structural Engineering Education
   for Qualitative Analysis of Statically Indeterminate Beams and Frames
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Hand-made physical models; Qualitative analysis; Structural analysis;
   Statically indeterminate; Beams and frames
ID STUDENTS; DESIGN
AB This study investigates the integration of hand-made physical models into structural engineering education, with a particular focus on the qualitative analysis of statically indeterminate beams and frames. Conducted as part of a third-year undergraduate module, the research highlights how these models significantly enhance students' understanding of structural behaviors, including deflection and internal force distribution, leading to improved accuracy in drawing axial force, shear force, and bending moment diagrams. By bridging theoretical instruction with practical, hands-on engagement, the models fostered deeper conceptual clarity and delivered measurable improvements, as evidenced by substantial gains in the postcourse assessment. Student feedback, collected through surveys and critical incident questionnaires, underscored the widespread appreciation for the tactile and interactive nature of model-based learning, which encouraged logical reasoning, teamwork, and academic growth. Despite challenges such as initial conceptual difficulties, the findings advocate for the use of physical models in engineering curricula to enhance comprehension, engagement, and preparedness for professional practice.

TI The Cultivation of International Engineering Graduate Students in China:
   A Study under the Belt and Road Initiative
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Civil engineering graduate education; International students;
   Exploratory factor analysis (EFA); Collaborative training model; Belt
   and Road Initiative
ID EDUCATION; FUTURE
AB To address structural challenges in international civil engineering graduate education under the Belt and Road Initiative, this study systematically evaluates current training systems and proposes a collaborative model. Employing a quantitative survey design, structured data were collected from 198 participants, including 118 faculty members and 80 international graduate students across 94 Chinese universities. Data were analyzed using exploratory factor analysis. The results reveal a fundamental cognitive gap between educational supply and demand: exploratory factor analysis (EFA) extracted a detailed five-factor structure for teachers-covering goals, competencies, teaching, platforms, and faculty-versus a macrointegrated three-factor structure for students. Quantitatively, notable discrepancies emerged in evaluating goal alignment (91% teacher approval versus 81% student approval for personal development relevance) and high-level competence acquisition, with only 22% of teachers rating academic communication training as highly effective. To bridge these supply-demand mismatches, this study introduces the "one body, two wings, four wheels" framework. Moving beyond broad pedagogical concepts, this study contributes specific, actionable policy pathways: mandating an annual curriculum update to integrate cutting-edge industry practices, institutionalizing cross-national dual-mentor collaborative platforms, and promoting the localized mutual recognition of Chinese Engineering Construction Standards. These targeted interventions provide an evidence-based roadmap for aligning institutional supply with students' developmental demands.

TI LLMs in Civil Engineering: Education Usage Patterns, Verification
   Practices, and Curriculum Implications from a Taxonomy-Aligned Student
   Survey
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Large language models (LLMs); Civil engineering education; Artificial
   intelligence literacy; Verification practices; Curriculum design
AB Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly entering civil engineering research and practice, yet little is known about their use in educational contexts. This study reports results from an institutional case study based on a taxonomy-aligned survey of 109 respondents (103 undergraduates, four graduate students, and two faculty) in civil engineering-related programs at a large US university. The survey examined adoption patterns, task functions, verification practices, disclosure norms, and training needs. Undergraduates primarily used LLMs for tutoring and concept explanation (83%) and design ideation (67%), with limited adoption in coding (7%) and technical reasoning (41%). Verification practices were robust: 86% recalculated manually, 52% checked against standards, and only 4% reported nonverification, yielding a median of two methods per user. Ethical orientations favored conditional disclosure for major contributions (53%) and placed primary responsibility for errors on the human user (75%). Demand for formal training was high, especially among those with greater adoption, familiarity, and verification breadth. Results reveal a developmental gap between student practices, which emphasize low-risk learning and ideation, and research and faculty practices, which emphasize technically rigorous applications. The study underscores the need for curricular pathways that guide students from exploratory uses toward responsibly verified technical tasks within similar educational contexts. By linking a civil engineering-specific taxonomy of LLM functions with educational survey data, this work offers institutionally grounded empirical evidence on artificial intelligence (AI) literacy in civil engineering education and highlights directions for curriculum and assessment design.

TI Experiential and Constructivist Learning in Structural Engineering: The
   Old Alton Bridge Module
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Experiential learning; Constructivist pedagogy; Structural engineering
   education; Field-based module; Bridge testing; SAP2000 modeling
AB This paper introduces a novel instructional module in structural engineering that distinctively integrates full-scale field testing, wireless sensing technologies, and finite-element modeling within an experiential and constructivist framework. Developed for undergraduate structural analysis and design courses, the module centers on the Old Alton Bridge, a historically significant, accessible structure that serves as a real-world platform for hands-on testing, data analysis, and engineering decision-making. Unlike laboratory-based studies, the use of a preserved historic bridge enhances both authenticity and heritage value, offering students exposure to real-world conditions rarely replicated in classroom settings. Students conducted physical load tests using wireless sensing devices and finite-element modeling software, linking classroom theory with practical application. Grounded in the experiential learning cycle and constructivist theory, the module was implemented in both junior- and senior-level courses, with activities mapped to each stage of the experiential cycle to encourage autonomy, engagement, and reflection. This case study emphasizes detailed implementation, including instructional sequencing, course integration, testing procedures, and student collaboration, to support replication in similar contexts. Evidence of impact is drawn from instructor observations and student reflections, highlighting increased engagement, improved applied skills, and deeper conceptual understanding. Lessons learned from multiple implementations are shared to inform educators considering similar approaches, including logistical planning, scaffolding strategies, and the value of integrating authentic field experiences into engineering curricula. The module supports Accreditation Board for Engineering and Technology (ABET)-aligned learning outcomes related to problem-solving, experimentation, and teamwork, offering a transferable model for civil and structural engineering education.

TI Unveiling Student Motivation in Construction Management Education:
   Drivers, Barriers, and Institutional Strategies for Support
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic performance; Academic success; Higher education; Professional
   success; Retention and attrition; Science, technology, engineering, and
   mathematics (STEM) education; Student motivation
ID SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; HEALTH
AB Fostering greater interest and engagement in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) and preparing students to succeed in industries shaped by rapid technological advancements are key goals of STEM education. Motivation plays a crucial role in student success, shaping engagement with coursework, persistence in demanding career paths, and perceptions of future opportunities. Therefore understanding the drivers of motivation is essential, not only to improve retention and reduce attrition, but also to enhance learning outcomes and overall academic and professional achievement. Although the importance of motivation is widely recognized, limited research has examined the specific factors that hinder STEM students' ability to sustain it, or the strategies needed to address these barriers. This study addresses this gap by exploring both the enablers and obstacles to motivation and identifying strategies for improvement. A survey of 135 Construction Management (CM) students at Florida International University (FIU) revealed that academic, financial, and social factors strongly influence motivation. Key challenges included the perceived difficulty of career paths, uncertainty about future opportunities, financial stress, poor work-life balance (WLB), and burnout. Based on these findings, the study recommends practical strategies to foster motivation, such as peer mentoring and tutoring, financial aid workshops, career fairs, and time management workshops. These approaches can help students overcome barriers, persist in their studies, and achieve both academic and professional success. The findings provide educational institutions and stakeholders with actionable strategies to strengthen motivation and improve outcomes.

TI Midproject Peer Assessment Effect on Group Dynamics and Transferable
   Skills
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Peer assessment; Transferable skills; Group work; Group dynamics
ID SELF; COHESION
AB Peer assessment has been widely used in educational settings, particularly in group projects. Despite its known benefits, there is limited evidence on how the design of peer assessment activities influences group dynamics or how it can be used as a mechanism to foster the development of transferable skills. In this study, we investigated the effect of a midproject intervention on group cohesion and overall peer satisfaction. The intervention consisted of an interim peer assessment, where students evaluated each other's performance using a structured rating scale, followed by a structured conversation to provide feedback. The intervention was implemented in a third-year civil engineering group design project module with a total duration of 15 weeks. We used the standard deviation of end-of-module peer assessment scores as a proxy to measure group cohesion and overall satisfaction with peer performance and compared this metric across groups from four consecutive academic years, including one year with the intervention and three without. Results reveal that the intervention positively impacted group dynamics, and that the feedback mechanism enables students to reflect on and enhance transferable skills, including communication, reliability, enthusiasm and contribution. These findings offer evidence to support the integration of peer assessment as a tool for enhancing group functioning and skills development.

TI Implementing Adaptive Instructional Strategies for Inclusive BIM
   Education: Graduate-Level Case Study
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Building information modeling (BIM) education; Learner diversity;
   Project-based learning; Engineering education; Formative assessment
ID CURRICULUM
AB Graduate-level building information modeling (BIM) courses often enroll students with widely varying technical skills and professional backgrounds, presenting challenges to educators in implementing equitable and effective instruction. This case study describes the development and implementation of an adaptive instructional method for a graduate BIM course that supports diverse student needs through inclusive teaching strategies grounded in educational best practices. Using Bloom's taxonomy and evidence-based instructional practices (EBIPs) such as project-based learning, peer collaboration, and scaffolded instruction, the course was structured to provide differentiated support across three learner profiles: experienced professionals, midcareer practitioners, and full-time students. Instructional adaptations were refined throughout the semester based on learner feedback and the aggregate quality of the deidentified course artifacts. The important lessons learned highlight structured flexibility, ongoing formative assessments, and differentiated project-based approaches to support diverse learners. Incorporating an adaptable curriculum into EBIPs may enhance the inclusivity and replicability of BIM. All analyses used deidentified aggregate artifacts produced as part of normal coursework, and no research-specific data collection was undertaken.

TI Service Learning through Rehabilitating a Green Roof
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID SUSTAINABILITY; IMPLEMENTATION; EDUCATION; STUDENTS; OUTCOMES
AB As climate change and increased development in urban areas increasingly impact communities, universities need to take a larger role in sustainability education, with a focus on green infrastructure solutions. This case study describes a cocurricular service-learning project on a neglected green roof of an academic building. Over three years, students from seven majors at all undergraduate levels voluntarily rehabilitated the green roof, which included removing weeds and replanting the green roof. Four engineering majors were represented in this effort: civil engineering, mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, and computer science. Students investigated plant selection, plant placement, and maintenance through planting 12 different species of sedum and one species of thyme in shady and sunny locations. They observed that thyme did not survive on the roof, and plants in the sunny location had more growth but higher die-off compared to the shady location. During the third year, it was clear that irrigation during the summer months and keeping the roof free of weeds was an important part of maintaining the green roof. Surveys indicated that students enjoyed working on the green roof, felt it was rewarding to make the green roof look better, enjoyed working with all grade levels and majors, and felt an increase in the sense of community in the School of Engineering. The green roof provided an opportunity for students to learn about sustainable green stormwater infrastructure, in addition to providing a greater sense of community and increased utilization of the green roof for other curricular purposes. Cocurricular service-learning opportunities incorporating campus or local community green infrastructure can leverage the benefits of service learning while improving community green spaces for the benefit of all students, staff, and faculty.

TI A Near-Peer Mentoring Framework for a CEE Curriculum: A Case Study
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID STUDENTS
AB Many innovative pedagogical strategies, such as near-peer mentoring, have been developed to address challenges of the first-year college curriculum. Near-peer mentoring involves upper-level students mentoring lower-level students and has been shown to improve student outcomes, such as increased sense of belonging, increased confidence in abilities, and enhanced academic and professional growth. However, many of these programs primarily focus on the mentee and often overlook the mentor. Additionally, these programs can have high barriers to entry and may require extensive administrative support and infrastructure, especially for large classes. This paper presents a curriculum-level near-peer mentoring framework with the goals of (1) enhancing both mentors' and mentees' sense of belonging and identities as engineers, and (2) improving the quality of mentees' semester-long team project solutions, conclusions, and final products. This framework was applied to a large first-year civil and environmental engineering (CEE) course with more than 210 mentees and uses more than 165 mentors primarily from fourth year CEE courses. Mentees and mentors were paired according to similar interests, and each pair met five times during a semester. After each mentoring session, both mentees and mentors completed mirrored surveys about their experiences. Both mentors and mentees somewhat agreed that the near-peer mentoring created a stronger sense of identity as a civil engineer, an increased sense of belonging, and higher quality project solutions, conclusions, and final products. Both groups rated the mentoring experience as beneficial with average self-reported scores of 3.7 out of 5, and both groups believed they helped their counterparts make connections with each other and to the project. Overall, this novel curriculum-level near-peer mentoring framework will allow all students to gain the many benefits of mentoring, and it scales well without additional faculty/teaching assistant (TA) resources.

TI A Qualitative Study of Students' Experiences and Perceptions of the Use
   of Social Presence-Enhanced Augmented Reality for Online Engineering
   Education
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Online engineering education; Augmented reality; Social presence
ID VIRTUAL-REALITY; CONSTRUCTION; COMPREHENSION; TECHNOLOGY
AB Although asynchronous online education offers flexibility, it can sometimes limit student engagement, especially in the absence of opportunities for interaction and collaboration. Emerging technologies like augmented reality (AR) show promise in addressing these challenges, yet their effectiveness in fostering collaborative learning and enhancing social presence remains underexplored. This study investigates the role of a novel Social Presence-Enabled Augmented Reality (SPEAR) tool, which integrates real-time voice chat and AR-based visualization, in improving student engagement, collaboration, and comprehension of complex engineering concepts. Seven focus group discussions were conducted with undergraduate engineering students who used the SPEAR tool in an online Strength of Materials course. The results reveal that the integration of AR with social presence cues significantly enhanced students' understanding of abstract concepts, reduced feelings of isolation, and fostered peer collaboration. Participants praised the tool's interactive features, such as real-time manipulation of three-dimensional (3D) structural models, which bridged the gap between theoretical learning and practical application. Voice chat further enriched the learning experience by facilitating instant peer support and fostering a sense of community. This study highlights the transformative potential of AR in online engineering education and proposes a framework for integrating social presence cues to optimize engagement and learning outcomes. Future research should explore scaling AR tools to diverse contexts and incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual reality (VR) for deeper immersion. These findings contribute actionable insights to the development of more interactive, collaborative online learning environments.

TI Online Construction Site Visits: Comparing Systematic and Nonsystematic
   Learning Progression in Students' Knowledge Development and
   Collaborative Problem-Solving
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID DECLARATIVE KNOWLEDGE
AB Virtual site visits have become an essential innovation in construction education, offering safe, repeatable, and flexible alternatives to physical site visits, which are often limited by safety concerns, logistics, and access restrictions. Although immersive technologies and collaborative virtual platforms have expanded these opportunities, the instructional organization of learning content within such environments remains underexplored. This study addresses this gap by comparing the impacts of systematic and nonsystematic learning progressions on students' knowledge development and collaborative problem-solving during online construction site visits. A virtual learning platform focusing on building mechanical systems was developed, incorporating four learning objectives progressing from declarative to procedural knowledge. Using a between-subject experimental design, undergraduate construction students experienced either a systematic or nonsystematic learning sequence. Results indicated that both learning progressions effectively supported students' knowledge development within the online construction site visit environment; however, notable differences emerged in higher-order reasoning and collaborative practices. Students in the systematic learning progression condition demonstrated stronger performance on tasks requiring conceptual integration and procedural reasoning. They also exhibited more structured collaborative behaviors, such as referencing two-dimensional (2D) drawings while manipulating three-dimensional (3D) models and collaboratively verifying calculations. These behaviors suggest that systematic sequencing may reduce cognitive load and facilitate schema integration during complex tasks. In contrast, learners in the nonsystematic condition engaged more freely in exploratory navigation but showed less coordinated reasoning and weaker linkage across concepts. Overall, these findings highlight the critical role of instructional sequencing design in virtual construction education and provide insights for designing adaptive scaffolding frameworks in future online site visits.

TI Feedback and Teaching Reform for the National College Students
   Structural Design Competition Course
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Structural design competition; Engineering education reform; Mechanics
   learning; Practice-oriented teaching; Student feedback; Higher education
AB This case study reports on a competition-linked elective course designed to support undergraduate preparation for the National College Students Structural Design Competition (NCSSDC) and to help students connect mechanics concepts with open-ended structural design decisions. Using an anonymous questionnaire survey of 100 undergraduates across civil engineering, architecture, and related majors, we examined students' competition participation, prior mechanics coursework, and their perceptions of the course components (short lectures, case-based discussions, supervised hands-on workshops, and peer mentoring). Results indicate that 76% of respondents had competition experience (mostly at the campus level) and 66% reported receiving awards. Although 64% had completed one or more mechanics courses, many still reported difficulty transferring theory to design-and-build tasks. Among students who enrolled in the elective, 97.3% reported that it supported their mechanics learning, and 67.6% rated the perceived benefit as "very significant." Open-ended feedback emphasized needs for more hands-on practice, integration of real competition cases, structured experience sharing from past competitors, and small-class instruction. We synthesize these findings into practical recommendations for implementing and scaling competition-linked electives in civil engineering programs.

AB This study evaluates the impact of course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs) on learning and retention in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields among engineering students at Tennessee State University (TSU), a public historically Black college and university (HBCU). TI How Virtual Reality Training Method Affects Learner Reactions: A
   Comparative Experiment-Based Investigation
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID CONSTRUCTION SAFETY; MOTIVATION; VALENCE; AROUSAL; SYSTEM
AB The construction industry is witnessing growing adoption of virtual reality (VR) for training and education. This study investigates how VR-based training compares with a traditional paper-based method in terms of learner reactions, including utility reactions, affective reactions, and biopsychological responses. We developed a realistic VR system and conducted a comparative experiment (N=26) in a VR environment and a paper-based setting. Utility and affective reactions were collected by validated questionnaires, and electroencephalogram (EEG) data were analyzed through a hybrid machine-learning pipeline. Results indicate that the VR condition was associated with higher perceived utility (+59.2%) and more positive affective reactions (+32.9%), as well as significantly higher EEG-derived scores across valence, arousal, dominance, and liking. These findings provide preliminary evidence that immersive VR may elicit stronger emotional, cognitive, and physiological engagement than traditional materials, highlighting VR's potential to enrich construction safety training research.

TI Construction and Teaching Practice of a Typical Case Library for the
   Advanced Tunnel Engineering Course
SO JOURNAL OF CIVIL ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Tunnel engineering; Professional degree education; Case-based teaching;
   Typical case library; Effectiveness evaluation
AB "Advanced Tunnel Engineering" is a key graduate-level course for students majoring in civil engineering and related disciplines, emphasizing the integration of theoretical instruction with engineering practice. However, challenges such as abstract content, weak engineering relevance, and low student engagement still exist in current teaching practices, limiting the development of students' engineering comprehension and analytical skills. The teaching team addressed these issues by developing a typical case library of 24 engineering cases across six categories, centered around core course knowledge. This case-based teaching approach has been systematically applied in classroom practice. Results show that it effectively stimulates student interest, enhances the course's practical orientation, and helps students build an integrated understanding of "structure-geology-construction-monitoring." Based on an anonymous survey of 196 postgraduate students (5-point Likert), the case library received consistently high ratings, with mean scores ranging from 4.68 to 4.75 out of 5, reflecting improved engagement and self-reported conceptual understanding. It also helps students connect theory with real engineering scenarios and supports the development of problem-analysis skills. The workflow provides a replicable template for building and embedding case libraries in other engineering disciplines and institutions.

TI Factor structure of artificial intelligence use in university teaching
   pedagogy
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; university pedagogy; exploratory factor
   analysis; reliability
ID TECHNOLOGY; ACCEPTANCE
AB The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education pedagogy has gained increasing relevance; however, there remains a shortage of psychometrically validated instruments capable of assessing, in a multidimensional and context-specific manner, faculty adoption of these technologies. The aim of this study was to identify the factorial structure and evaluate the psychometric properties of an instrument designed to measure AI use among university faculty. The instrument was developed based on the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology and was administered to a convenience sample of 330 university instructors. Exploratory factor analysis revealed a robust seven-factor structure explaining 66.90% of the total variance, allowing the refinement and optimization of the instrument from 50 to 30 items. The final scale demonstrated excellent overall internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.913). It is concluded that the developed instrument is a valid and reliable tool for higher education institutions to assess and diagnose faculty levels of AI adoption, thereby facilitating the design of contextpedagogy.

TI Designing and implementing teacher digital competence programs: An
   implementation science approach using CFIR 2.0
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE teacher digital competence; teacher education; implementation science;
   consolidated framework for implementation research 2.0; professional
   development
ID TRIAL
AB Teacher digital competence (TDC) is widely recognized as a key enabler of educational digitalization, yet many professional development initiatives do not lead to sustained changes in classroom practice. This study examines the contextual and organizational determinants that should inform the design and implementation of TDC programs in school education from an implementation science (IS) perspective. Drawing on the consolidated framework for implementation research 2.0, a three-round Delphi study was conducted with 23 specialists in educational technology, including teacher educators, school leaders, and system-level advisers. The findings suggest that effective TDC programs must extend beyond a narrow focus on individual skills, as their success also depends on leadership, organizational conditions, external support, contextual adaptation, and ongoing evaluation. The model provides a structured basis for designing, implementing, and evaluating programs that are realistic, context-sensitive, and sustainable. Overall, the study demonstrates the value of IS for strengthening teacher professional development in digital education.

TI Engagement trajectories in AI-supported learning: Sequence analysis and
   differential responses to instructor interventions
SO INTERNET AND HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Sequence analytics; Engagement trajectories; AI-supported learning;
   Learner clustering; Instructor intervention
ID STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; INTRINSIC MOTIVATION; ANALYTICS; PARTICIPATION;
   STRATEGIES; REMINDERS; EDUCATION
AB This study examines engagement trajectories in an AI-based problem-solving platform implemented within an extracurricular TOEIC program in higher education and their responsiveness to instructor interventions. Using 91 days of log data from an AI-based problem-solving platform, we discretized weekly learning activity into four states (NoAccess, Low, Mid, High), represented each learner's 13-week history as a behavioral sequence, and then applied sequence analysis and clustering to trace engagement trajectories over time. The analysis identified three clusters: Persistent Engagers, who maintained continuous high-level engagement; Fading Engagers, who began with moderate to high participation but gradually declined while showing renewed responsiveness to instructor interventions; and Nominal Participants, whose involvement remained minimal throughout. Cluster-level comparison revealed that interventions were most effective for Fading Engagers, whereas Nominal Participants exhibited diminishing sensitivity over repeated prompts. A Supplementary survey analysis further showed that intrinsic learning motivation significantly predicted cluster membership, while self-directed learning did not. These findings highlight the value of sequence-based analysis for capturing temporal engagement patterns and demonstrate how intervention effects vary by learner. This evidence provides a foundation for informing the design of adaptive, data-driven support systems in AI-enabled learning environments.

TI Learning with AI-animated pedagogical agents: The role of age and gender
   similarity in identification, situational interest, and learning
   outcomes
SO INTERNET AND HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pedagogical agents; Artificial intelligence; Age; Gender;
   Identification; Situational interest; Learning
ID VIDEO MODELING EXAMPLES; CHARACTER IDENTIFICATION; WISHFUL

   SELF; PERCEPTIONS
AB Educational videos featuring pedagogical agents (PAs) are considered effective teaching tools. Although theories suggest that sociodemographic similarity (e.g., age and gender) between PAs and learners can enhance learning, little is known about learners' perceptions of and interactions with AI-animated PAs. Accordingly, the present study investigates how the age and gender of AI-animated PAs interact with those of learners in shaping PA identification, situational interest, and learning outcomes. AB This pilot case study examines how a short-term hybrid study abroad program was intentionally designed to address inequitable participation in global learning among teacher candidates at a Hispanic-Serving Institution. In response to documented underrepresentation of Hispanic students and education majors in study abroad, the six-week program integrated pre-departure coursework, a two-week in-country immersion, and structured post-experience reflection to scaffold intercultural development. Guided by established intercultural competence frameworks (Deardorff, 2006; Hanvey, 1982) the instructional design emphasized sequencing, structured reflection, and theory-aligned assessment. Six undergraduate and graduate students completed a pre-and post-program Intercultural Literacy and Global Learning Survey that included Likertscale items and open-ended responses. Descriptive and thematic analyses indicated growth in students' recognition of cultural assumptions, confidence in engaging with diverse educational practices, and readiness to incorporate global perspectives into future teaching. Qualitative findings further suggested shifts from surface-level interest in new instructional strategies to deeper reflection on teacher identity, child autonomy, and inclusive practice. As a pilot case study, the findings offer pedagogical insights and design principles for faculty seeking to expand equitable global learning opportunities in educator preparation.

AB Teacher training in the Brazilian scenario has undergone transformations in recent decades, fostered by public policies aimed at narrowing the dialogue between Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) and Basic Education. From this perspective, the present study proposes a systematic analysis of the academic production regarding the Pedagogical Residency Program (PRP), with the purpose of mapping the knowledge produced within the scope of Pedagogy courses in the 2018-2023 timeframe. TI Positive emotions, digital skills and reflection predict academics'
   perceived development of online teaching expertise: An experience
   sampling study
SO INTERNET AND HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Online teaching; Teacher expertise; Experience sampling method; Higher
   education; Emotions; Bayesian modelling
ID UNIVERSITY TEACHERS; EDUCATION
AB The increasing adoption of online teaching in higher education (HE), especially in the post-pandemic era and with the rise of artificial intelligence, highlights the need to better understand how online teaching expertise evolves. Recognising that such developments may fluctuate across contexts and time, this study employed an experience sampling method (ESM) to investigate both within-teacher variability and between-teacher differences in time-variant predictors of perceived expertise development in online teaching. The sample consisted of 25 university teachers, representing a substantial size for intensive longitudinal research using ESM in HE. Participants provided repeated diary entries via a mobile app before and after teaching or planning sessions. These entries captured emotional valence, digital skills, reflection and perceived development of online teaching expertise. Bayesian cumulative mixed-effects analyses revealed that state positive emotions during teaching and planning sessions were positively associated with perceived development of online teaching expertise. Momentary perceptions of digital skilfulness during sessions were more influential than stable trait-level differences between individuals. Furthermore, teachers who engaged more frequently in reflective practices across sessions reported greater cumulative expertise development. These findings underline the importance of withinteacher dynamics in emotions and digital skills and between-teacher differences in reflection in shaping the development of online teaching expertise. The implications of the study and future research are discussed.

TI Bridging technology and education: The use of ChatGPT in grading
   pharmacy student exams
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Pharmacy education; Assessment
AB Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly being explored for educational applications. This study evaluates the use of ChatGPT, an artificial intelligence language model, in grading various types of assessment questions administered to pharmacy students, with the goal of improving efficiency while maintaining the quality and integrity of student assessment. Methods: This mixed-methods study evaluated the accuracy and consistency of ChatGPT-5 in grading 21 total multiple-choice (MC), listing, select-all-that-apply (SATA), fill-in-the-blank, short-answer, and essay questions administered to 16 pharmacy students during their adult medicine advanced pharmacy practice experience (APPE) rotations. ChatGPT-5 graded responses under specific conditions such as grading the full exam versus by question type, each with and without a rubric, and results were compared with human grading (gold standard) to assess agreement and reliability. All student data was de-identified, collected through REDCap, and analyzed using descriptive and comparative statistics. Results: Sixteen students completed a 21-item mixed-format examination graded by faculty (gold standard) and AI, with and without a rubric. AI demonstrated near-perfect accuracy and concordance for objective items. Performance declined for listing, short-answer, and essay questions. Providing a rubric did not consistently improve accuracy or agreement in mixedformat grading. When responses were grouped by question type, rubric use improved accuracy and concordance for listing questions but not for short-answer or essay items, where rubric-free grading often showed higher agreement. Conclusions: AI grading reliability is highly dependent on question type and grading context. AI performs well for objective assessments, while rubric effectiveness is context-specific and limited for subjective responses.

TI Do modes of presence matter? regulation and participation in graduate
   students' hybrid synchronous group-based collaboration
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Synchronous hybrid learning; Self-regulation; Group-regulation; Small
   group collaboration; Epistemic network analysis; Multimodal
   mixed-methods
ID SOCIALLY SHARED REGULATION; EPISTEMIC NETWORK ANALYSIS; SELF; ONLINE;
   COREGULATION
AB Background: Synchronous hybrid education offers flexibility and accessibility, but can also pose challenges for students in regulating group work and ensuring equal participation in collaborative activities. Understanding how students address the challenges of regulation and participation in hybrid collaboration settings is critical for designing and supporting students for hybrid education. Aims: This exploratory study examines how regulation strategies and verbal participation manifest across online and physical modes of presence in a collaborative project, and how students address challenges that emerge during hybrid synchronous group work. Sample: Four graduate-level student groups (16 students) participating in a 14-week hybrid legal education course. Methods: A multimodal exploratory mixed-methods approach combining Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA), speaking time analysis, and qualitative content analysis of group verbal and non-verbal interaction. Results: Findings revealed significant differences between the two modes of presence. Participants in the online mode engaged more in self-monitoring, self-planning, and group-monitoring behaviours. Groups employing adaptive strategies, such as shared visual aids, successfully mitigated challenges in hybrid collaboration. Conclusions: This study's findings offer exploratory insights relevant for both research and practice, providing guidance and tools for collaborative learning in hybrid settings, and ideas for thoughtful design of hybrid learning environments that enable productive collaboration.

TI Who will become teachers? Personal and social-environmental factors
   influencing preservice teachers' entry into teaching

LA English
DT Article

ID GRADE-POINT AVERAGE; SELF-EFFICACY; CONTEXT; CHOICE; SCALE
AB This longitudinal mixed-method study examines how preservice teachers' personal and social environmental factors predict their career decisions after graduation. The study investigated preservice teachers' background, cognitive attributes, non-cognitive attributes, and perceived social environment before graduation, tracking their careers ten months later. Career decisions were categorized as becoming teachers, pursuing professional degrees, or leaving teaching.    confidence and clinical assessment

   process (PPCP); Pharmacy education; Student confidence
AB Objective: To evaluate differences in self-perceived confidence and performance between oncampus (OC) and distance learning pathway (DLP) PharmD students completing a capstone course designed to integrate and assess the Pharmacists' Patient Care Process (PPCP). Methods: This prospective comparative study included third-year PharmD students enrolled in a capstone course that emphasized simulated patient care across community, ambulatory, and acute care settings. Conclusions: The capstone course effectively enhanced confidence and competency in both OC and DLP students, supporting the equivalence of distance learning when assessments and active learning strategies are standardized. These findings affirm that hybrid and distance models can achieve comparable outcomes to traditional instruction and provide a foundation for future work examining longitudinal performance and practice readiness.

TI Workplace learning and professional identity formation in
   university-allocated pharmacy placements: A scoping review to inform
   curriculum development
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Placement; Pharmacy students; Professional identity formation;
   Professionalism; Scoping review; Workplace learning
ID STUDENT; PERCEPTIONS
AB Background: Workplace learning is central to pharmacy education, offering authentic experiences that foster students' professional identity formation as they transition into the pharmacist role. Research in this area is growing but is methodologically varied, spanning multiple theories, student cohorts, and practice settings, without an overarching synthesis. This scoping review aimed to generate recommendations for pharmacy curriculum development from studies relating to professional identity formation and workplace learning opportunities, specifically university-allocated placements. Methods: Peer-reviewed journal articles were obtained from searching four databases, using synonyms for workplace learning, professional identity formation, and pharmacy students. Extracted data focused on key concepts and study design features that were analysed inductively, then findings were interpreted to generate recommendations. Results: Sixteen studies were analysed. Most research was exploratory, relied on qualitative or self-report methods, and focused on later-year students in hospital or community settings. Definitions of professional identity formation and workplace learning varied and most had to be inferred. Reported outcomes highlighted relationships among professionalism, placement experiences, and developing identity, but few studies used robust indicators or evaluative designs. Implications: This review highlights that research on pharmacy students' professional identity formation in workplace settings is largely exploratory. Greater use of evaluative, longitudinal, and mixed methods designs that integrate behavioural, reflective, and validated measures are needed to strengthen evidence quality. This area would benefit from clearer theoretical alignment, shared definitions, and broader sampling across learner stages and practice settings, to enable more robust comparisons and targeted curriculum development.

TI From information to experience: Using design thinking to support
   pharmacy students preparing for multiple mini interviews
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Design thinking; Multiple mini interview (MMI); Pharmacy education;
   Experiential learning; Student partnership; Professional readiness;
   Interview preparation; Curriculum design
AB Purpose: Preparing pharmacy students for the Foundation Training Year (FTY) Multiple Mini Interview (MMI) is a key component of supporting transition to professional practice. While MMIs assess non-academic competencies such as communication and ethical reasoning, preparation within curricula often emphasises informational support rather than experiential learning. This reflective work addresses this gap by exploring how a Design Thinking approach can be used to better understand and support students' preparation for MMIs. Description: This work draws on our experience as an educator responding to pharmacy students' concerns about MMI preparedness. Conclusions: Preparation for MMIs requires a shift from information delivery to experiential, practice-based learning. TI Emotion dynamics in online learning communities: Temporal networks,
   motifs, and links to achievement
SO INTERNET AND HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Emotion dynamics; Temporal networks; Motifs; Online learning
   communities; Learning outcomes
ID ASYNCHRONOUS ONLINE; SOCIAL PRESENCE; ANALYTICS; PATTERNS; FACILITATION;
   INSTRUCTORS; INQUIRY; MOOCS
AB This study investigates how emotions co-evolve with interaction structures in online learning communities using Emotional Temporal Networks (ETNs). Fifteen weekly ETNs captured learner-to-learner interactions and node-level emotions across a semester. Regression models related weekly emotions to network properties, and a motif-coloring analysis traced emotional roles within recurrent subgraphs. We also compared network-emotion patterns across learner groups with different achievement levels. Key findings include: (i) Positive emotions predominated but declined over time, while negative and confused emotions increased. The emotion-network association was dynamic and metric-specific, with stable positive links for centrality measures like indegree and eigenvector, but variable or null links for outdegree and betweenness under stress. (ii) Motifs revealed complementary "sharer" (outgoing) and "listener" (incoming) roles: sharers showed greater emotional volatility, whereas listeners maintained more stable positive affect shaped by group context. Two temporal junctures emerged-mid-semester shifts in affect and a pre-exam rise in closed triads and bidirectional ties supporting collaborative problem solving. (iii) High-achieving learners occupied more central, information-rich positions and sustained more stable positive emotions. The ETN framework offers a mesoscale lens for monitoring and guiding emotion dynamics and suggests interventions that enhance information flow, scaffold sharer-listener role dynamics, and use motif-based monitoring for timely instructional support.
