TI Gender equality in higher education: can leaders drive change?
SO HIGHER EDUCATION RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Gender inequality; gender competence; higher education; gender
   leadership; STEMM; HASS
ID WOMEN
AB Gender inequality in Australian universities is pernicious and entrenched. Higher Education (HE) leaders are widely recognised as potential change agents and key to creating workplaces which manifest gender equality, diversity and inclusion. Their capability to do so, however, is less certain. This article examines the capability of HE leaders to create respectful workplaces with the aim of better understanding their knowledge of the problem and know-how to drive change. Data are provided from in-depth, qualitative interviews with a discipline-diverse sample of Australian HE leaders. Drawing on the concept of gender competence, we find important limitations in how the nature and causes of gender inequality are understood and their concomitant solutions. Leaders often understand the problem narrowly, as numeric, with few recognising the systemic and structural drivers. Notably, Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics and Medicine (STEMM) leaders were more likely than Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences (HASS) leaders to externalise the problem and treat it as a pipeline issue. This research corroborates and extends current knowledge on gender inequality in HE, indicating new opportunities for universities to strengthen change efforts. Notably, our findings demonstrate the need for enhanced gender capability of HE leaders and further research-based, disciplinary relevant training and interventions.

AB This qualitative study, conducted in T & uuml;rkiye, explores graduate students' perceptions of and experiences with artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education contexts. TI A descriptive longitudinal investigation of EFL academic discussion
   writing following systemic functional linguistics-oriented genre-based
   instruction
SO LANGUAGE TESTING IN ASIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Descriptive longitudinal investigation; Delayed posttest; SFL-oriented
   genre-based instruction; Academic discussion writing; EFL higher
   education; Long-term retention
ID ENGLISH-LANGUAGE LEARNERS; STUDENTS; FAMILIES
AB Long-term evidence on the durability of genre-based writing instruction in EFL higher education remains limited, because most studies evaluate outcomes immediately after a single course and rarely track whether genre resources are maintained or reshaped across multiple years, evidence that is important for curriculum design and program-level decision-making. This exploratory, descriptive, small-scale longitudinal classroom investigation traces the development of EFL academic discussion writing following Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL)-oriented genre-based approach (GBA) instruction in a Japanese university context. Two cohorts of students who completed the same 15-week SFL-GBA course produced timed discussion essays at Time 1 (pre-course), Time 2 (immediate post-course), and Time 3 (delayed posttest 3-4 years later). To contextualize Time 3 performance under matched task conditions, a third cohort who completed a skill-based writing course completed the same Time 3 task and served as a cross-sectional reference group. Fifty-eight essays were analysed using mixed methods that combine corpus-based lexical indices (text length, lexical richness, and academic vocabulary use) with SFL-informed coding of discussion-genre resources. Across the SFL-GBA learning communities, several lexical and genre-related resources observed at Time 2 were broadly maintained at Time 3, while some interpersonal resources showed mixed trajectories, highlighting areas that may require sustained instructional support beyond the first year.

TI The importance of trust in mentoring relationships for women's outdoor
   leadership development
SO SPORT EDUCATION AND SOCIETY
LA English
DT Article
DE Mentoring; outdoor leadership; women; trust; gender
ID GENDER; CHALLENGES; WORK
AB Mentoring is an important tool that organisations can implement to help address gender barriers in women's progression in sport and the outdoors. However, there is much still to learn about what makes for effective mentoring in these contexts. This paper explores what makes for positive and 'successful' mentoring relationships within a formal mentoring programme for women's outdoor leadership development. A qualitative, interpretive approach was adopted. Twenty participants who took part in a ten-week women's outdoor leadership course and experienced mentoring by either a male or female mentor were interviewed using semi-structured interviews lasting 30-60 min. The data reveal the value of both male and female mentors but also highlight the ambiguities and uncertainties for women in cross-gender mentoring. In particular, we show the importance of the mentoring relationship as a psychologically safe space where women's experiences in the male-dominated context of the outdoors can be understood, recognised and validated. Recommendations for mentoring programmes are provided.

TI Relationships between students' perceptions of teacher enthusiasm and
   EFL classroom engagement: A self-efficacy mediation model with
   multi-group analysis of language mindsets
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Perceived teacher enthusiasm; Classroom engagement; Self-efficacy;
   Language mindsets; EFL classrooms
ID GROWTH MINDSET; ACHIEVEMENT; SCHOOL; MOTIVATION; ENGLISH; PERFORMANCE
AB This study investigated the impact of perceived teacher enthusiasm on student engagement in English as a foreign language (EFL) classrooms, exploring the mediating role of self-efficacy and the moderating influence of language mindsets. Data from 2,740 undergraduate students in China were analyzed using a self-efficacy mediation model and multi-group analysis. Findings revealed that teacher enthusiasm directly and indirectly influenced classroom engagement through selfefficacy, with self-efficacy enhancing behavioral, cognitive and affective engagement. Crucially, the study also found invariance of these relationships across growth and fixed mindset groups, underscoring that teacher enthusiasm can effectively foster engagement in the classroom regardless of students' mindset orientations. These findings highlight teacher enthusiasm as a beneficial and critical factor for enhancing engagement in EFL classroom settings. Implications for teacher education emphasize the need for strategies to express enthusiasm and build students' self-efficacy, creating a classroom environment that promotes engagement across different language mindsets.

TI Effects of the Elimination of the Grad PLUS Loan Program on Student
   Pharmacist Borrowers
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Access; affordability; federal student loans
AB Objective: Federal bill H.R.1 eliminates Grad PLUS loans and changes borrowing limits for Direct Unsubsidized loans for professional students, including student pharmacists. The study evaluates the total gap in pharmacy school cost of attendance (CoA), which would previously have been addressed by a Grad PLUS loan after applying the new federal Direct Unsubsidized loan limit. Methods: A secondary data analysis was conducted using publicly available CoA data for colleges of pharmacy (COPs) in the US. 2025-26 tuition and fees and indirect expenses were collected from the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy and each COP's university website, respectively, to calculate CoA for each COP. Annual cost gap (difference between annual CoA and the annual Direct Unsubsidized loan limit of $50,000) for each year of each program was summed to calculate total cost gap. The Kruskal-Wallis one-way analysis of variance was conducted to assess the effects of program classification (public in-state, public out-of-state, private 4-year, and private 3-year) on total cost gap. Results: A total of 133 COPs were included. The median total cost gap for public in-state PharmD programs ($17,948) was significantly lower than that for public out-of-state ($68,214), private 4-year ($102,087), and private 3-year ($132,609) programs. The median total cost gap for public out-of-state programs was significantly lower than that for private 4-year and 3-year programs. Conclusion: Loss of Grad PLUS loans may pose a significant financial barrier to pharmacy education. COPs should use multiple strategies to address students' financial challenges, including federal and state advocacy, private loan options, tuition reduction, philanthropy, financial assistance partnerships, and loan repayment and forgiveness programs.

TI Redefining and measuring student agency in AI-assisted learning:
   Development and validation of the agentic engagement with AI (AE-AI)
   scale
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Learner agency; Agentic engagement; Human-AI co-agency; Generative AI;
   Epistemic responsibility; adaptability; Scale validation
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; VALIDITY; INSIGHTS; MODEL
AB Student agency has become a central concern in learning with artificial intelligence (AI). With growing capability and adaptiveness, Generative AI (GenAI) tools are no longer merely passive tools but responsive participants in learning. This shift makes agency relational and reciprocal: students exercise agency through intentional engagement with AI, while AI responses shape how students express, adjust, and develop that agency. Existing instruments, however, continue to frame agency as student-centered control over external tools and environments, positing students as the primary initiators and regulators of learning. This misalignment leaves the relational and reciprocal nature of agency in AI-assisted learning unmeasured. To address this gap, the present study adopts the construct of agentic engagement and conceptualizes student agency in AIassisted learning as a proactive, adaptable, and reciprocal process enacted through ongoing exchanges between human intentionality and machine adaptivity. To develop the Agentic Engagement with AI (AE-AI) Scale, an integrated inductive-deductive approach was used to generate an initial pool of 28 items from student interviews (N = 26). The scale was refined and validated through expert review, exploratory factor analysis (N = 340), confirmatory factor analysis (N = 256), and criterion validity checking. The final 16-item scale comprises four factors: Adaptive Direction, Critical Integration, Cross-Source Inquiry, and Reflective Calibration. Together, these factors redefine student agency as a process of human-AI co-agency grounded in adaptability, epistemic responsibility, and distributed inquiry. The study provides a validated instrument for observing student agency and opens new directions for examining the evolving synthesis of human and machine intelligence in education.

TI Beauty is the eye of the beholder: Introducing the visual aesthetic
   principle for multimedia instructional design and how it is moderated by
   learners' creativity
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive load; Color; Creativity; Decorative shape; Emotional design;
   Motivation; Visual aesthetics
ID DUAL-CODING THEORY; EMOTIONAL DESIGN; DECORATIVE PICTURES; POSITIVE
   AFFECT; COLOR; ILLUSTRATIONS; METAANALYSIS; FEATURES; SCIENCE; IMPACT
AB Oftentimes, experimental studies manipulating colors and shapes link their materials to aesthetics. However, a gap exists in understanding what a truly aesthetic design is and how it influences learning. Moreover, the seductive detail effect states that learning-irrelevant details, such as additional aesthetic features, compromise learning. This research aimed to discover how presentation slides that vary in their perceived aesthetics influenced learners' motivation, cognitive processes, and performance. The personality trait of creativity was examined as a possible moderator. In the first experiment, 42 designs created by application of the visual aesthetic principle were evaluated according to their perceived aesthetics (n = 70). In the second study, 105 university students were randomly assigned to one of four conditions in a 2-decorative shape (round vs. abstract angular) by 2-color scheme (chromatic vs. achromatic) design. The results revealed that round decorative shapes and chromatic designs were independently perceived as aesthetically superior to abstract angular decorative shapes or achromatic designs. Further, while round decorative shapes reduced extraneous cognitive load and led to better learning performance, chromatic designs had a significant statistical effect on motivation. The interaction between independent variables was significant for motivation and performance ratings. Learners' trait of creativity strongly moderated the influence of round decorative shapes on learning performance. These results are interpreted within the frameworks of Emotional Design, Cognitive Load Theory, and the Cognitive-Affective Theory of Learning with Media. Future perspectives include exploring and applying the visual aesthetic principle in instructional design.

TI Profiles of ESL postgraduate students' use of artificial intelligence in
   writing: Antecedents and outcomes
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Latent profile analysis; Writing; Higher
   education; ChatGPT
ID CRITICAL THINKING
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely used to support academic writing. Prior research has demonstrated AI's general effectiveness at improving learning outcomes, but has tended to overlook how different AI-use pattens across groups may be associated with variation in specific outcomes. We therefore adopted latent-profile analysis (LPA) to examine AI-use profiles, their predictors, and the learning outcomes they are associated with. Specifically, we LPA analysis of survey data provided by 1073 postgraduate students from 21 countries studying in the United Kingdom revealed three AI-use profiles: transformation explorers, technical-support-focused users, and balanced users. Profile membership was significantly predicted by academic discipline and AI-use frequency: with humanities students and frequent users more likely to be transformation explorers. Self-reported learning outcomes varied across AI-use profiles, with transformation explorers claiming the highest overall level of critical thinking and the most perceived writing improvement, and technical-support-focused users, the highest motivation. Balanced users reported moderate outcomes across all measures. Our findings indicate that balancing AI use across multiple functions did not necessarily enhance learning: in other words, learning may depend less on the breadth of AI use, and more on how deeply and effectively each function is used. Moreover, AI, as a tool, is inherently neutral; its impact depends on how it is employed.

   distraction and self-reported learning loss
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION

ID MEDIA MULTITASKING; MOBILE PHONES; INTERNET USE; IMPACT; ATTENTION;

AB Access to personal technology in college classrooms has increased significantly. TI Instructor's pointing gestures promote learning more than guiding gaze
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pointing gestures; Guiding gaze; Video learning; Instructor; Multimedia
   learning
ID COGNITIVE ARCHITECTURE; PEDAGOGICAL AGENTS; EYE CONTACT; EXAMPLES
AB Previous research has found that an instructor's social cues (e.g., gestures and gaze) can have positive effects on learning when the content is presented in a video format captured from an actual instructor. This study utilized eye tracking in an attempt to provide a more fine-grained, precise analysis of the effects of pointing gestures and guiding gaze on learning outcomes during video-based instruction. More specifically, a 2 (Gaze: guiding gaze vs. no guiding gaze) & times; 3 (Gestures: specific pointing gestures vs. general pointing gestures vs. no pointing gesture) between-subjects design was employed to investigate the effects of these social cues in this context, as assessed during 2 separate tests-retention and transfer at 2 different time periodsimmediate and delayed (5 days later). 138 college students were recruited in this experiment. A significant effect was found for gestures on both the retention and transfer tests, wherein the learning outcomes were greatest when instructors utilized specific pointing gestures (i.e., pointing at specific knowledge points) vs. general pointing gestures (i.e., pointing at the whole learning material) or no gestures. No differences were found between guiding gaze and direct gaze. Eye tracking data revealed a similar pattern of findings, as students assigned to the specific pointing gestures group paid greater attention to the key material than did those students assigned to the other gesture conditions, which did not differ from one another. These findings suggest that the specific pointing gestures of instructors play a crucial signaling role in video learning by guiding students' attention to the learning content, thereby enhancing learning outcomes.

TI Transition shock trajectories and their reciprocal mediation with
   professional identity on nursing interns' retention: A longitudinal
   study with educational implications
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Transition shock; Professional identity; Retention intention; Students;
   Nursing; Longitudinal study
ID EXPERIENCES
AB Background Transition shock (TS) is a core stressor influencing nursing students career choices. However, its dynamic trajectories during internship and influence on retention intentions remain underexplored.<br /> Objectives: To identify heterogeneous TS trajectories in nursing interns, examine associations of psychological capital, internship bullying, and organizational support with trajectory categories, and investigate the longitu-dinal reciprocal effects between TS and professional identity (PI) and their subsequent impact on retention intentions.<br /> Design: A prospective longitudinal study with three time points.<br /> Settings University hospitals in Changsha, Hunan Province, China<br /> Participants: A total of 826 nursing interns were recruited.<br /> Methods Data on TS, PI, and retention intentions were collected at internship weeks 4 (T1), 24 (T2), and 40 (T3) between October 2024 and December 2025. Growth mixture modeling identified TS trajectories, multinomial logistic regression analyzed influencing factors, and cross-lagged panel models examined longitudinal mediating relationships.<br /> 1 Results: Three distinct TS trajectories were identified: low-shock stable group (45.096), high-to-low shock group (32.0%), and high shock stable group (23.0%). Lower psychological capital (OR=0.81, P<0.001) and higher internship bullying ( OR = 2.06 , P < 0.001 ) were significantly associated with high-shock stable trajectory. A bidirectional medikting relationship emerged: TS at T1 (beta -0.031, Bootstrap 95% CI [ -0.046, beta-0.017]) and T2 (beta-0.041, Bootstrap 95% CI [-0.057, -0.025]) indirectly reduced T3 retention intentions through their negative asociation with T2 PI; conversely, T2 PI indirectly diminished T3 retention intentions through its association with Ty at T2 (beta-0.047, Bootstrap 9596 CI [-0.067, -0.028]) and T3 (beta -0.041, Bootstrap 95% (-0.060, -0.023]).<br /> Conclusion: TS among nursing interns follows heterogeneous paths, with the high-shock stable group as priority for intervention. 15 and PI form a mutually reinforcing longitudinal relationship negatively associated with retention intentions. Nursing educators across academic and clinical settings should collaborate to strengthen psychological capital, reduce internship bullying, and repair PI during mid-internship, thereby interrupting this detrimental relationship and reducing early workforce attrition.

TI The mediating role of self-efficacy between time management disposition
   and deep learning ability among undergraduate nursing students: A
   cross-sectional study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Deep learning; Nursing; Time management disposition; Self-efficacy;
   Cross-sectional study
AB Background Deep learning ability is essential for nursing students to navigate complex knowledge acquisition and intelligent healthcare challenges. However, information overload in digital learning environments may hinder the mastery of complex knowledge. Objectives This study aims to investigate the current status of deep learning ability and its influencing factors among undergraduate nursing students, and to explore the mediating role of self-efficacy between time management disposition and deep learning ability. Design A cross-sectional, correlational study. Methods A total of 238 full-time undergraduate nursing students were recruited from medical colleges via convenience sampling between September and December 2025. Data were collected using the Deep Learning Ability Scale, Time Management Disposition Scale, and General Self-Efficacy Scale. Analyses included t-tests, ANOVA, Pearson correlations, multiple regression, and mediation analysis using the PROCESS macro (Model 4). Results The mean total scores for the 238 undergraduate nursing students were 105.17 +/- 19.03 for deep learning ability, 163.06 +/- 28.33 for time management disposition, and 27.03 +/- 5.11 for self-efficacy. Correlation analysis indicated that deep learning ability was significantly and positively correlated with time management disposition (r = 0.755, P < 0.001) and self-efficacy (r = 0.754, P < 0.001). Additionally, a significant positive correlation was observed between time management disposition and self-efficacy (r = 0.770, P < 0.001). Student leadership experience, self-efficacy, and time management disposition were identified as significant predictors, collectively explaining 66.2% of the variance in deep learning ability. Furthermore, self-efficacy partially mediated the relationship between time management disposition and deep learning ability (beta = 0.217, 95% CI [0.138, 0.303]), accounting for 41.41% of the total effect. Conclusion The deep learning ability of undergraduate nursing students is at a moderately high level. Self-efficacy serves as a crucial partial mediator between time management and deep learning. Nursing educators should adjust teaching strategies to enhance deep learning ability and improve the quality of nursing talent cultivation.

DT Article

AB Drawing on the Health Belief Model and labeling theory, we examined how mental health perceptions shape help-seeking intentions among Gen Z hospitality students. TI No more excuses: Mandating online learning competencies in all teacher
   preparation programs
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher preparation; Online learning; Blended learning; Emergency remote
   teaching; Pre-service teachers; Educational standards; Accreditation
ID K-12 ONLINE; VALIDATION; SCHOOLS
AB The COVID-19 pandemic exposed a critical systemic vulnerability in education - a widespread lack of teacher readiness for online instruction, which resulted in improvised 'emergency remote teaching' rather than high-quality online learning. In this article, we argue that such unreadiness is part of a long-standing pattern in which educational disruptions caused by pandemics, natural disasters, and civil unrest have necessitated transitions to remote learning. Despite decades of federal guidance advocating for a teaching force skilled in distance delivery, many teacher preparation programs have historically treated remote instruction as a temporary crisis response rather than a core professional competency. To break this cycle of reactive improvisation, the authors propose a comprehensive roadmap for the mandatory integration of online and blended learning competencies into teacher preparation programs. This agenda outlines six essential actions: (1) developing validated, research-based standards; (2) creating reliable metrics and assessment instruments; (3) ensuring sufficient specialized coursework; (4) requiring teacher candidates to experience online learning as students; (5) mandating supervised field experiences in online settings; and (6) establishing enforceable preparation requirements through accrediting bodies and state agencies. By transitioning from theoretical endorsement to rigorous, evidencebased integration, teacher preparation programs can ensure that all future educators are prepared for modern instructional realities and inevitable disruptions.

TI The DIPS model: GenAI integration in digital information problem solving
   by experts and novices
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Information problem solving; Information
   literacy; Instructional support; Authentic task; Higher education;
   Cognitive task analysis; GenAI
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; INSTRUCTION; STUDENTS; SUCCESS; SEARCH; IMPACT
AB In the digital age, academic success increasingly depends on information problem solving (IPS) competence: the ability to find, evaluate, process, and synthesize information into knowledge products. However, generative AI (genAI) transforms how higher education students engage with digital information, challenging models developed for web-based IPS, such as the IPS using Internet (IPS-I) model. Therefore, an empirically grounded model for the AI-mediated IPS process is needed. This study decomposes the cognitive activities of the AI-mediated IPS process and pinpoints where students need guidance and support. It empirically refines the IPS-I model through cognitive task analysis of think-aloud protocols from 14 novices (pre-service teachers) and 12 experts (teacher trainers) completing an authentic IPS task using genAI. Through bottom-up analysis of observed behaviors, we identified 25 cognitive activities distributed across six interrelated phases: Define, Search, Select, Process, Synthesize, and Create. Compared to the original IPS-I model, three new and four modified activities emerged, with Regulation remaining a central, cross-cutting metacognitive component. Additionally, experts and novices differed in time allocation across phases, AI tool usage, and sequencing of the IPS phases. Experts exhibited a more iterative process, integrating AI across all phases, including Regulation, and delayed the use of AI. In contrast, novices used AI early, mainly during Search and Create. The resulting Digital Information Problem Solving (DIPS) model provides a refined, empirically grounded framework for understanding and teaching IPS within the context of genAI. This model defines the intended learning outcomes for learning environments aimed at fostering responsible AI use in higher education.

AB Background: Although palliative and end-of-life care are increasingly integrated into nursing curricula, little attention is paid to how students experience and learn to care for dying or deceased persons and their relatives in emergency care settings. This lack of focus leaves students underprepared to navigate emotionally and ethically complex situations involving death. Aim: The aim was to explore nursing students' experiences in learning and providing care for dying or deceased persons and their relatives in emergency care settings. TI Nurturing an evolving identity through role transition: A hermeneutic
   phenomenological exploration of the lived experiences of nurse academics
   working in UK universities
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nurse academics; University higher education; Hermeneutic phenomenology;
   Professional identity; Workforce retention
AB Introduction: Worldwide, there are challenges in sustaining an effectively educated nursing workforce. The UK faces significant challenges recruiting and retaining nurse academics, with lack of role clarity, unclear career pathways and busy workloads contributing to attrition from higher education. A stable nurse professional role identity enhances role satisfaction however moving to a university work context can be challenging. More research was needed to understand experiences of this transition and the nurse academic role. Aim: This study aimed to understand registered nurse academics' perceptions of their university work experience, their experiences of transition from clinical practice and how this influenced their nursing identity. Design: A hermeneutic phenomenological research design within an interpretive paradigm enabled an in-depth exploration of the lived experience of participants. Participants and methods: A purposive sample of thirty registered adult nurses from three UK universities participated in individual semi-structured interviews. Data were transcribed verbatim and thematically analysed, informed by the hermeneutic circle. Findings: Four themes were identified: nurse academic identity, service culture of nursing, influence of others, and competence. Analysis showed that the early years of transition are a critical period of professional nurse identity redefinition. Inadequate support during this phase contributed to negative experiences affecting identity. A new nurse academic identity formation framework provides theoretical insights into how professional identity is influenced during transitions to a nurse academic role. It highlights the interplay of being a professional (in this case a nurse), organisational socialisation, social identity switching, and job satisfaction. Conclusion: Retention of nurse academics in roles in higher education can be supported through a nursing focused induction which is culturally and context sensitive, enabling them to develop a strong stable nurse academic identity. These findings have resonance for other professions where the transition of individuals from practice delivery settings to academic roles in universities.

TI A dual path driven change model of innovative ability for nursing
   students: A longitudinal four-year follow-up study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Innovative ability; Self-directed learning ability; Creative
   self-efficacy; Nursing; Student; Longitudinal study
AB Background: Self-directed learning ability (SLA) and creative self-efficacy (CSE) are potential predictors of innovative ability (IA) in nursing students; however, the longitudinal relationships among these variables across different stages of nursing education remain unclear. Aim: To examine the longitudinal relationships among SLA, CSE, and IA, and explore whether these relationships varied across four academic years among nursing students. Methods: A four-year longitudinal study was conducted with 163 first-year nursing students recruited through convenience sampling from a medical university in southern China. SLA, CSE, and IA were measured annually from 2021 to 2024 (T1-T4). Data were analyzed using SPSS and AMOS, and multiple-group structural equation modelling was conducted to examine longitudinal relationships among the variables across T1-T4. Results: Of the participants, 144 (88.3%) completed the four-year follow-up. SLA, CSE, and IA remained at lowto-moderate levels across T1-T4. The structural equation models demonstrated acceptable model fit across all time points. SLA consistently predicted IA at all time points ((3 = 0.501-0.663, P < 0.001) and significantly predicted CSE at T1, T3, and T4 ((3 = 0.306-0.413, P < 0.001). CSE directly predicted IA only at T1 ((3 = 0.248, P <0.001) and T2 ((3 = 0.157, P = 0.009), and mediated the relationship between SLA and IA at T1 ((3 = 0.076, P = 0.019). Most structural relationships remained stable across time points, with significant differences observed only for the effect of SLA on CSE between T2 and T3. Conclusions: This study supported a dual-path driven change model of innovative ability among nursing students, showing that self-directed learning ability demonstrated sustained associations with innovative ability across four academic years, whereas creative self-efficacy was more strongly associated with innovative ability during the early stages of nursing education. These findings provide empirical support for cultivating nursing students' innovative ability by strengthening self-directed learning while integrating creative self-efficacy training, particularly in the initial stages of education.

TI Association between generative artificial intelligence-related factors
   and self-directed learning ability among nursing students: a
   cross-sectional study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; Nursing students; Self-directed
   learning; Nursing education
ID ACCEPTANCE
AB Background: Generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) has emerged as an innovative tool in the healthcare and educational sectors and as an important tool for learning. Yet, limited empirical research has examined the related factors and associations of generative AI with self-directed learning ability among nursing students. Aim: This study investigated the association between generative AI-related factors and nursing students' self-directed learning ability, using the technology acceptance model (TAM). Design: A cross-sectional design. Setting: An online survey conducted in September 2024 in South Korea. Participants: A total of 219 nursing students completed the online survey. Methods: The key variables, based on the TAM, included perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, readiness to use, and intention to continue using generative AI. Multiple regression analysis was conducted to examine which variables were associated with self-directed learning ability. Results: Most participants (96.8%) had prior experience using AI. Among the variables, readiness to use generative AI (beta = 0.345, p < 0.001) showed the strongest association with self-directed learning ability, followed by perceived ease of use of generative AI (beta = 0.201, p = 0.003), and intention to continue to use generative AI (beta = 0.184, p = 0.004). Among the covariates included in the model, major satisfaction (beta = 0.216, p < 0.001) was also significantly associated with self-directed learning ability. These variables explained 62.6% of the total variance. Conclusions: There was a significant relationship between generative AI-related factors and self-directed learning ability. Future educational strategies should prioritize improving nursing students' readiness, perceived ease of use, and intention to use generative AI. Major satisfaction, identified as a significant covariate, should also be considered in designing these strategies. Through these strategies, nursing students' self-directed learning ability may be more effectively fostered.

TI Transforming challenges into opportunities: Students' incivility, the
   WHO nurse educator competencies, and perceptions of an ideal nurse
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nurse educator; Mixed methods; Competencies; Faculty retention;
   Incivility; Nursing education
AB Background: Global nursing education systems face significant structural and relational strain, characterised by faculty shortages and rising reports of student-faculty incivility. While the World Health Organization (WHO) Nurse Educator Core Competencies provide an international framework for excellence, empirical research into how students prioritise these competencies-particularly within unique cultural contexts-remains limited. Aim: To examine nursing students' perceptions of the 'ideal' nurse educator and determine how these perceptions align with WHO Nurse Educator Core Competencies. Methods: A convergent mixed-methods study grounded in pragmatic methodology was conducted at a rural university in Hawai'i. A purposive sample of junior Bachelor of Science in Nursing students (N = 37) completed a newly developed, competency-aligned survey (S-CVI > 0.90). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and reflexive thematic analysis, with integration achieved through comparative joint display analysis. Results: Quantitative findings demonstrated that students prioritised relational communication behaviours (M = 4.7, SD = 0.3) and professionalism enacted through fairness (M = 4.6, SD = 0.4). Qualitative themes converged with these patterns, highlighting four key pillars: Relational Presence, Fairness and Consistency, Clinical Credibility through Humility, and Psychological Safety. Integration revealed that relational enactment is the primary mechanism through which technical pedagogical competencies gain meaning. Conclusions: Relational competence is central to operationalizing global educator frameworks. In this context, the Aloha Spirit functions as a pedagogical ethic of reciprocity and compassion that transforms technical standards into transformative practice. Student incivility should be reframed as a 'diagnostic signal' to evaluate the relational climate rather than a mere behavioural issue. International faculty development must move beyond instructional technology to prioritise emotional intelligence and conflict resolution, fostering environments where both educators and learners can thrive.

TI Theory-practice gaps, factors and strategies in community nursing: A
   Knowledge-to-Action framework-guided qualitative study of interns'
   perspectives
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Community nursing education; Theory-practice gap; Knowledge-to-action
   framework; Undergraduate nursing students; Thematic analysis; COREQ;
   Community health education
ID PERCEPTIONS; INTERVIEW; EDUCATION
AB Background: The theory to practice gap (TPG) is a significant challenge in undergraduate community nursing education. Although TPG has been extensively studied in nursing education, research specifically examining these gaps in community nursing remains limited. Objective: The aim of this study is to explore the manifestations, contributing factors, and bridging strategies of the TPG in community nursing education from undergraduate nursing interns' perspectives. Design: A qualitative study guided by the knowledge-to-action (KTA) framework. Setting: This study was conducted at a medical university in China. Participants: Fifteen undergraduate nursing interns (12 females, 3 males) who had completed their 2-3-week community practicum were recruited using purposive sampling. Methods: Data were collected through face-to-face in-depth interviews conducted from October to December 2024. All interviews were audio-recorded and analyzed using Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis method. Results: The analysis identified three core themes: (1) gaps, manifesting in individual competencies, pedagogical aspects, and healthcare system; (2) factors, including individual aspects, environmental aspects, and systemic issues; (3) strategies, focusing on enhancing talent development, adjusting teaching plans, and building collaborative mechanisms. Notably, a majority of the respondents believe that adjusting the ratio of theoretical and practical courses, enhancing students' hands-on learning, and strengthening school-community collaborative education can quickly narrow the gap. Conclusion: This study found that the TPG in community nursing involves three dimensions including individual, environmental, and healthcare system, primarily influenced by factors such as the disconnect between theoretical and practical curricula, uneven teaching quality, and insufficient support from community institutions. It is recommended to increase the arrangement of practical courses in the curriculum design process and implement corresponding synchronization, and to improve educational quality through regular exchanges between teachers from both schools and communities.

TI Challenges and opportunities of micro-credentials in nursing: A
   qualitative study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Micro-credentials; Nursing; Continuing professional development
AB Background: Micro-credentials (MCs) present a new opportunity for improving continuing professional development (CPD), but their implementation in the field of nursing remains largely unexplored. The aim of this study was to explore the opportunities and challenges related to integrating MCs into nursing education in Slovenia. Methods: The study utilized a qualitative, exploratory design that involved conducting semi-structured interviews. A total of 19 interviews were conducted with representatives from different parts of the MCs ecosystem. The data collected were subsequently analysed through inductive thematic analysis. Results: Three main themes were identified: potential challenges in MCs implementation, opportunities and advantages of MCs, and the scope of potential areas for MCs application. Each of the three main themes was divided into three separate subthemes, which were then divided into associated codes. The most commonly mentioned potential challenges of MCs implementation were the regulation of knowledge output, accreditation of MCs, funding, and a lack of workplace communication. The most frequently occurring opportunities and advantages were the accessibility of education and training, competence improvement, career development, and standardisation. MCs could help develop better competence in specialised fields of healthcare, individual interventions, and non-technical skills, as well as fields that are not strictly related to nursing, such as management and mentor training. Conclusion: MCs hold significant promise for advancing nursing practice. Effective implementation of MCs could impact CPD for nursing practitioners, which is a known field that needs improvement. For this to be realized, we need to take into consideration challenges such as a lack of regulation, funding, and communication between stakeholders. Further research is still required to determine how to best implement MCs into nursing practice.

TI Trajectories and determinants of caring behaviours in nursing students:
   A longitudinal study over three academic years
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Caring; Caring behaviour; Nursing education; Nursing instructors;
   Nursing students
ID PERCEPTIONS; EDUCATION; INVENTORY; IMPACT
AB Background: Caring is a key concept in nursing care, divided into Expressive and Instrumental Caring. Learning caring competencies during nursing education is influenced by numerous factors, but these are not clearly defined in literature. Moreover, the trend/trajectories of competencies are not described in the literature. Understanding these elements is essential for developing effective educational strategies to promote the strengthening of caring in nursing students and, therefore, nurses. The study aims to describe the caring trajectories of nursing students throughout their three-years program and to identify caring determinants. Methods: A three-year observational study was conducted, enrolling a cohort of nursing students in four teaching hospitals in Northern Italy. The Caring Behaviours Inventory measured caring, with a score ranging from 1 to 6 for the dimensions of Being with and Responding to individual needs (Expressive Caring), and Doing with competence and Providing effective care (Instrumental Caring). Mixed-effects models estimated caring trajectories and their determinants. Results: A total of 274 students (median age: 20 years; 84% female) were enrolled. Over the three-year period, Instrumental Caring increased significantly (Doing with competence: (3 = 0.66; 95% CI = 0.56; 0.76 and Providing effective care: (3 = 0.90; 95% CI = 0.73; 1.06), while Expressive caring, which had already shown high scores at baseline, remained stable. The following variables were identified as determinants of increased levels of caring: perceiving trust from the instructor in a positive learning environment (Providing effective care: (3 = 0.29; 95% CI = 0.11; 0.47), being female ((3 male = -0.19; 95% CI = -0.35; -0.03), and living with the family of origin ((3 = -0.11; 95% CI = -0.22; -0.01). Conclusion: Nursing education could provide a significant contribution to the increase in Instrumental Caring and maintains high levels of Expressive Caring. The trust instilled in students by the instructor and, consequently, a positive learning environment are essential in increasing students' levels of caring over time.

TI Differences in teaching modalities and the effect on undergraduate
   nursing students' knowledge about, attitudes toward, and intent to work
   with older adults: A longitudinal study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Attitudes; Curriculum; Education; Gerontology; Intent; Knowledge;
   Nursing
ID PEOPLE; SCALE
AB Background: As the older adult population in the United States grows, demand for nurses prepared in gerontological care is rising. Yet many nursing students are reluctant to pursue this specialty, often owing to limited exposure and persistent age-related stereotypes. Aim: To compare knowledge about, attitudes toward, and intent to work with older adults among students in two accelerated BSN programs: one with a stand-alone gerontology course and one in which gerontological content is integrated throughout the curriculum. Methods: A two-group, longitudinal quasi-experimental study surveyed undergraduate nursing students at program entry, six months into their program, at program completion, and six months post-graduation. Validated instruments measured students' knowledge, attitude, and intent. Multiple multivariate linear mixed models examined curriculum and time effects. Results: Students in the stand-alone course achieved significantly higher knowledge scores and more positive attitudes toward older adults across all time points compared to those in the integrated curriculum. While both groups showed improvements in knowledge and attitude over time, attitude consistently predicted stronger intent to work with older adults. Conversely, higher knowledge scores were associated with lower intent in one model. Most intent questions remained stable across time points, with some showing slight declines six months after graduation. Conclusion: Focused gerontological coursework enhances nursing students' knowledge and attitudes, yet sustaining intent to enter geriatric practice may require additional post-graduate support. Findings underscore the value of explicit gerontology content in undergraduate curricula and highlight the need for transition-to-practice strategies that reinforce positive attitudes toward older adult care.

TI Equity, diversity, and inclusion in nursing educational institutions: A
   Walker and Avant concept analysis
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Equity; Diversity; Inclusion; EDI; DEI; Nursing; Nursing educational
   institution
ID STUDENTS; STRATEGIES; OUTCOMES; COLLEGE; JUSTICE
AB Aim: This study aimed to examine the concepts of equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI) within nursing educational institutions (NEIs) and to propose a definition of these concepts in this context. Design: This study was guided by Walker and Avant's concept analysis approach. Method: The eight-step approach identified the attributes, antecedents, and consequences of equity, diversity, and inclusion within the context of nursing educational institutions. Data sources: Twenty articles published between 2015 and 2025 were selected and analyzed from a search of five databases (MEDLINE, CINAHL, ERIC, Education Research Complete, and Scopus). Results: Our analysis shows that EDI is embedded in NEIs through compassion, techniques, and pedagogical approaches. Critical steps, such as strategy and clearly defined methods, come before it. Well-structured EDI plans and procedures have a positive impact on both individuals and organizations within NEIs. Conclusion: Seven key elements will advance equity, diversity, and inclusion in nursing educational institutions, clearly defining the construct within the context of nursing education. Implications for the nursing profession: In nursing educational institutions, equity, diversity, and inclusion are still in the early stages of understanding and application, with no universally accepted definition yet. Clearly defining and understanding the key elements of equity, diversity, and inclusion can help improve their implementation in this context.

TI The opportunities and experiences of interprofessional education for
   undergraduate nursing students on professional experience placement: An
   integrative literature review
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Interprofessional education; Interprofessional collaboration;
   Professional experience placement; Undergraduate student nurse;
   Literature review
ID CLINICAL PLACEMENT; PERCEPTIONS; IDENTITY; QUALITY; IMPACT; MODEL
AB Aim: This Integrative review aimed to identify the interprofessional education opportunities for undergraduate nursing students on clinical placement and to understand their experiences of undertaking them. Design: This study used an Integrative Review design following the process outlined by Whittemore and Knafl (2005). Data sources: Five electronic databases were searched: CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE Complete, ERIC, Web of Science Core Collection and ProQuest Health and Medicine Collection. Review methods: The PRISMA principles were used for reporting the review. Quality assessment was undertaken using an adapted version of the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Braun and Clarke's (2020) six-step reflexive thematic analysis approach was adopted to interpret the study characteristics and main themes. Results: A total of 32 articles were included in the review. Interprofessional education in clinical placement has variability in lengths of placement, placement settings, and interprofessional education activities. The length of placement and activities were linked to a lack of placement availability and the financial impact on a facility. The three main settings for interprofessional placements were primary health care, residential aged care and rehabilitation wards. Most articles reported the creation of temporary multidisciplinary placements for interprofessional education research. Five main themes were classified during data analysis including: 'authentic and valuable learning experience'; 'communication and collaboration'; 'constraints and challenges'; 'professional hierarchies'; and 'professional identity'. Conclusions: Student nurses value interprofessional education opportunities and believe they support the development of communication and collaboration skills, their own role perceptions and perceptions of other professions, although professional hierarchies remain a concern. Opportunities for interprofessional education are mainly artificially created for research projects. Research is lacking on actual opportunities or experiences for nursing students in standard clinical placements. Further research is needed on Interprofessional education focusing on the acute setting and the length of time required to support interprofessional education in practice.

TI Healthcare students' personality traits, readiness for interprofessional
   learning and self-efficacy for competence in interprofessional
   collaborative practice - a cross-sectional study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Attitudes; Competencies; Education; Interprofessional; Personality
AB Introduction: Interprofessional learning can enhance self-efficacy for competence in interprofessional collaborative practice among healthcare students. Research shows that healthcare students enter interprofessional learning with varying prerequisites. However, little is known about how these factors influence self-efficacy for competence in interprofessional collaborative practice. Aim: To explore healthcare students' self-efficacy for competence in interprofessional collaborative practice related to readiness for interprofessional learning, personality traits, gender and healthcare education. Method: A cross-sectional survey was conducted, involving healthcare students from four different programmes at two universities in Sweden. The Interprofessional Education Collaborative Competency Self-Efficacy Tool (IPECC-Set 9), the Readiness for Interprofessional Learning Scale (RIPLS) and the Neuroticism, Extraversion, and Openness to Experience Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI) were used. The IPECC-Set 9 correlated positively with the RIPLS dimensions of Teamwork and Collaboration and Roles and Responsibilities, and the personality traits Extraversion and Conscientiousness, and negatively with Neuroticism. The personality traits Extraversion and Conscientiousness were identified as positive predictors for higher scores on the IPECC-Set 9, (R2 = 0.09, adjusted R2 = 0.08). Medical students had lower scores in the RIPLS than students from the other programmes, while women scored higher than men. Conclusion: Personality predicts studentsself-efficacy for competence in interprofessional collaborative practice, while gender and education influence students' readiness for interprofessional learning. These factors should be considered when designing interprofessional learning activities to maintain student motivation and educational quality.

TI Task-oriented incivility and its impact on nursing students' safety
   behaviors in intensive care units: A qualitative study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Intensive care units; Nursing students; Patient safety; Qualitative
   research; Workplace incivility
ID EXPERIENCE; EDUCATION; VIOLENCE
AB Background: In high-acuity intensive care units (ICUs), production pressures often normalize incivility, prioritizing efficiency over education and compromising patient safety. While the psychological toll on students is well-documented, limited research explores how such environments shape safety decision-making and professional integrity. Objectives: To explore the underlying dynamics of ICU incivility, analyze its influence on professional identity across diverse student backgrounds, and examine the defensive strategies adopted and their implications for clinical safety behaviors. Design: A qualitative descriptive design was employed, adhering to the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (SRQR) checklist. Settings and participants: The study was conducted between November 2025 and January 2026 in the ICUs of three public teaching hospitals in xxx. Purposive sampling was used to recruit 26 participants, including 19 nursing interns and 7 clinical preceptors/administrators. Methods: Data were collected through semi-structured in-depth interviews. Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis was utilized for coding and theme generation. Results: The analysis identified "contextualized survival strategy" as the overarching theme, comprising four interrelated themes: (1) Professional marginalization and academic devaluation: Students experienced status incongruence and were frequently functionalized as labor supplements; (2) Prioritization of clinical production over educational needs: Instructors' efficiency imperatives contributed to pedagogical rationing and physical takeover of tasks; (3) Adoption of defensive coping strategies and performative compliance: Students navigated the hierarchy through strategic silence and regulating work pace; and (4) Influence of fear-based silence on patient safety: Fear of incivility prompted defensive simplifications, such as non-disclosure of errors and documentation workarounds. Conclusions: Task-oriented incivility appears to function as a latent structural force, prompting students to prioritize social survival over strict compliance. Addressing these adaptive deviations requires more than moral education; institutions must critically examine the efficiency imperative, establish non-punitive safety feedback channels, and provide structural support to rectify environmentally shaped behavioral deviations.

TI Comparative effectiveness of cybernetic-based instruction and
   traditional lecture method on nursing students' academic achievement: A
   quasi-experimental study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Cybernetics; Feedback; Self-regulated learning; Nursing education;
   Academic achievement; Quasi-experimental; Nigeria
AB Background: Cybernetics describes how systems regulate performance through feedback control by setting goals, monitoring current states, comparing against a standard, and adapting actions to reduce discrepancies. In teaching, this feedback-loop logic can be operationalized as structured cycles of goal clarification, guided information seeking, peer sense-making, and formative feedback. However, evidence on a cybernetic-based instructional approach (CBI) for undergraduate nursing achievement remains limited in low-resource higher-education settings. Aim: To compare the effects of Cybernetic-Based Instruction and the traditional lecture method on the academic achievement of undergraduate nursing students in maternal and child health nursing. Method: A quasi-experimental, non-equivalent group pretest-posttest study was conducted among fourth-year nursing students at Bayero University, Kano, Nigeria. Two intact cohorts from successive academic sessions received the same course content over a 13-week module. The 2024/2025 cohort received CBI (objective-driven inquiry, explicit credibility appraisal, peer synthesis, and iterative instructor/peer feedback), while the 2023/2024 cohort received conventional didactic lectures (PowerPoint/whiteboard with scheduled Q&A). Achievement was measured using a 50-item Maternal and Child Health Nursing Achievement Test (MCHNAT) administered pre- and post-instruction under supervised conditions. Analyses used within- and between-group tests and ANCOVA adjusting for pretest scores (alpha = 0.05). Results: Both groups improved significantly from pretest to posttest (p < 0.001). The CBI cohort achieved higher post-test scores and larger gains than the lecture cohort (73.12 +/- 8.96 vs 60.62 +/- 4.49; p < 0.001) and greater mean gain (31.59 +/- 8.37 vs 17.94 +/- 4.54; p < 0.001), and the adjusted between-group difference remained significant after controlling for baseline scores. ANCOVA confirmed a significant adjusted advantage for CBI (B = 13.13; 95% CI: 11.30-14.97; p < 0.001; partial eta p(2) = 0.554; R-2 = 0.605). Conclusion: A structured cybernetic feedback-loop approach was associated with higher short-term achievement than lecturing. Further multi-site studies should examine longer-term retention and transfer, and strengthen internal validity where feasible.

TI Co-designing a student-led digital assessment resource (SCAR-V) to
   enhance clinical reasoning in undergraduate nursing education: A
   qualitative study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Co-design; Clinical reasoning; Assessment literacy; Nursing education;
   Double diamond; Interpretive description; Student partnership
ID MODEL
AB Background: Developing clinical reasoning and assessment literacy is central to undergraduate nursing education, yet students often struggle to demonstrate higher-level reasoning in written assessments. This study explored how co-design, guided by the Double Diamond framework and Interpretive Descriptive analysis, could inform the creation of a digital resource to support this progression. Objectives: To examine students' and educators' experiences of assessment and learning across Levels 5 and 6, and to co-design a peer-led digital resource to enhance clarity, authenticity, and inclusion in assessment guidance. Methods: A qualitative co-design workshop was conducted with five students and three educators from an undergraduate adult nursing programme at a UK university. Participants highlighted the need for transparent scaffolding, accessible multimodal guidance, and peer-led exemplars to enhance confidence and academic progression. Conclusions: Integrating co-design with interpretive analysis enabled collaboration between students and educators to translate lived experiences into tangible educational innovation. The resulting Student Curated Assessment Resource Video (SCAR-V) exemplifies how partnership-driven design can strengthen assessment literacy, foster belonging, and promote inclusive learning cultures in nursing education.

TI The unacknowledged challenge of moral distress for nurse academics
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Moral distress; healthcare; education; nursing
ID EDUCATORS
AB The pluralistic nature of healthcare presents nurses with situations challenging their moral values which nurses must navigate. Challenges to moral values can result in the experience of moral distress, a problem that is common within the clinical nursing context. Moral distress is a known and well-researched phenomenon within nursing and has long contributed to detrimental effects such as frustration, anger, anxiety, decreased job satisfaction, burnout and ultimately attrition. However, despite extensive research in clinical environments, minimal research exists detailing this concept within the context of nursing academics and educators. Nurses can experience moral distress if they are in or exposed to work situations that are at odds with their own ethical and moral values. We contend here that moral distress is experienced regardless of practice context, and therefore we discuss moral distress in the context of nursing academics who are impacted by moral distress. Nursing academics experience moral distress, and this distress emerges from a variety of sources including insufficient resourcing, interpersonal relationships, misalignment of values, and student attitudes to learning. The psychological impact is profound and contributes to interrupted career progression and attrition. Opportunity for improvement remains but ultimately relies upon systemic change. Moral distress emanating from student behaviours is a unique factor for the nursing academic workforce. The nursing academic workforce is experiencing increasing workplace stress, expanding expectations from consumers, and increasing fiscal constraints; a situation likely to exacerbate the occurrence and the experience of moral distress for this population. Nursing academics recognise the occurrence of moral distress and propose solutions to address this concern. However, very limited evidence supports this assertion. Further research is needed within this population to ascertain the scale and the nature of the challenges faced in higher education, and more importantly to develop, test and evaluate interventions to ameliorate moral distress.

TI An informatics competency model for undergraduate nursing students: A
   quasi-experimental study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Informatics competency; Nursing informatics; Nursing students; Project
   Management; Training; Undergraduate
AB Background: Developing nursing informatics competencies in undergraduate nursing students is critical. However, existing curricula often emphasize basic computer and internet skills rather than competency-based preparation aligned with authentic informatics roles and project-based practice, contributing to a persistent theory-practice gap. The Nursing Informatics Competency Organizational (NICO) model provides a structured framework for competency development in nursing informatics. Aim: To examine the effectiveness of a NICO model-based nursing informatics course in improving nursing informatics competency among first-year undergraduate nursing students. Design: A quasi-experimental study. Methods: Instructional materials were developed based on the "Nursing Information System Project Management" component of the NICO model, emphasizing user-centered needs and experiential learning. Participants were allocated to an experimental group (n = 40), which received NICO-based project management training in addition to computer literacy, or a control group (n = 40), which received general computer courses only. The intervention comprised nine weekly 90-minute sessions. Outcomes were measured using a nursing informatics competency self-assessment scale, a project experience assessment questionnaire, student feedback, project outputs, and a self-developed scoring tool. Results: Participants in the experimental group showed significantly greater improvements in nursing informatics competencies compared with those in the control group (t = 2.770, P = 0.007). Significant gains were observed in informatics roles, basic computer knowledge and skills, and wireless device competencies (t = 2.279, 2.461, and 3.118, respectively, all P < 0.05). No significant differences were found in applied computer skills or clinical informatics attitudes. Six group-based projects were completed, with reports graded at a B level. Learning satisfaction was high (mean score 96.03 +/- 9.10 out of 105). Conclusions: Integrating a NICO-based approach into undergraduate nursing education may support the development of selected nursing informatics competencies and promote high learner satisfaction. These findings provide practical insights for refining project-based informatics training in nursing education.

TI Developing open innovation competency in Gen Z entrepreneurship
   students: Roles of absorptive capacity, AI literacy and algorithmic
   thinking skills
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Absorptive capacity; AI literacy; Algorithmic thinking skills; Open
   innovation competency; Gen Z entrepreneurship students
AB This study aims to examine the relationships among absorptive capacity, AI literacy, algorithmic thinking skills, and open innovation competency. The research sample comprised 308 undergraduate senior students majoring in entrepreneurship from both public and private higher education institutions in Thailand. Data were collected using a questionnaire developed based on a comprehensive literature review and validated for reliability and content validity. The findings, analyzed through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), revealed that absorptive capacity significantly and positively influences AI literacy and algorithmic thinking skills. Furthermore, AI literacy and algorithmic thinking skills play crucial mediating roles in linking absorptive capacity with open innovation competency, with algorithmic thinking skills emerging as the most prominent structural factor contributing to open innovation success. The results underscore the importance of developing absorptive capacity, AI literacy, and algorithmic thinking skills to enhance open innovation competency among Gen Z entrepreneurship students. These findings provide actionable insights for educational institutions and organizations to design curricula or training programs that focus on technology skills and complex problem-solving capabilities, thereby preparing young entrepreneurs for the challenges of the digital economy.

TI Open- versus closed-response methods of measuring students' reasoning: A
   case study using the Physics Measurement Questionnaire
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID MULTIPLE-CHOICE; POINT
AB We compare open- and closed-response versions of two questions that measure students' reasoning on the Physics Measurement Questionnaire, same mean different spread (SMDS), and different mean same spread (DMSS). We conducted an experiment in one class (N 1/4 248) to test if asking students for their reasoning on an open-response question changes their answer to the closed-response question. To test whether answering the open-response question alters students' closed-response answers, we prompted half of the students to explain their reasoning before seeing the closed-response options, while the other half went straight to the closed-response reasoning options. We find no effect of asking students their reasoning in an open-response question on their subsequent closed-response answers. Additionally, we investigated whether we measure students' reasoning differently on the closed-response versus openresponse versions of the question by evaluating the consistency between the students' open-response and closed-response answers. Although we measure similarities in students' reasoning across the two methods, the differences indicate that the open-response and closed-response questions provide different information. The results inform the need for critical judgment when deciding between open- and closed-response assessment formats.

TI Exploring students' perceptions of their learning experience and
   self-efficacy in online physics class with project-based learning: An
   interpretative phenomenological analysis
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
AB Project-based learning (PBL), recognized as an active learning strategy, has been linked to students' self-efficacy in prior studies, including those within physics education research. Meanwhile, technological advancements have significantly facilitated the optimization of diverse learning modes, including online learning. However, comprehensive investigations addressing questions such as how students perceive PBL and their self-efficacy, what forms of PBL design they prefer, and what benefits and challenges they encounter during its implementation remain underexplored in existing literature. This work presents the results of 1- and 2-year pedagogical research on 10 students as preservice physics teachers in an online PBL physics class, focusing on its influence on their self-efficacy within a phenomenological study. Data were collected via semistructured, in-depth interviews. Social cognitive theory, Bandura's self-efficacy theory, and a theoretical framework for the impact of project-based learning on educational outcomes were employed as guiding frameworks to shape the interpretation of students' experiences and perspectives. Through interpretative phenomenological analysis, the researchers identified three primary themes representing the students' experiences. There are (1) variety of unique learning experiences based on students' perceptions about their character, (2) pivotal experiences as catalysts in the learning process, and (3) student self-awareness. The findings contribute novel insights for educators in implementing PBL, particularly in online contexts, by highlighting strategies to accommodate diverse student personality characteristics. Moreover, the latest findings in this study, compared with relevant research that has been done previously, are discussed. The study offers valuable references for research on the interplay between PBL and self-efficacy. Possible directions for further research are discussed.

TI Exploring preservice teachers' use of ontologies and stances toward the
   wave function through a classical-quantum analogy lesson
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
AB Physics students, teachers, and preservice teachers (PSTs) struggle with the abstract nature of quantum mechanics (QM), which has led to calls for a more conceptual approach to QM teaching and learning. In response, this study uses a novel analogy between Kundt's tube and the infinite quantum well to elicit discussion of ontological issues. We investigated PSTs' use of ontologies, including their interpretation of the wave function. Nine PSTs participated in the analogy lesson; dialogues were recorded, transcribed, and thematically analyzed. We identified five different ontologies: one classical and four quantum ontologies. The importance of probabilities in PSTs' quantum ontologies stood out. Three ontologies (probabilistic particle, particle-wave, and probabilistic wave) expand the particle-wave duality, while the fourth (wave collapse) added a dynamic element to this axis. PSTs often used a single ontology in response to one aspect of the analogy but switched flexibly between ontologies across aspects of the analogy that they discussed. Concerning the wave function, we found both realist and formalist stances, revealing a diversity of interpretations that contrasts with the uniformity of the formalist QM courses PSTs had attended. We conclude that explicit attention to ontological issues in QM, supported by classical-quantum analogies, provides insight into PSTs' ontological reasoning and offers a conceptual approach to teaching and learning QM. We present recommendations for PST training and implications for QM teaching reform.

TI Comparing teacher-centered and student-centered agents based on prompt
   engineering: Effects on learning performance, cognitive load, flow
   experience, and empathy perception in physics learning
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID ARCHITECTURE; CHATGPT
AB Large language models (LLMs) often face challenges in generating accurate and coherent explanations when solving physics questions. Prompt engineering serves as an effective strategy for human-artificial intelligence communication, guiding LLMs to generate precise and contextually relevant responses with well-designed instructions. The study utilized prompt engineering on the Coze platform to construct two types of instructional agents: a teacher-centered agent and a student-centered agent. They were designed to respond to students' questions in accordance with their respective roles and communication styles. Specifically, the teacher-centered agent tended to provide authoritative, professionally grounded, and content-focused responses, whereas the student-centered agent was designed to be more attentive to students' prior knowledge and learning needs, offering adaptive and supportive guidance. The study compared the effects of these two agents on students' learning performance, cognitive load, flow experience, and empathy perception. The results revealed differential effects between the two promptengineered agent conditions. Compared with the teacher-centered agent, students interacting with the student-centered agent condition showed higher learning performance, lower extraneous cognitive load, stronger germane cognitive engagement, greater flow experience, and higher empathy perception.

TI Toward thinking quantumly: Student reasoning about the enigma of QM
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID VIDEO RESEARCH; RESOURCES; TEACH
AB The physics education research (PER) literature on quantum mechanics (QM) often acknowledges and minimizes what we refer to as the enigma of QM, viewing these aspects of QM as a challenge to overcome, rather than an inherent feature to be leveraged for learning. Using the overlapping theories of knowledge-inpieces and resource theory as connected to an epistemological framing perspective, we focus on students' descriptions of the enigma of QM and the epistemological frames that students view as relevant when approaching QM. Data comes from interviews with 10 undergraduate physics students who had learned quantum physics topics across different courses in the curriculum, ranging from sophomore-level modern physics to an advanced undergraduate-level QM course. To elicit students' ideas on QM, the interview protocol emphasized their perspectives and empowerment when possible. Iterative rounds of qualitative analysis coded the data for how students described enigmatic aspects of QM, along with three epistemological frames students identified as their reasoning strategies: reasoning about scale, reasoning about the connections between QM and mathematics, and reasoning about the connections between QM and classical mechanics. The results document that students are aware that something about QM is unexplainable, an enigma to acknowledge. We argue that acknowledgment of the enigma of QM is a key part of what we refer to as thinking quantumly. Additionally, the epistemological frame of reasoning about scale has not been widely discussed in the QM-PER literature, which students use to distinguish QM from classical mechanics and to explain why mathematical models are needed. These results are important for amplifying students' voices in how they approach enigmatic aspects of QM. Thus, our results begin to move the QM-PER literature beyond viewing enigmatic aspects of QM as obstacles to be corrected through refined instruction, toward an asset-based orientation as a source of meaningful insights for the learning process.

TI Organizing energy instruction around the work and energy relation to
   support knowledge integration in secondary physics
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID LEARNING PROGRESSION; CATEGORIZATION; DIFFICULTIES; SYSTEMS; EXPERTS
AB Energy is a central idea in physics, but students often learn energy as a set of loosely connected terms, equations, and conservation statements rather than as an integrated explanatory framework. Prior physics education research (PER) has shown that students have persistent difficulty identifying appropriate systems, tracing energy changes across systems and forms, and applying energy conservation in unfamiliar contexts. Drawing on the knowledge integration perspective and on research on systemsbased energy reasoning, this study developed a conceptual framework for a ninth-grade energy unit in which the work and energy relation served as the central organizing relation linking energy change, energy conservation, and contextualized problem solving. We implemented a conceptual-framework-based instructional intervention and compared it with regular textbook-sequence instruction in a quasiexperimental study involving two intact ninth-grade classes in China. Both groups studied the same curriculum content for the same amount of instructional time and were taught by the same teacher. Analysis of covariance showed that, after controlling for pretest performance, the intervention group significantly outperformed the control group on the overall post-test score and on the three conceptual categories of energy change, energy conservation, and the work and energy relation. Statistical mediation analyses further showed that the intervention group's post-test advantage was associated with students' performance on the work and energy relation. In the post-test mediation model, this indirect association was larger for atypical context performance than for typical context performance. These findings provide classroom-based evidence that reorganizing energy instruction around a core conceptual relation can support students' integrated understanding and application of energy ideas. The study contributes to PER by extending conceptual-framework-based instruction to a broader secondary energy unit and by clarifying how a work-centered organization may support reasoning beyond familiar surface features.
