TI Effect of scale comprehension on student reasoning about astronomical
   phenomena. II. Moon phases
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID SPATIAL ABILITY; TEACHERS CONCEPTIONS; EARTH; UNDERSTANDINGS; KNOWLEDGE;
   EDUCATION; IMPACT; IDEAS; SUN
AB This paper is the second in a two-part series that investigates students' reasoning on astronomical phenomena. In this work, we examined how (if at all) students rely on spatial scale assumptions when reasoning about Moon phases. To that end, we conducted N 1/4 25 semistructured interviews with last-year high school students. A personalized, physical scale model of the Sun-Earth-Moon system was constructed for every participant individually and placed on the interview table. Students were encouraged to clarify their thoughts by interacting with the scale model or by making a drawing. The scale estimates underpinning the scale model on the table were assessed through an interactive online survey, which was administered several days to weeks prior to the interviews. Only students with severely underestimated values for the relevant sizes and distances were selected for an interview. This selection procedure was motivated by both pragmatic and empirical considerations. We observed a wide variety of explanations for Moon phases, some of which were not found in the existing literature. Several students used their (inaccurate) scale ideas to reason about Moon phases. However, occasionally an interviewed student expressed arguments inconsistent with the scale model on the table. In these cases, scale assumptions seemed to be not taken into account when reasoning about Moon phases. The implications of these findings are discussed.

TI Effect of scale comprehension on student reasoning about astronomical
   phenomena. I. The apparent sizes of Moon and Sun and Solar Eclipses
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID SPATIAL ABILITY; MISCONCEPTIONS; KNOWLEDGE; TEACHERS; MODELS; PHASES;
   ANGLES
AB This paper is the first in a two-part series that investigates students' reasoning on astronomical phenomena. We interviewed N 1/4 25 last-year high school students to uncover their reasoning on three observable phenomena, two of which will be discussed in this paper. The first phenomenon was the apparent sizes of the Moon and the Sun (as seen from Earth) and potential causes for their variation. The second phenomenon regarded the event of a solar eclipse and the difference between total and annular eclipses. The interviews were held in light of the students' understanding of spatial scales in the Earth-Moon-Sun system. Based on their answers on a prior online survey assessing students' estimates of these scales, a personal to-scale model of the Earth-Moon-Sun system was provided for every student. The students selected for interviews were those who showed a substantial underestimation of these scales. Students were repetitively encouraged to illustrate their reasoning on both phenomena by using the scale model or by providing a drawing. For both discussed astronomical phenomena, we encountered several alternative explanations that-as far as we know-were not previously documented in the research literature. Many of these relied on an inaccurate comprehension of the involved scales. Although for some students these explanations were in line with the scale model on the interview table representing their substantial underestimations, others did not seem to take spatial scales into account when making suggestions on the causes for these astronomical phenomena. The implications of these findings are discussed.

TI Nature of heat inventory: Assessing students' understanding of thermal
   processes in kinetic molecular terms
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE basic heat processes: heat transfer; convection; melting
ID CONCEPTIONS; PERFORMANCE; INSTRUMENT
AB The present study describes the development and field testing of the nature of heat inventory (NOHI) that examines high school and undergraduate students' understanding of heat transfer processes in the terms of kinetic molecular theory. NOHI comprises 10 items. Based on preliminary study and the history of science, the 30 distractors of NOHI were designed to reflect the following three categories of possible misconceptions regarding heat: (a) materialistic views, (b) hot atoms, and (c) expanding atoms. Field testing, carried out on 81 students for science teaching, showed the materialistic misconceptions of heat still to be the most popular. NOHI has been proven to be a valid and reliable tool that could be used to determine students' thinking regarding classical heat processes.

TI Exploring how reducing the weight of low exam scores impacts average
   grades and equity gaps
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID COLLEGE; GENDER
AB Students interpret grades as signals of their strengths, and grades inform students' decisions about majors and courses of study. Differences in grades that are not related to learning can impact this judgment and have real-world impact on course-taking and careers. Existing work has examined how an overemphasis on high-stakes exams can create equity gaps where female students and Black, Hispanic, and Native American students earn lower grades than male students and Asian and white students, respectively. Yet, minimal work has examined how the weighting of individual midterm exam scores can also contribute to equity gaps. In this study, we examine how three midterm exam score aggregation methods for final grades affect equity gaps. We collected midterm exam data from approximately 6000 students in an introductory physics course over 6 years at a large, research-intensive university. Using this dataset, we applied common midterm exam score aggregation methods to determine their impact on aggregated midterm exam grades: dropping the lowest midterm exam score, replacing the lowest midterm exam score with the final exam score if higher, and counting the highest midterm exam score more in the final grade calculation than the lowest midterm exam score. We find that dropping the lowest midterm exam score resulted in the largest increase in final grades, with students with lower grades benefiting the most. However, we find no evidence that these alternative midterm exam aggregation methods close equity gaps. Instead, we find some evidence that such practices could increase equity gaps between male and female students, though the effect is very small in relation to the overall grade increase. Implementing the alternative midterm exam aggregation methods examined here may be useful for instructors wanting to raise course grades or give lower-scoring students a boost. However, they do not appear to be effective in reducing equity gaps.

TI Unlocking Morphology: A Case Study of Morphological Knowledge Growth in
   a Deaf Student Using Computer-Delivered Intervention
SO AMERICAN ANNALS OF THE DEAF
LA English
DT Article
DE language development; morphology; spelling; vocabulary
ID HARD-OF-HEARING; ENGLISH READING-COMPREHENSION; AWARENESS INTERVENTION;
   ACADEMIC VOCABULARY; PHONOLOGICAL AWARENESS; LITERACY ACQUISITION;
   LANGUAGE; CHILDREN; INSTRUCTION; SKILLS
AB Morphological knowledge (MK), or awareness of word structure and morphemic relationships, is a critical component of literacy for students who are D/HH. However, it has been explored to a lesser extent than other literacy components, such as phonological awareness and vocabulary. This case study examined the responsiveness of an 11-year-old bilingual student who is deaf to a computer-delivered supplemental morphology intervention, the Morphological Analysis Pathway to Reading (MAP-R). TI Fostering career awareness and self-directed learning through an
   AI-Induced Disruptive Learning Environment
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-Induced disruptive learning environment; AI substitution;
   Self-directed learning; Learning anxiety; Career awareness
AB As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly substitutes for human tasks, higher education must address changing skill demands. However, the emotional and cognitive processes activated when students confront AI substitution remain insufficiently examined. This study conceptualizes and implements an AI-Induced Disruptive Learning Environment in which structured human-AI performance contrasts are designed as psychologically salient learning events. Using a three-wave quasi-experimental mixed-methods design, this study examined undergraduate students enrolled in a product design and manufacturing course. The findings indicate that AI substitution exposure was linked to heightened career awareness and stronger acceptance of skill transformation. Although learning anxiety increased temporarily during the intervention, it appeared to function as an informational signal when supported by guided reflection. Structural equation modeling supported a theoretically consistent pattern of associations linking emotional activation, career awareness, skill transformation acceptance, and self-directed learning, while qualitative findings showed a non-uniform progression from disruption to adaptive repositioning. These findings suggest that AI substitution can be understood not only as a technological capability, but also as a pedagogically structured learning event that shapes emotional, cognitive, and behavioral adaptation. The study contributes to AI-in-education research by clarifying how structured exposure to AI-driven disruption, when instructionally scaffolded, may support reflective adaptation and self-directed learning orientation.

TI Defining a physics person: Tensions in the identity development of
   undergraduate women in physics
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID SCIENCE IDENTITY; STUDENTS; GENDER; SENSE; EXPERIENCES; VALUES; COLOR;
   WORK
AB This qualitative study explores how undergraduate women define what it means to be a physics person alongside how they describe their own physics identity. Our team analyzed 120 survey responses (97%, or 116 of the 120 respondents, identified as women or non-binary) to understand what factors are associated with an individual's physics identity. Those surveyed were attendees of Conferences for Undergraduate Women in Physics, who attended 88 unique institutions in 30 states. Our participants' conceptions of what it means to be a physics person fell into two themes: (1) people who are skilled academically and in research and (2) those who have an interest in physics ranging from an enjoyable interest to a life-devoting passion for the subject. When asked to explain their own physics identities, students responded through a personal and social lens more frequently than through an academic lens. Our analysis revealed three tensions in the development of undergraduate women's physics identity: (1) the tension between identifying entirely as a physics person and having other identities that are important to who they are, (2) the tension between the need for belonging in the physics community and their view of themselves as a physics person, and (3) the tension between their expectations of a physics person and their beliefs about their own abilities or interest.

TI Understanding and enhancing students' use of evaluation strategies
   during physics problem solving through reflective prompts
SO PHYSICAL REVIEW PHYSICS EDUCATION RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
ID METACOGNITIVE SKILLS; ONLINE
AB The Disciplinary Learning Companion (DLC) is an online reflection tool designed to enhance students' engagement in metacognitive activities during physics problem solving. It achieves this through providing reflective discipline-and topic-specific prompts on the solving process. This study focuses on evaluation strategies and aims to understand whether, how, and when students use evaluation strategies during physics problem solving, whether the DLC's reflective prompts trigger the use of evaluation strategies and the extent to which this use is transferred to future problem solving. A total of twelve first-year bioscience engineering students each participated in four think-aloud interviews over a four weeks period. This study focuses on students' use of evaluation activities as part of their metacognitive process. In addition, we evaluated the impact of the DLC by studying the evaluation strategies students used after being prompted and those transferred to subsequent problem-solving attempts. The analysis revealed that students spontaneously applied evaluation strategies to numerical problems but rarely to symbolic problems. The DLC's reflective prompts successfully triggered the use of evaluation strategies, though infrequently. Similarly, there were few instances of transferring evaluation strategies from one think-aloud interview to another.

TI The Use of Artificial Intelligence with d/Deaf and Hard of Hearing
   Students: A Systematic Review
SO AMERICAN ANNALS OF THE DEAF
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; reading text; reading comprehension;
   vocabulary; d/Dhh students
AB The major purpose of the present systematic review is to critically evaluate the literature on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) with d/Deaf and hard of hearing (d/Dhh) students. It is also of interest to analyze any existing studies on the use of AI to improve the reading skills of these students. In light of limited available investigations, it is important to describe the development of a funded AI reading project to be proffered as a model for future research. The studies reviewed provide various examples of the use of deep learning, machine learning, and AI applications for d/Dhh individuals. It was also emphasized that the system not only facilitates alphabet recognition, but also can be extended to the teaching of more complex reading units that form the basis of literacy. In the funded AI reading project model, reading texts were developed for d/Dhh students. The Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (Turkish version) readability formula was used to determine whether the texts were suitable for the first-and second-grade levels. The model has the potential to serve larger groups of students through more comprehensive databases with its scalable structure.

TI Eye Tracking Shows Deaf and Hard of Hearing Children with Cochlear
   Implants Read Like Hearing Peers
SO AMERICAN ANNALS OF THE DEAF
LA English
DT Article
DE deaf and hard of hearing children (DHH); eye tracking; reading; cochlear
   implants
ID PHONOLOGICAL PROCESSING SKILLS; ENHANCED PERCEPTUAL SPAN; VOCABULARY
   KNOWLEDGE; PRESCHOOL-CHILDREN; MOVEMENT PATTERNS; EMERGENT LITERACY;
   SPOKEN LANGUAGE; CONTENT WORDS; AWARENESS; ATTENTION
AB This study investigated the reading processes of deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) children with cochlear implants (CIs) in comparison to typically hearing (TH) peers using eye-tracking methodology. While prior research on CI users has primarily focused on the level of reading performance, our approach captured word-by-word reading behavior to examine fixation durations, fixation counts, and regressions. Twenty-two DHH children with CIs (14 female; Ma9e = 10.25 years, SD = 1.31) and 26TH children (16 female; Ma9e = 10.5 years, SD = 0.95), silently read an age-appropriate Polish text while their eye movements were recorded. We analyzed eye movements by word type (content vs. function words) and word length. Consistent with established reading research, both groups devoted more attention to content words than function words, and to longer than shorter words as evidenced by more fixations, longer dwell time, and more regressions. Interestingly, however, there were no differences in first fixation duration or average fixation duration. Finally, no significant between-group differences were observed in any eye-tracking metrics, indicating similar cognitive processing during reading. These findings align with the qualitative similarity hypothesis, suggesting that with appropriate support, DHH children with CIs can achieve reading processes comparable to TH peers. Similar first and average fixation durations indicate unimpaired word decoding, while increased fixation counts, regressions, and dwell times for content and longer words reflect higher demands during post-lexical semantic and syntactic integration.The results highlight the value of eye tracking as a sensitive tool for detecting reading strategies, and they underscore the potential of early implantation combined with holistic educational support to promote literacy development.

TI Nursing students making sense and meaning of norm-criticism in a
   campus-based clinical learning environment: A narrative analysis
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Aesthetic learning; Critical reflection; Erving Goffman; Health equity;
   Norm-criticism; Nursing education; Nursing students; Sense-making
ID SOCIAL-JUSTICE
AB Background: Nursing education institutions have sought to incorporate health equity and social justice into curricula. However, nursing students report limited opportunities to engage with these perspectives during their studies. In a campus-based clinical learning environment, efforts have been made to support students in the advancement of health equity and social justice by integrating a norm-critical approach. Aim: This study aimed to explore how nursing students made sense of norm-criticism in a campus-based clinical learning environment. Design: The design of the study was qualitative, informed by narrative inquiry and a Goffmanian theoretical framework. Setting: The study was carried out in a campus-based clinical learning environment for nursing education in a mid-sized university college. Participants: The participants of the study consist of 14 undergraduate nursing students. Methods: This study adopted a narrative methodology where the data was analyzed both structurally and thematically. Results: This study demonstrates that students made sense of norm-criticism by framing it in three distinct phases. First, students encounter norm-criticism through norm-critical photographs, then they engage in critical reflection on norm-criticism, both in collaboration with peers and through personal reflection on their own positionality, and lastly, they find meaning in norm-criticism as a tool to change unequal nursing practices and provide person-centered nursing care. Conclusion: This study highlights that, by mechanisms of impression management and reframing, nursing students regard and use norm-criticism as a reflective tool that empowers them to change healthcare structures and supports them in understanding how to provide person-centered care.

TI Indigenous health and cultural safety in interdisciplinary tertiary
   education: A multi-method evaluation of student learning
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Cultural safety; Decolonising curriculum; Interdisciplinary tertiary
   education; Aboriginal ways of knowing; Being and doing; Anti-racism;
   Indigenous health
ID CAPABILITY MEASUREMENT TOOL
AB Background Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples experience persistent health inequities shaped by colonisation and its ongoing impacts, including racism, and structural and social determinants of health. Culturally safe tertiary education is essential for preparing a responsive health and human services workforce. Objectives To explore shifts in undergraduate and post-graduate nursing, midwifery, and social work students' knowledge, attitudes, beliefs and learning experiences during a mandatory Cultural Safety and Indigenous Health and Wellbeing interdisciplinary course at an Australian university. Methods A sequential multi-method research design used a pre-and post-curriculum online survey (Ganngaleh nga Yagaleh) alongside open-ended qualitative questions. Quantitative data were analysed using non-parametric tests and mixed-effects models; qualitative responses were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results Of 481 enrolled students, 182 (37.8%) completed all survey components. While no significant change was observed in Commitment to Culturally Safe Practice (coefficient 1.11, 95% CI -0.32-2.53, p = 0.13), significant improvements were found in Understanding of History and Power (co-efficient 2.59, 95% CI 1.55-3.62, p < 0.001), and Attitudes, Values and Beliefs (coefficient 3.44, 95% CI 1.95-4.92, p < 0.001). Qualitative findings demonstrated richer, more nuanced shifts: students moved from general awareness to more contextualised understandings of colonisation, systemic inequity and their own positionality. Many described emotional journeys characterised by discomfort, vulnerability, empathy, and renewed commitment to ethical and culturally safe practice, while others expressed resistance or uncertainty. Students emphasised the importance of Indigenous-led teaching, yarning-based learning environments and relational, reflective pedagogy in supporting transformative learning. These data also indicated the need for indigenising curriculum beyond one course to enable students' earlier exposure to racially determined negative health outcomes. Conclusion The course fostered meaningful cognitive, emotional and reflective shifts in students' understandings of cultural safety. Findings emphasise the value of Indigenous-led, relational, and decolonising pedagogies and the importance of embedding cultural safety education earlier and more consistently across health curricula.

TI The role of inhibitory control in creative cognition: exploring a
   multifaceted relationship
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creativity; Inhibition; Executive functions; Divergent thinking;
   Convergent thinking; Cognitive inhibition; Creative cognition
ID LATENT INHIBITION; DIVERGENT THINKING; EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; DEFAULT
   NETWORK; WORKING-MEMORY; BRAIN NETWORKS; RISK-TAKING; FUNCTIONAL
   CONNECTIVITY; ORIGINAL IDEAS; SELF-REPORT
AB Creative cognition is often argued to involve inhibitory control, but it remains unclear what amount, and type, of inhibitory control is relevant to which type of creative cognition. Some evidence suggests that creative performance benefits from stronger inhibition (particularly in laboratory settings), while other evidence suggests that it benefits from weaker inhibition. Supposing that this variation in findings might be due to the multifaceted nature of both inhibitory control and creative cognition, we sought to clarify the relationship between these constructs using several measures of each, with factor analysis and regressions. We examined creative cognition using two measures of divergent thinking (the alternative uses task and a figural completion drawing task), and a measure of convergent thinking (the remote associates test). We examined inhibitory control using two measures of response inhibition (the Stroop and the Emotional Stroop), a measure of cognitive inhibition (retrieval-induced forgetting), and a measure of latent inhibition. Participants (N = 151) also completed measures of personality, intelligence, self-monitoring, and real-world creative achievement. Results revealed that cognitive inhibition was a significant predictor of divergent thinking after accounting for both trait openness and fluid intelligence, but was unrelated to convergent thinking or real-world creative achievement. Meanwhile, response inhibition and latent inhibition were not significantly related to any measure of creative cognition. These findings shed light on the nuanced relationship between inhibitory control and creative cognition, and highlight the importance of assessing these multifaceted constructs with a variety of measures.

TI Creative and neurocognitive profile of adults with developmental
   dyslexia
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creativity; Developmental dyslexia; EEG; Divergent thinking; Convergent
   thinking; Executive functions; Working memory; Inhibition
ID COGNITIVE INHIBITION; EXECUTIVE FUNCTIONS; DIVERGENT THINKING;
   WORKING-MEMORY; CONVERGENT; ATTENTION; BRAIN; CHILDREN; EEG;
   INTELLIGENCE
AB Research on creativity in developmental dyslexia has produced mixed findings, with some studies suggesting enhanced creativity and others reporting no differences relative to typical readers. The present study examined behavioral and electrophysiological mechanisms underlying various creativity tasks in adults with developmental dyslexia. Forty-two adults (12 with dyslexia, 30 controls) completed divergent and convergent creativity tasks alongside executive-function assessments, while electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded during divergent thinking. Behavioral results revealed comparable divergent thinking performance across fluency, flexibility, and originality measures. In contrast, adults with dyslexia demonstrated lower performance on the convergent thinking task and reduced working memory capacity compared with controls, whereas inhibitory control did not differ between groups. Electrophysiological analyses indicated increased alpha event-related synchronization (ERS) during divergent thinking in the dyslexia group, with the strongest effects observed bilaterally, particularly in the right hemisphere. Correlation analyses showed associations between executive functions and creativity performance primarily in the control group, whereas no significant relationships were observed in the dyslexia group. Taken together, the findings reveal a dissociation between divergent and convergent creativity processes in dyslexia. While working memory limitations appear to constrain convergent problem-solving, divergent thinking performance remains preserved and is accompanied by increased right-hemisphere alpha synchronization. These results suggest that creative idea generation in dyslexia may rely on alternative neural mechanisms that support internally directed attention during creative cognition, highlighting multiple cognitive pathways underlying creativity in neurodiverse populations.

TI Differential effects of embodied unplugged programming activities on
   computational thinking in K-12 students: A meta-analysis
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Embodied learning; Unplugged programming; K-12; Computational thinking;
   Meta-analysis
ID EFFECT SIZE; SKILLS; ENVIRONMENTS; FOUNDATIONS; ENGAGEMENT; FRAMEWORK;
   ROBOTICS; DESIGN; IMPACT
AB Unplugged programming is emerging as an effective approach to cultivate computational thinking among K-12 students by lowering technical barriers and mitigating health risks associated with excessive screen time. However, consensus remains elusive regarding its implementation effectiveness across different levels of embodiment. Embodied learning refers to instructional approaches that involve physical movement, sensory engagement, or bodily interaction to enhance cognitive processing (i.e., unplugged programming tasks that involve varying degrees of students' bodily movement, physical manipulation, or role enactment). This meta-analysis, synthesizing 97 studies (198 effect sizes, 23,168 participants), reveals that embodied unplugged programming effectively enhances computational thinking in K-12 students with a moderate effect size (Hedges' g = 0.636, 95% CI [0.545, 0.728], p < 0.05) Differences exist among weak, moderate, and strong embodied unplugged activities (Q(B)=4.829, p < 0.05). Within weak embodiment activities, a 0-6 weeks instructional intervention using game-based learning in formal classroom settings with 21-40 students most effectively enhances computational thinking among elementary students. For moderately embodied activities, project-based learning interventions lasting over 12 weeks in formal learning settings with class sizes of 0-20 students yielded the greatest computational thinking gains for middle school students. For highly embodied activities, elementary students benefited most from over 12 weeks of game-based learning in informal settings with class sizes of 0-20. These findings provide theoretical and empirical guidance for designing unplugged programming activities with varying embodiment levels and formulating computational thinking education policies.

TI Can media multitasking enhance creative performance? Insights from
   self-determination theory
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Autonomous motivation; Creative performance; Media multitasking;
   Perceived autonomy; Self-determination theory
ID AUTONOMOUS MOTIVATION; INTRINSIC MOTIVATION; DIVERGENT THINKING;
   COGNITIVE CONTROL; SUPPORT; COMPETENCE; TEAM
AB The widespread use of portable media devices has made media multitasking increasingly common in learning, work, and daily life. However, previous studies have largely focused on its negative effects from a cognitive perspective, overlooking the possibility that media multitasking may enhance creative performance through motivational process. Drawing on self-determination theory and a situational-trait interaction perspective, the present study systematically examined the promotive effects of media multitasking on creative performance, as well as the mediating and moderating roles of perceived autonomy and autonomous motivation, across three preregistered simulated behavioral experiments (N = 415). Results indicated that individuals engaged in media multitasking demonstrated higher levels of creative performance compared to those engaged in non media multitasking (Experiment 1 and 3). This effect was mediated by an increase in perceived autonomy, which subsequently enhanced creative performance (Experiments 1 and 2). Interestingly, this enhancement effect was more pronounced in individuals with low autonomous motivation than in those with high autonomous motivation (Experiment 3). These findings illuminate the constructive functions of media multitasking, extend non-cognitive perspectives on its underlying mechanisms, and provide practical implications for creatively disadvantaged individuals to leverage media affordances to regain a competitive advantage.

TI Same AI, different pathways: Unpacking mechanisms of AI-mediated
   learning across discipline-institution contexts
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; Prompting proficiency; Verification behavior; Trust
   calibration; Perceived task-related cognitive load; Large language
   models; Higher education; Mixed-methods
ID COGNITIVE ARCHITECTURE; INSTRUCTIONAL-DESIGN; AUTOMATION; TRUST
AB Large language models (LLMs) are transforming higher education, yet their learning benefits likely depend on students' AI literacy and how they prompt and verify AI outputs. This mixed-methods study investigates how AI literacy relates to prompting proficiency and verification behavior, and how these behaviors operate through two mechanisms, AI-supported calibration accuracy and perceived task-related cognitive load, to predict coursework performance across two discipline-institution contexts in Thailand. The author surveyed Design students (n = 221) and Business students (n = 222) and analyzed the data using multigroup structural equation modeling, complemented by thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews. Results indicated that AI literacy significantly predicted both prompting proficiency and verification behavior (p < .001). Prompting proficiency was positively associated with trust calibration, whereas verification behavior was negatively associated with perceived task-related cognitive load, and the corresponding indirect effects were supported. Context-specific patterns also emerged: in the Design context, verification behavior showed a stronger direct association with task quality, while in the Business context, AI-supported calibration accuracy was the stronger predictor of assignment quality. Interview evidence helped explain these differences. Design students used ChatGPT primarily to accelerate ideation and refinement, whereas Business students used it to support structured analysis and to make their work more auditable. Across both contexts, verification functioned as a metacognitive safeguard that reduced overload and stabilized accuracy. These findings suggest that teaching AI literacy in higher education should emphasize rubric-guided prompting, verification routines, and calibrated trust to balance efficiency with deeper engagement, with attention to context-specific pedagogical demands.

TI Six basic image schemata of creative design thinking from the
   perspective of categorization
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creative design thinking; Design fixation; Categorization; Image
   schemata; Grounded theory
ID INTEGRATION; PSYCHOLOGY; FIXATION
AB This study investigates the cognitive basis and differentiated patterns of creative design thinking. From the perspective of categorization, and drawing on classic theories in cognitive linguistics, it develops a typological and image-schematic account of how creative design thinking unfolds. Using Grounded Theory, the study analyses representative and influential inventions from modern human history. Through data collection, grounded coding, and category relationship construction, six principal types of creative design thinking are identified in the creative unfolding phase: analogy, blending, negation, reverse, conversion, and restoration. Corresponding basic image schemata are then constructed to represent these different pathways of thinking, showing how categories are expanded, reconfigured, and transformed in the design process. In this way, the study contributes a meso-level cognitive framework for explaining how creative design thinking develops and overcomes design fixation.

TI A review of literature on dropout in tertiary-level continuing
   professional development e-learning courses
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Dropout; e-learning; Online learning; MOOCs; Adult education; Continuing
   professional development; Systematic mapping study
ID OPEN ONLINE COURSES; CLASSROOM INSTRUCTION; OPEN-UNIVERSITY; MOOC;
   PREDICTION; PERFORMANCE; ENGAGEMENT; PATTERNS; SUPPORT; SYSTEM
AB The increasing importance of lifelong learning and professional development is linked to the growing usage of tertiary-level continuing professional development (CPD) through e-learning. However, high dropout rates remain a significant challenge both for adult learners seeking to update their skills and for institutions aiming to provide effective online education. This mapping review analyses 216 articles on dropout in e-learning courses for tertiary-level continuing professional development, published between 2007 and 2023. The review addresses three key research questions: what has been researched regarding dropout, how the research has been conducted, and what findings have emerged concerning dropout rates, causes, and interventions. The review finds that research in this field is dominated by quantitative methods and the focus is largely on MOOCs and on courses in information and communication technology (ICT), business, and STEM subjects. High dropout rates are common, though they varied widely, based on differences in how dropout was defined and measured. Time constraints, insufficient motivation, and course workload were cited more frequently as contributing factors. Persistence is associated with motivational support, high-quality course design, effective feedback, and social interaction. Interventions such as encouragement and guidance showed some success, but remain understudied. The review highlights a need for more qualitative methodologies, theoretical frameworks, and research on interventions, particularly outside the MOOC context and in professional/commercial adult education. To improve retention, practitioners should focus on flexible course structures, social features, assessment and feedback implementations, and approaches that foster motivation and self-regulation.

TI Junior high school student perspectives on the use of ChatGPT in music
   education
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT; Lyric learning; Experience marketing; Technology acceptance
   model
ID MEDIATION; ADOPTION; PRODUCT; AI; ACCEPTANCE
AB In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly been integrated into educational contexts. This study examines the integration of ChatGPT with experiential marketing (XM) theory in music education, with a particular focus on lyric learning activities that emphasize emotional engagement. The application of ChatGPT combined with XM in lyric learning in music education remains relatively underexplored. This study addresses two research objectives: (1) to evaluate students' attitude toward use of ChatGPT in post-pandemic music education by integrating XM theory with the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and (2) to identify factors influencing junior high school students' acceptance and adoption of ChatGPT as a learning tool. Structural equation modeling was employed to analyze the data. The results indicate that the integrated XM-TAM model explains 53% of the variance in students' adoption attitudes. While traditional technology acceptance models primarily emphasize rational evaluations, the findings demonstrate that XM serves as a complementary framework by capturing affective and experiential dimensions. Specifically, experiential marketing and perceived enjoyment show significant positive associations with students' attitudes toward adopting ChatGPT, highlighting the central role of emotional engagement. These findings support an integrated framework for understanding student acceptance of AI-supported music education and offer implications for instructional design and future research in emotionally oriented arts education contexts.

TI Advancing nursing education through social and emotional learning: A
   systematic review guided by the Collaborative for Academic, Social, and
   Emotional Learning framework
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing education; Social and emotional learning; CASEL framework;
   Generation Z; Systematic review
AB Background: With Generation Z entering the nursing workforce in growing numbers, strengthening social and emotional learning is critical for academic success, professional adaptation, and safe practice. However, the existing evidence remains fragmented because of varied interventions and inconsistent approaches. Objectives: This systematic review examined (1) the social and emotional learning essential for nursing students and nurses within the Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning framework, (2) their impact on educational and clinical outcomes, and (3) implications for advancing nursing education and practice. Methods: Following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines, five international (PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Cochrane) and three Korean (RISS, KoreaMed, KMBASE) databases were searched up to June 2025. Eighteen studies involving 2,952 participants met the inclusion criteria, including quasi-experimental quantitative studies, descriptive quantitative studies, qualitative studies, and mixed-methods studies. The methodological quality of the included studies was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Results: Within the Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning framework, relationship skills and self-management were the most frequently studied competencies, emphasizing teamwork, communication, and stress regulation. Self-awareness and social awareness were underexplored, despite their importance in empathy, resilience, and reflective practice. Responsible decision-making was the least studied competency, despite its importance in ethical reasoning. Social and emotional learning was consistently associated with enhanced adaptation, communication, leadership, relationships, and clinical performance. Effective strategies included blended learning, simulation, reflective activities, and mentorship, which are aligned with Generation Z's learning preferences. Conclusion: Although social and emotional learning integration is associated with improvements in educational and clinical outcomes in nursing, current research has largely centered on relational and stress-related competencies while underrepresenting responsible decision-making. To cultivate reflective, empathetic, and ethically grounded nurses, curricula should integrate social and emotional learning through a balanced and structured approach. Registration: This study was registered on PROSPERO (ID: CRD420251005683).

TI Erasmus in undergraduate nursing students: A scoping review of mobility
   experiences
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Erasmus; Undergraduate nursing students; Study abroad; Erasmus mobility;
   Nursing education
ID ABROAD PROGRAMS; HEALTH-CARE; EXCHANGE; DECISIONS
AB Background: The Erasmus Mobility programme offers university students opportunities for academic development, professional training, and intercultural exchange. However, research exploring the impact and implications of Erasmus Mobility among undergraduate nursing students remains fragmented, methodologically heterogeneous, and lacking a comprehensive synthesis specifically focused on nursing education contexts. Aim: To systematically map and synthesise the existing research on Erasmus Mobility among undergraduate nursing students within the European context, with a particular focus on students' personal, academic, professional, and intercultural experiences, as well as the methodological approaches, challenges, and research gaps related to mobility programmes in nursing education. Mobility durations ranged from one to three months and destinations included the United Kingdom, Turkey, and Northern Europe with activities (study or clinical placements). Reported outcomes included language improvement, cultural adaptation, and autonomy development, alongside language barriers and disparities in clinical assessment methods. Conclusion: Erasmus Mobility fosters cultural competence and professional development among undergraduate nursing students. Future research should prioritise investigating post-Erasmus Mobility reintegration challenges and participation barriers.

TI Promoting critical thinking in Vietnamese EFL classrooms: Teachers'
   perceptions and challenges
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical thinking; Teacher perceptions; Resource constraints; Cultural
   influences; Barriers; Vietnam; Replication study; EFL Classroom; EFL
   teachers; mixed-methods research
AB Critical thinking (CT) is widely promoted in English language teaching, yet evidence on how in-service teachers conceptualize and enact CT in non-Anglophone secondary settings remains limited. This study offers an embedded mixed-methods approximate replication of prior CT work to examine Vietnamese secondary EFL teachers' CT perceptions, perceived barriers, and context-sensitive solutions. A survey of 122 in-service teachers (8 CT-perception items; 24 barrier items across six domains) was paired with open-ended prompts. Given Likert data and non-normality, we report medians/IQRs and use Mann-Whitney<bold>,</bold> Kruskal-Wallis (epsilon & sup2;), and Friedman with Wilcoxon follow-ups (Holm), alongside effect sizes. Scale reliability was examined at the domain level. CT perceptions were favourable (composite Mdn = 4.00, IQR = 0.50<bold>;</bold> alpha = 0.88) with mild ceiling tendencies. Perceptions did not differ by gender (U = 1743.50, p = .626, r = 0.04) but varied by experience (H(3) = 17.96, p < .001, epsilon & sup2; = 0.13); teachers with 10+ years scored higher than those with 4-6 years (p_Holm = 0.003, r = 0.41) and 7-10 years (p_Holm = 0.026, r = 0.29). Barriers differed within-person (Friedman chi & sup2;(5) = 221.73, p < .001, Kendall's W = 0.36): Student Readiness ranked highest, followed by Resource Availability and Teacher Training. Domain reliability was high for Student Readiness (alpha = 0.95) and acceptable for Cultural Influences (alpha = 0.73) but weak for several barrier composites, indicating heterogeneous content. Qualitative themes emphasized language scaffolding<bold>,</bold> assessment signals that reward reasoning, targeted professional development (PD), and resource provision. Teachers expressed strong conceptual support for CT, yet systemic and classroom constraints,especially student language andreadiness, limit enactment. Strengthening CT integration in EFL requires PD that couples CT with language scaffolds, alignment of assessments with reasoning, and resourcing for CT-rich tasks. Regional, snowball sampling (Mekong Delta), self-report measures, and mixed-valence barrier items constrain generalizability; classroom observations and instrument refinement are recommended.

TI Integrating heutagogy and critical thinking: A conceptual model for
   higher education
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical thinking; Heutagogy; Learner autonomy; Ultra-orthodox (Haredi)
   women; Higher education
AB This study examines how a heutagogical learning design was associated with the emergence of critical thinking practices among ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) Jewish women in higher education. The study focused on an Academic Writing course that encouraged students to exercise autonomy, select topics, and engage in reflective inquiry. Within this context, personal choice was conceptualized as self-voice, paralleling antilogos, whereby learners articulate positions while engaging with alternative perspectives. Using a qualitative case study, data were collected from 23 students through written assignments, reflective journals, and oral presentations. Thematic analysis identified five themes: conflict as a basis for identity development, value reflection and boundary setting, gender awareness and critique, argumentative deliberation, and emotional tensions. The findings suggest that learner autonomy, combined with engagement in controversial issues, was associated with critical thinking practices, including formulating counterarguments, evaluating evidence, and considering multiple perspectives. Participants described emotional tensions addressed through reflective and argumentation-based processes. Building on these findings, the study proposes the Heutagogical Critical Thinking Emergence Model, a context-sensitive framework explaining how autonomy, engagement with controversial issues, and dialogic interaction may support the emergence of argumentation-based critical thinking practices within culturally structured learning environments. The model conceptualizes critical thinking as a situated, dialogic, and identity-mediated practice and suggests that critical inquiry may emerge through engagement with identity commitments rather than detachment from them. Implications highlight the importance of combining learner choice with analytic criteria and culturally responsive dialogue. The findings offer a context-sensitive account of critical thinking and provide insights for research in higher education settings.

TI The effects of VR digital gaming on multidimensional engagement among
   EFL students: Immediate and delayed evidence
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION: X REALITY
LA English
DT Article
DE VR digital gaming; EFL students; Behavioral engagement; Emotional
   engagement; Cognitive engagement; Social engagement
ID COGNITIVE-LOAD; SCHOOL; ARCHITECTURE
AB The present study investigated the effects of Virtual Reality (VR) digital gaming on English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students' engagement across behavioral, emotional, cognitive, and social dimensions. Although VRmediated language learning has been widely advocated, prior evidence on engagement remains mixed, and little is known about whether engagement gains are sustained over time, particularly for social engagement. Fifty-six EFL first-year university students participated in the study and were randomly assigned to either a VR group or a control group. The VR group (n = 28) completed a 50-min session using an English-language VR visual novel game, whereas the control group (n = 28) completed matched printed materials covering the same narrative content and comprehension questions. Engagement was assessed using a multidimensional self-report questionnaire capturing behavioral, emotional, cognitive, and social engagement. All participants completed a pretest, an immediate posttest, and a delayed posttest. Linear mixed-effects modeling showed that students in the VR group reported significantly higher overall engagement than those in the control group. Within the VR group, engagement increased from pretest to immediate posttest and remained stable at the delayed posttest, suggesting that the engagement gains were sustained over one month. Dimension-specific analyses further showed that emotional engagement was significantly higher than cognitive engagement, whereas no significant differences were found among the other engagement dimensions. These findings suggest that even a single-session VR digital gaming task can promote short-term sustained engagement among EFL students when task demands are appropriately managed.

TI Personalized neural cognitive architecture search: AutoML-driven
   diagnostic model generation for heterogeneous learner profiles
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Personalized learning; Neural architecture search; Automated machine
   learning; Learner portrait; Cognitive diagnosis
AB With the rapid advancement of digital transformation in education, personalized learning has become a central objective for improving educational quality. However, traditional educational models struggle to effectively process multi-source heterogeneous learning behavior data, resulting in limited learner profiling and inefficient diagnostic model development. In addition, existing teaching quality evaluation systems mainly rely on static examination outcomes and simple statistical indicators, lacking the capability to dynamically analyze learning processes. To address these challenges, this study proposes a personalized neural cognitive architecture search framework driven by automated machine learning. The framework integrates multi-modal educational data using heterogeneous information network technology to construct dynamic learner profiles incorporating cognitive states, behavioral sequences, and contextual factors. A hierarchical neural architecture search space is then designed, combining differentiable search strategies with a Bayesian performance predictor to automatically identify optimal diagnostic model structures. Experimental results based on 28.45 million educational records show that the proposed method achieves an AUC of 89.1%, accuracy of 85.3%, and F1-score of 84.7%. The model significantly outperforms traditional psychometric approaches and surpasses mainstream deep learning and AutoML baselines. Ablation experiments further confirm the importance of multi-source data fusion and automated architecture search. Despite strong performance, challenges remain regarding computational efficiency and fairness validation across diverse learner populations.

TI Human-AI collaboration in higher education: Exploring the impact of
   technology expectations and distrust
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Human-AI collaboration; Generative AI; distrust; Expectation
   confirmation theory; Conceptual model; responsible use of AI
ID TRUST; CONFIRMATION; CONTINUANCE; ACCEPTANCE
AB Drawing on expectation confirmation theory (ECT), this study explores the factors that impact Human-Artificial Intelligence (AI) collaboration and investigates the effect of students' distrust towards GenAI. An online survey was administered to students in higher education using GenAI (N = 245). This study found positive and significant relationships between effort expectation and performance expectation, as predicted by ECT, with positive confirmation of GenAI collaboration significantly influencing intentions and positively impacting student behavior. This study further revealed that GenAI distrust negatively moderates the relationships between (1) effort expectation and performance expectation; and (2) expectation confirmation toward collaborating with GenAI and intentions to collaborate with GenAI. Accordingly, this research contributes to the understanding of the role of distrust into Human-AI collaboration and extends the theoretical boundaries of ECT in higher education context. Practically, our findings provide insights for educators and GenAI practitioners to develop strategic approaches that effectively bridge students' distrust and initial expectations with responsible Human-AI collaboration behaviors.

TI Hauntology and absent presences in contemporary nursing education
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing education; Hauntology; Caring science; Absent presences;
   Technology in nursing education
ID STUDENTS
AB Background: Nursing education is undergoing ongoing transformation, particularly through competency-based curricula and digital technologies. However, persistent ethical and relational tensions remain insufficiently explained within existing frameworks. Aim: This paper aims to explain why ethical and relational tensions persist in nursing education despite ongoing reform. Methods: A conceptual analysis grounded in Derrida's hauntology is undertaken, drawing on interdisciplinary literature in health and education. Hauntology is used as both a theoretical foundation and a sensitizing concept. Results: The analysis introduces the concept of absent presences to describe displaced yet influential dimensions of practice. These are examined across ethical, epistemological, and pedagogical domains, including caring as ethical residue, marginalized knowledges, inherited pedagogies, and imagined futures. These dynamics are further explored in relation to digital transformation. Conclusion: Persistent tensions in nursing education are not simply failures of reform but reflect ongoing ethical commitments that resist resolution. A hauntological perspective offers a novel conceptual lens that complements existing frameworks and supports more ethically responsive educational practices.

TI Beyond the Mozart effect: The influence of musical predictability on
   creativity pathways
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Musical predictability; Creativity; Flexibility; Persistence; Task
   engagement
ID COGNITIVE CONTROL; TASK ENGAGEMENT; POSITIVE AFFECT; HEDONIC TONE; DUAL
   PATHWAY; MOOD; FLEXIBILITY; MODEL; ACTIVATION; IDEATION
AB Listening to background music during non-musical tasks is a common practice, yet its effects on creative performance remain to be fully understood. Previous research has predominantly focused on its mechanisms, notably emotional mechanisms, overlooking the role of music's structural properties. This study investigates how musical predictability, i.e. the extent to which a musical structure aligns with the listener's expectations, influences creative cognition by applying the Dual Pathway to Creativity model, which distinguishes between flexibility and persistence pathways. In a controlled experiment, 61 participants were randomly assigned to listen to one of two Mozart pieces differing in musical predictability while performing creative tasks. Measures included flexibility and persistence components of divergent thinking, as well as persistence in convergent thinking. Results indicate that higher musical predictability enhances persistence in both divergent and convergent thinking, but this increased engagement comes at a cost: flexibility is reduced through task engagement mechanisms, even though no direct effect of musical predictability on flexibility is observed. Importantly, this effect is mediated by task engagement rather than emotional mechanisms. These findings offer practical insights for individuals curating music to support creative work and for organizations designing auditory environments to strategically foster specific types of creative cognition.

TI Predicting creativity from personality traits and overexcitabilities:
   Cross-cultural evidence from Lebanon and the United States
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creativity; Personality traits; Overexcitabilities; Cross-cultural;
   Creative domains
ID BIG 5; DOMAINS
AB This cross-cultural study examined how demographic factors, the Big Five personality traits, and overexcitabilities predict creativity across five domains: everyday, scholarly, performance, scientific, and artistic. Data were collected from 1020 university students (407 males, 613 females) enrolled at four universities across the United States (n = 505) and Lebanon (n = 515). Using domain-specific self-report measures of creativity, the study investigated the relative contributions of age, gender, country, personality traits, and five forms of overexcitability (psychomotor, intellectual, sensual, emotional, and imaginational). Results showed that creativity is both domain-specific and culturally embedded. Creativity domains were predicted by varying combinations of nationality, personality, and overexcitability factors, with some straightforward relationships. For instance, although scholarly creativity was associated with intellectual overexcitability, performance and artistic creativity were related to greater sensual and imaginational overexcitabilities. Results suggest a new avenue for investigating individual differences in creative domains, along with demographics and personality traits.

TI Advancing Sustainable Development in management education through online
   learning: Evidence from a Chinese business school
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Sustainability education; Education for sustainable development;
   Transformative learning; Online learning; Responsible management
   education; Action research; Sustainability competencies
ID SPORT MANAGEMENT; EMPOWERMENT; LEADERSHIP; DOCTORATE; NEED
AB Integrating sustainability into management education has become a central institutional priority for higher education and a recognised pillar of the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Yet evidence on whether and how online pedagogies can foster transformative sustainability learning in undergraduate management programmes remains scarce, particularly across emerging economies where digital instruction expanded rapidly after the pandemic. Drawing on transformative learning theory and education for sustainable Development, this study examines an online course in social and environmental management delivered over 13 weeks at a Chinese business school between January and May 2022, integrating a qualitative case study with action research across five triangulated data sources from 53 undergraduates and applying thematic coding in ATLAS.ti version 8.4. Findings show that a structured pedagogical model blending flipped learning, group projects, and reflective dialogue produced measurable shifts across the three transformative dimensions, with most of the 53 students reporting an expanded understanding spanning environmental, social, and wellbeing aspects and a clear reorientation of career intentions toward ethically responsible employers. The study contributes a pedagogical framework that connects online learning design to transformative learning processes and sustainability competencies, offering management educators a transferable model for cultivating responsible future leaders.

TI Enriching intercultural language learning through high immersion social
   virtual reality
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION: X REALITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Virtual reality; Virtual exchange; Intercultural communication; Blocking
   & threading narratives; threading narratives; Multimodal (inter)action
   analysis
ID TELECOLLABORATION; MULTIMODALITY; COMPETENCE
AB Virtual reality (VR) has emerged as a promising tool in language education, offering immersive, interactive, and motivational learning experiences (Dhimolea et al., 2022; Sadler & Thrasher, 2023). High-immersion social virtual reality (HISVR) further enhances these affordances by enabling real-time, embodied collaboration through avatar-based interaction (Gruber & Kaplan-Rakowski, 2020; Lee et al., 2024). This exploratory case study investigates how learners negotiate intercultural meaning in an HISVR-mediated virtual exchange (VE), using Norris's (2004, 2019) Multimodal (Inter)action Analysis and Holliday's (2016) concepts of blocking and threading narratives to frame the analysis. Drawing on a qualitative case study of two international student groups engaged in three VE tasks in AltspaceVR, data were collected through VR session recordings, student reflection diaries, and focus group interviews. The multimodal analysis examined how students used linguistic and embodied resources-such as gesture, spatial positioning, and object manipulation-to construct intercultural understanding. Findings show that while blocking narratives were present-often expressed through conversational rigidity, cultural distancing, or spatial dominance-threading narratives were more frequent. These were characterised by inclusive language use, curiosity, collaborative movement in the environment, and coordinated multimodal actions. Students leveraged the affordances of HISVR to build rapport, clarify cultural references, and manage interactional challenges. The results demonstrate that HISVR fosters a dynamic, embodied form of intercultural communication that extends beyond the capabilities of other conventional technologies like videoconferencing. The study highlights the potential of HISVR for innovating language education by supporting task-based, interculturally oriented pedagogies that integrate multimodal and spatial dimensions of communication.

SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Igba-Boi system; Management education; Indigenous knowledge;
   Apprenticeship; Decolonisation; Experiential learning
ID MANAGEMENT EDUCATION; LEADERSHIP; WESTERN
AB Western management education has evolved significantly since the early nineteenth century, with innovations such as case studies and business simulations shaping teaching methods. However, it continues to face recurring criticisms, including abstract theorising, limited contextual relevance, elitist accessibility, and inadequate integration of alternative knowledge systems. This paper proposes the Igba-Boi apprenticeship system of Eastern Nigeria as a relational institutional model of management learning that embeds mentorship, capital transfer, and ethical accountability within entrepreneurial training. The Igba-Boi system represents a form of relational pedagogy in which learning occurs through sustained social relationships, community accountability, and practice-based engagement. Through an integrative literature review and comparative analysis, we demonstrate how the Igba-Boi model complements conventional management curricula by fostering character development, practical skill acquisition, ethical entrepreneurship, and socially responsible decision-making. The analysis highlights how structured mentorship, staged responsibility, and reciprocal learning relationships enable apprentices to acquire not only technical business skills but also social and moral competencies necessary for entrepreneurial success. Conceptually, the study contributes to ongoing debates on the future of management education by foregrounding relational pedagogy as an important but underexplored dimension of management learning. Incorporating relational learning structures inspired by the Igba-Boi system can help reimagine management education as a more practice-oriented, socially embedded, and context-sensitive field of knowledge.

TI Numeracy, major choice, and the likelihood of graduation
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE College major choice; Business majors; Math requirements; Program
   requirements; Remedial math; Prerequisites
ID COLLEGE; STUDENTS; SUCCESS; PERFORMANCE; MOTIVATION; 1ST-YEAR; BUSINESS;
   GENDER; SCHOOL
AB Mathematics preparation is a key determinant of success in business and other quantitatively oriented majors, yet many students enter college underprepared and are placed into remedial coursework. This paper examines how mathematics placement shapes academic trajectories. Using administrative data from a mid-sized public university and a fuzzy regression discontinuity design, we estimate the causal impact of placement just below versus above key thresholds. Students placed into remediation are significantly less likely to enroll in gateway math courses, pursue quantitatively intensive majors, or graduate within six years. These differences emerge among students with nearly identical placement scores, suggesting that placement itself-through added time, cost, or discouragement-alters behavior. We find little evidence that remediation improves course success, indicating limited academic benefit relative to its costs. Traditional prerequisite-based remediation may therefore act as a barrier rather than a support. We conclude by discussing alternatives appropriate to business schools, including co-requisite models and integrated quantitative instruction, that may better support progression and completion.

TI From problem-solving to problem-posing: Are the ways in which
   11-12-year-old students solve pattern problems related to the types of
   problems they pose?
SO JOURNAL OF MATHEMATICAL BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE Pattern problems; Problem posing; Problem solving; Problem-solving
   strategies; Early algebra
AB We understand pattern problems as non-routine problems that require finding implicit regularities and mathematical structures to generalize beyond immediate evidence. Our study examines in what ways 11-and 12-year-old students' approaches to solving pattern problems are related to the types of pattern problems they pose in an unstructured task. Data were collected during four sessions in which fifty students first solved a sequence of pattern problems requiring near and far generalization and later engaged in a problem-posing task. We analyzed students' written productions to characterize the strategies they used and the extent to which they were able to generalize. We also categorized the problems they posed into null, incomplete, variation of a solved problem and new problem. Results reveal that those who did not pose any problems, or who posed null or incomplete problems, in the problem-solving task had mainly resorted to strategies that had little to do with generalization, such as extending the given drawing. In contrast, students who posed variations of previously solved problems or entirely new problems, had mainly used strategies oriented toward generalization, such as mixed strategies and the continuation of arithmetic progression. Although our findings are context-specific, they contribute to ongoing efforts to better understand how problem-solving experiences relate to students' ability to pose new problems. We conclude that research seeking to explore problem-posing processes should provide students with opportunities not only to pose problems, but also to discuss and solve them, thereby facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of their reasoning processes.

TI Attribution linking creative self-efficacy and resilience in a STEAM
   competition context
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creative self-efficacy; Attribution style; Resilience; STEAM
   competitions
ID CAUSAL ATTRIBUTIONS; CONSEQUENCES; SCALE; STYLE
AB Background: : Attribution theory explains how students interpret success and failure, shaping motivational orientations and behavioral responses in learning contexts. Such interpretations are closely related to creative self-efficacy and resilience in performance-oriented settings Purpose: : This study examined how attribution styles attributing failure to intelligence versus effort are associated with creative self-efficacy and resilience in a science, technology, engineering, art, and mathematics (STEAM) competition context Method: : Data were collected from 703 primary and secondary school students participating in the i-STEAM PowerTech Contest in which participants designed and assembled wooden robots under time constraints for head-to-head performance tasks. A structural model was tested to examine relationships among attribution styles, creative self-efficacy, and resilience Results: : Creative self-efficacy was negatively associated with intelligence-based attributions and positively associated with effort-based attributions. Students who attributed failure to effort also reported higher resilience Conclusions: : Attribution styles are important psychological correlates of students' creative confidence and resilience in STEAM competitions. Promoting effort-focused interpretations of failure may support adaptive psychological responses in short-term, high-pressure, design-based learning environments.

TI How Constituents' Identical and Opposite Relations Influence Creative
   Performance in Conceptual Combination Activities
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE creativity; conceptual combination; synonym; antonym; fluency;
   originality
ID STRUCTURAL ALIGNMENT; SIMILARITY; DIFFERENCE; CONFLICT; SYNONYMS; DESIGN
AB This research, comprising two studies, examined how identical and opposite semantic relations between two stimulus words influence creative performance in conceptual combination tasks. In Study One, 163 college students from southern Taiwan participated, and in Study Two, 151 fifth graders from the same region were recruited. Both studies employed repeated-measures designs. Results from Study One indicated that college students produced significantly higher fluency and originality scores when combining antonyms than synonyms, and when combining nearantonyms than near-synonyms. In Study Two, fifth graders did not show significantly higher fluency or originality when combining antonyms compared with synonyms; however, their scores were significantly higher when combining near-antonyms than near-synonyms. Overall, participants tended to prefer oppositional (antonymous) relations over identical (synonymous) relations when these two relation types were presented together. Moreover, the results suggest that fifth graders' abstract reasoning abilities may not yet be sufficiently developed to support the effective combination of strongly opposed concepts, consistent with cognitive-developmental accounts of formal operational thought. Accordingly, educational practitioners need to apply activities involving diametrical opposites with younger learners cautiously, even though antonymy can facilitate creative thinking under appropriate levels of relational strength.

TI Secondary students' use of creative problem-solving strategies prior to
   intervention
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creative problem solving; Creativity; Self-regulated learning; Strategic
   planning; Strategy use; Microanalysis interview
ID ACHIEVEMENT; THINKING
AB Creative problem solving (CPS) is a critical skill for success in school and life, yet little is known about the strategies students use before receiving formal instruction. This study examined which CPS strategies secondary students plan and use when generating and selecting ideas and which strategies are most predictive of creative outcomes. We recruited 89 secondary students to complete a CPS microanalysis interview protocol, including two open-ended prompts-one before and one after a creative problem-solving task-to assess strategic planning and strategy use. Responses were coded for strategies, and CPS performance was scored on fluency, flexibility, originality, and usefulness. Findings revealed that participants listed few strategies overall, with perspective-taking, dissecting the problem, and connecting to past experiences among the most common. Several strategies predicted fluency and flexibility, but few were associated with originality or usefulness. Results suggest that students approach CPS with a limited but varied set of strategies, offering valuable insight into how CPS skills develop prior to formal instruction. This formative approach may inform process-based assessments and support targeted strategy instruction. Implications are discussed for educators, interventionists, and researchers seeking to support creativity and problem-solving in secondary education.

TI From playtime to potential: A meta-analysis on the developmental role of
   play in creativity
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Play; Childhood play; Social play; Adult-directed play; Creativity;
   Meta-analysis
ID PRETEND PLAY; DIVERGENT THINKING; CHILDREN; LANGUAGE; BEHAVIOR; IMPACT;
   SKILLS; ACQUISITION; PEDAGOGY; PROGRAM
AB Fostering creativity in young people is critical to their success in life. This meta-analysis synthesized findings from 16 studies (m = 90 effect sizes) investigating the relationship between play and creativity in children. The overall effect size was small but not significant, g = 0.15, CI95% [-0.08, 0.38] and the data were heterogeneous, Q(T)(89) = 304.1, p < .001, suggesting that variation in effect size could be explained by examining different characteristics of the studies included in the meta-analysis. Moderator analyses revealed that adult-guided play (g = 0.41) significantly enhanced creative outcomes, whereas child-guided play shows negligible effects. Notably, age also moderated the relationship between play and creativity: elementary-aged children (5-11 years) benefited from play (g = 0.47), while preschool-aged children (< 5 years) exhibit a negative association (g =-0.27), potentially due to limited cognitive development and executive functions. The significant moderators and their interaction were further examined using meta-regression, which revealed no significant difference between adult-guided and child-guided play in preschool children. However, adult-guided play interventions produced a significantly larger effect on creativity for elementary students when compared to child-guided play. Additionally, the significant interaction between play direction and age group suggested that adult-guided play has a medium effect (g = 0.77) on creativity in elementary students. The findings underscore the multifaceted nature of play and highlight the role of structured guidance in fostering creativity. The results have important implications for educational practice and parenting, suggesting that integrating guided play into curricula can bolster creative skills essential for future innovation. Further research is needed to explore how different play types and developmental stages influence creative outcomes.

TI Digital storytelling versus oral storytelling in mathematics education:
   effects on knowledge construction, creative thinking, and cognitive load
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital storytelling; Knowledge construction; Creative thinking;
   Cognitive load; Network analysis
ID DESIGN THINKING; MULTIMEDIA; IMPLEMENTATION; MEDIA
AB A longitudinal quasi-experimental design was employed, and 177 students were assigned to an experimental group and a control group that differed only in storytelling modality (digital storytelling vs. oral storytelling). The Clarify-Ideate-Develop-Present (CIDP) framework was used to structure students' mathematical story-creation activities. The results indicated that, for both groups, posttest scores in mathematical knowledge construction and creative thinking were significantly higher than pretest scores, whereas cognitive load was significantly lower at posttest. Effect size analyses further showed that, compared with oral storytelling, digital storytelling substantially reduced students' cognitive load and enhanced their level of mathematical knowledge construction, although its direct effect on creative thinking was relatively modest. In addition, cross-lagged panel network (CLPN) analysis revealed cross-temporal causal relationships and interaction patterns among the variables, demonstrating not only temporal stability but also a stronger connection between mathematical knowledge construction and creative thinking under digital storytelling conditions. Building on these findings, the instructional mechanisms of digital storytelling were theoretically interpreted from the perspectives of multimedia learning, the learning sciences, psychology, and sociology. Practice-oriented strategies for digital story creation aimed at fostering knowledge construction, promoting creative thinking, and regulating cognitive load were further proposed to inform the future optimization of digital storytelling in elementary mathematics classrooms.
