TI Amplifying vulnerable youths' voices: Transforming thinking skills
   through inclusive pedagogies
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Student voice; Thinking skills; Teacher education; Vulnerable youths;
   Sociocultural theory; Participatory action research; Inclusive pedagogy;
   Dialogic learning
AB This article reports on participatory action research that explored how implementing empathically responsive pedagogical practices amplified vulnerable youths' voices and cultivated the development of their higher order thinking skills. Conducted within a partnership between a teacher-education college and a therapeutic boarding school, the study examined how educators could turn instances of pupils' negativistic behaviors (such as resistance, withdrawal, and defiance) into opportunities for cultivating higher-order cognitive processes. We used a participatory action research methodology to ensure the involvement of all stakeholders (namely, pupils, student-teachers, and cooperating teachers) in a process of collaborative knowledge coconstruction. Vygotsky's sociocultural theory provided the theoretical grounding as we used his dual stimulation pedagogical method (involving two complementary stimuli, a challenging task and a mediating tool) to demonstrate how teachers could facilitate students' cognitive development. Engaging in a dialogic inquiry, wherein a self-generated metaphor based on the students' personal experience served as the second stimulus, led both learners and teachers to develop higher-order thinking skills. Specifically, findings illustrated how interpretive thinking developed through metaphorical reasoning, metacognitive awareness through self-reflection, and collaborative reasoning through joint meaning-making. The dual stimulus approach required participants to operate on multiple cognitive levels simultaneously, analyzing negativism while interpreting the mediating metaphor, promoting cognitive flexibility. The findings reveal how this process cultivated transformative thinking and agency in learners and educators alike. Pupils demonstrated symbolic reasoning (the cognitive ability to use symbols, metaphors, and abstract representations to interpret and make meaning of lived experiences) by mapping abstract representations and concrete experiences, while student-teachers developed inquiry-based thinking through responsive practices. The discussion emphasizes that addressing educational challenges by combining an empathically responsive pedagogy with a collaborative approach provided the necessary conditions for amplifying pupils' voices and creating a sense of agency, an experience which, in turn, cultivated transformative thinking and the development of higher order thinking skills, in learners and educators alike. We conclude by noting that allowing for students' authentic voices to emerge can serve as a powerful mechanism for the development of critical and creative thinking skills among vulnerable youth who demonstrate negativist behaviors. This study contributes to thinking skills scholarship by showing that negativism, when approached through participatory, metaphor-mediated inquiry, represents emerging cognitive complexity rather than deficits.

TI Examining critical thinking in EAP speaking assessment: An
   argument-based validation study
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical thinking; EAP speaking; Language assessment; Argument-based
   validation; Many-Facets Rasch Measurement; rating scale
ID ENGLISH
AB It is widely believed that critical thinking (CT) ability should be part of any assessment of spoken English for academic purposes (EAP); however, few validated tools exist for evaluating it. Without validation, it would not be possible to draw meaningful, appropriate, and useful inferences from the assessment. In this study, CT is operationalized by validating a rating scale for a large-scale EAP speaking test in China, i.e., the College English Test-Spoken English Test. Guided by an argument-based validation approach, multiple sources of evidence were collected to validate the rating scale. Six trained raters assessed university students' CT ability on 128 individual presentations and 64 paired discussions using a fully crossed rating design. Many-Facets Rasch Measurement was used to examine rater consistency, rater bias/interaction, scale functioning, and dimensionality. The findings revealed that the CT rating scale is a valid and reliable instrument. By systematically interrogating the underlying validity evidence, this study extends the limited body of CT validation research in the EAP context and offers empirical support for broadening the EAP speaking assessment construct to explicitly incorporate CT.

TI Unveiling the two-stage neural mechanism of creative thinking: An
   ecological study from generation to 3D modeling validation
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creative thinking; Geneplore model; 3D modeling; Dynamic functional
   connectivity (dFC); State transition frequency; Frontal-temporal; fNIRS
ID DIVERGENT THINKING; BRAIN; COGNITION; NEUROSCIENCE; SIGNATURE; NETWORKS
AB Research on the cognitive neural mechanisms of creative thinking has mostly focused on idea generation, with far less attention to the exploration-verification stage (where ideas become concrete solutions or prototypes). This gap arises mainly from difficulties capturing or measuring this phase's dynamic characteristics in controlled labs. This study innovatively used ecologically valid three-dimensional (3D) modeling and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to dynamically monitor neural activity across the two creative phases (generation and exploration) in 36 college students. Key findings revealed that compared to non-creative tasks, creative tasks exhibited significantly enhanced fronto-temporal functional connectivity during generation, which was positively correlated with sketch novelty. During the exploration phase, we observed significantly increased transition frequencies of low-coupling (State 1, S1) and intermediatecoupling (State 2, S2) states in brain functional connectivity. Notably, S2 transition frequency positively correlated with new elements in 3D models (vs. initial sketches) but negatively with similarity and reproduction fidelity. In summary, these results reveal stage-specific brain network activities and their dynamics in creativity, providing new neurodynamic evidence for the Geneplore Two-Stage Model. This study also offers an ecologically valid, neurointerpretable, robust paradigm for exploring neural temporal mechanisms underlying the entire creative process (from generation to exploration), thereby advancing beyond traditional conceptual research paradigms.

TI Generative AI as a logic scaffold: why video-based project learning
   requires a redesign of task structure and learning difficulty
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; Logic scaffolding; Video-based project learning; Task
   structure; Instructional design; Higher education
ID FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT
AB This study examines how generative AI reshapes learning processes in video-based project learning by introducing the concept of logic scaffolding. Rather than viewing AI as a tool for motivation or outcome enhancement, we conceptualize it as an embedded execution-level support that restructures task organization and sequencing. Using a quasi-experimental pre-post design in undergraduate marketing courses, we analyze students' perceived procedural burden reduction, logic scaffolding outcome (i.e., logical organization and narrative clarity), theory application, and perceived professional output. The results show that AI is not directly associated with learning outcomes but instead operates through a process mechanism: it reduces procedural burden, is associated with improvements in logic scaffolding outcome, and redirects cognitive resources toward theory application and professional performance. Moreover, AI efficacy beliefs, rather than usage frequency alone, play a critical role in the adoption of this form of scaffolding. The findings highlight the need to reconsider how learning difficulty should be configured in project-based instructional design.

TI Unlocking Calm Minds: Critical Thinking Reduces Academic Anxiety via the
   Learning Motivation Pathway - Neural and Behavioral Evidence
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical thinking dispositions; Critical thinking skills; Learning
   motivation; Academic anxiety
ID DORSOLATERAL PREFRONTAL CORTEX; NEAR-INFRARED SPECTROSCOPY;
   DECISION-MAKING; STATISTICS ANXIETY; COGNITIVE CONTROL; ACHIEVEMENT;
   STUDENTS; SKILLS; BRAIN; DISPOSITIONS
AB Academic anxiety poses a significant threat to student well-being and performance globally. While critical thinking and learning motivation are theorized to mitigate anxiety, their interplay across critical thinking dimensions (critical thinking dispositions, CTD; critical thinking skills, CTS) and underlying neural mechanisms remain inadequately characterized. This study addresses this gap by conducting a multimodal investigation of 65 undergraduates, integrating validated psychometric assessments with effort-based behavioral tasks (EEfRT paradigm) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) monitoring of prefrontal dynamics to explore the problem from an integrated perspective. After controlling for gender effects, analyses revealed both critical thinking disposition (CTD) and skills (CTS) significantly reduced academic anxiety, with learning motivation partially mediating CTD's anxiolytic pathway but not CTS'. Neurally, both dimensions enhanced activation in dorsolateral prefrontal regions (CH25/CH34) while CTS uniquely suppressed Broca's area (CH50). Resource optimization was evidenced by decreased posterior DLPFC activity (CH6), freeing metabolic resources for core integrative hubs. This study confirmed, through both behavioral and neural evidence, that learning motivation mediates the relationship between critical thinking and academic anxiety. Furthermore, it highlighted the distinct characteristics of different critical thinking dimensions, particularly emphasizing the significant role of CTD in motivation and emotion regulation. Results advocate for dimension-specific interventions targeting critical thinking and learning motivation to alleviate academic anxiety.

TI Fostering critical thinking and argumentative writing in EFL learners: A
   collaborative reading-based creative writing approach
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE EFL learners; Collaborative reading-based creative writing; Critical
   thinking dispositions; Argumentative writing
AB This study examines a pedagogical approach for critical thinking and writing training, combines reading-based creative writing, role-structured collaboration, and rubric-guided review. Conducted over 16 weeks in an advanced English course, it involved two classes Chinese students majoring in English (total N = 49; experimental group n = 26, control group 23) in a quasi-experimental mixed-methods design. Critical thinking dispositions were assessed using the Chinese version of the Critical Thinking Disposition Inventory (CTDI-CV), while mentative writing performance was evaluated using the TEM8 writing task, with the students' compositions scored according to rubrics that measured both writing proficiency and thinking quality. Results showed fluctuating, inconsistent, and/or non-significant changes writing performance and critical thinking within the control group, whereas participants experimental group demonstrated significant improvements, with notable gains in dispositions such as open-mindedness, analytical thinking, and self-confidence. Reflective thematic analysis also indicated that strategies such as collaborative engagement, effective communication, metacognitive regulation were crucial for linking collaboration with improved argumentation. The findings suggest that integrating pedagogical techniques, including role-based collaboration and criterion-referenced feedback, into structured critical thinking and argumentative writing tasks can significantly improve EFL students' writing skills and foster their critical thinking habits.

TI How toxic leaders undermine innovation: Evidence from IT firms and the
   protective role of leisure crafting
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Corporate psychopathy; Innovative work behaviour; Employee well-being;
   Leisure crafting; Conservation of resource theory
ID CONSERVATION; RESOURCES; PSYCHOPATHY; MODEL
AB This study examines how corporate psychopathy undermines employee innovative work behavior (IWB) and psychological well-being in technology-based organizations, drawing on Conservation of Resources (COR) theory and a Thinking Skills and Creativity perspective. We conceptualize innovative work behavior not only as a performance-related outcome but also as a cognitive and motivational resource reflecting employees' creative capacity and cognitive flexibility that supports creative problem-solving under adverse leadership conditions. Using a three-wave time-lagged survey design, data were collected from 350 employees working in software houses, digital services, and technology consulting firms in Lahore, Karachi, and Islamabad, employing a stratified sampling approach. Hypotheses were tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM 4.2). The findings reveal that corporate psychopathy functions as a chronic resource-depleting context that significantly reduces both innovative work behavior and employee well-being. Innovative work behavior positively predicts well-being and mediates the relationship between corporate psychopathy and well-being, indicating that the erosion of creativity-related cognitive resources represents a key mechanism through which toxic leadership harms employees. Moreover, leisure crafting emerges as a critical boundary condition that enables cognitive reenergization and buffers the negative effects of corporate psychopathy on innovative work behavior, preventing innovation demands from becoming a source of strain in high-pressure technological work environments. Overall, this study extends creative resource theory by demonstrating how employees mobilize thinking skills and self-directed recovery strategies to cope with leadership toxicity and protect well-being.

TI Why do young children struggle to draw non-existent objects?
   Experiential constraints on imaginative representation
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Children's drawing; Creativity; Representational procedures; Imaginative
   representation; Experiential constraints; Experiential realism
ID REALISM; FLEXIBILITY; LEARN; CANT
AB Creativity research often assumes that young children possess a rich imaginative capacity, enabling them to easily depict fictional or non-existent objects. However, studies consistently show that young children struggle with such tasks, usually producing images closely tied to familiar real-world objects. While common explanations attribute these difficulties to limitations in drawing skills or representational procedures, this paper offers a complementary perspective. It argues that children's difficulties reflect an orientation toward experiential realism, in which imaginative representation is constrained by lived experiences rather than being freely generated. From this perspective, children's drawings of novel entities emerge primarily arise through the transformation and recombination of their experienced reality. This framework provides new insights into the development of creativity in children's drawing and highlights how educational practices can better support imaginative expression.

TI Are PISA 2022 creative thinking items fair? A tree-based approach to
   detecting DIF
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Differential item functioning; Recursive data partitioning; Partial
   credit tree; Creative thinking; PISA 2022
ID POWER; MODEL
AB Creative thinking is recognized as a pivotal 21st-century competency and was introduced as a new assessment domain in PISA 2022. Ensuring fairness in such large-scale assessments is essential for valid cross-national interpretations. This study examined differential item functioning (DIF) in 15 Creative Thinking (CT) items in PISA 2022 using a tree-based approach that applies recursive partitioning to explore subgroup differences beyond predefined groups. Responses from 10,779 students across all countries that administered Form 37 were analyzed with the Partial Credit tree (PCtree) model. DIF items identifying subgroups were examined by using the logistic ordinal regression model. The PCtree model identified six distinct subgroups defined by complex interactions of immigrant background, gender, and economic, social and cultural status (ESCS), with ESCS emerging as the primary partitioning factor. All 15 CT items exhibited DIF across multiple subgroup comparisons; however, individual effect sizes were negligible according to established criteria. Nevertheless, small DIF effects may accumulate across items, potentially resulting in differential bundle functioning (DBF) or differential test functioning (DTF) at the assessment level. These findings reveal complex intersectional patterns of DIF that traditional single-variable DIF approaches would miss, demonstrating how multiple demographic characteristics combine to create measurement inequities. The study emphasizes the importance of exploratory validation strategies in creativity assessment and highlights the need for comprehensive fairness validation before interpreting PISA 2022 CT results across groups and countries.

TI Expectation and perceived performance during the creative ideation
   process: The interplay between cognitive, metacognitive, and
   motivational components
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Metacognition; Ideation process; Creativity; Education; Creative
   problems; Self-regulation
ID MINDSETS; DEFINITION
AB Education has been interested in understanding the creative process and teaching basic creative skills. One of these skills is idea generation. In one study, we tested the connections between growth mindsets and the development of expectation to solve a creative problem. We also examined the role of expectations on creativity scores and feelings of ease of idea generation. In addition, we also tested the relationships between growth mindsets, metacognitive feelings, and creativity scores as rated by judges and perceived performance while considering initial expectations and differences in attribution of a function of perceived performance. 687 business students completed a short battery of questionnaires and a divergent thinking task to help a brand solve a business problem. Results showed a positive relationship between growth mindsets and expectations. Expectations then showed a positive relationship with creativity scores and feelings of ease of idea generation. In addition, results showed positive relationships between creativity scores and feelings of ease and perceived performance. Individuals who perceived a good performance on the ideation task were more likely to attribute it to ability rather than effort. Our results have theoretical implications for the field of metacognition in creativity and educational implications.

TI The effect of integral emotions on subjective creativity evaluation of
   everyday products: Evidence from the entropy weight method
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Subjective creativity evaluation; Product pleasure; Integral emotions;
   Evaluation criteria; Entropy weight method
ID POSITIVE EMOTIONS; BUILD THEORY; CORE AFFECT; AROUSAL; BIAS;
   INFORMATION; PSYCHOLOGY; BROADEN; VALENCE; MODEL
AB Subjective creativity evaluation (SCE) involves integrating multiple criteria, yet how this integrative process is modulated by emotional states remains poorly understood. Moving beyond incidental emotions, we used two studies to examine how integral emotions, more specifically, product-induced pleasure, shape creativity judgments and their underlying evaluative structure. In Study 1, we found that products eliciting positive or neutral integral emotions were consistently rated as highly creative than those eliciting negative emotions and that there was no significant difference in creativity between the positive and neutral conditions. In Study 2, we employed the Entropy Weight Method (EWM) and found that as pleasure decreases, ratings across all creativity criteria decline and the evaluative structure is reorganized, with the discriminative contributions of novelty and interestingness decreasing, the contribution of aesthetics increasing, and the distribution of appropriateness remaining stable. Together, these findings characterize SCE as an affect-sensitive evaluative process, in which integral emotions shape both the magnitude and the informational weighting of creativity judgments. Methodologically, this work demonstrates the use of EWM in uncovering emotion-contingent shifts in evaluative structure that remain invisible in conventional mean-level analyses.

TI A cross-linguistic examination of critical thinking and written
   production in comparative continuation tasks of argumentative writing
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical thinking disposition; Critical thinking performance; Writing
   performance; Cross-linguistic perspective; Comparative continuation
   tasks
ID COGNITIVE LOAD; DISPOSITIONS; PROFICIENCY; EDUCATION; STUDENTS; SKILLS;
   ESSAY; L2
AB This study explored how critical thinking disposition (CTD), critical thinking performance (CTP), and writing performance (WP) in L1 (Chinese) and L2 (English) are interconnected in comparative continuation tasks using a mixed-methods design that included a questionnaire among 209 Chinese-speaking English-as-a-foreign-language students and in-depth interviews with eight of them. TI Cultural scripts and the curricular positioning of business ethics in
   management education: A cross-national analysis
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Business ethics education; Management education; Responsible management;
   Curriculum design; Cultural narratives; Ethical readiness
ID RESPONSIBLE MANAGEMENT; PSYCHOLOGICAL SAFETY; ORGANIZATIONS
AB Business ethics (BE) has become an increasingly visible component of undergraduate management education as universities confront rising expectations for responsible leadership, sustainability transitions, and ethical judgement under conditions of uncertainty. Yet despite these pressures, the institutional positioning of BE remains uneven across countries and programmes. This study examines how curricular structures and cultural scripts jointly shape students' ethical readiness by combining a cross-national scan of 128 undergraduate management programmes across 32 countries with an interpretive analysis of obedience-related proverbs and cultural indicators drawn from Hofstede, GLOBE, and the World Values Survey. The findings reveal marked cross-regional variation in the curricular positioning of BE. Anglo and Nordic universities more frequently embed (BE) as a mandatory component of management curricula, whereas Eastern European, Middle Eastern, and Asian programmes more often position it as an elective course or integrate it within broader modules. Mandatory provision appears more common in low power distance and self-expression contexts, suggesting that curriculum design aligns with wider cultural expectations regarding authority, student voice, and moral agency. Although students express support for ethical values across contexts, obedience-related proverbs, including variants of "The bowed head avoids the sword," continue to shape how learners interpret responsibility, conflict, and ethical voice in hierarchical collectivist environments. The study develops a diagnostic framework explaining when BE operates as a corrective, consolidative, or future-oriented pedagogical anchor, offering both conceptual insight for research on management education and practical guidance for culturally responsive ethics pedagogy.

TI Embodied and entangled creativity with tablet computers: A multimodal
   ethnography in pre-schoolers' homes
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Home; Pre-school; Tablet computer; Posthumanism; Creativity
ID YOUNG-CHILDREN
AB This study expands upon current understanding of pre-schoolers' creative use of tablets with their family members in the home environment, providing conceptual and empirical contributions. A nuanced posthuman theoretical framework was constructed to examine pre-schoolers' creativity while they use tablets with their families. This combined Barad's (2007) theory of intra-action, Deleuze and Guattari's (1988) rhizomatic creativity and Craft's (2000) possibility thinking. The methodology involved developing and applying a multi-case multimodal ethnography with eight families over 18 months, drawing upon transcription and diffraction to analyse experiences with tablet computers through a range of theoretical lenses. Multimodal transcription and embodiment were used to ground posthumanism empirically. Findings suggested that 1) most tablet use in the home was not creative 2) an equal balance of power distributed across child, family member and tablet facilitated collaborative creativity and 3) multi-touch functionality aided in children's ability to co-create and collaborate on tablet computers. Implications for parents, educators and app designers are discussed.

TI How does emotional valence influence the interpretation of conceptual
   combinations?
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Conceptual combination; Emotion; Emotional valence; Creativity
ID FRENCH WORDS; CHILDREN; CREATIVITY; MEMORY
AB Conceptual combination (CC) is a key component of creativity. While most research has examined the cognitive processes and representations underlying this ability, an alternative perspective suggests that CC may also result from interactions between linguistic and emotional systems. The present study investigates the effect of the emotional valence of nouns on the interpretation of novel CCs. Seventy university students in education were asked to interpret 90 CCs. These combinations were categorized according to emotional valence (30 negative, 30 positives, and 30 neutral) and semantic similarity (15 similar and 15 dissimilar combinations within each valence category). The results show that emotionally valenced combinations (positive or negative) are interpreted differently from neutral ones. More specifically, pairs of nouns with no emotional valence, or neutral nouns, tend to lead participants toward more complex, elaborate interpretation strategies involving the reduction of a concept to one of its salient properties (destructive interpretations). In contrast, both positive and negative emotional combinations give rise to a wider range of interpretations, more often involving simple interpretations such as relational interpretations that preserve both concepts (non-destructive interpretations). Furthermore, the effect of emotional valence depends on the complexity of the CC: it was only observed for simple (dissimilar) CCs, and not for more complex (similar) ones. These results are discussed in the light of the theory of embodied cognition, and their implications for creative thinking processes are considered.

TI A quick way of counting the muses in German speakers: Evaluation of a
   20-item short version of the German-language translation of the Kaufman
   Domains of Creativity Scales (K-DOCS)
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creativity; K-DOCS; Measurement invariance; Creativity assessment;
   Kaufman Domains of Creativity Scales
ID INITIAL ASSESSMENT; ADULT PLAYFULNESS; VALIDATION
AB The Kaufman Domains of Creativity Scale (K-DOCS) is a standard self-report instrument for the assessment of creativity. The original K-DOCS comprises 50 items that assess five domains of creativity and it is available in numerous languages, including a German-language version. Recently, a 20-item short form of the K-DOCS, assessing each domain with four items, was introduced, and we evaluate the psychometric properties and structural validity of this proposed short form in the German-language version. We re-analyzed data from three samples and provide new data from two additional samples (Ntotal= 2144). We used confirmatory factor analyses and measurement invariance analyses, which showed that (a) the factorial structure of the original version can be retained and (b) invariance was found regarding gender and presentation mode (i. e., presenting the 20-item subset or the full 50 item set). The internal consistencies were in line with expectations for brief measures, with alpha s >= 0.64 and omega s >= 0.63. Finally, there were only minor changes in the pattern of correlations with external measures when using the short version (<= 0.15). Overall, our findings support the usage of the 20-item short version of the K-DOCS, with the typical limitations and benefits associated with brief measures. The K-DOCS-20 is useful in large-scale surveys or repeated-measures designs with limited testing time.

TI Uncovering the effect of Gen AI-assisted learning on students'
   creativity: A meta-analysis from quasi-experimental evidence

DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; Creativity; Meta-analysis;
   Quasi-experimental; ChatGPT
ID HIGHER-ORDER THINKING; GENERATIVE AI; SKILLS
AB While technology-supported learning has traditionally facilitated aspects of higher-order thinking and creativity, emerging generative artificial intelligence (Gen AI) holds significant potential for further development in this area. However, whether Gen AI-assisted learning could effectively foster students' creativity has not yet achieved a consensus. To answer this question, this paper adopted meta-analysis to investigate 32 relevant (quasi-)experimental studies and evaluate the potential effect of Gen AI-assisted learning on students' creativity. These results contributed insights for advancing future studies and practices in leveraging Gen AIassisted learning to foster students' creativity.

   students: A digital game application

   learning; Teaching aids
ID ADAPTIVE GAMIFICATION; VIDEO GAMES; LITERACY; COMPETITION; PLAY
AB Computational thinking (CT), which emphasizes problem-solving, programming, and STEM disciplines, has become a key focus in educational institutions worldwide to help students develop essential technical skills. Digital games are increasingly recognized as educational environments that can be deconstructed into manageable components, enabling players to complete tasks and identify patterns that reveal underlying rules. This study introduces the CT game-to-play (CT-G2P) teaching aid, which integrates four commercial web games to assess their impact on CT skill development. This study highlights the importance of game selection and instructional guidance in CT education and provides insights for educators and researchers developing game-based computational thinking curricula.

TI Exploring the relationship between mathematical convergent and divergent
   thinking
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Convergent thinking; Divergent thinking; Mathematical creativity;
   Domain-specific assessment; Mathematical achievement; Creative problem
   solving; Argumentation
ID CREATIVITY; ORIGINALITY; PROOF
AB The relationship between convergent and divergent thinking in mathematics remains largely unknown, yet understanding this relationship is critical for educational practice and theory. This cross-sectional study examined performance patterns and relationships between convergent and divergent thinking using domain-specific mathematical tasks, with data collected at two time points approximately eight months apart to assess replication across task operationalizations and stability of individual differences. At T1, 374 students from grades 5-13 (ages 10-19) in northern Norway participated; T2 data were collected from 359 students. Convergent thinking was measured through pattern generalization and claim evaluation tasks scored for correctness and argumentation quality. Divergent thinking was assessed through problem-posing, redefinition, and problem-solving tasks scored for fluency, flexibility, and originality. Results revealed substantial individual variation in both thinking types, with students showing particular challenges in mathematical argumentation. Convergent and divergent thinking demonstrated a moderate positive correlation, consistent with theoretical models positioning them as related but distinguishable cognitive abilities. Component-level analyses revealed that argumentation quality showed stronger associations with divergent thinking dimensions than simple correctness. Both convergent and divergent thinking were significantly associated with mathematical achievement across all models, with age and gender as non-significant predictors. These findings establish baseline performance patterns for domain-specific measures and suggest that mathematical convergent and divergent thinking are linked but not redundant. The results have implications for mathematics education, suggesting that fostering both convergent reasoning and divergent creative thinking may support mathematical achievement.

TI Generative AI and creative self-efficacy: A systematic review
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creative self-efficacy; Creative confidence; Generative AI; Artificial
   intelligence; Human-AI Collaboration; Systematic Review; Creativity
   Education
AB Creative self-efficacy shapes motivation, persistence, and engagement in creative work. As generative artificial intelligence systems become increasingly integrated into educational, professional, and artistic contexts, questions have emerged regarding how these technologies influence individuals' creative self-beliefs. This systematic review synthesizes research published between 2021 and 2025 to examine how generative AI is associated with creative self-efficacy, creative confidence, and related constructs during a period of widespread adoption. Following PRISMA guidelines, we analyzed 42 peer-reviewed studies across educational, professional, and creative domains. Fourteen studies directly examined relationships between the use of generative AI and creative self-beliefs, while additional studies provided contextual insight into how creative self-efficacy was conceptualized and measured during the AI integration period. Findings across the reviewed literature were heterogeneous, varying across domains and study designs. Across studies, recurring patterns indicate that perceived control, attribution clarity, and opportunities for human agency are frequently associated with differences in reported creative confidence and self-efficacy. When generative AI was positioned as a supportive tool within transparent co-creation processes, studies more often reported neutral or positive associations with creative self-beliefs. When AI outputs were perceived as displacing human authorship or obscuring individual contributions, studies more commonly reported uncertainty or reduced confidence. Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy remain relevant in AI-mediated contexts but appear to operate differently in human-AI collaboration. Overall, the review suggests that generative AI does not uniformly enhance or diminish creative self-efficacy; its psychological implications depend on contextual, pedagogical, and design-related factors.

TI Solving the paradox between the generalized partial credit model and
   PISA's rating instructions: A generalized IRTree approach to
   within-rating multidimensionality
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Psychometrics; Creativity; Item response theory; Measurement
ID ITEM-RESPONSE; CREATIVITY; VARIABILITY
AB In the PISA 2022 Creative Thinking test, students produce open-ended responses that are scored by human raters as no credit, partial credit, or full credit. As in many large-scale assessments, PISA scales these ratings using the generalized partial credit model. We show that the rating instructions conflict with the GPCM assumption of within-rating unidimensionality: raters are asked to consider different attributes at different thresholds, such as appropriateness and originality or diversity. Using multidimensional generalized item response tree (IRTree) models, we account for the sequential nature of the ratings and disentangle the attributes contributing to each threshold. Multidimensional models outperformed unidimensional ones, indicating within-rating multidimensionality. The latent traits were strongly correlated, but only at levels comparable with those observed between creative thinking and mathematics, reading, and science. We discuss whether collapsing attributes remains reasonable, and other implications for score validity and interpretation.

TI Predicting Key Factors Influencing Students' Creative Thinking: A
   Machine Learning Analysis Based on PISA 2022 Data from East Asia
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE PISA 2022; creative thinking; machine learning; LASSO; Random Forest
ID EDUCATION; CONFUCIANISM; ACHIEVEMENT; EXPLORATION; INNOVATION
AB In the contemporary educational landscape, identifying the key factors that influence students' creative thinking has become a critical issue. While much of the existing research has focused on single-variable analyses, this study adopts a broader perspective by simultaneously examining a wide range of potential factors. Drawing on data from the PISA 2022 creative thinking assessment in East Asia and framed by Socio-Ecological Theory, this study employs two machine learning methods-LASSO regression and Random Forest-to predict and analyze the determinants of students' creative thinking. The analysis considers 26 factors across three dimensions: individual, microsystem, and mesosystem. Meanwhile, the results also show that the explanatory power of the models varied among economies (with R2 values ranging from 0.2241 to 0.3656), as did the rankings of predictor importance: for Macao (China) (R2 = 0.3656) and Singapore (R2 = 0.3649), the top three predictors consistently included ESCS, self-efficacy in digital competencies, and school size; for Hong Kong (China) (R2 = 0.2887), the top three were school size, ESCS, and participation in creative activities outside school; for Chinese Taipei (R2 = 0.3194), they were self-efficacy in digital competencies, ESCS, and class size; and for South Korea (R2 = 0.2241), the top predictors were ESCS, curiosity, and imagination. The findings provide empirical evidence for policymakers, educators, and families, helping them target educational resources more effectively to the areas most likely to enhance students' creative thinking.

TI Value co-creation in AI-influenced management education: Gamification as
   a relational mechanism
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gamification; Value co-creation; Management education; Service-dominant
   logic; Artificial intelligence; Student engagement; Educational
   technology
AB This study examines how gamification facilitates value co-creation in management education within learning environments where artificial intelligence tools are increasingly integrated into students' study routines. Drawing on service-dominant logic, learning is conceptualized as a cocreated process shaped by relationship quality and student engagement. The study investigates how utilitarian, hedonic, and social gamification elements contribute to these mechanisms. Survey data were collected from 409 management students across five universities in South India who had prior exposure to gamified classroom activities. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was employed to test the relationships among gamification elements, relationship quality, student engagement, and value co-creation. The findings indicate that recognition and social influence strengthen both relationship quality and engagement, while playfulness enhances engagement. Utilitarian elements such as usefulness and ease of use exhibit limited direct effects. Relationship quality and student engagement, in turn, strongly predict value co-creation. These results suggest that gamification supports co-creation through interaction-oriented features that reinforce relational ties and visible participation, rather than solely through instrumental or usability-focused elements. The study extends service-dominant logic in management education by clarifying how classroom-level design features shape co-creation in AI-influenced learning environments and offers practical guidance for educators seeking to balance technological efficiency with human-centered engagement.

TI Improved Activity Evaluations: An Iterative Process Using the Rasch
   Model
SO JOURNAL OF CONTINUING EDUCATION IN THE HEALTH PROFESSIONS
LA English
DT Article
DE outcomes; evaluation; psychometrics; measurement; assessment
ID EDUCATION
AB Introduction: Traditional evaluation models, often linear and outcome-focused, are increasingly inadequate for the complexities of modern medical education, which demands more comprehensive and nuanced assessment approaches.Methods: A standardized continuing professional development activity evaluation instrument was developed and implemented. An iterative process was performed, using a repeat Rasch analysis, to improve reliability of the evaluation instrument. Category Probability Curves and Test Information Function were generated by the Rasch analysis to refine the construction of the assessment. All educational activities completed between 2022 and 2024 were eligible for inclusion. The study incorporated a diverse range of educational activities and included multiple health care professions.Results: The pilot analysis included 250 educational activities with 26,554 individual learners completing evaluations for analysis. Initial Rasch findings demonstrated a need to remove redundancies and change from a five to four-point rating scale. The final instrument validation included 21 activities and 529 learners. Improvement was seen in reliability after modifications, with an increase in Cronbach alpha from 0.72 to 0.80.Discussion: Use of psychometrics to improve assessments can yield a more reliable and less redundant evaluation instrument. This research demonstrates a psychometrically informed, flexible evaluation tool that can inform future educational efforts and serve as a data driven metric to enhance the quality of continuing professional development programs.

TI Vape Counseling at Pediatric Practices: The Rethink Vape Toolkit
SO JOURNAL OF CONTINUING EDUCATION IN THE HEALTH PROFESSIONS
LA English
DT Article
DE vaping; adolescent substance use; tobacco use prevention; ENDS;
   qualitative
ID HIGH-SCHOOL-STUDENTS; TOBACCO PRODUCT USE; YOUTH TOBACCO; UNITED-STATES;
   ADOLESCENTS; MIDDLE
AB Introduction: E-cigarettes (Vapes) represent the most common form of tobacco used by adolescents, with one out of every 29 (3.5%) middle school students and one in every 13 (7.8%) of high school students vaping daily. This project aimed to increase vape screening and prevention education in youth visits at pediatric practices, to increase provider comfort with the topic of vaping, and to evaluate this educational process.Methods: A provider training and resource modules (talking points, billing codes, and shareable parent/teen-tailored resources) were developed. Providers (N = 32) completed an anonymous pre/postsurvey regarding their knowledge, comfort levels, barriers, and practices related to teen vaping. The frequency of providing vaping information in the Depart Summary was monitored.Results: Reported barriers to providing vape prevention counseling, including lack of knowledge, lack of resources, discomfort with topic, and patient resistance, were significantly reduced after participation. Time constraints continued to be the greatest barrier to preventive counseling. Physicians who indicated they often or always provide vape prevention information during a visit increased from 9 to 50 percent. Average resources provided increased from 1 to 94 per month.Discussion: Tailored provider-training and resources increased physician knowledge of and confidence with the topic of vaping as well as the frequency of screening and preventive guidance provided to teens and their families.

TI Spaced Repetition Enhances Self-Rated Learning Confidence: A Large
   Randomized Trial Among Practicing Family Physicians
SO JOURNAL OF CONTINUING EDUCATION IN THE HEALTH PROFESSIONS
LA English
DT Article
DE metacognition; confidence; learning
ID MEDICAL-STUDENTS; PERFORMANCE; COMPETENCE; KNOWLEDGE; ACCURACY
AB Introduction: Metacognitive accuracy-the extent to which individuals' perceptions of their knowledge align with actual performance-is critical in clinical decision making. Overconfidence can lead to diagnostic errors, while insufficient confidence may delay decisions or prompt unnecessary testing, increasing health care costs. Although longitudinal knowledge assessments with spaced repetition have been shown to improve learning and knowledge transfer, their impact on metacognition remains underexplored. This study investigates changes in confidence under different spaced repetition strategies in a large cohort of family physicians.Methods: Data were drawn from the American Board of Family Medicine's Continuous Knowledge Self-Assessment, a longitudinal assessment administered quarterly. Participants rated their confidence on a 6-point scale after each question. In total, 16,751 physicians who completed assessments at baseline, quarter 6, and quarter 10 were included. Participants were randomized to control or intervention groups receiving repeated or clone questions at various intervals. One-sample t tests assessed confidence changes for questions initially answered incorrectly but subsequently answered correctly. Multivariate regression controls demographic factors.Results: Confidence increased significantly for repeated questions, with moderate effect sizes in single repetition groups and large effect sizes in two-time repetition groups. Clone questions also showed gains, though smaller in magnitude. After adjusting for clinician demographics, male and younger physicians generally reported higher confidence.Discussion: Spaced repetition enhances both learning and metacognitive accuracy. Two spaced repetitions yielded larger gains. These findings support incorporation of metacognitive-enhancing strategies into CME to improve clinician self-assessment and potentially reduce diagnostic error.

TI Pediatric Emergency Department Provider Experience Using the Revised
   Safer Dx for Self-Directed Feedback on Diagnostic Performance
SO JOURNAL OF CONTINUING EDUCATION IN THE HEALTH PROFESSIONS
LA English
DT Article
DE feedback; diagnostic excellence; diagnostic error; calibration; patient
   safety; self-assessment; clinical reasoning; emergency department
ID DECISION-MAKING; ERROR
AB Introduction: Well-calibrated diagnostic performance requires feedback on decisions. Emergency department and urgent care (ED/UC) clinicians infrequently receive diagnostic performance feedback. We explored clinician experience with self-directed diagnostic performance review compared with diagnostic safety expert review. Methods: Single-center, cohort study of pediatric ED/UC clinician self-directed case review involving possible diagnostic errors (DxEs). Participants reviewed their care of patients admitted within 10 days of an index ED/UC visit at risk of DxEs. The Revised Safer Dx provided structure for DxE identification and was compared with expert review by two diagnostic safety experts using Cohen kappa. Participants also reported their experience using the Revised Safer Dx. Results: During the 1-year study period, 187 patients at risk of DxEs received index visit care from 260 ED/UC eligible clinicians. Seventy-one clinicians submitted reviews for 97 patient-clinician encounters (37.4% response rate). Agreement on the presence of DxEs ranged from 84.8% to 87.5%; Cohen kappa for expert 1 = 0.51 (95% confidence interval = 0.25-0.76); expert 2 = 0.54 (95% confidence interval = 0.17-0.92) indicating moderate agreement. More than 60% of participants agreed that the Revised Safer Dx provided a useful framework for reviewing diagnostic performance regardless of the presence of a DxE. Participants self-identifying a DxE were significantly more likely to have altered their diagnostic approach than those who did not (75.0% vs 5.7%; P < .001). Discussion: ED/UC clinicians performing self-directed structured review for DxEs demonstrated moderate agreement with diagnostic safety experts indicating this method may aid diagnostic reasoning calibration. Promoting self-directed reviews may improve feedback delivery among ED/UC clinicians.

TI From Theory to Practice: Evaluating the Integration of Adult Learning
   Theory in Continuing Medical Education Activities
SO JOURNAL OF CONTINUING EDUCATION IN THE HEALTH PROFESSIONS
LA English
DT Article
DE adult learning theory; continuing medical education; educational theory
   integration; health care workforce development; program evaluation;
   interprofessional education; theory adoption
ID DELIBERATE PRACTICE; PROFESSIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; HEALTH; PERFORMANCE;
   PHYSICIAN; OUTCOMES; IMPACT; CME
AB The underpinnings of adult learning theory are foundational to continuing medical education (CME). Several widely studied learning theories are relevant to medical providers including deliberate practice, situated learning theory and community of practice, social cognitive theory and self-determination, adaptive expertise, and experiential learning theory. The Accreditation Council for Continuing Medical Education recognizes 11 types of CME activities each integrating these learning theories to some degree. Provider preferences are shaped by accessibility, cost, flexibility, and opportunities for networking leaving many balancing the convenience of online programs with the value of in-person interactions. The degree to which learning theories are integrated within CME activities is widely understudied despite their interwoven relationship and association to provider preferences. This analysis aims to (1) evaluate the degree various CME models integrate learning theory; (2) identify theory-led strengths and limitations of CME models; and (3) extrapolate themes for CME planners to strengthen theory integration. The three most common types of CME activities are enduring material (ie, web-based courses, web-based courses with simulation), live courses (ie, conferences, webinars, simulations), and regular scheduled series (ie, Project Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes, speaker series). Integration of learning theory across 7 CME models was evaluated through a content analysis using a trichotomous classification system (fully integrated, partially integrated, or no integration). Results varied, with Project Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes and live simulations having the highest degree of theory integration. A thematic analysis identified five themes for improving theory integration including feedback mechanisms, structured self-reflection, adaptability to promote autonomy, repeat exposure to complex skills, and practice of humility.

AB Point-of-care ultrasound proficiency requires the integration of spatial anatomic knowledge, technical hands-on image acquisition, and the ability to interpret images and incorporate findings into clinical decision-making. TI Integrating Continuing Professional Development, Continuing Education,
   and Quality Improvement: A Case Study and Implications for Practice
SO JOURNAL OF CONTINUING EDUCATION IN THE HEALTH PROFESSIONS
LA English
DT Article
ID MEDICAL-EDUCATION; HEALTH; IMPACT; CARE; CME
AB Continuing professional development (CPD) and quality improvement (QI) are both dedicated to improving clinical practice and health outcomes. Although leaders in both disciplines have long recommended closer alignment, few case studies have demonstrated how such alignment can be developed and sustained within a health care system. Kaiser Permanente Colorado is an integrated health care delivery system in the United States that has worked toward coordination of CPD and QI for >20 years. Alignment of departmental reporting structures, interdisciplinary teams of educators, incorporation of quality concerns into continuing education (CE) activities, coordination of CE activities with implementation of decision support tools, and reliance on evidence-based educational practices have all contributed to a unique organizational culture of education. Published research has shown that their approach can lead to sustainable practice change. Many elements of this approach are potentially applicable to other systems, including consistent use of interprofessional teams, recognizing the organizational context, development of a theory of change to address education and quality gaps, coordination of CE and quality interventions, and using educational and clinical data to evaluate the effectiveness of these interventions. Because these changes have occurred within an evolving environment of real-world practice, the effectiveness of specific components or the interactions between them are difficult to establish. Nonetheless, the Kaiser Permanente Colorado model provides one example of coordination between CPD and QI experts to achieve their shared goal of improving clinician practice, patient care, and system performance.

TI Enhancing Naloxone Reach Through Innovative Training Strategies at an
   Academic Medical Center in Arkansas
SO JOURNAL OF CONTINUING EDUCATION IN THE HEALTH PROFESSIONS
LA English
DT Article
DE naloxone education; opioid-overdose prevention; harm reduction;
   continuing professional development; academic detailing; RE-AIM;
   implementation science
ID FUTURE; MODEL
AB The Arkansas Naloxone Education and Training (ANET) program, based at the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences, was developed to address the urgent need for opioid-overdose prevention across the state. Funded by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Administration (SAMHSA), ANET uses a train-the-trainer model to equip health care professionals with the knowledge and tools necessary to deliver naloxone education in their local settings. In its first year, the program launched a three-module curriculum, accredited for continuing education, of health care professionals and delivered using an academic detailing teaching strategy, prioritized recruitment from counties through a needs assessment including the highest rates of opioids dispensed and of overdose deaths, and implemented a comprehensive evaluation plan that is grounded in an evidence-based framework that facilitates continuous evaluation and improvement (ie, RE-AIM framework-Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance). Knowledge and attitudes were assessed before and after health care professionals completed the training program. All trainers received technical support and outreach materials. The program also fostered strategic statewide partnerships to support recruitment, implementation, and community engagement. ANET is embedded within an academic medical center and aligned with continuing professional development infrastructure, offering a replicable model for community-centered overdose prevention. Lessons learned during the program's implementation underscore its potential to inform future design, delivery, and sustainability of similar interventions.

TI Clinical Educators Professional Development Utilizing Clinical Educators
   Milestones-Qualitative Thematic Analysis
SO JOURNAL OF CONTINUING EDUCATION IN THE HEALTH PROFESSIONS
LA English
DT Article
DE Clinician Educator Milestones; professional development; goal setting;
   self determination theory
ID SELF-DETERMINATION
AB Introduction: Medical educators often face challenges in planning and prioritizing professional development due to a lack of structured guidance. The Clinician Educator Milestones (CEMs) were introduced to address this gap, providing a roadmap for educators' growth and development. This study explores the effectiveness of CEMs as a tool for self-assessment and goal setting in medical education.Methods: Participants in a medical education course at our University undertook self-assessment using CEMs and used this to develop educational development plans. Interviews were conducted to gather feedback and insights. The data were transcribed and analyzed thematically.Results: Participants reported that CEMs supported effective goal setting, identifying development needs and recognizing support required. Thematic analysis revealed themes on the use of CEMs related to developing a clear vision for professional development, identifying new perspectives, relating theory to practice, reflecting on their own understanding and capabilities, and recognizing educational role models.Discussion: The structured approach facilitated by CEMs aligns with the principles of Self-Determination Theory, empowering educators to take control of their development, enhance competence, and foster a sense of belonging within the medical education community. This research supports the efficacy of using CEMs to promote educators' growth and well-being.

TI Learning Together From Uncertainty: An Evaluation of Practice Inquiry
   Groups in a Nationwide Primary Care Practice
SO JOURNAL OF CONTINUING EDUCATION IN THE HEALTH PROFESSIONS
LA English
DT Article
DE uncertainty; primary care; practice inquiry
AB Practice inquiry (PI) is a structured method of discussion that helps primary care clinicians explore uncertainty and learn from challenging cases. An understanding of what aspect of PI primary care clinicians value could guide leaders who are contemplating implementation of collaborative discussion formats in their clinical systems. We administered a survey examining clinicians' perceptions of PI in a large nationwide membership-based primary care service. Two hundred ninety-six surveys (61%, N = 296/482) were received from participants and 69 surveys (75%, N = 69/92) were received from facilitators. Most respondents (>70% across five queries) felt that PI led to enhancement of knowledge and management skills and helped them become more comfortable managing uncertainty. Colleagues in PI groups provided validation and reassurance, valuable health system information, and insights into reasoning and patient-clinician relationships. Participants and facilitators outlined ways PI sessions could be improved (eg, case follow-up) and how the organization could support PI sessions (eg, enhanced facilitator training). This is the first program evaluation of PI in a large, community primary care setting. Future directions include examining what group-level characteristics mediate PI efficacy and how clinicians and patients fare after PI discussions. Such insights could inform enhancements to the group facilitation process.

TI Quality of Life in Six Words: An Arts- and Narrative-Based Approach for
   Centering Patient Voices in a Health Care Education Session
SO JOURNAL OF CONTINUING EDUCATION IN THE HEALTH PROFESSIONS
LA English
DT Article
DE knowledge translation; narrative medicine; narratives; illness; rare
   disease; quality of life; storytelling; patient-engagement
AB A participatory arts- and narrative-based approach for knowledge translation was utilized in a rare disease educational session at a medical conference, combining stakeholder storytelling with the presentation of relevant empirical evidence and frameworks to deepen clinicians' understanding of patient and caregiver quality of life. Before the conference, patient/caregiver perspectives were solicited via a six-word story creative writing prompt (n = 94); during the session, clinicians utilized these stories to cocreate three visual pieces representing the complexity of patient and caregiver experiences and symbolizing the common threads that appear when many "rare" experiences come together. Session attendees reported highly positive feedback, with most clinicians reporting that the knowledge gained from the session would result in a change in their clinical practice. We propose arts- and narrative-based approaches hold great promise for centering patient voices in health care education.

TI We Sit Side by Side: How Course Peers Shape the Achievement and Success
   of At-Promise Students
SO REVIEW OF HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE At-promise students; peer effects; learning communities; academic
   achievement; network analysis
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; COMPLEX-SYSTEMS; NETWORK;
   OUTCOMES; IMPACT; GRADES; FRIENDSHIPS; CENTRALITY; RETENTION
AB Higher education scholarship reflects no consensus on the impact of peers on academic outcomes. This inconsistency may stem from the absence of a common methodological approach to estimate peer effects. Using administrative records of two cohorts of low-income students participating in a comprehensive college transition program across three campuses, we employ complex systems network thinking to estimate if students impact and are impacted by their peers' performance in loose-cohort learning community courses. Findings provide evidence of peer/spillover effects in cumulative GPA, persistence, and credits attained. TI Caught in a Double Bind: Toward an Understanding of Undergraduate Women
   Engineers Early Experiences
SO REVIEW OF HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE gender; undergraduate students; engineering; women of Color;
   intersectionality
ID GENDER; SCIENCE; PERFORMANCE; TECHNOLOGY; CHALLENGES; MOTIVATION;
   IDENTITY; CAREERS; MAJORS; RACE
AB Women's experiences in engineering are fraught with issues beyond their underrepresentation. Utilizing the concept of the double bind and intersectionality, this interpretive phenomenological study examined data from interviews with 32 first-year women undergraduate engineering students during their first few weeks of college to understand how women's early experiences inform the ways they position themselves in engineering. We were concerned with how women's self-understanding is inherently intertwined with how they make calculated moves based on contradictory messaging about their competence and suitability for engineering both prior to and early on in their college experience. We found that women engineering students of all races and ethnicities begin college already caught in a double bind that forces them to navigate conflicting social expectations, which are intensified and reified during their early college experiences as they face the entrenched gender expectations in engineering. For women of Color, the whiteness of the space uniquely heightened, differentiated, and situated their experiences. We conclude our discussion with implications that center equity in both experiences and outcomes

TI Workplace learning in civil-military crisis exercises: constructive
   alignment, context support and defensive routines
SO JOURNAL OF WORKPLACE LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Workplace learning; Civil-military exercises; Constructive alignment;
   Psychological safety; Defensive routines; Training transfer; Emergency
   preparedness
ID COLLABORATION; TEAM
AB Purpose-This paper aims to examine how constructive alignment, context support, psychological safety and defensive routines are associated with observable indicators of workplace learning in civil-military crisis exercises and why exercise participation should not be equated with demonstrated learning. Design/methodology/approach-This study is a comparative qualitative reanalysis of two previously studied Swedish exercise settings conducted between 2022 and 2024. No new empirical data was collected for this study. The structurally nonequivalent cases are compared using the same deductive workplace-learning framework; the comparison is used to elaborate theory rather than to estimate causal effects. Findings-Case A exhibited more observable indicators of learning progression, along with clearer objectives, sequenced activities, feedback opportunities and stronger contextual support. Case B displayed fewer such indicators alongside vague objectives, limited assessment, heterogeneous participant experience and recurring defensive routines. Because the cases also differ in duration, immersion, group stability, participant composition and unit of analysis, these patterns are interpreted as associations rather than causal effects of exercise design. Research limitations/implications-The comparison concerns one five-day exercise and a composite of seven exercises, uses unequal qualitative corpora and lacks independent pre-and postmeasures or behavioral evidence of transfer. This study therefore identifies theoretically relevant patterns and observable learning-process indicators, not verified individual learning outcomes or causal effects. Practical implications-Exercise planners should connect specific learning objectives to role-relevant activities and structured feedback, while deliberately providing legal expertise, role clarity, facilitation and conditions for speaking up. Evaluation should distinguish immediate exercise outputs from subsequent transfer to ordinary work. Originality/value-This study does not add new empirical data. Its contribution is a standardized cross-case reanalysis that integrates constructive alignment with workplace-learning affordances, psychological safety, defensive routines and training-transfer research and specifies the boundary conditions under which exercise outputs can be interpreted as indicators of learning progression.

TI Educators' sensemaking about mathematics equity and ability grouping
SO QUALITY EDUCATION FOR ALL
LA English
DT Article
DE Ability grouping; Equity; Mathematics education; Mental models; SDG 4;
   Sensemaking
ID IMPACT; POLICY
AB Purpose - This study aims to examine how educators in one private prekindergarten through Grade 8 (PK-8) school conceptualized mathematics equity and reasoned about the equity of ability grouping. Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) provides the broader context. Design/methodology/approach - An interpretive qualitative single-case study used semi-structured interviews with 11 educators, supplemented by the school's equity document and one participant-confirmed field note. Analysis combined in vivo and provisional coding with cross-participant comparisons. Sensemaking and mental models served as analytical lenses; the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics' conception of mathematics equity provided the conceptual foundation; and a meso-level framing located the analysis at the school level. Findings - Most participants defined equity as meeting individual needs and drew on overlapping evidence sources but emphasized different indicators when reasoning about need and readiness. They also differed in what counted as a resource. Participants evaluated grouping conditionally: it could support equity through appropriate support and challenge but pose risks through inaccurate placement, fixed labels or constrained opportunities. Accounts also revealed tensions between professional judgment and parent influence and variation in placement review. Originality/value - This study shows that similar needs-based conceptions of equity and overlapping evidence sources can coexist with different interpretations of need, readiness and resources and different views of grouping, placement authority and review. It situates school-level sensemaking about mathematical opportunities within SDG4's broader equity commitment.

   gap
ID EDUCATION; MATHEMATICS; KNOWLEDGE; INSIGHTS; SUPPORT
AB Purpose - Addressing a gap in the current research, this study aims to capture pre-service teachers' perceptions regarding the nature and impact of Lesson Study in the longer term, one year after completion, thus informing the continued development and refinement of Lesson Study as an embedded, institutionally supported feature of initial teacher education (ITE). Design/methodology/approach - A semi-structured focus group interview was selected as the most appropriate data collection method to capture pre-service teachers' perspectives regarding the Lesson Study process one year on, and the impacts of engaging in Lesson Study on their practice in the interim. The study highlights the enduring power of Lesson Study in challenging beliefs about mathematics teaching and in closing the theory to practice gap by activating inert knowledge. Research limitations/implications - The findings and implications of this study are relevant to all teacher educators who grapple with the logistical challenges of facilitating Lesson Study within initial teacher education. SO QUALITY EDUCATION FOR ALL
LA English
DT Article
DE Basic digital education; Belonging; Teachers' attitudes; Educational
   inequality; Digital divide; Postdigital condition
ID ENGAGEMENT; SCIENCE; SIZE
AB Purpose The sudden implementation of Basic Digital Education (BDE) in lower secondary education in Austria called for teachers without subject-specific training to instruct BDE. Thus, BDE is currently highly influenced by teachers' attitudes and personal experiences with digitality. The purpose of this study is to investigate teacher's social practices within the new school subject, centring the question what attitudes teachers hold toward students' belonging and how teachers' beliefs underpin these evaluations. Design/methodology/approach This paper focuses on eight semi-structured interviews with Austrian BDE teachers. The data were analysed with a combination of reflexive thematic analysis to categorise overarching themes and documentary method for in-depth understanding of tacit, social knowledge. While type I teachers focus on academic achievement and rely on power imbalances, type II teachers try to break with these norms by focusing on strong relationships and participatory learning. The data further suggest teachers' ambition to include all students. Originality/value The findings of this study show that BDE offers a freedom to learn - meaning a shift from direct teaching into participatory learning - which opens the opportunity to break with structural norms and mitigate inequalities. To further support this movement, the conclusion suggests implications for more inclusive practice in BDE.

DT Article

   Sustainable entrepreneurship; Sustainable business models; Higher
   education
ID EDUCATION; MODEL; MANAGEMENT; STUDENTS
AB Purpose-This study aims to present a teaching methodology that integrates sustainability and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) into entrepreneurship education to foster the development of sustainable business models (SBMs) through challenge-based learning (CBL) in higher education. Design/methodology/approach-The methodology was implemented over five years at the University of Valencia and the University of Turku, combining CBL with a proprietary framework for designing, testing and scaling SBMs. A systematic literature review (2003-2024) was conducted to support the approach. Industry engagement was facilitated through the European Center for Innovative Enterprises, which participated in project feedback sessions. Originality/value-This study offers a structured, replicable model for sustainable entrepreneurship education, incorporating tools such as the Triple Layered Business Model Canvas, the Common Good Matrix and the Sustainable Lean Startup. It addresses a gap in entrepreneurship education by embedding sustainability as a core element.

TI Bridging knowledge gaps in agri-food sustainability: stakeholder
   perspectives on transforming vocational education and training in
   Ireland
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SUSTAINABILITY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Vocational training; Lifelong learning; Education for sustainable
   development (ESD); Curricular innovation; Education in sustainability;
   Sustainable collaborative learning
ID WASTE; INNOVATION; BEHAVIORS; BARRIERS; IMPACT
AB Purpose - This study aims to examine the role of vocational education and training (VET) in supporting sustainability within Ireland's agri-food sector. While sustainability is increasingly prioritised, limited research has explored how agri-food stakeholders conceptualise sustainability-related knowledge, skills, and competencies, and how these insights can inform VET provision. Specifically, this study aims to (1) explore stakeholder perspectives on sustainability challenges within the Irish agri-food sector, (2) identify key knowledge gaps and competencies required to support sustainability transitions and (3) examine how these insights can inform the design of VET programmes. Design/methodology/approach - Conducted as part of the Erasmus + Train to sustain project, it draws on qualitative insights from four semi-structured focus groups involving 26 stakeholders from across the agri-food value chain. Participants represented diverse perspectives, including educators, farmers, food entrepreneurs, sustainability practitioners, and policymakers. Discussions focused on four pillars of food sustainability: food waste management, food production, farming practices, and food packaging. Data were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke's six-phase framework. Findings - Findings identified four overarching themes: (1) Educating for Sustainability: Building knowledge, awareness, and behavioural change. (2) Policy and structural supports. (3) Stakeholder engagement. (4) Innovation as a driver of transformation in the agri-food sector. The results underscore the importance of integrating sustainability across VET curricula and governance structures while fostering collaboration among educators, industry, and policymakers. Embedding transformative learning principles and systems thinking within VET can cultivate the skills, attitudes, and values essential for sustainable food systems. Research limitations/implications - The study was conducted within the Irish context, and while Ireland provides a useful case for examining VET's role in sustainability transitions, structural, cultural, and policy differences across countries may influence the applicability of these findings elsewhere. In addition, the perspectives captured reflect a snapshot in time within a rapidly evolving policy landscape. However, the study contributes to sustainability and vocational education research by highlighting the value of stakeholder-informed, qualitative approaches for understanding how sustainability competencies are conceptualised within VET. Future research would benefit from longitudinal or comparative studies examining how these competencies evolve across VET systems and national contexts. Practical implications - This study identifies practical strategies for embedding sustainability within agri-food VET programmes, demonstrating how educators can integrate sustainability through experiential, sensory, and systems thinking pedagogies aligned with industry practice. Policymakers are encouraged to consider coherent policy frameworks, targeted incentives, and infrastructural supports that enable sustainable behaviour across the food system. Strengthening collaboration between VET providers, industry, and community stakeholders can support skills development, innovation, and lifelong learning, positioning VET as a key driver of Ireland's transition to sustainable food systems.
   Originality/value - This study contributes original stakeholder-informed insight into how sustainability competencies are understood, prioritised, and operationalised across the Irish agri-food sector. By capturing perspectives across the food system, it highlights the importance of collaboration and supports the development of education aligned with sector needs and global sustainability priorities. The research highlights how stakeholder perspectives can inform more contextually relevant approaches to VET curriculum design, policy alignment, and sustainability learning in the agri-food sector.

TI Appraising the role of students' industrial work experience scheme
   (SIWES) in developing employable skills: Nigerian higher education
   institutions' stakeholders' perspective
SO HIGHER EDUCATION SKILLS AND WORK-BASED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Employable skills; Hindrances; Nigeria; Students; SIWES; Sustainable
   development goals
AB Purpose-Despite several policies, studies have revealed that the unemployment rate among Nigerian Higher Education Institution (HEI) graduates is the highest on the continent. Evidence shows that a comprehensive, practice-based Students' Industrial Work Experience Scheme (SIWES) within HEIs' academic programmes may enhance the skills required for engagement, particularly in engineering, technology and environmental science. However, attempts to enhance skills development via SIWES within HEIs' programmes may be challenging. This study explored perceived issues in the implementation of SIWES in HEIs and proposed measures to improve its implementation, enhance employable skills and, by extension, advance the achievement of the SDGs. Design/methodology/approach-The researchers employed a qualitative design and collected data from 48 eligible Nigerian participants via virtual interviews. They also used an investigative method to engage participants and conducted a thematic analysis to analyse the data. The study achieved saturation. Findings-The research results show that an improved SIWES Scheme can develop HEIs students' employable skills. Poor incentives and delays in SIWES payments, inadequate sensitisation of SIWES students, inadequate placement of SIWES students, chronic institutional corruption, poor funding and poor collaboration between academia and industry were identified as hindrances to implementation, and measures were proposed to address them. Originality/value-The adopted theories (Vygotsky and Piaget) support the framework for revamping the SIWES Scheme for engineering and technology, as well as environmental science, to align with best practices, develop graduates' employability skills and, by extension, improve the achievement of SDGs 3, 4, 8 and 9.
