TI Skills and competence assessment in higher education: a case study in
   Hungary on employer expectations
SO HIGHER EDUCATION SKILLS AND WORK-BASED LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Higher education; Soft skills; Hard skills; Labour market; Competences;
   Challenges; Employer expectations; M30; I21; J01
ID UNIVERSITY
AB Purpose The purpose of this study is to identify the key labour-market skills, the challenges graduates face and recommendations for aligning higher education with employer expectations in Hungary, a Central European country. This study underscores the importance of soft skills, such as adaptability, problem-solving and independence, for graduates in the Hungarian labour market.Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey was conducted among all students of a Hungarian university involved in work placements (n = 1,556). The research subjects were the organisations where undergraduate students from a Hungarian university completed their practical semester, and a total of 1,556 student evaluations were processed. The study analysed 15 distinct skills suggested by NACE and identified four factors: agility, professional knowledge, interpersonal skills and generic skills.Findings The study's findings indicate that agility, encompassing adaptability, problem-solving skills and independence, emerged as the paramount criterion in employers' evaluations. The findings indicate substantial disparities in the perceived significance and assessment of skills across diverse academic disciplines. The research findings show that, in the labour market, soft skills may be more significant than technical expertise. The subsequent development of the skills and competence measurement tool identified in the literature review is proposed, particularly with respect to the hard and soft skills of the field of study.Research limitations/implications The main limitation of this research is the use of a non-validated measurement instrument developed for internal quality management, which may lack scientific rigour. Additionally, the application of a uniform competency framework across all disciplines prevents the study from capturing the specific skill nuances required by different professional fields.Practical implications Universities should move beyond simply adding soft skills modules and instead embed cognitive and interpersonal development across all curricula. Key mechanisms for this include structured industry partnerships, work-integrated learning and a shared competency framework that aligns academic content with specific labour-market expectations.Social implications By addressing the skills mismatch, these findings foster a more efficient transition from education to employment, ultimately enhancing graduate career prospects. Recognising the hierarchical structure of skills, where technical knowledge is the baseline but agility and interpersonal skills drive advancement, helps society better prepare a workforce capable of long-term professional growth.Originality/value This study underscores the significance of soft skills in the Central European/Hungarian labour market context, offering direct evidence from employer evaluations of student work placements. The implications of this phenomenon extend to the need for educational reform that integrates soft skills training. Furthermore, there is a compelling need for enhanced collaboration between universities and employers. Additionally, policy adjustments are imperative to ensure the successful implementation of these changes. Aligning educational curricula with employer expectations can help mitigate the skills gap and stimulate economic growth in Central Europe.

TI A framework for interdisciplinary blockchain training: bridging the
   skills gap in supply-chain education
SO JOURNAL OF APPLIED RESEARCH IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Blockchain education; Supply chain management; Curriculum design;
   Experiential learning; Emerging markets; Higher education
AB Purpose This article addresses the skills gap in supply chain management (SCM) education, particularly in emerging markets, where traditional curricula lack the technical expertise required for blockchain technology. The study identifies key challenges hindering blockchain adoption in SCM curricula and proposes an empirically grounded, interdisciplinary, modular training framework suitable for non-technical learners.Design/methodology/approach A qualitative exploratory design within an interpretivist paradigm was adopted. Data included a review of South African SCM curriculum documents, consultations with external stakeholders and learning artefacts from lecturers and students involved in blockchain-integrated teaching. Data were thematically coded in ATLAS.ti and triangulated across sources. The framework was developed iteratively and examined through comparative cross-case analysis and a South African classroom pilot.Findings The study identified interrelated constraints: limited curricular coverage of blockchain concepts and laboratory exposure; uneven faculty readiness and institutional resource limitations; and learner heterogeneity that increases cognitive load for non-technical cohorts. These findings informed a three-tier modular framework comprising foundational literacy; applied simulations and platform familiarisation; and industry-linked capstone projects. Cross-case comparison and classroom pilot evidence indicate that staged, use-case-driven learning supports progression from conceptual understanding to applied competence within resource-constrained contexts.Research limitations/implications This study is exploratory in nature and based on a single institutional case. Further empirical testing and comparative studies across institutions and geographies are recommended to validate the framework's generalisability and long-term impact.Practical implications The framework provides a roadmap for integrating blockchain into non-technical programmes, enabling universities, government and industry to co-develop scalable skills development interventions. It supports employability, innovation and national digital transformation agendas.Social implications This study contributes to social inclusion by proposing an accessible, non-technical pathway for integrating blockchain education into SCM programmes. By lowering technical entry barriers, the framework supports skills development for diverse learner groups, including students from non-IT backgrounds and working professionals engaged in upskilling and reskilling. In the South African and broader African context, this approach has the potential to enhance graduate employability, reduce digital skills inequalities and support youth participation in digitally enabled supply chains. The framework also aligns higher education curricula with inclusive Fourth Industrial Revolution agendas and workforce transformation goals.Originality/value The article contributes a stakeholder-centred, practice-informed approach to curriculum innovation in SCM education. It integrates Technology-Organisation-Environment, stakeholder theory and learning theory to explain adoption feasibility and pedagogical progression and offers a scalable framework and implementation roadmap for resource-constrained institutions seeking to align SCM education with digital transformation and employability demands.

AB Purpose Higher education is expected to prepare students both academically and professionally. In non-vocational programs, this entails fostering academic and generic competencies, lifelong learning and the development of professional identity. The purpose of this study was to evaluate a student-centered longitudinal curriculum intervention in a non-vocational bachelor's program in southern Sweden. It was designed to enhance student empowerment, professional identity and employability through increased awareness of professional competencies.Design/methodology/approach The intervention was a 7.5-credit program-based assessment implemented over three years and organized into four interconnected sub-courses. TI Quality of work-integrated learning and employability in Henan TVET:
   serial mediation via career self-efficacy and adaptability, moderated by
   proactive personality
SO EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
DE Work-integrated learning; Placement quality; Career self-efficacy;
   Career adaptability; Employability; Proactive personality; Serial
   mediation; Moderated mediation; Social cognitive career theory; Chinese
   TVET
ID SKILL DEVELOPMENT
AB Purpose-This study critically examines how the quality of work-integrated learning (WIL) placements enhances Chinese technical-and-vocational-education (TVET) students' employability and for whom the benefits are greatest, by testing a social-cognitive-career-theory model that links WIL to employability through career self-efficacy (CSE) and career adaptability (CAD) and examines proactive personality (PRO) as a boundary condition. Design/methodology/approach-Survey data were collected from 477 final-year students at public TVET colleges in Henan Province. Validated Chinese instruments captured WIL quality (15 items), CSE (8 items), CAD (12 items), PRO (10 items) and self-perceived employability (8 items). PROCESS Model 59 with 5,000 bias-corrected bootstraps estimated a first-stage moderated serial-mediation structure (WIL -> CSE ->? CAD -> employability; PRO & times; WIL on CSE). Findings-Higher-quality WIL significantly increased CSE (b = 0.439, beta = 0.437, p < 0.001); stronger CSE raised CAD (b = 0.512, beta = 0.592, p < 0.001); and CAD was the principal driver of employability (b = 0.728, beta = 0.730, p < 0.001). The serial indirect effect WIL -> CSE -> CAD -> employability was 0.147 (95% CI [0.115, 0.185]) and fully absorbed WIL's direct influence. PRO strengthened the WIL -> CSE path (interaction b = 0.197, p < 0.001); the slope rose from 0.182 at low PRO (16th percentile) to 0.685 at high PRO (84th percentile). Originality/value-This is the first multi-college Chinese TVET investigation to validate the Placement Quality Measure in Chinese TVET, to model serial mediation via self-efficacy and adaptability, and to uncover proactive personality as a boundary condition, integrating motivational, self-regulatory and dispositional explanations of WIL-driven employability.

TI The human impact of crisis in business schools in higher education: the
   role of belonging dissonance
SO EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
DE Business schools; Higher education; Crisis; Cognitive dissonance; Sense
   of belonging; Belonging work
ID COGNITIVE-DISSONANCE; MANAGEMENT
AB PurposeThis study investigates how business school academics experienced and navigated disruptions to their sense of belonging during the COVID-19 crisis. Responding to limited research on academic belonging in times of institutional upheaval, the study develops the concept of belonging dissonance to explain the tensions created when academics' expectations of collegiality, identity affirmation and institutional support diverge from crisis-driven organisational practices.Design/methodology/approachThe study draws on 153 qualitative survey responses and 12 in-depth interviews with business academics across multiple countries. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we identify the mechanisms that triggered cognitive dissonance during the pandemic and analyse how academics enacted "belonging work" to manage, repair or reorient their sense of belonging.FindingsThree contributions emerge. Firstly, the study demonstrates that cognitive dissonance is central to understanding how academics evaluate and respond to belonging disruptions during crisis. Secondly, we introduce belonging dissonance, a relational and identity-based form of cognitive dissonance that arises when institutional actions undermine expectations of collegiality, recognition and shared governance. Thirdly, we show that academics employed varied forms of belonging work at classroom, organisational, relational and external community levels to sustain or reframe belonging, while others disengaged due to workload pressures and emotional strain. These processes produced divergent belonging trajectories, ranging from significant belonging loss to heightened forms of academic belonging.Practical implicationsFindings highlight belonging as a form of relational infrastructure that requires intentional institutional investment. Universities should prioritise relational connection, reduce crisis-driven workload intensification, strengthen recognition practices and design participatory decision-making processes. Supporting staff capacity for belonging work can enhance resilience, well-being and continuity in academic communities.Originality/valueThis study advances theory by conceptualising belonging dissonance as a crisis-specific manifestation of cognitive dissonance and by identifying belonging work as a key mechanism for dissonance resolution. It offers a nuanced, processual understanding of academic belonging and provides actionable insights for sustaining belonging in volatile higher education environments.

AB PurposeRapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) technology have brought about numerous opportunities and challenges in various fields, including education and research. TI Soft skills as durable-adaptive capital: industry insights for career
   construction across the lifespan
SO HIGHER EDUCATION SKILLS AND WORK-BASED LEARNING

DT Article
DE Soft skills; Lifelong learning; Career adaptability; Labour market;
   Digital transformation; Career construction
AB PurposeThis study analyses the increasing demand for soft skills from an integrated perspective, aiming to explain their function as durable-adaptive capital and enhance evidence-based career guidance and lifelong learning strategies, thereby supporting work adjustment and career construction across the lifespan.Design/methodology/approachEmploying a qualitative research design, the methodology triangulated industry perspectives with economic perspectives and vocational psychological framework, grounded in career construction theory regarding adaptive capital. DT Article
DE Transformative lesson study incorporating open approach model;
   Pedagogical content knowledge; Fractions; Professional learning
   community
ID STUDENTS
AB PurposeThis case study examines how primary teachers develop Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) on fractions within the Transformative Lesson Study incorporating Open Approach (TLSOA) model. It identifies key PCK characteristics and how TLSOA model fosters them.Design/methodology/approachA Lesson Study team of six members (two student teachers, two in-service teachers, one researcher, and one expert) engaged in weekly cycles of collaborative planning, observation, and reflection across 10 fraction lessons in a Thai primary school. Participation across multiple years and varied professional learning communities (PLCs) with experienced reflection teams could enhance teachers' PCK awareness and development through broader collaborative experiences.Practical implicationsThe use of the TLSOA model in developing teachers' PCK on fractions through student-centered collaborative lesson design strengthened the effectiveness of teacher professional development approaches in mathematics education.Originality/valueThis study demonstrates how collaborative PLCs foster dynamic integration of content and pedagogical knowledge in mathematics education, contributing to PCK literature by showing the TLSOA model's specific mechanisms for developing fraction instruction through student-centered collaborative practice.

ID JOB MISMATCHES; LABOR-MARKET; MATCH; ENTERPRISES; MANAGERS; GENDER
AB PurposeThis paper aims to examine the role of workplace learning in mitigating the wage penalties associated with horizontal mismatch - also known as field-of-study mismatch - which occurs when a worker, educated in one field, works in another field.Design/methodology/approachUsing data from manufacturing workers in 23 countries from the Program of International Assessment of Adult Competencies (PIAAC), this study applies Mincer's equation to assess how workplace learning moderates the relationship between horizontal mismatch and earnings, controlling for demographic and job characteristics and country fixed effects.FindingsOn-the-job training and workshops or seminars significantly alleviate wage penalties for horizontally mismatched workers. The mitigating effect of workplace learning is pronounced among managerial workers. By firm size, on-the-job training is particularly effective in small and medium-sized firms, whereas workshops or seminars are more beneficial in larger firms.Research limitations/implicationsThis study is based on cross-national data, which does not allow for causal inference regarding the effect of horizontal mismatch on wages.Practical implicationsThe findings reveal context-specific workplace learning strategies that enhance productivity for mismatched workers. Complementarity between learning and training and adaptive partnerships with educational institutions and industry are highlighted.Originality/valueDespite growing research on wage penalties associated with education-occupation mismatches, few studies focus on practical solutions to mitigate the penalty. This study highlights workplace learning as a strategy to mitigate wage penalties for the mismatched workers.

TI Instrumental or transformative? An exploratory analysis of
   sustainability competences and pedagogy in European micro-credentials
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SUSTAINABILITY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Micro-credentials; Sustainability; Active learning; Pedagogy;
   Competences
AB PurposeSustainability-focused micro-credentials delivered by European universities are growing. However, it is unknown how and to what extent sustainability competences are being taught within these programmes. The purpose of this study is to explore the nexus of European micro-credentials, sustainability competence integration and active learning pedagogies to examine how they interact in practice and whether they provide a transformative or instrumental education for professional learners.Design/methodology/approachA mixed-method analysis using quantitative content analysis and qualitative thematic analysis of 100 European sustainability-focused micro-credential course descriptions and learning objectives was used. A coding framework based on the GreenComp sustainability competence framework was collaboratively developed and directed content analysis was conducted in NVivo. Pedagogical approaches were coded and analysed.FindingsMicro-credentials sampled addressed an average of three GreenComp competences displaying low breadth of competences, with instrumental competences more present than value-based competences. Less than half used active learning pedagogies. A positive relationship (r = 0.43) was found between active learning and the number of embedded competences. Poor communication of competences and reliance on transmissive pedagogies challenge micro-credentials' potential for transformative sustainability education. Tensions are apparent between the interrelatedness of sustainability competences and the narrow, instrumental focus of many micro-credentials. Active learning and improved transparency of competence communication may enhance their educational and transformational value.Originality/valueTo the best of the authors' knowledge, this study is the first to analyse how sustainability competences and pedagogical strategies are embedded in a large data set of university-provided, publicly available European sustainability micro-credential course descriptions using the GreenComp framework between March and April 2025. This study contributes a novel understanding of the presence and teaching of sustainability competences within European micro-credentials.

TI Disability inclusivity in employment transition programmes: perspectives
   of African graduates with disabilities

ID INDIVIDUALS; EDUCATION; STUDENTS; BARRIERS
AB PurposeThis study evaluates the effectiveness of African Career Networks (ACN) disability inclusion efforts by examining barriers and facilitators experienced by youth with disabilities participating in employment transition programmes, assessing the role of reasonable accommodations and analysing stakeholder attitudes that influence employer and university engagement.Design/methodology/approachA mixed-methods study employed an online survey (n = 92), focus group discussions and individual interviews with youth with disabilities who were current students and alumni of African Leadership Academy or Mastercard Foundation Scholars programme. Data analysis utilised a critical occupational perspective informed by the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health framework. Qualitative methods of research, however, emphasises the transferability of findings to similar contexts over statistical generalisability. The reliance on online data collection methods through MS Teams and Zoom platforms may have inadvertently excluded youth with disabilities who lack reliable Internet access or appropriate assistive technology, potentially underrepresenting the experiences of those facing the most significant digital barriers to participation.Originality/valueThis research provides contemporary empirical evidence from an African context on employment transitions for youth with disabilities, addressing a knowledge gap in disability employment research from African scholars. The study contributes novel insights into the effectiveness of targeted inclusion strategies and offers evidence-based recommendations for improving equitable access in graduate employment transition programmes across Africa. The findings inform policy implications for programme design of youth with disabilities' transitional efforts that challenge standardised approaches to support of this marginalised group.

TI Facilitator positioning work in a Chinese-US high school virtual
   exchange: "a way to learn about themselves in the world"
SO QUALITY EDUCATION FOR ALL
LA English
DT Article
DE Virtual exchange; Cultural awareness; UN SDGs; Facilitators; Classroom
   discourse; Cross-cultural communication; Positioning theory
ID LANGUAGE; EDUCATION; STUDENTS; INQUIRY
AB PurposeInstantiated in UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4: Quality Education for All is the target that all learners acquire skills necessary for global citizenship. Cross-cultural virtual exchanges (VEs) using problem-based learning can be valuable for students' global awareness and, relatedly, their intercultural communication competencies. In a VE, facilitators from diverse contexts collaborate to guide student discourse by making discursive decisions (planned and impromptu) that shape the course of conversation. This study aims to explore facilitator positioning, including their discursive choices, during a problem-based, SDG 4-focused VE that brought together secondary students situated in the USA and China, two countries facing heightened geopolitical tensions.Design/methodology/approachThis case study used discourse analytic methods to examine the discursive roles that three facilitators took on during a cross-cultural VE between Chinese and US secondary students in fall 2023. Data sources included semistructured interviews with facilitators; transcripts of VE facilitator work sessions; and transcripts of VE sessions, including multimodal artifacts produced and shared by VE student participants.FindingsFacilitators described "charged" moments as emotionally and socially tense instances, often triggered by student comments on geopolitically sensitive topics. Results revealed that facilitators enacted patterned, discursive positioning roles - e.g., framer, repair maker and amicable host - to manage these moments. Facilitators struggled to balance open dialogue with perceived geopolitical sensitivities; at times, conversations were constrained, limiting the intended purpose of shared exploration of SDG 4: Quality Education for All. The results point to some incongruence between facilitators' beliefs in the value of open discourse and their impromptu and planned discursive choices, indicating value for improved preparation for VE facilitators. Positioning, as an anticipatory pedagogical frame for VE facilitators, is discussed as a tool to align facilitator discursive choices with pedagogical aims.Research limitations/implicationsAs is true for any case study, the findings are not generalizable to a broader population and instead should be interpreted as a close analysis of phenomena that occurred in this bounded setting with this bounded population. The study demonstrates the value of research studies that examine discursive interactions and the ways facilitators influence dialogic, problem-based global learning experiences.Practical implicationsThe study examines facilitator discourse and positioning work in a problem-based cross-cultural VE. It explores facilitator discursive positioning during perceived "charged" dialogue and introduces positioning theory as a useful anticipatory pedagogical tool for improved facilitator preparation.Originality/valueThe study examines facilitator discourse and positioning work in a problem-based cross-cultural VE. It explores facilitator discursive positioning during perceived "charged" dialogue and introduces positioning theory as a useful anticipatory pedagogical tool in preparing VE facilitators to navigate sensitive topics, promote inclusive dialogue and cultivate students' global citizenship competencies.

DT Article

ID ECONOMIC-GROWTH
AB PurposeThis paper investigates the relationship between education and economic growth in Egypt, with a particular focus on the role of education within the framework of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4 (Quality Education). TI Factors affecting the industry-academia collaboration: a case study of
   higher education institutions (HEIs) in Islamabad, Pakistan

DT Article

   Academic entrepreneurship (ENT); Research-related interactions (RRI);
   Higher education institutions (HEIs)
ID UNIVERSITIES; LINKAGES
AB Purpose - The industry-academia collaboration (IAC) at the higher education level is greatly impacted by various factors. This study aims to investigate the factors influencing IAC in higher education institutions (HEIs) in Islamabad, focusing on educational interactions (EDU), academic entrepreneurship (ENT) and research-related interactions (RRI). Design/methodology/approach - This study adopted a quantitative approach by forming research questions using a critical study of literature and collected data from 80 faculty members selected through stratified sampling across public and private HEIs through the survey method. Statistical analyses, including reliability tests, descriptive tests, correlation, ANOVA, multiple regression and multicollinearity, reveal that while all three factors significantly contribute to IAC, ENT emerges as the strongest predictor (beta = 0.586, p < 0.01), followed by RRI (beta = 0.194, p < 0.01) and EDU (beta = 0.152, p < 0.05). Findings - The findings indicate moderate engagement in educational initiatives such as guest lectures and field visits, but limited efforts in RRI and ENT activities. These factors explain 76.2% of the variability in collaboration outcomes. Key barriers include the lack of structured policies, insufficient funding and misaligned academic outputs with industry needs. This study highlights the need for a robust entrepreneurial system, targeted policies and strengthened collaboration frameworks to enhance IAC. Research limitations/implications - This study is limited to the perspectives of faculty members from a small sample of HEIs in Islamabad, which may not fully capture the industry's viewpoint, ignoring the viewpoint of industrial experts because of limited resources. Additionally, it does not address external factors such as government policies or global market dynamics. Practical implications - This research contributes to the broader discourse on sustainable innovation and provides actionable strategies for bridging the academia-industry gap. Originality/value - This pilot study provides valuable insights for researchers interested in a larger IAC. It also provides insights for HEI managers who want to understand the motivations of industry participants in RRI. These insights are not only relevant for Pakistan but also for other developing nations seeking to leverage IAC for sustainable innovation. This research contributes to the broader discourse on sustainable innovation and provides actionable strategies for bridging the academia-industry gap.

TI What remains of the relative age effect? Selection, achievement, and
   educational tracking
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Relative age; tracking; gender; socioeconomic status; school entry rules
ID SCHOOL STARTING AGE; ENTRY; CHILDHOOD; MATURITY; CHILDREN
AB Relative age effects (RAEs) arise because students within the same grade may differ in age by up to one year. While a large literature documents substantial RAEs in educational achievement, it typically pays less attention to how compliance with school-entry rules and subsequent grade progression shape the RAE that remains observable later in students' school careers. Using linked administrative and achievement-test data from Switzerland, we examine RAEs at the end of primary school, for students who entered school on time and progressed through primary school without grade repetition. We show that selection, particularly at school entry, substantially alters the observed RAE and generates pronounced heterogeneity across student groups. Among students with regular school trajectories, significant RAEs are concentrated among girls and students from socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds. Yet even among girls, for whom the RAE is most pronounced, the achievement advantage of relatively older students is too small to translate into a higher probability of entering the most academically demanding track at the lower-secondary level.

TI Are cardinal and transcendent virtues associated with human flourishing?
   A study of university students
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Flourishing; cardinal virtues; transcendent virtues; SFM; higher
   education; integral formation
ID CONCEPTUAL-FRAMEWORK; RELIABILITY; LEADERSHIP; EDUCATION; LIFE
AB This study examines the extent to which cardinal and transcendent virtues are associated with human flourishing among university students, responding to the growing interest in how character development contributes to well-being in higher education. A sample of 1,159 first-year students from a Mexican university completed three validated self-report instruments: the Secure Flourishing Measure (SFM), the Questionnaire of Competencies and Cardinal Virtues (QCV), and the Questionnaire of Transcendent Virtues (MHM). Factor analyses indicated that the SFM was best represented by a four-factor structure in which happiness and life satisfaction, health, and meaning/purpose loaded onto a broader wellbeing factor. Regression analyses showed that, among the cardinal virtues, fortitude and justice were significantly related to flourishing, with fortitude showing the strongest association. Among the transcendent virtues, magnanimity and humility showed significant associations with flourishing, particularly magnanimity. When both virtue sets were considered jointly, fortitude and magnanimity remained the most strongly associated with flourishing. These findings are consistent with flourishing in emerging adulthood being more strongly associated with agency, perseverance, and hopeful striving than with reflective deliberation alone. The results also inform the ongoing debate on whether flourishing should be considered an educational aim and provide evidence that virtue-based assessment tools can guide educational practice and support integral formation. The findings further suggest that flourishing may depend not on isolated virtues but on their integration within broader patterns of character development.

   pressure; environmental
AB This study investigates accounting students' perceptions of the effectiveness of role-plays in facilitating ethics education and preparing them for ethical dilemmas in the workplace. Two role-plays were designed to simulate technical and ethical issues that accountants could face. The study took place at a South African university. Thirty senior accounting students participated in 10 role-plays. Perceptions of the role-plays' effectiveness were obtained through surveys and focus group discussions. AB Values education has long been central to Bhutan's education system. However, there is limited research examining how values are represented in teaching materials in early primary education.    review; Gross National Happiness; Bhutan
ID BHUTAN; PERSPECTIVES; COCITATION
AB The development of education based on the philosophy of Gross National Happiness (GNH) transferred into the education system in Bhutan and influenced international education. The study aimed to explore the knowledge base landscape, to determine the leading impacting authors and literature, and visualize the intellectual structure of education for GNH knowledge base. Several implications and recommendations were proposed to improve the literature review towards future studies.

TI Teaching for critical thinking under constraint: Secondary science
   teachers' pedagogical practices and systemic barriers in Pakistani
   Public schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical thinking; science education; secondary school teachers;
   pedagogical practices; public schools; Pakistan; Qualitative study
ID ARGUMENTATION; INSTRUCTION; DISCOVERY; FAILURE
AB Critical thinking is widely recognized as a central goal of contemporary education, yet in many school systems it remains overshadowed by syllabus coverage, examination preparation, and content transmission. This qualitative study explored how secondary school science teachers conceptualize critical thinking, the pedagogical practices they report using to foster it, and the systemic constraints shaping its implementation in Pakistani public secondary schools. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with 12 science teachers teaching Biology, Chemistry, and Physics across four public secondary schools. Interview data were analyzed using qualitative content analysis. Findings indicate that teachers generally conceptualize critical thinking as independent reasoning, questioning, explanation, problem-solving, and applying scientific knowledge to real-life situations. Participants reported using inquiry-oriented questioning, classroom discussions, collaborative learning, demonstrations, activities, and structured problem-solving to promote these skills. However, implementation was constrained by curriculum overload, limited instructional time, high-stakes examinations, overcrowded classrooms, inadequate resources, and insufficient sustained professional support. The study concludes that lecture-based teaching should not be interpreted simply as teacher resistance to change but as an adaptive response to systemic pressures. Sustainable development of critical thinking requires closer alignment among assessment practices, curriculum pacing, resource provision, and continuous professional development within secondary science education.

TI Investigating the effects of school meals, textbooks, and uniforms on
   enrolment and attendance: evidence from basic education pupils in Ghana
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Free school meals; free uniforms; free textbooks;; school enrolment;
   school attendance
ID REGRESSION
AB Access to basic education in Ghana is constrained by nutritional, material, and learning resource constraints. In-school non-cash transfer programmes, providing free meals, uniforms, and textbooks seek to mitigate these constraints, yet most prior studies have examined single interventions in isolation. This study advances the literature by simultaneously evaluating both the individual and combined effects of these supports on enrolment and attendance.. Drawing on nationally representative data from 16,122 school-aged children from the Ghana Living Standards Survey Round Seven, and applying Propensity Score Matching (PSM) and Inverse Probability Weighted Regression Adjustment (IPWRA), we estimate average treatment effects (ATE/ATT) for each intervention. Free school meals increase enrolment by approximately 0.4-0.9 percentage points, with standard errors between 0.002 and 0.003, underscoring the role of nutritional support in school entry. Free uniforms raise attendance by 3-4.4 hours per week, with confidence intervals excluding zero, indicating robust effects on regular participation. Free textbooks yield enrolment gains of 0.5-0.8 percentage points and attendance improvements of 2.2-3.9 hours, both statistically significant at the 1-5% level. Combined interventions outperform standalone programmes: meals paired with uniforms generate the largest enrolment gains, while textbooks combined with uniforms produce the greatest attendance improvements. Findings suggest that education policy should prioritise strategically bundled in-kind support, as integrated interventions more effectively reduce multiple barriers to school participation than isolated programmes.

TI Policy implementation at the margins: affect, agency, and boundary work
   in global democratic precarity
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Autoethnography; democratic precarity; disability studies; policy
   implementation; boundary work
AB Global democratic precarity is reshaping how policies are interpreted, enacted, and resisted within higher education, particularly as universities confront polarization, austerity, and intensified scrutiny of academic labor. This autoethnographic study examines how policy implementation is experienced from the margins by tracing my journey as an international scholar with a visual impairment navigating U.S. academic institutions. Through critical autoethnography grounded in disability studies and critical policy analysis, I draw on personal narratives, institutional correspondence, reflective journals, and embodied accounts to illuminate how belonging and exclusion, access and erasure, and growth and vulnerability intersect within spaces of declining public investment and rising ideological hostility. The analysis highlights how affective and sensory experiences reveal the subtle yet powerful mechanisms through which democratic erosion is lived through inaccessible systems, shifting institutional priorities, and boundary work required to maintain legitimacy. Findings suggest that disability, precarity, and transnational identity offer unique epistemic vantage points for understanding policy enactment under conditions of democratic uncertainty. This study expands policy implementation scholarship by foregrounding marginalized positionalities as sources of theoretical insight and by demonstrating how autoethnography can capture the affective and structural complexities shaping contemporary academic life. It argues for more humane, inclusive, and democratically grounded approaches to policy and institutional practice.

   comparative analysis
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Physical education; curriculum; public health; health and wellbeing;

   Education; Education; Secondary Education; By Subject;
   Primary/Elementary Education; Curriculum Studies
ID CURRICULUM; HEALTH; CONTEXTS
AB This study compares how physical education (PE) is conceptualised in official curriculum texts across Greater China, specifically Mainland China, Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan. Drawing on a comparative, discourse-oriented approach, the study examined curriculum documents written to inform teachers' curriculum planning and enactment. Analysis combined deductive and inductive elements, with findings organised around three themes: health and the broader purposes of PE; performance and movement competence; and curriculum structuring, pedagogy, and teacher mediation. The study contributes to comparative curriculum research by moving beyond identifying overlapping discourse resources to showing how they are differently weighted and configured across related yet distinct contexts. In doing so, it extends comparative discourse analysis into Greater China and provides a common language for cross-jurisdictional curriculum reflection and dialogue.

TI Genitive constructions across Somali dialects: Northern, Benadiri, and
   Maay
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Somali dialects; genitive constructions; morphosyntactic variation;
   cushitic typology; possessive structures; Social Sciences; Education;
   Education Policy & Politics; Education Policy; Curriculum; Philosophy of
   Education; Moral & Values Education; Primary/Elementary Education; By
   Subject; Geography
AB This study examines genitive constructions across Northern Somali (Maxaa Tiri), Benadiri, and Maay, addressing the limited comparative evidence on dialectal variation in Somali nominal possession. A comparative descriptive design was employed using elicited examples, translation tasks, sentence-judgement prompts, oral narratives, written texts, and prior grammatical descriptions. The 21 speakers constituted the participant sample; the 45 selected core examples (15 per dialect) constituted the analytical sample. The selected examples were coded for marker type, morphosyntactic attachment, constituent order, overt nominal concord, semantic relation, and possible contact influence. Northern Somali primarily employs noun-bound definiteness and nominal concord morphology within a construct-state-like possessed, possessor configuration rather than dedicated genitive case marking. Benadiri exhibits reduced, provisionally clitic-like attachment and discourse-conditioned variation in constituent order. Maay relies more extensively on relational markers and analytic constructions and permits possessor-before-possessed order in part of the dataset. Although all three varieties share a Cushitic tendency toward head-dependent organization, they encode possession through distinct combinations of attachment, relational marking, nominal concord, and word order. Contact-based explanations remain hypotheses requiring stronger historical and sociolinguistic evidence. These findings advance Cushitic typology and support dialect-responsive teaching, multilingual pedagogy, literacy development, and the preservation of Somali linguistic heritage.

TI Learning analytics and mathematics performance: the mediating role of
   student engagement and self-regulated learning
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Engagement; higher-order thinking skills; learning analytics; mathematic
   performance; self-regulated learning
ID FEEDBACK
AB Learning analytics is widely regarded as a tool for enhancing academic performance, yet empirical evidence on this relationship remains inconsistent, leaving it unclear whether learning analytics improves performance directly or through underlying psychopedagogical processes such as student engagement and self-regulated learning. This gap is especially evident in mathematics education, a cognitively demanding field in which the mediating roles of engagement and self-regulated learning have rarely been examined. This study therefore investigated how learning analytics affects mathematics performance, with student engagement and self-regulated learning as mediating variables. Data were collected from 126 undergraduate students enrolled in Learning Management System (LMS)-supported mathematics courses at Universitas PGRI Mpu Sindok, Indonesia, using a quantitative method with an explanatory survey design. We used questionnaires and essay-based math tests to collect data on higher-order thinking skills, then analysed the data using Partial Least Squares-Structural Equation Modelling. The results showed that learning analysis had a positive and significant effect on student engagement, with a path coefficient of 0.939. Student engagement and self-regulated learning significantly affected math performance, with coefficients of 0.494 and 0.359, respectively. However, learning analysis did not show significant direct effects on self-regulated learning or mathematical performance. The indirect influence of learning analysis on mathematics performance through student involvement was found to be significant, with a coefficient of 0.464. These findings highlight the significant role of student engagement in leveraging learning analytics to improve math performance.

TI Local knowledge and climate change in Ethiopian secondary school
   geography and biology textbooks
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Climate change; local knowledge; indigenous knowledge; geography;
   biology
ID INDIGENOUS KNOWLEDGE; CURRICULA; TEACHERS
AB Education is crucial in addressing the climate crisis, with textbooks shaping students' knowledge and skills. However, little research examines how Ethiopian textbooks integrate climate change concepts with local perspectives, despite the importance of local knowledge. This study conducts a content analysis of Ethiopian secondary school biology and geography textbooks to investigate the portrayal of climate change, with particular attention to the incorporation of local knowledge. Six textbooks, four geography and two biology, were selected for analysis. The study employed theoretical frameworks including green governmentality, ecological modernization, civic environmentalism, and the political ecology of education. Findings indicate that climate change is predominantly framed through global scientific perspectives, with minimal incorporation of local knowledge systems. The textbooks primarily reflect climate change problems related to agriculture, hydrology, and biodiversity. Causes of climate change are presented as both anthropogenic and natural, while proposed solutions are categorized into mitigation and adaptation measures, with adaptation strategies receiving greater emphasis. However, the portrayal of climate change dynamics lacks meaningful connections to local practices, thereby failing to cultivate contextually relevant climate literacy. We recommend revising Ethiopian textbooks to integrate local knowledge, promote culturally grounded learning, and empower students as active agents in addressing climate change.

TI Building blocks for STEM education: investigating students' and parents'
   attitudes toward tablet-based literacy and numeracy learning initiative
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Tablet-based learning; Literacy and Numeracy Drive; attitudes; students;
   parents; primary education
ID TECHNOLOGY; ACCEPTANCE; PERFORMANCE; MOTIVATION; INTERNET; PCS
AB In the contemporary digital era, digital learning technologies have become increasingly integral to education systems worldwide. Tablet-based learning tools have gained attention for their portability, interactivity, and potential to support foundational literacy and numeracy skills, regarded as precursors to later STEM learning. This study investigated students' and parents' attitudes toward the government-implemented Literacy and Numeracy Drive (LND), a tablet-based initiative for teaching and assessing foundational literacy and numeracy skills in public primary schools in Punjab, Pakistan. Data were collected from 216 fifth-grade students and 151 parents using a self-developed Tablet Attitude Questionnaire measuring overall attitudes, educational benefits, technical awareness, negative potential, and prior experience. Descriptive statistics, independent-samples t-tests, and multiple regression analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics. Results showed that students demonstrated highly positive attitudes toward LND, whereas parents expressed moderately positive but more cautious attitudes. Significant differences emerged between students' and parents' attitudes across all measured constructs. Educational benefits were positively associated with favourable attitudes among both groups, while technical awareness showed significant indirect associations through perceived educational benefits. The findings provide context-specific evidence of stakeholder acceptance of tablet-based foundational learning, supporting readiness for later STEM education rather than demonstrating improvements in STEM achievement.

TI Prevalence and patterns of sedentary behaviours among University of Dar
   es Salaam students
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic activities; screen-based activity; sedentary activity; sitting
   time; university students
ID PHYSICAL-ACTIVITY
AB Sedentary behaviour is rising among university students because of lifestyle changes, modernisation, and academic demands. This paper examined the prevalence and patterns of sedentary behaviour among the University of Dar es Salaam students in Tanzania. The study employed a cross-sectional research design. Using a simple random sampling technique, the study involved 600 students studying various degree programmes from the School of Education. The researchers collected data using questionnaires and analysed them using descriptive and inferential statistics. Findings indicate that social networking emerged as the most prevalent activity, followed by academic activities, while board and card games were the least prevalent. Therefore, students need to control social networking chatting time and replace it with physical activity.

TI Enhancing cybersecurity curricula through Dark Web education with
   AI-based hands-on labs
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Darknet; Dark Web; Tor network; cybersecurity curricula; artificial
   intelligence; educational framework; Bloom's Taxonomy
AB As cybersecurity threats evolve, adversaries increasingly utilize anonymizing technologies like the Dark Web, creating an urgent need to align cybersecurity education with emerging realities. Current curricula reveal significant knowledge gaps, leaving graduates ill-prepared for roles in threat intelligence and digital forensics. This paper presents a novel pedagogical framework that integrates structured Dark Web instruction supported by AI-driven, hands-on laboratory activities. Using a mixed-methods approach, the study surveyed 85 undergraduate students pre-implementation to assess baseline knowledge and evaluated 75 students post-pilot. Initial assessments revealed substantial deficits, with 93.5% of students reporting low confidence in their understanding of Dark Web technologies. Following the pilot, results demonstrated significant improvements in student engagement, conceptual understanding, and satisfaction. The proposed framework incorporates legal, ethical, and technical safeguards to ensure responsible instruction while demonstrating the potential of AI to support scalable, sound education in emerging threat domains.

TI Multiple intelligence profiles vis-à-vis speaking achievements: evidence
   from Ethiopian EFL university students
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Multiple intelligence; students' intelligence profile; speaking
   achievement; Ethiopian higher education; EFL speaking instruction
AB This research examined the correlation between EFL learners' multiple intelligence types and their speaking achievements in two Ethiopian universities. To achieve the intended objective, a correlational study design was used involving fifty (50) undergraduate EFL students chosen purposefully from Hawassa and Madda Walabu Universities. To collect the necessary data, multiple intelligence inventory survey and document analysis acquired from the teachers' course grade submitted data were used. The information gathered through these tools were statistically examined using descriptive statistics and Chi-square testing. The findings showed that the most prevalent student profiles were bodily-kinesthetic and visual-spatial intelligences. The results of the Chi-square testing revealed a statistically meaningful relation, chi(2)(21, N = 50) = 34.07, p =0.036, Cramer's V = 0.48, showing a moderately substantial statistically significant correlation between speaking achievement and predominant MI types. The results underline the significance of recognizing student variability in EFL speaking courses and imply that students' intelligence types are linked to variations in speaking achievement.

TI The role of teacher concern in teacher emotions and grit
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher grit; positive emotions; negative emotions; teacher concern; EFL
ID SELF-EFFICACY; ENJOYMENT
AB Teaching is a cognitively and emotionally demanding profession, especially in English as a foreign language (EFL) contexts. While traits like grit are known to influence teacher performance, their interaction with emotional constructs such as teacher concern and emotions remains underexplored. This study investigates how teacher concern is associated with positive and negative emotions and grit among teachers. Participants were 499 EFL teachers from various cities in Iran who completed three validated measures: the Teacher Concern Scale (TCS), the Teacher Academic Emotions (TAE) scale, and the L2 Teacher Grit Scale (L2TGS). Data were analyzed using Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), correlation analysis, and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). Two models were tested: a direct model examining the associations of variables with grit, and an indirect model testing the mediating roles of emotions. Results showed that teacher concern and positive emotions were positively associated with grit, whereas negative emotions showed a negative association. The indirect model revealed a significant indirect association from concern to grit through positive emotions. The validated TCS identified three subcomponents: apathy, sympathy/empathy, and metapathy. These findings highlight the importance of both emotional and cognitive factors in sustaining teacher perseverance. Implications include incorporating emotion regulation training into teacher education programs .

TI Using digital tools to teach grade 7 mathematics in under-resourced
   schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Constructionism; digital tools; mathematics education; pedagogical
   strategies; under-resourced contexts
AB In mathematics classrooms, teachers are expected to employ various pedagogical strategies supported by diverse teaching and learning materials to facilitate an understanding of this unique discipline. However, South African mathematics education continues to face various challenges, including the influence of conventional teaching strategies in under-resourced settings. The lack of resources in schools is largely due to inequities in access to resources that are often associated with socioeconomic factors. Therefore, this study aims to explore whether digital tools could improve mathematics learning in Grade 7. This study is grounded in the theory of constructionism and employs a qualitative approach. Eight Grade 7 mathematics teachers were purposively sampled from the four schools. Data collected through observations and semi-structured interviews were analysed using thematic analysis. This study's findings indicate that the use of online videos, Kahoot! GeoGebra and Google Forms seem to foster mathematics learning, promote learner engagement, and are conducive to allowing learners to think critically. The use of digital tools can offer holistic instruction on different mathematics content; however, there is limited access to these vital tools in South African schools. This study recommends increased priority in the provision of digital tools in schools as they improve the teaching and learning of mathematics. Future studies could focus on narrating the implementation of tools in mathematics classrooms. This study is essential in that it offers valuable insights into the integration of technology in mathematics pedagogy and provides practical implications for mathematics instructors.

TI Beyond grades: a questionnaire for measuring student-centered success
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student success; student-centered assessment; questionnaire development;
   academic goals; higher education
ID UNIVERSITY
AB Given the critical role of higher education in fostering new competencies and addressing students' evolving needs amidst societal change, it has become increasingly important to expand the definition of student success. In this study, a questionnaire was developed to measure higher education students' subjective perceptions of success. Participants were invited to evaluate the importance of various success dimensions retrieved from a previous qualitative study and subsequently assess their own level of achievement in each area. This instrument is closely aligned with students' academic goals and seeks to illuminate their personal experiences and interpretations of success. The questionnaire was validated using a sample of N = 213 students studying at public universities in Austria. The results confirmed the construct validity, as well as convergent and discriminant validity of the questionnaire. This instrument can be utilized to assess student success at universities and simultaneously serve as a self-reflection tool for students.

TI Language shifts as a catalyst for social and educational cohesion in
   multilingual societies
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Language shifts; IKN; social cohesion; educational cohesion
ID MULTIPLE LANGUAGES; CAPITAL CITY; INDONESIA; DIALECT
AB Although the Indonesian New Capital City, or Ibu Kota Nusantara (IKN), is a potential living laboratory of a multilingual society, studies investigating the extent to which language shift conditions stimulate educational cohesion remain limited. To fill this gap, this research aims to investigate language shifts at schools in IKN to achieve equitable education. The participants were teachers and high school students who lived in three subdistricts of IKN (Sepaku, Penajam Pasir Utara, and Muara Jawa). We conducted eight interviews and two classroom observations to capture the participants' linguistic backgrounds and to document language shifts. The interviews were then developed into a 2-million-word corpus of spoken language (Spoken Corpus Data of Vernacular Indonesian). The corpus was analyzed using frequency and concordance features in AntConc to capture patterns of language shift. The findings reveal that regional migrants from Java Island (Central and East Java ethnicities), South Kalimantan Island (Banjar ethnicity), and South Sulawesi Island (Bugis ethnicity) constitute the dominant demographic in IKN. This study also found that some linguistic shifts occurred, including phonological changes such as consonant softening, morphological simplification, and syntactic adjustments aimed at building stronger community ties both within schools and in society.

TI IDEOLOGICAL CONTESTATION IN ISLAMIC EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS: canonical
   and apocryphal dynamics in Muhammadiyah and Nahdlatul Ulama schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Ideological contestation; Islamic educational institutions; canonical
   and apocryphal ideology; Muhammadiyah and Nahdlatul 'Ulama;
   transnational Islamic influence; Social Sciences; Education; Education
   Policy & Politics; Education Policy; Pedagogy; Arts & Humanities;
   Humanities; Philosophy; Phenomenology; Religion
AB This study explores ideological contestation in Islamic educational institutions, focusing on Muhammadiyah and Nahdlatul Ulama's schools in Indonesia, with the aim of understanding how competing religious ideologies interact, are negotiated, and shape institutional identity and practice. Using a qualitative approach with case study, data were collected through in-depth interviews, participant observation, and document analysis across selected schools representing diverse socio-cultural contexts, and analyzed through iterative processes of coding and thematic interpretation. The findings reveal that these institutions are not static sites of ideological transmission but dynamic arenas where external ideological influences enter through informal channels and interact with established beliefs, generating subtle yet persistent tensions. These tensions are expressed through discursive negotiation, variations in practice, and the formation of informal alignments, rather than open conflict. Institutional responses involve reinforcement of core values, selective adaptation, and boundary-making processes that distinguish between canonical ideology, which is legitimized and integrated, and apocryphal ideology, which is perceived as external and contested. This study offers an original contribution by reframing education as a site of ideological contestation and introducing the conceptual distinction between canonical and apocryphal ideology. The study also demonstrates how ideological contestation operates through subtle, non-confrontational processes embedded in everyday educational practices. It provides a new lens for understanding how institutions manage competing beliefs, while suggesting future research on broader contexts, comparative cases, and mixed-methodological approaches.

TI I found myself Diggin': integrating Black feminist theory into archival
   methodologies to uncover historically silenced narratives
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Black feminist theory; critical archival studies; archival
   methodologies; educational history
AB This paper develops speculative nonfiction as a Black feminist archival methodology to recover historically silenced narratives of Georgia's Jeanes Teachers, rural African American women educators who led transformative community-based educational work from 1908-1968. Moving beyond institutional archives, this approach integrates Black feminist theory and qualitative social network analysis to excavate dispersed documents, sorority archives, and intergenerational memory. Through case studies of Maenelle Dempsey, Frances McBride, and Susie Wheeler, I show how rural Black women created political infrastructures of care, resistance, and educational innovation. This work reimagines archival epistemology and argues for liberatory methods that restore agency to historically marginalized subjects.

TI Evaluating perceived obstetric anesthesia training needs in residency
   education: a Taiwanese national survey
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Declining birthrate; medical education; needs assessment; obstetric
   anesthesia; residency training
ID NUMBER
AB Background Taiwan's declining birthrate has reduced obstetric case volume and may threaten obstetric anesthesia training. We examined training experiences, self-perceived competencies, and educational needs in Taiwan to inform feasible curricular strategies. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional nationwide anonymous online survey of anesthesiology residents and attending anesthesiologists in Taiwan (October 1-December 31, 2024). The 37-item questionnaire covered demographics, self-assessed competencies and confidence, satisfaction with current training, and future training preferences, with open-ended items on barriers to additional training. Descriptive statistics, independent-samples t tests, one-way ANOVA, Pearson correlations, and linear regression were performed. Results A total of 145 valid responses were analyzed (112 attendings, 33 residents), yielding an overall response rate of 8.3% (attendings 7.8%, residents 10.4%). Self-assessed competence increased with greater clinical seniority and longer obstetric anesthesia training duration. Highest-rated competencies were neuraxial anesthesia for cesarean delivery (mean 7.93) and airway management during general anesthesia in obstetric patients (7.82), whereas confidence was lower for managing cardiac parturients (6.21) and neonatal resuscitation (5.89). Attendings reported higher overall confidence in independently performing obstetric anesthesia than residents (8.00 vs 6.52, p < 0.001). Male respondents were significantly older than female respondents (mean 41.9 vs. 35.4 years, p < 0.001). Correspondingly, male respondents reported higher confidence than female respondents for independent practice (8.05 vs 7.08, p < 0.001) and for managing cardiac parturients (6.63 vs 5.59, p = 0.001). In multivariable regression, confidence in managing cardiac parturients (beta = 0.61, 95% CI 0.217-0.997; p = 0.002) and competence in neuraxial anesthesia for cesarean delivery (beta = 1.214, 95% CI 0.190-2.238; p = 0.020) independently predicted overall confidence. Conclusions Obstetric anesthesia competence and confidence were associated with training exposure, yet gaps persisted in high-risk and emergency domains and differed by gender. Programs should prioritize simulation-based training for rare critical events and develop inter-institutional collaborations to strengthen competency acquisition amid declining obstetric volumes.

TI Niche-making in intersectional spaces of Ilonggo women in mathematics:
   groundwork for a liberatory curriculum framework
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Liberatory mathematics; intersectionality; narrative inquiry;
   mathematics education; global South
AB Gender inequality in mathematics persists despite global commitments to equity, with women's participation shaped by intersecting socio-cultural, economic, and institutional conditions. Limited research examines how women's lived experiences, particularly in localized Global South contexts, can inform curriculum development. This study explores the lived experiences of Ilonggo Women in Mathematics and translates their narratives into a Liberatory Mathematics Curriculum Framework. Anchored in subjectivism and feminist inquiry and guided by critical theory and intersectionality, the study employed qualitative narrative inquiry. Four Ilonggo women in mathematics were purposively selected and engaged in multiple in-depth life story interviews. Data were analyzed through iterative coding, restorying, and cross-narrative analysis to generate key themes.i Findings reveal that participation in mathematics is shaped by the interplay of intersectionality, niche-making, and empowering structures. Socio-economic constraints and gendered representations influence access and belonging, while participants actively reconfigure their roles through teaching, mentoring, and community engagement. Mentorship and family encouragement are critical in sustaining persistence and identity formation. These insights informed a Liberatory Mathematics Curriculum Framework integrating contextualized content, critical engagement, identity affirmation, transformative practice, and relational support. The framework contributes a grounded approach to rethinking mathematics education through decolonizing perspectives in the Global South.

TI Addressing educational quality in nursing home placements: exploring
   nurse educators' time-commitments. A qualitative study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE nurse educator; nursing education; nursing home; student nurse;
   supervision; time management
AB Nurse educators play a critical role in maintaining educational quality by supervising first-year student nurses during their initial clinical placements in nursing education. Nurse educators' time-commitments, defined as the time dedicated to fulfilling educational responsibilities, can either enhance or hinder the efficiency of supervision. Hence, addressing educators' time-commitments is essential in aiming for high-quality education. This study aimed to explore nurse educators' experiences with time-commitments while supervising first-year student nurses during their initial clinical placements. A qualitative, exploratory and descriptive research design was used, based on five focus group interviews with 22 nurse educators, conducted in spring 2019. The data were analysed using Malterud's framework for systematic text condensation. The study found that nurse educators experienced important time-related pressure caused by fragmented placement structures, extensive travel between sites and the need to balance physical and digital supervision. Additionally, educators reported a high demand for continuous availability for both students and registered nurse mentors, often extending beyond contracted hours. The results highlight a need for organisational strategies that acknowledge educators' workload and support sustainable supervision practices.

TI Learning-oriented generative AI use and student agency in Chinese higher
   education: the roles of self-directed learning and assessment climate
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; self-directed learning; student agency; assessment
   climate; higher education; Social Sciences; Education; Development
   Studies; Environment; Social Work; Urban Studies; Criminology and
   Criminal Justice
ID MOTIVATION
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in higher education, but its relationship with students' capacity to act intentionally in learning remains underexplored. This study examined whether learning-oriented GenAI use was associated with student agency, and whether this association was mediated by self-directed learning and moderated by assessment climate. A cross-sectional survey of 742 undergraduates from six Chinese universities was analysed using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling. The four focal constructs showed adequate empirical distinctiveness. Learning-oriented GenAI use was positively related to both self-directed learning and student agency, and self-directed learning partially mediated this relationship. Assessment climate also moderated the link between GenAI use and agency: the association was stronger when students perceived assessment as supporting feedback, reflection and improvement. These findings suggest that GenAI is more likely to support student agency when students use it for understanding and self-regulated learning, and when assessment environments encourage constructive engagement rather than simple task completion.

TI 'I've got that autonomy on how I want to manage my day as long as I'm in
   for teaching': a follow up of teaching practices in post Covid-19 higher
   education sport
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Face-to-face; self-determination theory; technology enhanced learning;
   autonomy; confidence; a staff motivation
AB Covid-19 and ensuing lockdowns severely disrupted all sectors of society, including higher education. In the United Kingdom (UK), universities rapidly transitioned to remote delivery, requiring significant changes in teaching and assessment practices. Using semi-structured qualitative interviews and the lens of self-determination theory, this study investigated the post-pandemic teaching and working practices of nine sports educators employed across seven UK higher education institutions. The aim was to explore the post Covid-19 teaching and working practices of educators delivering sports provision in UK higher education settings. Findings indicate that participants improved their competence in online teaching during the pandemic through the adoption of diverse digital tools and are now experiencing greater autonomy in structuring their working days but have not necessarily extended their alternative content and delivery styles since the pandemic. The resumption of in-person teaching promoted stronger connections and a renewed sense of relatedness with students but less so with other colleagues. Overall, the participants showed a clear understanding of the benefits and challenges of hybrid work. While they greatly valued having the freedom and choice to work from home on days when not teaching, some reported missing the informal, day-to-day interactions and community engagement that occur in campus settings.

TI Preservice teachers' experiences of using ICT in English education
   programmes at Nepali universities
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE English language teaching; ICT in the classroom; ICT tools; interactive
   learning; Nepali universities; pedagogical skills; preservice teachers;
   professional development; teaching-learning activities; technical skills
   for teachers
ID TEACHING PRACTICUM; CONTENT KNOWLEDGE; FRAMEWORK
AB The growing use of information and communication technology (ICT) in education has created new opportunities for English language teachers by enhancing the accessibility of educational resources and fostering interactive pedagogical practices. In this context, this study examines how preservice English teachers in Nepali universities experience ICT use in their teacher education programmes. Adopting an interpretive paradigm, it employed a qualitative design using semi-structured interviews with ten purposively selected preservice English teachers pursuing a master's degree in English education at two campuses in Karnali Province. The data were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis, flexing four themes: (1) ICT as a means of promoting professional and pedagogical competences, (2) a shift from traditional instruction towards student-centered learning, (3) developing interaction and collaboration among teachers and students, and (4) resilience in navigating institutional and technical constraints. While preservice English teachers valued the use of ICT in teaching and learning, they reported challenges, such as their inadequate technical skills, poor ICT infrastructure in educational institutions, irregular electricity supply, and a lack of institutional initiatives for teachers. The study suggests that ICT integration in teaching English has significant value; however, its success requires not only technological access but also the alignment of preservice teachers' techno-pedagogical competencies, institutional supports, and contextual readiness at Nepali universities. IMPACT STATEMENT This study contributes to understanding how preservice English teachers in a resource-constrained context perceived the role of ICT in transforming traditional pedagogy into student-centred teaching-learning approaches, and how they sustained using it with resilience and grit despite persistent challenges.

TI Influence of servant leadership on organisational commitment, work
   engagement and job performance in teacher education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational leadership; job performance; organisational commitment;
   servant leadership; and teacher education
AB Teacher education occupies a central role in higher education as it prepares teachers for all levels of the education system. It equips prospective teachers with knowledge, skills and methods needed for teaching. In this light, this study examined the influence of servant leadership (SL) on organisational commitment (OC), work engagement (WE) and job performance (JP) in teacher education. Data were collected from 416 faculty members in colleges of education in Ghana. The analysis was done using structural equation modelling with the partial least squares (PLS) technique. The study recommends that management in colleges of education design policies that enhance faculty satisfaction, engagement and commitment by addressing the factors that genuinely motivate academic staff.

TI What works in values-based education? Evidence from basic education in
   Kenya
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Values-based education; integration; assessment; teacher training;
   competency-based education
ID METAANALYSIS; IMPACT
AB Kenya's transition to Competency-Based Education (CBE) renews emphasis on values and life skills alongside academic learning, yet little evidence exists on their integration across formal, non-formal, and informal dimensions of school life. This study examined how Values-based Education (VbE) is understood, integrated, and assessed in 16 of 79 schools in a Kenya Institute for Curriculum Development (KICD) pilot across Nairobi, Kajiado, Isiolo, and Bungoma counties. Data were collected through key informant interviews (education officers, school heads), focus group discussions (teachers and Grade 4-6 learners), and paired classroom observations of trained and untrained teachers. Participants commonly recognised core values such as love, respect, responsibility, and unity, and these were most visibly enacted in informal and non-formal school spaces: teachers modelled responsibility and integrity in 93% of observed classrooms, and learners displayed collaborative, respectful behaviour during breaks in 86% of schools. By contrast, formal lesson-level integration was less consistent, values-oriented pedagogy was observed in 89% of lessons, but structured assessment tools such as rubrics or reflective journals were used in only 29%. As a cross-sectional, purposively sampled pilot evaluation, these findings are descriptive rather than causal. The study recommends school-embedded coaching, simple standardized assessment rubrics/checklist, pragmatic resourcing, stronger parent-community partnerships, and routine monitoring with incentives for good practice to enhance reliable VbE integration at scale.

TI Amplifying teachers' voices? An innovative collaborative book project
   foregrounding perspectives from practice
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Theory-practice relationship; researcher-practitioner collaboration;
   knowledge production; preschools; power; collaborative writing
ID EDUCATION
AB The voices of preschool and school teachers have been largely absent from knowledge production, creating a gap between research and practice and limiting the potential of research to enhance education. While collaboration between researchers and teachers has been promoted to bridge the research-practice gap, its promise can be undermined by power imbalances, in which researchers' higher status risks silencing teachers' contributions to knowledge production. This is especially the case when collaboration unfolds in traditional research settings. Therefore, there is a need for research on attempts to collaborate in new ways. This study examines the possibilities of a collaborative book project to mitigate asymmetries in collaboration and amplify teachers' voices in knowledge production. The model used in the project was intentionally designed to foreground practitioners' perspectives while integrating both research and professional insights. Grounded in cultural-historical activity theory and based on observations and interviews conducted by an external researcher, the study shows that the collaboration process provoked tensions in relation to differences in practices, status and positionings. Yet its organisation enabled participants to address these tensions and develop agency. The collaboration model showed potential to amplify teachers' voices, fostering a more democratic knowledge infrastructure by positioning teachers as active knowledge producers.

DT Article
DE Arab international students; identity negotiation; investment;
