ID CHALLENGES
AB This qualitative study examines how Arab international students experience studying at a Turkish-medium university in T & uuml;rkiye, focusing on motivations, identity negotiation, and intercultural engagement in a non-Anglophone context. Drawing on poststructuralist theory and a phenomenographic research design, the study analyses in-depth interviews with eight students to identify qualitatively different ways of experiencing international study. TI Beyond unstructured use: scaffolded integration of generative AI in
   assessment for learning
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; assessment for learning; evaluative
   judgement; higher education; assessment design; Social Sciences;
   Education; Development Studies, Environment, Social Work, Urban Studies;
   Criminology and Criminal Justice
AB This study examined how scaffolded integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) within an assessment task influenced students' experience, evaluative engagement, learning, confidence, and competence. A cross-sectional quantitative survey was completed by 164 first-year undergraduate students in a fully online health communication course. The assessment required students to generate, critically evaluate, and revise GenAI-assisted outputs, and reflect on their use. The questionnaire comprised Likert-scale and multiple-response items assessing students' experiences, learning, confidence, competence, challenges, and perceived skill development. Composite scales were analysed descriptively and compared against neutral midpoints using non-parametric tests. Students reported positive technical experiences (64%) and learning benefits, particularly in critique writing (67%), critical thinking (83%), and responsible GenAI use (82%). Evaluative skills, including critical appraisal (71%) and source verification (69%), were frequently reported. Perceptions of reliability were cautious, and confidence and competence did not differ from neutral. Composite analyses indicated positive experience and learning without corresponding increases in confidence. Scaffolded integration of GenAI within assessment can support assessment for learning by promoting evaluative engagement and critical AI literacy without encouraging uncritical reliance. These findings position assessment design as a central mechanism for guiding responsible and effective GenAI use in higher education.

TI Imagined identity, investing, and harvesting the return: narratives of
   English language teachers
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher development; imagination; English language; teachers'
   narratives; life history; Nepal
ID EXPLORING LANGUAGE; INVESTMENT; INQUIRY
AB Teacher identity is an emerging field in educational research, with studies primarily examining the influence of teacher education and training, reflective practices, sociocultural environment, teachers' experiences, and agency. Limited research exists on English language teachers' imagination, imagined identity, investment, and their influence on professional development and identity construction. Underpinning Norton's notion of investing, this study foregrounds the storied lives of four secondary-level English language teachers, drawn from informal conversations and in-depth interviews. Their life history revealed that the learning environments at home and school, the role models they identified, their dreams for the future, and their aspirations to attain symbolic, economic, and cultural capital positively influenced their choice of subjects and their investment in imagined and idealized futures. Hence, their engagement in teacher education, practicum, professional communities, observation, reflection, and feedback should be understood as their investment in imagined identity. In return, they achieved an idealized future and an identity beyond their imagination. The article concludes that teacher identity, investment, and the return on that investment are interrelated and mutually influence one another, implying the need for role modeling in teaching to shape students' imagination and, thereby, investment and identity construction.

AB This study explored the lived experiences of counselor educators who strive to integrate social justice advocacy (SJA) amidst systemic challenges. TI Learning, memory, and belonging: how older adults use conversational AI
   beyond information seeking
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Older adults; large language models; conversational interaction;
   lifelong learning; digital divide; human-centred AI; Social Sciences;
   Education; Adult Education and Lifelong Learning; Work-based Learning;
   Philosophy of Education; Research Methods in Education
AB When a chatbot becomes a companion, learning in later life changes shape. This study examines how older adults converse with a large language model (LLM) in lifelong learning sessions across 4 Colombian municipalities with unequal digital infrastructures, asking which domains emerge and whether response depth varies by topic and territory. We analyzed 1,135 interactions from 273 older adults using semantic embeddings and unsupervised clustering (UMAP, HDBSCAN, and K-Means), topic modelling (BERTopic), and statistics (Wilcoxon with Bonferroni correction, chi-square, and multiple correspondence analysis). Overall, conversational AI use in later life is socio-affective, culturally situated, and territorially mediated, informing human-centered agent design and inclusive digital ageing and lifelong learning initiatives.

TI Establishing valid criteria for assessing transversal competencies in
   aircraft maintenance education: a Delphi study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Competency-based training and assessment; transversal competencies;
   valid assessment criteria; European Qualification Framework;
   international standardisation
ID PROFESSIONAL COMPETENCE
AB Global aircraft maintenance education and licensing standards are transitioning from theory- and time-based models to competency-based training and assessment (CBTA). Going beyond mere technical knowledge and skills, CBTA requires valid assessment of transversal competencies such as communication, teamwork and work management. Yet, defining measurable and standardized assessment criteria remains challenging. This study proposes a framework to operationalise transversal competencies into performance-based standards using a four-round Delphi study with 22 international aircraft maintenance experts. The study also positions aircraft maintenance license education within the European Qualifications Framework (EQF). Results indicate that education should be provided at minimally EQF Level four, with elements at Level five. Additionally, for the most crucial and difficult transversal competencies and associated observable behaviours, the study specifies assessment contexts and performance levels, reaching between 81% and 100% expert agreement. The consensus-based results address a key gap in aircraft maintenance education and supports international standardisation for consistent practice worldwide.

TI Financing education for children with autism Spectrum disorder in
   Tanzania: Perspectives from parents and teachers
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Financing education; children with ASD; financial challenges; inclusive
   education; parents of children with ASD; teachers of children with ASD;
   Social Sciences; Education; Behavioral Sciences; Educational Psychology;
   Cognitive Psychology; Motivation
ID CHALLENGES; MOTHERS
AB Families and schools face significant financial pressure in meeting the needs of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This qualitative study explored the financial challenges encountered by parents and teachers in providing support to children with ASD in Tanzanian inclusive primary schools. Purposive sampling was used to select 20 parents and seven teachers of children with ASD from two schools. Semi-structured interviews were employed to collect data, and analysis was conducted thematically. The findings suggest that parents experience financial difficulties covering hospital-based therapeutic and rehabilitation expenses, paying school fees, and managing transportation costs to and from schools. Also, teachers encounter financial hardships covering transportation costs for home visits, emergency medical care when children fall sick or get accidents at school, and purchasing resources to support teaching and learning for children with ASD. Thus, the study recommends that the Tanzanian Government strengthen financial protection for children with ASD by expanding health insurance coverage to include therapies, rehabilitation, and educational services. to provide financial support to parents and teachers of children with ASD. This will reduce their financial pressure and enhance their capacity and motivation in the provision of consistent care and support for children with ASD.

TI Negotiation as discipline: the constitution of the early childhood
   subject in Thai digital households
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Foucault; technologies of the self; governmentality; digital media;
   early childhood; discourse analysis; parental negotiation
AB Within the cultural politics of digital childhood, much is now known about what young children do with screens and how much. Less attention has been paid to what kind of self the child is being given the conditions to become where parental authority operates through negotiation rather than prohibition. Drawing on Foucault's technologies of the self and Rose's account of governmentality, this study treats Thai early childhood households - where Buddhist-influenced norms of krengjai and extended-family caregiving sustain a long-standing repertoire of indirect, contingency-based parenting - as a revealing site for re-examining the cultural politics of negotiated authority in digital family life. In-depth interviews with five mothers and two early-childhood teachers, recruited through a single centre in north-eastern Thailand, were analysed alongside a reference corpus of publicly accessible YouTube and TikTok material that these adults named as the focal four- and five-year-old children's most frequently watched content. The children were neither interviewed nor observed, and account-level recommendation histories were unavailable; the study is therefore an interpretive reading of adult accounts rather than a demonstration of effects. Within these bounds, a Foucauldian discourse analysis generated three interpretive claims: (a) screen access is governed through a negotiated economy whose 'if-then' logic schools children in a particular operation upon the self; (b) imitation is best read not as social learning but as self-practice, a rehearsal of platform-supplied subject positions and (c) the parent functions as a relay through whom platform rationalities are translated into the child's emerging moral self-government.

TI Student experiences in a Sino-foreign cooperative undergraduate nursing
   programme: a qualitative study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Sino-foreign cooperative education; nursing education; undergraduate
   nursing students; hidden curriculum; qualitative research
ID EDUCATION
AB Background: Sino-foreign cooperative undergraduate programmes are an important form of internationalised nursing education in China, yet little qualitative research has examined how students experience them in practice. Objectives: To explore how undergraduate nursing students experienced and made sense of Sino-foreign cooperative undergraduate nursing programmes in China, and to identify perceived areas for improvement. Methods: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with undergraduate nursing students. Participants were purposively sampled. Interview questions were informed by the Context-Input-Process-Product (CIPP) framework. Data were analysed using inductive and framework-informed thematic analysis, with the CIPP framework supporting interpretation. Results: Students reported mixed experiences. Many valued internationalised learning and described gains in broader perspectives, resilience and proactive learning habits. They also reported challenges, including a hidden curriculum arising from perceived inconsistencies in expectations and standards across teaching teams. These difficulties were compounded by bilingual assessment demands and challenges in English academic expression, with students often relying on peer 'translation work' to interpret requirements. Limited opportunities to apply internationalised learning in local placements contributed to weak classroom-clinical transfer and uncertainty about readiness and future pathways. Students prioritised clearer assessment alignment, stronger classroom-clinical connections, and structured support for English development and internationally recognised licensure preparation. Conclusions: The findings suggest that the value of internationalised nursing education is shaped not only by access to international curricula or bilingual learning opportunities, but also by how students interpret and connect these experiences to assessment, local clinical practice, and future pathways. Greater alignment across these areas may strengthen the practical value of Sino-foreign cooperative nursing programmes.

TI Organizational cognitive overload and the production of everyday
   inequities in primary education: an integrative review Target article
   collection: Social Practices and (In)Equity in Primary Education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Organizational cognitive overload; educational inequity; teacher
   workload; social practices; institutional structures; policy
   implementation; school improvement
ID EMOTIONAL EXHAUSTION; STUDENT; CLASSROOM; EFFICACY; BURNOUT; LOAD
AB Primary schools are institutions of educational opportunity, yet routine practices of instruction, documentation, discipline, intervention, and accountability may also reproduce inequity. This integrative narrative review develops organizational cognitive overload as a framework for explaining how accumulated and fragmented demands may exceed a school's attentional, relational, interpretive, and implementation capacity. Literature was identified through targeted searches of ERIC, Education Source, APA PsycINFO, Scopus, and the Web of Science Core Collection conducted from January through July 2026, supplemented by Google Scholar citation tracing. Purposive conceptual sampling organized scholarship across seven domains, and a three-stage process of identification, comparison, and integration was used to synthesize recurring constructs and qualifying evidence. The synthesis distinguishes organizational cognitive overload from individual workload and burnout and proposes five dimensions of demand and five practice-level mechanisms: attentional fragmentation, interpretive narrowing, surface compliance, relational thinning, and institutional destabilization. Rather than treating overload as an independent cause of inequity, the framework explains how a demand-capacity imbalance may reduce the organizational resources available for contextual judgment, responsive relationships, and coherent implementation. Its distinctive contribution is a testable organizational model that integrates dispersed evidence while separating established component relationships from causal pathways that remain theoretical.

TI Becoming professional teachers: innovative practicum in
   school-university partnerships
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher education; innovative practicum; school-university partnerships;
   practice architectures; professional learning
ID EDUCATION
AB Practicum is a key component of teacher education (TE), yet student teachers often reproduce established practices rather than develop innovative approaches. This study explores how an innovative practicum in school-university partnerships enables student teachers to develop ownership of their practice and reshape their role within the professional community. The context for the study is an innovative practicum model developed through collaboration between partner schools and a TE institution. The data comprise meetings involving student teachers, mentor teachers and campus teachers and were analysed using thematic analysis, informed by the theory of Practice Architectures. The findings suggest that ownership emerged not simply through opportunities to experiment with innovative teaching approaches, but through a practicum design that deliberately redistributed responsibility for pedagogical decision-making. This supported student teachers in contributing expertise recognised by mentors and colleagues, reshaping traditional mentor-student relationships and supporting inquiry-oriented professional learning. The study contributes to research on TE by demonstrating that the potential of innovative practicum lies in the practice architectures that enable professional responsibility, reciprocal learning and collaborative inquiry. The findings have implications for the design of practicum in school-university partnerships seeking to prepare student teachers for increasingly complex and innovative educational contexts.

AB The study focuses on the experiences of undergraduate students with Learning Management Systems (LMSs) at a rural South African university, where digital pedagogy is constrained by infrastructural limitations, socio-cultural diversity, and historical inequalities. TI The effect of school climate on high school students' physics
   achievement using academic engagement as mediator
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE School Climate; Academic Engagement; Physics Achievement; Structural
   Equation Modeling; Parallel Mediation
ID PERFORMANCE; RELATEDNESS; CONTEXT; MATTERS
AB This study examines the mediating role of academic engagement in the relationship between school climate and physics achievement among secondary school students in Northwest Ethiopia. Using a correlational research design, data were collected via Likert-scale questionnaires from randomly selected Grade 11 and 12 students enrolled in the science stream. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was performed using AMOS version 24 to test the proposed theoretical model. The results revealed that the direct effect of perceived school climate on physics achievement was not statistically significant. Instead, perceived school climate influenced physics achievement indirectly through students' academic engagement. A more detailed analysis indicates that while the overall relationship is fully mediated, specific dimensions of academic engagement play distinct roles. Specifically, emotional engagement, characterized by student interest and enthusiasm, emerged as the most critical mediating factor compared to other dimensions. These findings emphasize that cultivating a positive school climate is a prerequisite for fostering the deep engagement required to improve student outcomes in a challenging subject like physics. Theoretically, this study contributes to a discipline-specific model of academic achievement, providing an evidence base for educators and policymakers to improve STEM performance by optimizing school climate quality.

TI Teacher-perceived multi-level influences on preparedness for inclusive
   vocational education in Namibia: basic prevocational skills course
   implementation
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Inclusive vocational education; teacher preparedness; theory of planned
   behaviour; basic prevocational skills course; teacher-perceived
   multi-level influences; special educational needs; Social Sciences;
   Development Studies, Environment, Social Work, Urban Studies; Education;
   Behavioural Sciences; Cognitive Psychology; Learning
ID SELF-EFFICACY; ATTITUDES; BELIEFS
AB Inclusive vocational education remains challenging in Namibia, where learners with diverse needs continue to experience unequal access to vocational learning opportunities. The Basic Prevocational Skills Course (BPVSC) was introduced to develop practical and foundational skills supporting employability, independent living and progression to further training. Although teachers are central to implementation, limited research has examined how they perceive preparedness for inclusive vocational teaching. This study examines teacher-perceived multi-level influences on preparedness for BPVSC implementation. Using qualitative, theory-informed content analysis, it analyses open-ended survey responses from 29 teachers across four regions in Namibia. The analysis focuses on perceived psychological, institutional and systemic influences, with institutional and policy processes interpreted through teachers' written responses. The findings suggest strong normative commitment to inclusion, alongside variation in confidence and perceived capability. Participants described tensions between inclusive intentions and classroom practice, linked to limited self-efficacy, resource constraints and uncertainty about adapting practical vocational tasks. Leadership practices, collegial relationships and institutional routines were described as enabling or constraining professional agency, while policy misalignment, uneven resource distribution and deficit-oriented perceptions of vocational education were perceived as shaping implementation. The study identifies sustained professional learning, supportive school conditions, coordinated implementation and policy-resource alignment as necessary for strengthening inclusive vocational education.

TI From policy to practice: Educator perspectives on the design and
   delivery of mental health education in independent Victorian secondary
   schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mental health education; mental health literacy; educator perspectives;
   curriculum; pedagogy; education policy
ID INTERVIEW; LITERACY; IMPROVE; PROMOTION; PROGRAMS
AB Mental health education in schools is widely recognised as critical to improving adolescent mental health; however, limited research has examined its design and delivery within Australian secondary schools. The policy context for mental health education exhibits fragmentation and ambiguity, alongside variability in approaches and limited evidence to guide practice. This study explored how educators within a single school sector navigate this complexity, drawing on interviews with eight educators across six independent Victorian secondary schools. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, informed by Bernstein's theories of curriculum and pedagogy and Kutcher et al.'s Mental Health Literacy model, to examine how educators interpret policy, construct curriculum, and enact pedagogical approaches. In this context, educators engaged in complex recontextualising work to establish local coherence within structural and practical constraints. While pedagogy generally aligned with research on effective pedagogical practices, variability was evident in curriculum content coverage when examined through a Mental Health Literacy lens. These findings highlight the interpretive and organisational demands placed on educators, the equity implications of locally contingent curriculum decisions, and the value of the Mental Health Literacy model in supporting coherent, comprehensive curriculum design.

TI Bridging minds and futures: the transformative power of innovative
   mathematics pedagogy in South African high schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Innovative pedagogy; learner-centered education; conceptual
   understanding; Critical Pedagogy; humanistic psychology; South African
   high schools
AB South African high school mathematics classrooms continue to face persistent conceptual underachievement and low learner engagement, particularly in under-resourced contexts. This mixed-methods study evaluates the effectiveness of an innovative learner-centered mathematics teaching strategy operationalized through the REACT teaching approach in bridging conceptual gaps among Grade 11 learners in South African high schools. Integrating principles of Critical Pedagogy and Humanistic Psychology, the research aims to empower learners through enhanced critical thinking, motivation, and self-directed growth, while challenging conventional teacher-centered methods. Employing a convergent parallel design, the study combines quantitative measures of conceptual understanding with qualitative insights into learner confidence, motivation, and agency. The sample includes 84 Grade 11 learners and four mathematics educators from diverse semi-rural and urban schools. Data collection involved pre-and post-intervention assessments on functions, alongside semi-structured interviews, learner reflections, focus groups, and classroom observations. Results indicate statistically significant improvements in learners' conceptual grasp of functions, with corresponding moderate effect sizes, complemented by qualitative evidence of heightened motivation, emotional engagement, and active participation. The findings underscore the value of blending cognitive and affective approaches in mathematics instruction. The study recommends sustained teacher professional development, improved resource provision, and the wider use of learner-centered, contextually relevant pedagogy to strengthen conceptual understanding and learner agency.

TI Reimagining doctoral supervision and mentorship in sub-Saharan Africa:
   evidence from Ethiopia, Kenya and Rwanda
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Doctoral education; PhD training; supervision; mentorship; gender
   equity; sub-Saharan Africa; Higher education; Policy; Social science
ID STUDENTS; UNIVERSITY; EDUCATION; CAPACITY; CONTEXT; WOMEN; PHD
AB Doctoral education is central to strengthening research capacity and advancing knowledge production in Sub-Saharan Africa. However, challenges in supervisory quality, mentorship systems, and institutional governance continue to constrain doctoral completion, productivity, and equity. Comparative empirical evidence on supervision and mentorship systems in African higher education remains limited. This study examines how governance arrangements, supervisory practices, and mentorship structures shape doctoral supervision ecosystems in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Rwanda. Using a mixed-methods design, it integrates survey data (n=154), interviews (n=27), and policy dialogues under the Regional Scholarship and Innovation Fund (RSIF). Guided by the Doctoral Supervision Ecosystem Framework, the study explores institutional dynamics influencing supervision practices. Results reveal three patterns. Supervision in Ethiopia and Kenya is largely individualized and administratively assigned, with limited accountability and uneven engagement. Rwanda demonstrates a more coordinated model characterized by supervisory teams, structured monitoring, and institutional oversight. Mentorship remains predominantly informal across contexts, with limited integration into governance systems. Gender disparities constrain access for female doctoral candidates. By conceptualizing supervision as an institutional ecosystem rather than an individual supervisory relationship, the study extends doctoral education scholarship by demonstrating how governance structures, mentorship systems, and gendered institutional dynamics collectively shape doctoral outcomes in Sub-Saharan African universities.

TI Governing the environment through language: agency, responsibility and
   silence in Pakistani state educational discourse
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical discourse analysis; environmental discourse; educational texts;
   ideology; agency; quality education; climate action
AB This article investigates how environmental issues are discursively governed in state-produced English textbooks used at the secondary level in Pakistan. The corpus comprises two English textbooks (Grades 9 and 10) published by the Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board and the Punjab Education, Curriculum, Training and Assessment Authority (PECTAA), which are officially prescribed for secondary-level education in Pakistan. Adopting a Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) approach, the study draws on Fairclough's three-dimensional framework . The analysis focuses on textbook units that address environmental themes, such as pollution, conservation and climate change. The findings suggest that environmental degradation is represented without clearly identifiable agents, while responsibility is framed as generalized and individualized. Institutional, political and economic actors are consistently backgrounded or omitted. These discursive patterns function to naturalize environmental harm and limit the scope of accountability within educational discourse. This study suggests that textbooks operate not only as pedagogical resources but also as sites of ideological work, where understandings of environmental responsibility are normalized. By foregrounding both linguistic patterns and strategic silences, the study contributes to ongoing debates on discourse, power and environmental governance in education, while also highlighting its relevance to global priorities such as quality education and climate action.

TI Youth moral development in a Chinese context: an empirical study of
   Self-Other Knowledge Asymmetry between self, parents, and teachers
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Moral development; self-report; significant others; SOKA; collective
   perceived traits
ID COLLECTIVE-EFFICACY; POSITIVE PSYCHOLOGY; PERSONALITY-TRAITS
AB Moral education and fostering youth character development have become the foci of Chinese moral education; yet most existing studies are confined to the Chinese education community and not shared with an international audience. This paper aims to bridge the gap between Chinese and Western explorations of moral education by engaging with the Self-Other Knowledge Asymmetry (SOKA) framework, thereby fostering cross-cultural dialogue and advancing theoretical understanding. More specifically, the objectives of the present study were twofold: first, to use a tried-and-tested instrument based on the Chinese Code for Primary and Secondary School Students to measure the moral status of primary and secondary school students in Suzhou, China. Second, instead of administering only a student self-report survey, as used in previous studies, the present study's design also involved the 'significant others' of these students, such as their teachers and parents, to observe the convergence and divergence between students' self-evaluations and those of their significant others. The study included 1040 students, 811 parents, and 276 teachers of these students. The study used multivariate analysis of variance and individual differences, as well as multidimensional scaling, to test five hypotheses. Although the significant others were not directly paired with the individual students, but explored on a whole-cohort basis, the results offer some interesting findings for further discussion. The results indicated that this study's hypotheses were not fully supported. However, these findings have significant implications for understanding SOKA from a collective perspective.

TI Assessing digital health curriculum needs: a mixed-methods study of
   student and faculty perspectives in a Singapore medical school
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence in healthcare; digital health; electronic health
   records; mixed-methods research; undergraduate medical education
AB Background The rapid advancement of digital technologies has transformed healthcare delivery, creating an imperative for medical education to integrate digital health (DH) competencies into undergraduate training. Despite growing recognition of its importance, progress in embedding DH literacy within formal medical curricula has been uneven and slow.Objective This study examined DH education within an undergraduate medical programme by integrating faculty and student perspectives to identify curriculum development needs and inform evidence-based educational strategies.Design A mixed-methods study was conducted at a Singapore medical school offering a 5-year undergraduate curriculum. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with four faculty members as DH content experts, exploring curriculum design, pedagogical strategies, and competency expectations. A 24-item survey assessing knowledge, attitudes, and usage of DH tools was administered to students across pre-clinical and clinical training, with 131 responses from 848 eligible participants. Qualitative data were analysed using grounded theory-based thematic analysis, whilst survey data were analysed using descriptive statistics.Results Faculty interviews identified three key themes: curriculum gaps requiring more practical and clinically-oriented DH teaching, structural barriers including time constraints and rapid technological change, and complex stakeholder ecosystem influencing curriculum development. Student survey results revealed a persistent theory-practice gap across DH domains. Students reported high self-perceived knowledge in DH applications and artificial intelligence (AI) but consistently lower confidence in practical application, particularly in electronic health records (EHR) and telemedicine. Clinical students paradoxically rated their EHR knowledge lowest despite greater clinical exposure. Students expressed strong interest in programming, data analytics, and hands-on AI, favouring applied DH skills with direct clinical relevance.Conclusions Medical curricula struggle to translate DH conceptual knowledge into practice, reconcile divergent competency expectations between students and faculty, and remain current amid rapid technological change. Tiered competency models, coupled with experiential learning approaches and continuous faculty development, represent a promising strategy for preparing future physicians for digitally enhanced healthcare delivery.Clinical trial number Not applicable.

TI Empowering chemistry and physics teachers' pedagogical knowledge through
   computer based simulations integrated with predict-observe-explain
   approach
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Computer-based simulations; predict-observe-explain; pedagogical
   knowledge; chemistry teaching; and physics teaching
AB Chemistry and Physics teaching in Rwanda's lower secondary schools is constrained by limited resources and conventional instructional approaches that may limit students' engagement and understanding of scientific concepts. This study examined the effects of integrating Computer-Based Simulations (CBS) combined with Predict Observe Explain (POE) approach on teachers' pedagogical practices. The study involved 40 Chemistry and Physics teachers purposively selected from public schools across 10 districts. Quantitative data were collected through surveys, lesson-plan analysis, and classroom observations, while qualitative data were obtained through semi-structured interviews. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively and qualitatively through thematic analysis. The results showed that regular use of simulations increased from 7.5% to 18.7%, furthermore, classroom observations indicated substantial improvements in content delivery (55.1% to 81.3%) and lesson design and implementation (52.5% to 78.1%). Classroom culture also improved significantly (p < 0.05; d = 0.47), while lesson-planning scores increased from 70.5% to 81.3% (p < 0.05; d = 0.28). Interview findings further indicated increased student participation and engagement. Thus, integrating CBS with the POE approach strengthen teachers' pedagogical practices and support more interactive science instruction. The study recommends sustained professional development in technology-enhanced pedagogies to strengthen science teaching in resource-constrained contexts.

TI Students' academic-integrity anxiety in the GenAI ethical grey zone
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; academic integrity; AI-related
   academic-integrity anxiety; higher education; Grammarly; writing anxiety
AB The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has created confusion about proper scholarly behaviour in assessment and research writing. The current study explores the perceptions and coping strategies adopted by university students regarding academic integrity fears under unclear expectations about the use of GenAI. Qualitative phenomenological research with personal, in-depth interviews was conducted with 14 students from an Australian university, using purposive sampling and phenomenological thematic analysis. Six themes emerged: Changing AI rules, Varying degrees of AI assistance, Efforts to use AI ethically, Defending authorship, Fear of asking for support, and Differing academic stakes. Uncertainties regarding authorship, disclosure, the potential for false-positive detections by AI detection software like Turnitin, and whether the AI-assisted work genuinely represented their intellectual contribution were the main causes of students' worries and dilemmas about the use of GenAI. Research students were anxious about their scholarly identity, credibility as researchers, and becoming independent scholars, whereas coursework students were more worried about grade consequences and potential accusations of misconduct. These findings imply that anxieties about academic integrity may extend beyond a fear of misconduct. We recommend that universities should provide fair procedures to address AI detection issues, clear and task-specific guidelines, and a secure space where students can ask questions without fear of suspicion.

TI Disability prevalence, disclosure, and accommodation use in pediatric
   residency: results from a pilot study
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Disability; residency; pediatrics; accommodations; disclosure
AB Introduction Disability inclusion in residency is essential to building a diverse and equitable physician workforce. Recent Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education requirements mandate that programs maintain formal disability policies and provide reasonable accommodations. However, residents with disabilities continue to face barriers, including stigma, complex documentation processes, and limited institutional infrastructure, challenges that differ from medical school settings. Specialty-specific data are necessary to identify gaps in inclusion, especially given that national data show higher rates of disability among trainees entering pediatrics. This pilot study reports the prevalence and accommodation practices of four pediatric residency programs.Methods In collaboration with the Association of Pediatric Program Directors Longitudinal Educational Assessment Research Network, we conducted the first pilot survey examining disability prevalence, disclosure patterns, and accommodation use among pediatric residents. The survey was distributed to four programs between April and October 2024. Data were analyzed descriptively, with Fisher's exact tests used to examine group differences.Results Of the sixty-nine respondents, 36% self-identified as having a disability, more than triple the national average for residents with disabilities. ADHD, chronic health conditions, and psychological disabilities were the most reported. Fear of stigma and lack of documentation issues emerged as barriers to requesting accommodations. First-generation college graduates were significantly more likely to be unsure of their disability status.Discussion This pilot study provides preliminary and important insights into disability prevalence, disclosure, disability uncertainty, and accommodation use in pediatric residency programs. While these findings suggest encouraging rates of accommodation receipt among disabled residents, they also highlight stigma and uncertainty around disability identity and disclosure. Findings should be interpreted in the context of the small sample size, the self-selected participation of programs, and potential response bias.

TI Promoting scientific problem-solving skills of Grade 7 students using
   phenomenon-based learning enhanced by argument-driven inquiry (ADI): a
   classroom action research model
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Phenomenon-based learning; argument-driven inquiry; scientific
   problem-solving skills; classroom action research; weather change
   processes
ID SCIENCE; FRAMEWORK; PHYSICS; DESIGN
AB This classroom action research aimed to (1) improve Grade 7 students' scientific problem-solving skills on the topic of weather change processes, and (2) evaluate learning management approaches using phenomenon-based learning (PhBL) enhanced by argument-driven inquiry (ADI). The participants were 35 Grade 7 students during the 2024 academic year, selected through purposive sampling. The study followed six cycles of action research. Research tools included six PhBL-based lesson plans (18 hours), pre- and post-tests with three open-ended problem scenarios and students' learning journals. Qualitative data from reflective notes and journals were analyzed using content analysis, while quantitative data from tests were examined through mean scores and relative development indices. Findings revealed significant improvement in students' problem-solving skills. The average score increased from 55.62% (good level) before the intervention to 80.67% (excellent level) after the PhBL-ADI activities, with a relative development index of 37.57% (moderate level). The six stages of PhBL instruction - exploring, understanding, investigating, modeling, synthesizing and communicating scientifically - were found to effectively support skill development. Correspondingly, students developed six sub-skills of problem solving: identifying problems, analyzing causes, searching for information, connecting relationships, evaluating solutions and presenting conclusions. This finding indicate that integrating PhBL with ADI can effectively - enhance scientific problem-solving skills in lower-secondary science education.

TI The intergenerational transmission of advantage: parental education,
   out-of-school engagement and mathematics achievement in 81 countries
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Parental education; students' out-of-school engagement; gendered
   mediation; non-linear effects; mathematics achievement
ID HABITUS
AB Parental education predicts academic success, but its transmission is often oversimplified. This study examines how students' out-of-school engagement, what Bourdieu called internalized family dispositions or 'habitus', mediates this relationship for mathematics achievement. Using 2022 PISA data from 613,744 students across 81 countries and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), we found that parental education positively impacts both engagement and achievement. However, specific engagements varied: studying and exercise improved scores, while household chores and paid work harmed them. Crucially, studying also served as a key pathway explaining how parental education translates into higher mathematics achievement. For practice, these findings suggest that raising parental education alone is insufficient. Schools and policymakers should focus on improving the quality of student engagement, providing financial support to reduce students' reliance on paid work and designing interventions that address gender-based differences in how maternal education versus paternal education benefits sons versus daughters.

TI Toward a resilient digital learner: examining institutional enablers and
   academic resiliency in online higher education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital resiliency; digital literacy; institutional support; academic
   resiliency; online learning; Arts & Humanities; Humanities; Media & Film
   Studies; Journalism & Professional Media; Publishing; Arts; Music; Music
   & Education; Early Years; Social Sciences; Education
AB The rapid growth of online learning has transformed higher education while increasing students' exposure to technostress, underscoring the need for stronger digital adaptation skills. This study examines how digital literacy (DL), learning flexibility (LF), institutional support (IS), and academic resiliency (AR) shape digital resiliency (DR) in online learning environments. Grounded in self-determination theory (SDT), this study integrates individual competencies and institutional enablers into a unified framework. Using a cross-sectional design, data were collected from 286 students at a public university in Indonesia and analysed with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The results show that DL and IS significantly enhance DR, while LF does not exhibit a direct effect. Additionally, AR strengthens the positive influence of IS on DR, indicating that resilient students are better able to translate institutional resources into adaptive digital behaviours. However, AR does not moderate the relationship between LF and DR. These findings highlight the essential roles of digital competence, institutional support, and psychological resilience in enabling students to cope with technological demands and thrive in digital learning environments. The study contributes to theory by integrating motivational, technological, and institutional factors and offers practical guidance for universities to align digital literacy initiatives, support services, and resilience-building strategies.

TI Developing teacher expertise through the Change Laboratory in a Japanese
   elementary school
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cultural-historical activity theory; Change Laboratory; teacher
   expertise; school transformation; expansive learning; transformative
   agency
AB This study investigates how a Change Laboratory intervention fostered teachers' professional learning and the emergence of new forms of expertise in a Japanese elementary school. Grounded in cultural-historical activity theory and its formative intervention methodology, it analyzes six Change Laboratory sessions conducted between September and December 2025 with the participation of all 23 teachers at the school. Through transcript-based chronological and contradiction analyses, the study traces how teachers' learning expanded without following a linear developmental trajectory. The findings indicate a shift from improving individual lessons to transforming the school as a collective activity system. By using conceptual tools such as the triangular model of the activity system and the four-field model, teachers developed collaborative and transformative expertise through the collective redesign of the object, instruments, rules, community, and division of labor of the school's activity system. These findings suggest that the Change Laboratory offers a powerful methodological framework and concrete methods to support teachers' collaborative and transformative agency in whole-school educational changes.

TI Positive thinking-integrated research-based learning in a digital
   ecosystem for promoting growth mindset among pre-service teachers: a
   randomized controlled trial
SO COGENT EDUCATION

DT Article
DE Research-based learning; positive thinking; digital learning ecosystem;
   growth mindset; pre-service teachers; Social sciences; Education;
   Teachers and teacher education; Higher education; Assessment; Teaching &
   Learning
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; INTERVENTIONS; ACHIEVEMENT
AB Pre-service teachers often struggle with research methodology due to anxiety and fixed beliefs rather than limited ability. This randomized controlled trial examined a multi-component instructional model integrating positive thinking dispositions and growth mindset characteristics within a six-phase Research-Based Learning framework delivered through a digital learning ecosystem. TI Construction and application of evaluation models for online learning
   behaviour
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Online learning behaviour; learning effectiveness; factor analysis; SVM;
   evaluation model
AB Online learning not only makes full use of online resources to meet the diverse learning needs of students but also enhances their autonomy and information acquisition abilities. Through learning analysis techniques, the quality of online learning can be improved, thereby enabling evaluation, diagnosis, prediction, and intervention in learning. Based on the Ulearning platform, this study used 792 undergraduate course score data from 2023, divided students' online learning behaviours into different indicators, and performed exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) on the students' online learning data to verify the feasibility of the learning evaluation model indicators. Then, through the demand analysis of teaching decisions, the dataset was split by K-fold cross-validation, a nonlinear support vector machine (SVM) was used to optimize the hyperparameters to establish an online learning behaviour evaluation model. The experimental results show that factor analysis effectively extracts three core factors (Platform usage intensity, Learning behavior, Effective learning intensity) affecting academic performance and greatly reduces data dimensionality. The proposed model achieves a high coefficient of determination (R-2) of 0.960 and a low root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.194, demonstrating outstanding predictive performance and strong generalization ability. This method provides a reference basis for further improving students' online learning effectiveness and can be extended to student modeling in other types of learning activities. More importantly, it can capture the interdependence between different aspects of students' learning experiences and learning outcomes, thereby guiding teachers to better carry out teaching work, make early interventions, and allocate resources more effectively.

TI Data subject access requests as an interdisciplinary learning tool
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Interdisciplinary education; technology regulation; data protection;
   personal data; data access rights
AB The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) gives data subjects the right to obtain a copy of their data, as well as information regarding the purposes of the processing, categories of personal data collected, recipients to whom this data has been disclosed, data retention periods and whether automated decision-making or profiling have been undertaken. This article describes our experience using data subject access requests (DSARs) as a learning tool in an international higher education setting. Our pedagogical practice centred around a group-based assignment in which students performed DSARs, recorded the fulfilment process, and examined the received data. This format enabled the deployment of DSARs for practice-based learning by students from different disciplinary backgrounds. In the three years during which we have used DSARs in this manner, we have established that they provide a starting point for fruitful discussions regarding the legal and technical aspects of personal data processing. The pedagogical value of DSARs derives from their ability to motivate the students to navigate the complexities of obtaining and understanding data about them held by various platforms. This radically transforms the discussion about data rights from potentially fairly abstract into a tangible, close and relevant exploration of complex categories and concepts.

TI Enhancing pre-service teachers' self-efficacy to educate critical online
   readers
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pre-service teachers; teacher self-efficacy; online credibility
   evaluation; design principles; intervention; Basic Education; Education;
   Educational Psychology; Higher Education; Literacy; Social Sciences;
   Teacher Education
ID REFLECTION; BELIEFS; IMPACT
AB With growing concerns about mis- and disinformation online, teachers play an important role in educating critical online readers. To fulfill this responsibility, they must feel confident in teaching online credibility evaluation skills. To address this issue, we conducted two studies in two Finnish universities among Finnish-speaking pre-service teachers. In Study I, we developed a teacher self-efficacy measure for online credibility evaluation, including three dimensions: self-efficacy in discipline-specific online credibility evaluation, self-efficacy in general online credibility evaluation, and self-efficacy in teaching online credibility evaluation. Results indicated that three dimensions were distinct but highly correlated. In Study II, we applied the developed measure to assess the efficacy of a university course grounded in five design principles for enhancing pre-service teachers' self-efficacy in online credibility evaluation. We employed a quasi-experimental pre-post test design with intervention and control groups and conducted a qualitative analysis of pre-service teachers' written reflections to enrich quantitative results. The course enhanced pre-service teachers' self-efficacy, particularly in teaching online credibility evaluation skills, as also evidenced by their reflections on benefits of several course elements. Results suggest that pre-service teachers benefit from opportunities to practice and reflect on their own credibility evaluation skills and, in collaboration with peers, to carefully design and implement classroom instruction for online credibility evaluation.

TI Surveilled childhood: a Foucauldian-Vygotskian critique of youth
   development in the digital age
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Youth development; digital surveillance; Foucauldian-Vygotskian
   framework; identity formation; digital panopticon; emotional regulation
ID DATAVEILLANCE; TECHNOLOGIES; DATAFICATION; EDUCATION; CHILDREN
AB This paper examines how digital surveillance reshapes youth development through a Foucauldian-Vygotskian lens, synthesizing Foucault's concepts of disciplinary power and biopolitics with Vygotsky's theories of social mediation and internalization. It argues that surveillance technologies-ranging from algorithmic monitoring to biometric tracking-embed disciplinary power into developmental processes, shaping identity formation, emotional regulation, and agency. By comparing historical precedents, such as the Soviet youth project, with contemporary digital surveillance, the paper demonstrates the continuity of power dynamics in shaping childhood experiences. This Foucauldian-Vygotskian synthesis highlights the paradox of digital surveillance, revealing how normative regulation and youth agency emerge simultaneously within surveilled environments. Youth navigate these conditions by curating digital identities, strategically performing algorithmically acceptable behaviors while cultivating private selves. The paper concludes by proposing strategies for educational reform, privacy protections, and ethical technology design, emphasizing the need to balance the benefits of surveillance with youth autonomy and emotional agency to mitigate harms and support self-determination.

TI Socioeconomic and academic correlates of dropout intention in higher
   education: Cross-sectional evidence from a colombian public university
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student retention; dropout intention; higher education; logistic
   regression; academic satisfaction; first-generation students
ID LEARNING ANALYTICS
AB Student retention is a major challenge for higher education because withdrawal is associated with substantial academic, social, and financial costs. This cross-sectional study examines demographic, socioeconomic, academic, and support-related factors associated with dropout intention among undergraduate students at the National University of Colombia, La Paz campus. Using a web-based survey of 333 students collected between August and December 2025, representing 25.2% of the target population of 1,323 enrolled undergraduates, the analysis constructs a five-point dropout intention index and estimates nested ordered logistic regression models, Spearman correlations, and average marginal effects. First-generation status (OR = 1.76, 95% CI [1.17, 2.65], p = 0.007) and living in rented housing (OR = 1.55, 95% CI [1.02, 2.35], p = 0.040) were associated with higher dropout intention. In contrast, program satisfaction (OR = 0.64, 95% CI [0.49, 0.83], p = 0.001) and positive perceptions of labor-market opportunities (OR = 0.79, 95% CI [0.63, 0.99], p = 0.037) were associated with lower dropout intention. Average marginal effects indicate that first-generation students had a 7.18 percentage-point higher predicted probability of reporting high dropout intention, whereas each additional point in program satisfaction was associated with a 4.31 percentage-point lower probability. The findings should be interpreted as associational evidence from a single regional campus and suggest that retention strategies should address both academic experience and socioeconomic vulnerability.

TI Student misbehavior and teacher coping strategies in EFL classes in
   Iranian High Schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Classroom management; coping strategies; EFL teachers; demographic
   characteristics; student misbehavior; organizational characteristics;
   Social Sciences; Education; Teachers & Teacher Education
ID CLASSROOM MANAGEMENT; PERCEPTIONS
AB Foreign language teaching faces numerous pedagogical challenges, with student misbehavior being a major concern. Considering its effects on teaching and learning, teachers need effective strategies to manage student misbehavior. Thus, this study explored the most common student misbehaviors experienced by Iranian high school English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers and probed the types of and differences in their coping strategies based on demographic and organizational characteristics. To this aim, data was collected from 144 high school EFL teachers through an adapted questionnaire. The results of the study revealed talking with friends and making noise as the most frequent student misbehaviors in classrooms . Additionally, addressing misbehaving students by name to gain attention, staring, and moving closer to students to manage behavior were the most frequently used coping strategies among EFL teachers. The study also indicated that while EFL teachers' experience of student misbehavior differed with differences in demographic (educational degree) and organizational characteristics (school type), their coping strategies differed just with changes in their demographic characteristics (marital status, age, experience). This study also provides valuable insights into the student misbehavior-coping strategies used by different groups of EFL teachers to address student misbehavior, and offers practical implications for EFL teachers, teacher educators, teacher trainers, and administrators.

TI Sentiment and collaboration in online learning: positive interactions
   predict higher relational satisfaction
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Sentiment; group relational satisfaction; collaborative performance;
   task typology; virtual collaboration; online meeting; online interaction
ID PSYCHOLOGICAL SAFETY; EGO DEPLETION; TEAMWORK; MODEL; SELF
AB In the evolving landscape of educational and professional settings, effective collaboration emerges as a cornerstone of success, particularly in hybrid environments that blend virtual and in-person interactions. However, the competencies that need to be developed to support effective online collaborations remain elusive. This study employs a 15-category custom sentiment lexicon analysis to distil whether specific interpersonal competencies in pairs of undergraduate students during a naturalistic online seminar could influence both group relational satisfaction and task performance. 30 pairs of undergraduate participants (N = 60) participated in a structured 40-minutes online seminar that included a pre-recorded lecture, a discussion activity and a presentation of the discussed content. To capture the different types of collaborations that could occur in the real-world, three types of between-subject discussion activities were conducted: Cognitive Conflict, Brainstorming and Problem-solving, with 10 pairs assigned to each task condition. Recorded transcripts during the discussion activity were analysed for positive, negative and neutral clusters of sentiments. Presentation slides were scored based on a standardised rubric. Our results showed that the Cognitive Conflict task evoked greater negative sentiments compared to the other tasks. Findings demonstrated that positive sentiments (e.g. providing verbal agreement on task process, words of encouragement, greetings and praise for work completed) were found to significantly enhance group relational satisfaction. These findings have direct pedagogical application, as educators can hone these distilled behavioural competencies to better support collaboration in online learning settings.

TI Second-year undergraduate student engagement scale development: a
   proof-of-concept study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student engagement; wellbeing; scale development; student engagement
   scale; second-year undergraduates
AB This article reports on the Second-Year Undergraduate Student Engagement Scale (SU-SES), developed during a mixed-methods study of second-year undergraduate students. The SU-SES comprises 50 statements measuring five dimensions of engagement: (1) personal growth, (2) class engagement (CE), (3) beyond class engagement (BCE), (4) relational engagement (RE) and (5) preparedness and transition engagement. Scale development was informed by a review of the literature, eight focus groups with second-year students (n = 19) and the professional expertise of the author team. Following focus groups, a sample of 415 second-year students completed the SU-SES. Cronbach's alpha (alpha) and Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) were used to test the reliability and validity of the SU-SES. Cronbach's alpha indicated moderate to high reliability of SU-SES items. EFA was conducted with the items using Principal Axis Factoring extraction and Promax rotation. Findings indicated that the SU-SES demonstrated acceptable psychometric properties, with factor analytic procedures supporting the retention of 42 items across five dimensions of engagement and reliability coefficients indicating moderate to high internal consistency, indicating that the SU-SES appears to be a reliable and valid measure of engagement among second-year undergraduate students. A more robust study is needed to confirm this and further explore the SU-SES.

TI How do students seek feedback in the generative AI era? Exploring the
   role of generative AI affordances and social motivations
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Feedback-seeking behavior; generative artificial intelligence;
   affordance; communion motivation; defensive image motivation
ID GOAL ORIENTATION; RESOURCE; MOTIVES
AB Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping students' feedback-seeking behavior (FSB) in higher education through its capacity for adaptive content generation and immersive collaborative dialogue. However, the specific mechanisms through which GenAI influence FSB remain underexplored. Drawing on affordance theory and motivation frameworks, this mixed-methods study examined the influence of GenAI affordances and students' social motivations on FSB. We surveyed 286 university students with GenAI experience in China, followed by semi-structured interviews with 12 selected students. The principal findings emerged. (1) Among the two motivations examined, defensive image motivation inhibited FSB, while communion motivation promoted FSB. (2) Field affordance emerged as the most critical aspect of GenAI's impact on FSB, significantly reducing inhibition of defensive image motivation to some extent. (3) Technology affordance solely statistically enhanced feedback monitoring, while content affordance demonstrated no significant impact on FSB. (4) FSB in GenAI contexts was a strategic, situated decision process. The implications for designing GenAI-enhanced feedback environments and cultivating GenAI-enabled feedback literacy were discussed.

TI Smart starts: a curriculum-based screening tool for at-risk students
   with learning disabilities in Thai language at the early elementary
   level
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning disabilities; early screening tool; Thai language education;
   primary education; early intervention; Social Sciences; Education;
   Behavioral Sciences; Educational Psychology; Cognitive Psychology;
   Motivation
AB This study presents the development and validation of a curriculum-based screening tool to monitor and identify early elementary students at risk of learning disabilities in Thai reading. The research consisted of three phases: (1) designing and validating the tool; (2) pilot testing; and (3) revising for efficiency. Participants were 2,955 students in Grades 1-3 in Bangkok selected through simple random sampling. Six tool versions were created, tailored to grade levels and semesters. The tools showed strong psychometric properties. Content validity achieved high IOC scores. Pilot testing indicated item difficulty of 0.17-0.93, discrimination indices above 0.35, and high internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha = 0.87-0.98). The finalized tools included T-score conversion tables and classified students into four proficiency levels. This tool provides teachers with a reliable mechanism for early identification and timely intervention, supporting inclusive practices. By directly mapping the four T-score proficiency tiers onto a Response to Intervention (RTI) framework, the tool enables teachers to deliver immediate, differentiated classroom support ranging from targeted small group drills to intensive specialist interventions. However, since the participants was restricted to urban Bangkok, caution is warranted regarding its generalizability to rural or linguistically diverse regions, and future studies should explore its predictive validity.

TI Motivation and barriers to physicians' academic career in
   gastroenterology in France
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic motivation; career advancement; gastroenterology; gender
   inequities; glass ceiling; medicine
ID MEDICINE; LEADERSHIP; STUDENTS; FACULTY; PROGRAM; GENDER; SCALE; TIME
AB Background The decline in residents' interest in academic career, as well as high rates of dissatisfaction and intention to leave among academic physicians, have been reported in various medical specialties. Academic motivation remains underexplored among residents and university hospital faculty staff, particularly in gastroenterology, where the private sector is highly developed.Objective We aimed at investigating (i) motivational drivers and potential barriers to academic career decidedness in gastroenterology residents, and (ii) professional achievement and challenges experienced by academic physicians in gastroenterology in France.Design We conducted a descriptive cross-sectional quantitative study by distributing structured online questionnaires to all French gastroenterology residents and university hospital faculty staff between June 2024 and November 2024. Factors associated with academic motivation and perceived difficulties in career progression were identified by regression analysis.Results Seventy-five graduate physicians and 136 medical residents participated. A large proportion of gastroenterology residents (36.0%) declared considering the academic career, with a significant underrepresentation of female residents. The only differential barriers between females and males to academic decidedness were the lack of self-confidence in scientific skill for females and the insufficient salary for male residents. The academic motivation of university hospital faculty staff was lower in women and in early- and mid-career physicians. Decreased academic motivation was associated with poor confidence in scientific skill, no or few mentors, increased time dedicated to clinical activity, and perception of gender inequities in career advancement, reported by 57.6% of female physicians. Maintaining work-family balance was a major challenge for all.Conclusions This study suggests the need to improve exposure to research among medical trainees, with a specific focus on women, to enhance the appeal of their academic career. In tenured and non-tenured university hospital faculty staff, mentoring development, workload adjustment including protected time for research, and combating gender inequities are major challenges for improving academic gastroenterology.

TI Both privileged and disadvantaged: multiple identities of a Japanese
   female academic in an Australian university
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Japanese female academic; Australian higher education;
   intersectionality; multiple identities; privilege; disadvantage; Social
   Sciences; Education; Education Policy & Politics; Education Policy;
   Curriculum; Philosophy of Education; Moral & Values Education;
   Primary/Elementary Education; By Subject; Geography
ID AUTOETHNOGRAPHY; INTERSECTIONALITY; COLOR; TESOL
AB The study is an autoethnography of the researcher's multiple identities as a Japanese female academic who works at an Australian university, focusing on her feelings of both privilege and disadvantage. Asian female academics who work for universities in Western countries tend to find their ethnicities and cultural backgrounds a disadvantage, especially in the current competitive neoliberal environment. The researcher considers her own self-narratives about her different identities, experiences related to those identities, and her consequent feelings of privilege or disadvantage. She analyzes the narratives with thematic analysis and discovers four major themes related to her identities: (1) identities as a native speaker of Japanese and as a user of English as a second language; (2) identities related to her cultural background; (3) identities as a group member of the university and related to her roles; and (4) identities related to her gender. Using intersectionality as a theoretical framework, the study contributes to our understanding of the experiences of minority academics in Western universities by uncovering the intersectional complexities of the researcher's multiple identities, which are affected by sociopolitical and institutional structures and by issues of power, as well as by her linguistic and cultural background and her gender.

TI "It was kind of abusive": gender, power and inequity in Australian
   tertiary jazz education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gender; discrimination; tertiary education; jazz; consensual sexual
   relationships; microaggressions
ID MUSIC
AB Recent feminist research is identifying how the gendered power dynamics of creative industries are replicated within tertiary education programs. This article contributes to this scholarship by examining problematic aspects of jazz and improvisation at tertiary institutions in Australia. It presents a close reading of interviews in which four jazz musicians - of whom three identify as female and one as trans - reflect on their tertiary education experiences. Extending Amia Srinivasan's concept of gendered 'pedagogical failures' beyond consensual sexual relationships to also take in gendered microaggressions, our analysis focuses on how the actions of predominantly male teaching staff negatively impact the wellbeing of female and gender minority students. Our identification of the gendered harms arising from the intersection of academia and jazz in this localised setting allows us to articulate cultural and structural measures institutions can take to foster student wellbeing.

TI Intersection of diagnosis strategy and support in the educational
   journey of students with learning disabilities
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Labels; learning; diagnosis; strategy; support; educational journey;
   students with learning disabilities; Social Sciences; Education;
   Behavioral Sciences; Educational Psychology; Cognitive Psychology;
   Motivation
AB The purpose of this study was to understand how the combination of accurate diagnosis, good teaching methods, and supportive systems affects the learning experiences of students with learning disabilities. The study used a quantitative approach to describe the situation. A questionnaire based on existing research and local conditions was given to 330 teachers. Teachers were chosen randomly from different schools. The questionnaire was checked for accuracy by experts, and its reliability was confirmed using Cronbach's Alpha, which was more than 0.70. The data was analyzed using SPSS with both descriptive and statistical methods. The results showed that teachers generally agreed on the importance of proper diagnosis, effective teaching, and a supportive learning environment. However, there were differences in how teachers viewed these aspects, depending on factors like their age, education level, job position, experience, and where they worked. Teachers in urban areas and those with a master's degree had more positive views, while teachers in rural areas were also very committed, possibly because of the challenges they face. The study highlights the need for better training for teachers, smart use of available resources, and efforts to make all education settings more inclusive.

TI Challenges, safeguards, and professional learning needs for AI
   integration: insights from a two-week AI literacy module with preservice
   teachers
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; preservice teachers; teacher education; professional
   learning needs; challenges of AI; safeguards of AI
AB Preservice teachers (PSTs) often have limited preparation for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) in pedagogically meaningful and ethically responsible ways, while teacher education programs face practical constraints in providing sustained, practice-based AI preparation. This exploratory single-case study examined how 29 PSTs participating in a two-week, ethics-embedded AI literacy module within a required technology integration course anticipated and/or experienced challenges, proposed and/or enacted safeguards, and identified professional learning supports for responsible AI integration. Using a qualitatively driven mixed-methods design, data were drawn from reflections, structured AI tool evaluations, group lesson plans, and a post-module questionnaire. Findings showed that PSTs' challenges clustered around ethical, pedagogical, and technical issues. Across artifacts, PSTs most readily translated concerns into visible, teacher-led safeguards related to data protection, verification of AI outputs, bounded use, teacher mediation, and attribution or critique, but were less consistent in operationalizing safeguards related to bias, fairness, and AI's instructional authority. PSTs also identified ongoing needs for professional learning related to ethical use, technical fluency and prompting, foundational AI understanding, and curriculum-aligned integration. The findings offer design-relevant insight into how AI-related concerns surfaced in PSTs' evaluative and instructional design work, including which safeguards were more readily operationalized and which required more support.

TI The future of CALL in Pakistan: digital inequality, institutional
   support and global solutions female students in public women's
   universities
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE CALL adoption and perception; higher education; Pakistan; socioeconomic
   barriers; global solutions; women students
AB This study investigates barriers to the adoption of Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) and explores equitable policy solutions to enhance digital language learning in Punjab, Pakistan. It focuses on three objectives: (1) analyzing CALL adoption and students' perceptions, (2) identifying socioeconomic and institutional barriers to access and use and (3) evaluating systematic solutions from both developed and underdeveloped countries. A mixed-method approach was used, including a quantitative cross-sectional survey and a qualitative literature review. A structured questionnaire was distributed via Google Forms to 84 final-year undergraduate students from three public women universities in three major cities of Punjab including Sialkot, Lahore and Faisalabad, selected through purposive sampling. Descriptive statistics were analyzed using the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, while a critical discourse analysis of literature offered global insights. Results show occasional use of CALL tools, with Google Classroom (28%), Duolingo (22%) and Moodle (18%) being the most used; however, only 26% of students reported weekly use. Major barriers include financial constraints, reliance on mobile data, limited institutional support, lack of CALL integration in curricula and insufficient faculty training. The study recommends government-funded digital infrastructure, faculty training, localized CALL content and public-private partnerships to reduce the digital divide and promote equitable access to digital language education.

TI Understanding mechanisms of learning: a realist evaluation of the MRes
   research methods module
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teaching-research nexus; realist evaluation; research methods;
   supervisory support; context-mechanism-outcome; higher education;
   student learning
ID FRAMEWORK; NEXUS
AB This study conducted a realist evaluation of an MRes Research Module to identify what mechanisms enable or hinder learning, for whom, and in what contexts, to inform more effective and equitable postgraduate research training. Research methods training is a cornerstone of postgraduate education supporting students in independent research. However, its effectiveness varies, and there is limited understanding of how teaching strategies produce different outcomes for diverse students. A qualitative, realist evaluation approach was employed, analysing postgraduate student experiences through the Context-Mechanism-Outcome (CMO) framework to explain how and why specific strategies succeeded or failed. Ten MRes Bioengineering students were purposively recruited to ensure representation across a wide range of disciplines. Data were collected through a qualitative survey capturing their perceptions and experiences of the Research Methods Module. Workshops, authentic assessments and field-specific supervision were identified as effective mechanisms for learning. However, generic materials and inconsistent support hindered progress. This study proposes the 'Adaptive Nexus Model for Postgraduate Training', a practice-oriented framework that maps context-sensitive learning pathways across dry-lab, wet-lab, and computational disciplines. It shows that teaching effectiveness depends on disciplinary alignment and supervisory engagement, offering programme leaders actionable guidance to improve equity of learning outcomes across diverse cohorts.
