TI Tracing positive psychology threads in ELT textbooks through the lens of
   EMPATHICS vision
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE EMPATHICS; English language teaching textbooks; learner well-being;
   positive psychology; Q-method; Social Sciences; Education; Adult
   Education and Lifelong Learning; Work-based Learning; Philosophy of
   Education; Research Methods in Education
ID LEARNER AUTONOMY; LANGUAGE; EMOTIONS
AB This study seeks to explore the extent to which positive psychology (PP) principles, particularly those expressed in Oxford's () 'EMPATHICS' model, have been applied in two English Language Teaching (ELT) textbook series: Headway and Touchstone. The EMPATHICS model consists of nine dimensions, each of which represents psychological constructs that contributes to learner well-being and language acquisition. Utilizing sequential exploratory mixed-methods design, the study drew on expert consultation using Q methodology to operationalize the selected dimensions of EMPATHICS model (i.e. Emotion and Empathy, Meaning and Motivation, Agency and Autonomy, Time, and Intelligences) into observable indicators for textbook evaluation and assessed content validity of indicators using the Content Validity Index. The results show the frequency of incorporated PP principles in ELT materials which can potentially contribute to learner well-being. Findings revealed differences in the degree to which PP principles were embedded across the two series. While Touchstone integrated broader range of EMPATHICS dimensions - particularly Emotion and Empathy, Meaning and Motivation, and Agency and Autonomy - Headway demonstrated more uneven representation, with stronger emphasis on linguistic form and less attention to these dimensions. Pedagogical implications and future research directions centered on affective and cognitive dimensions of ELT materials are also presented.

TI Teacher support and parental support as key predictors of early
   childhood social-emotional development: the role of teacher
   certification and training
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher support; parental support; social-emotional development; early
   childhood education; PLS-SEM; Social Sciences; Education; Childhood;
   Behavioral Sciences; Developmental Psychology; Moral Development
ID EDUCATION
AB Early childhood social-emotional development represents a critical foundation for long-term academic and psychosocial outcomes. Despite extensive research on teacher-child relationships and parental involvement, limited empirical models have integrated interpersonal support and structural professional factors within a unified predictive framework. This study investigates the roles of Teacher Support (TS) and Parental Support (PS) as key predictors of Social-Emotional Development (SED), while examining the contributions of Teacher Certification and Training within an integrated structural model. A quantitative explanatory design was employed involving 411 early childhood teachers selected through stratified random sampling. Data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that parental support significantly predicts children's social-emotional development, while teacher support exerts both direct and indirect effects through increased parental involvement. Conversely, Teacher Certification and Training do not demonstrate significant direct or moderating influences on developmental outcomes. The model explains 78.3% of the variance in social-emotional development, indicating strong predictive capability. Importantly, it should be noted that Parental Support and Social-Emotional Development were assessed through teacher-reported proxy measures, reflecting teachers' perceptions of parental involvement and children's observable social-emotional behaviours, rather than through direct parent or child self-reports. These results highlight the dominant role of relational support mechanisms over formal structural qualifications in shaping early childhood developmental trajectories.

TI From surface to deep learning: a comparative experiment into digital
   learning effectiveness
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Learning effectiveness; surface learning; deep learning; digital
   learning & conventional learning; digital learning; conventional
   learning
ID EDUCATION; COURSES
AB This study investigated whether online learners demonstrate learning gains comparable to those of on-campus learners in terms of lower- and higher-order thinking skills when taught by the same lecturer in the same subject area. Using a quasi-experimental design, a real-time, head-to-head comparison was conducted involving 37 online and 40 on-campus students enrolled in a Bachelor of Construction Management. Although no statistically significant differences were found in the mean scores of the two groups across the three assessment levels (i.e. 0.618 > 0.05, 0.174 > 0.05, and 0.865 > 0.05), the interview results indicated that the effectiveness of online learning varied significantly depending on the strategies employed. Gamified exercises and guided learning activities, supported by reinforcement strategies were more effective for surface learning, whereas roleplay simulations, reflective writing, and self-directed problem-solving activities supported deep learning. The study concludes that learning effectiveness is influenced less by the mode of delivery and more by teachers' creativity in tailoring instructional strategies to students' learning pace and needs, as well as, students' readiness and timing. While the study findings are transferable to similar educational contexts, generalisations should be made with caution, as the experiment was limited to a single subject and involved non-randomised participants.

AB This study develops and empirically validates an integrated Child-Friendly Islamic Boarding School (Pesantren Ramah Anak [PRA]) model by synthesizing *maq & amacr;sid al-syar & imacr;'ah* with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). TI Anti-racist approach to participant observation methods in educational
   research
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Participant observation; anti-racist paradigm; equity; community-based
AB This conceptual paper examines how participant observation in communitybased educational research can either reproduce racial inequities or advance anti-racist commitments. Drawing on a methodological rupture experienced by our research team while working alongside out-of-school time educators in a racial equity initiative, we critically examine the tensions between conventional participant observation practices and anti-racist, community-centered research. We consider how researcher positionality, institutional affiliation, power, and traditional notions of observation can inadvertently reproduce racialized surveillance and outsider-driven knowledge production. In response, we propose an anti-racist participant observation framework that reimagines observation as a relational, reflexive, and equity-centered practice. The framework emphasizes critically examining power, challenging deficit perspectives, centering community knowledge and lived experiences, and aligning research processes with anti-racist commitments.

TI Initial psychometric validation of the Critical Thinking Disposition
   Scale for Indonesian university students
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical thinking disposition; initial psychometric validation;
   exploratory factor analysis; higher education; Indonesian university
   students
ID RECOMMENDATIONS
AB Critical thinking disposition is a key component of students' reasoning and decision-making in higher education. However, validated instruments for assessing this construct in the Indonesian context remain limited. This study aimed to adapt the Critical Thinking Disposition Scale (CTDS) into Indonesian and to provide initial psychometric validation among university students. A total of 504 students from 24 universities across Indonesia participated in the study. Data were analyzed using exploratory factor analysis with Principal Axis Factoring and Direct Oblimin rotation. The results indicated adequate sampling suitability, with a high Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin value and a significant Bartlett's Test of Sphericity. A two-factor structure emerged, explaining 53.94% of the total variance, and the 11-item scale demonstrated strong internal consistency. These findings provide initial evidence that the Indonesian version of the CTDS is a reliable instrument for assessing students' critical thinking dispositions. However, the absence of confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) limits the strength of the structural validation, and future research is recommended to further examine the scale using CFA and more diverse samples.

AB This qualitative case study examines how technologically enriched Innovative Learning Environments (ILEs) support the development of Innovation Consciousness (IC) among in-service teachers. TI Validating the HEQAM model in a post-conflict higher education system:
   Evidence from Somalia
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Higher education quality; career Prospects; E-service; infrastructure;
   HEQAM; Social Sciences; Education; Higher Education; Study of Higher
   Education; Teaching & Learning
AB This study assesses the measurement and structural validity of the Higher Education Quality Assessment Model (HEQAM) in Somalia's post-conflict context, examining eight quality dimensions: curriculum structure, academic staff quality, career prospects, infrastructure, administrative services, library services, e-services, and institutional location. Using a quantitative cross-sectional survey of 1,803 undergraduate students from five universities in the Benadir region, partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) evaluated the measurement model and structural paths, with career prospects as the focal outcome. The measurement model demonstrated adequate reliability and construct validity. In the structural model, infrastructure (beta=0.346), academic staff quality (beta=0.330), and curriculum structure (beta=0.306) were the strongest positive predictors of career prospects, explaining 48.6% of its variance (R<^>2=0.486). Library services (beta=-0.057) and institutional location (beta = -0.064) showed small, statistically significant negative associations with career prospects, reflecting potential mismatches with student employability expectations. Additionally, curriculum structure and staff quality positively predicted e-services (beta=0.121; beta=0.288), but e-services did not predict career prospects, yielding no support for mediation. Overall, findings validate HEQAM in a fragile-state setting, highlighting curriculum relevance, staff quality, and infrastructure as priority levers to enhance student-perceived employability in Somalia.

AB This study examined university students' discontinuance intention towards AI-mediated informal digital learning of English (AI-IDLE). Grounded in the cognition-affect-conation (CAC) framework and informed by appraisal-based accounts of emotion, the study modelled disconfirmation, perceived complexity, and perceived risk as post-adoption cognitive appraisals; dissatisfaction and frustration as distinct affective responses; and discontinuance intention as the conative outcome. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 746 Chinese university students who had experience using AI tools for informal English learning. Data were analysed using structural equation modelling (SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). The SEM results showed that dissatisfaction and frustration positively predicted discontinuance intention, with frustration showing the stronger effect. All three cognitive appraisals positively influenced both affective responses. The fsQCA results identified multiple sufficient configurations leading to high discontinuance intention, demonstrating causal complexity and equifinality. The findings specify an appraisal-emotion-withdrawal mechanism for AI-IDLE while indicating that negative affect is not inherently discontinuance-producing: it is more likely to become inhibitory when learners experience persistent goal obstruction and limited perceived control. The study extends AI-IDLE research from adoption and engagement to post-adoption disengagement and offers implications for designing more manageable, trustworthy, and pedagogically useful AI-supported learning experiences.

TI Intersecting vulnerabilities: factors contributing to pregnancy among
   learners with disabilities in two Namibian resource schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Resource schools; inclusive education; learners with disabilities;
   inclusive and equitable quality education; SRHRE
ID INTELLECTUAL DISABILITIES; ADOLESCENTS
AB Learners with disabilities face compounded vulnerabilities that increase their risk of pregnancy while at school. Yet, research on the factors contributing to learner pregnancy in Namibian resource schools remains scarce. This qualitative study, guided by an intersectional, examined the factors contributing to learner pregnancy in two Namibian resource schools. Two Life Skills teachers and eight learners with disabilities were sampled purposively. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and learner-generated collages to accommodate diverse communication needs. Data were analysed thematically and four themes emerged: inadequate sexual and reproductive health and rights education and limited teaching resources, limited access to contraceptives, sexual abuse and poverty-driven exploitation, and lack of parental guidance. The findings reveal that disability intersects with poverty, inadequate sexual and reproductive health and rights education, poverty and absent parental support to create layered, compounding vulnerabilities rather than isolated risk factors. The study concludes that pregnancy among learners with disabilities cannot be addressed through a single-issue intervention. It recommends intersectional, multi-level interventions that simultaneously address educational, economic and protective measures. These should include accessible sexual and reproductive health and rights education materials, on-site contraceptive access and caregiver education on disability responsive child protection measures.

TI From AI readiness to course chatbots: explaining students' intentions to
   use instructor-developed generative tools in higher education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI chatbots; behavioral intention to use; formative feedback; technology
   acceptance; technology acceptance model (TAM); unified theory of
   acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT)
ID INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; ACCEPTANCE
AB This study examines college students' behavioral intention to use an instructor-developed, course-specific generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot for formative feedback. A total of 146 students from Biotechnology and Management courses used the chatbot while completing an assignment. Drawing on the technology acceptance model (TAM) and the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT), the study tested whether students' intention to use the course chatbot (BIUC) was predicted by their general intention to use AI tools (BIU), perceived usefulness, perceived value, perceived ease of use, trust, and enjoyment. The findings showed that BIU was the strongest predictor of BIUC, followed by perceived value and perceived usefulness. Trust and enjoyment were positively correlated with BIUC but were not significant predictors in the full regression model. Group comparisons indicated higher adoption intentions among Biotechnology students, native-language speakers, and older students, while no gender differences were found. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between general AI readiness and course-specific chatbot adoption in higher education.

TI Comparing technology-enhanced and conventional Van Hiele Phased
   Instruction in advancing learners through Van Hiele levels in
   transformation geometry
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Technology-enhanced instruction; Geometric reasoning; Transformation
   geometry; Van Hiele levels; GeoGebra; Mathematics Education; Pedagogy;
   Curriculum; Geometry Education
ID MATHEMATICS; GEOGEBRA
AB Developing learners' geometric reasoning remains a persistent challenge in secondary mathematics education, particularly in transformation geometry, where many learners struggle to progress through the hierarchical Van Hiele levels of geometric thinking. Although technology-enhanced instruction has been associated with improved mathematics learning, limited evidence exists on how integrating GeoGebra within the phases of Van Hiele instruction influences learners' progression through these levels. This study compared Technology-Enhanced Van Hiele Phased Instruction (TVHPI) with Conventional Van Hiele Phased Instruction (CVHPI) in promoting learners' progression through the Van Hiele levels in transformation geometry. Guided by Van Hiele theory and constructivist learning principles, a quasi-experimental design involving 483 Ugandan secondary school learners (TVHPI = 238; CVHPI = 245) was employed. Both instructional approaches significantly improved learners' geometric reasoning; however, learners receiving TVHPI demonstrated greater progression through the Van Hiele levels than those receiving CVHPI. The findings suggest that integrating GeoGebra within the phases of Van Hiele instruction is associated with higher levels of geometric reasoning and provides empirical support for technology-enhanced, competency-based geometry instruction that promotes deeper conceptual understanding.

TI The integration of artificial intelligence in the academic writing of
   EFL students in higher education: a case study at Fergana State
   University
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic writing; EFL students; higher education; ChatGPT; technology
   acceptance Model (TAM); Sociocultural Theory; learner autonomy; Arts &
   Humanities; Language & Literature; Language Teaching & Learning; Social
   Sciences; Education; Higher Education; Educational Psychology
ID TECHNOLOGY ACCEPTANCE MODEL; USER ACCEPTANCE
AB The rapid growth of AI-assisted writing tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly and QuillBot is reshaping academic writing practices in higher education. While these technologies offer immediate linguistic support for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners, they also prompt ongoing pedagogical debate concerning learner autonomy, critical engagement and potential overreliance. Despite expanding global scholarship, little empirical research has examined how AI integration unfolds within post-Soviet Central Asian EFL contexts, where distinct pedagogical traditions and linguistic backgrounds may mediate its impact. This convergent mixed-methods case study explores how 351 EFL students at Fergana State University, Uzbekistan, used AI tools in academic writing and investigates the effects on writing quality, cognitive independence and technology acceptance. Drawing on Sociocultural Theory (SCT) and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the study combined questionnaire data, comparative writing tasks and semi-structured interviews (n = 30). Quantitative analyses indicate that AI assistance was associated with substantial improvements in grammatical accuracy (35% error reduction, d = 1.27) and lexical sophistication (53% increase in Academic Word List coverage, d = 1.40). At the same time, reductions were observed in warranted argumentative claims (24% decline, d = 1.06) and measures of originality (d = 0.96). Perceived usefulness emerged as the strongest predictor of continued AI use (beta = 0.47, p < 0.001). Qualitative findings revealed tensions between scaffolding and substitution, a perceived performance-competence gap, institutional ambiguity and increasingly strategic use among advanced learners. The findings suggest that AI may enhance surface-level performance while being associated with weaker indicators of independent academic reasoning under assisted conditions.

TI We feel you: affect-regulation strategy in Indonesian legal-entity state
   university lecturers
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Affect-regulation framework; work stressor domain; emotion; stress;
   legal-entity state university; Autonomous University; Continuing
   Professional Development; Higher Education; Institutional Change
ID EMOTION REGULATION; MINDFULNESS; STRESS
AB Despite the expansion of Indonesia's leading public campuses into legal-entity state universities (Perguruan Tinggi Negeri Berbadan Hukum: PTN-BH), the impact of greater autonomy on academic personnel remains uncertain. This study examines the utility of the affect-regulation framework for understanding the interplay between occupational stress and emotions among PTN-BH lecturers. Participants (N = 144 lecturers from 18 PTN-BH; 69.4% female; M age = 38.74, SD age = 7.86) completed questionnaires assessing daily work-related stress and natural affect-regulation tendencies, then were randomly assigned to learn about one of three affect-regulation strategies - expressive suppression, reappraisal, or mindful regulation - while viewing animated videos illustrating four common sources of workplace stress: interpersonal relationships, research, teaching, and career development. Those with a natural inclination toward mindfulness reported lower daily stress, less tendency to suppress emotions, and lower negative affect. However, they did not necessarily favor reappraisal or report increased positive affect. Stress levels varied by domain, but mindful regulation consistently reduced stress and emotional arousal across all domains. Reappraisal was particularly effective for less emotionally charged stressors, attenuating the adverse effects of expressive suppression. These findings underscore the importance of integrating coping strategies with emotion-regulation approaches in highly competitive educational institutions.

TI Cross-cultural validation of the social empathy index: a psychometric
   study among Japanese medical students
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Social empathy index, social determinants of health; psychometrics,
   scale validation, cross-cultural validation
ID DETERMINANTS; EDUCATION; HEALTH
AB Background Assessing and fostering social empathy among medical students is crucial for advancing health equity. While education on the social determinants of health (SDH) has become increasingly important in medical curricula, its impact has been evaluated mostly through qualitative approaches. Quantitative assessment tools that assess social empathy remain limited in medical education. The Social Empathy Index (SEI) is a self-report instrument designed to assess interpersonal and social empathy and may have relevance for medical education.Objectives This study aimed to examine the psychometric properties of the Japanese version of the SEI (SEI-J) among medical students and explore its potential application in medical education in Japan.Methods A total of 414 medical students from three academic years at a private medical school in Tokyo completed the SEI-J and a self-developed sociodemographic questionnaire. Confirmatory factor analysis was conducted to examine structural validity based on the original SEI framework. Internal consistency was assessed using McDonald's omega coefficients. Known-groups validity was examined using one-way analysis of variance.Results Of the participants, 279 completed the survey (response rate 67.4%); 230 responses were included in the final analysis. Confirmatory factor analysis provided partial support for the original multidimensional structure of the SEI-J, and McDonald's omega coefficients indicated acceptable to high internal consistency across subscales. Higher SEI-J scores were associated with female gender, volunteering or study-abroad experience, interest in the arts or literature, people-oriented specialty preference, and greater self-rated understanding of SDH, consistent with prior research.Conclusions The findings demonstrate that the SEI-J is a psychometrically valid and reliable tool for measuring social empathy. This study provides preliminary evidence supporting the applicability of the SEI in a Japanese medical education context, identifies factors associated with the development of social empathy, and offers an outcome measure that supports the evaluation and iterative improvement of SDH- and equity-oriented curricula.

   education in religious and non-religious schools in Indonesia

ID DE-RADICALIZATION
AB Religiosity and religious tolerance are strongly related to the intensity of radicalism. In this context, schools, as institutions that provide religious education, need to foster a character of tolerance grounded in the normative values of religious doctrine. However, religious education is delivered through an inclusive education system oriented toward openness and egalitarianism. This study focuses on constructing an inclusive education model that fosters a character of tolerance in religious and non-religious schools. Between the theoretical and practical dimensions, there is a continuous process that strengthens religious education in constructing a character of tolerance.

   classrooms and school choice

DE Swahili-medium primary school; english-medium primary school;
   overcrowded classroom; school choice; classroom management
ID INSTRUCTION; EDUCATION
AB Many teachers in Swahili-medium primary schools enrol their children in English-medium primary schools. This choice is notable in Tanzania. Swahili-medium primary schools serve most pupils but face overcrowded classrooms and little chance for individualised instruction. This study explored Swahili-medium primary school teachers' experiences with overcrowded classrooms and how these influence their decisions to choose English-medium primary schools for their children. The study applied a qualitative research approach using a phenomenological research design to explore the problem. A purposive sampling strategy was applied, followed by a simple random sampling strategy to select 20 Swahili-medium primary school teachers, who were then interviewed using semi-structured interviews. Organisational culture theory, rational choice theory, and cultural capital theory were applied together to guide the study. The findings revealed that overcrowded classrooms create noisy and disruptive teaching and learning environments, limit teachers' ability to provide personalised instructional support, reduce opportunities to motivate pupils to learn, and constrain the use of diverse learner-centred teaching strategies. Swahili-medium primary school teachers reported that these classroom challenges, combined with broader systemic and cultural factors related to educational quality and future opportunities, influence their decision to enrol their children in English-medium primary schools. The results suggest that targeted policy and school level interventions to improve classroom conditions in the Swahili-medium primary schools could improve the quality of instruction and lead to a decrease in the teachers' preference to enroll their children in English-medium primary schools.

TI Bad feelings in queer and trans participatory research
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Emotions; critical methodologies; arts-based educational research;
   schools
ID STIGMA; PRAXIS
AB In schools, educators commonly accept that messiness is part of our work. Yet, researchers are often trained to see feelings as things to be excised. When engaging in participatory research with students and educators, mess is an inescapable part of the process. Participatory researchers navigate competing interests, conflicting schedules, gaps in knowledge, and complex power dynamics. AB This autoethnography examines the experiences of a 1.5th generation Asian American sibling broker navigating the K-12 special education system alongside a brother with autism and Korean-speaking immigrant parents. Drawing on eight years of reflective data and guided by AsianCrit and DisCrit, this study traces how race, language, and disability intersect to shape the author's positioning within institutional processes. This study contributes to emerging scholarship on sibling brokers and extends DisCrit and AsianCrit frameworks to special education family engagement.

TI From policy to practice: examining disability inclusion in a university
   quality assurance context
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Disability-inclusive practices; higher education quality assurance;
   institutional logics; Capability Approach; policy-practice gap; Ghana
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; INSTITUTIONAL ISOMORPHISM; STUDENTS; DESIGN;
   ORGANIZATIONS; PARTICIPATION; PERCEPTIONS
AB This qualitative case study examines disability-inclusive quality assurance practices at University of Cape Coast in Ghana, investigating the gap between formal policy commitments and disabled students' lived experiences. Through interviews with fifteen disabled students and five institutional officers, analysed using institutional theory and the Capability Approach, the study reveals systematic decoupling between policy and practice across three domains: assistive technology provision, assessment processes, and lecture room environments. Despite formal inclusivity policies, disabled students encounter inadequate assistive technologies requiring personal financial investment, inaccessible assessment scheduling, and unwelcoming environments characterized by attitudinal and infrastructural barriers. These implementation failures reflect competing institutional logics of compliance versus resource optimization that perpetuate symbolic rather than substantive inclusion. The findings demonstrate that quality assurance operates reactively rather than proactively, failing to systematically identify barriers or build institutional capacity for inclusive practices. To address these challenges, the study proposes comprehensive reforms, including establishing a disability inclusion committee with decision-making authority, mainstreaming disability indicators in quality assurance frameworks, implementing mandatory Universal Design for Learning faculty training, conducting accessibility audits with funded remediation plans, and transforming institutional culture through awareness campaigns and robust feedback mechanisms. The study underscores that achieving genuine inclusion requires fundamental transformation of institutional logics, embedding disability inclusion as a core value throughout organizational structures and practices.

AB This study investigates how digital ecosystem development in Kyrgyz higher education contributes to sustainability education and the preparation of future leaders. Although digital transformation in higher education has been widely studied, limited empirical evidence exists on how digital ecosystems function in resource-constrained contexts such as Central Asia. The findings indicate that inclusive and well-coordinated digital ecosystems can strengthen sustainability competencies and leadership development. This study provides one of the first empirical analyses of digital ecosystem development in Central Asian higher education. It demonstrates how resource-constrained countries can leverage digital transformation to advance sustainability education and offers policy-relevant insights for building resilient, inclusive, and digitally connected higher education systems.

   enhancing pre-service teachers' critical thinking

LA English
DT Article
DE STEM-PjBL; deep learning; product differentiation; critical thinking;
   pre-service teachers
AB In recent years, teacher education has placed increasing emphasis on critical thinking as a key 21st-century competency. However, the integration of STEM, project-based learning (PjBL), deep learning and product differentiation is often fragmented, leaving a gap in supporting pre-service teachers' critical thinking development. This study examines the effectiveness of a STEM-PjBL Deep Learning Model integrated with product differentiation. A sequential explanatory mixed-method design was applied to 70 undergraduate students in Indonesia, divided into experimental and control groups. Qualitative findings indicate that STEM integration supports analytical reasoning, product differentiation enhances ownership and reflection strengthens metacognitive awareness. Results should be interpreted with caution, as this study used convenience sampling from a single institution with SCM undergraduates and may not generalise to other disciplines or contexts. Recommendations include redesigning institutional frameworks for AI-assisted learning, developing effective AI use guidelines and curriculum adaptations emphasizing critical thinking alongside technological literacy.

AB Cybersecurity is a multifaceted challenge that cannot be addressed solely through technological solutions. A critical factor in the field of cybersecurity is individual behaviour. TI Assessing global leadership competency in international undergraduate
   education: a contextualized scale developed in China
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Global leadership competency (GLC); scale development; international
   undergraduate students; Chinese higher education; leadership development
ID INTERCULTURAL COMPETENCE
AB This study developed and initially validated a six-factor global leadership competency (GLC) scale assessing self-perceived GLC among international undergraduates in Beijing, China. Existing instruments are largely grounded in Western managerial contexts and may not adequately reflect student development in culturally diverse higher education. A 50-item scale was developed through literature synthesis, expert review, item-objective congruence-based content validation, and pilot testing. Data from 314 international undergraduates across 28 Beijing universities were analyzed using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. Principal axis factoring with Promax rotation identified six dimensions: global mindset, strategic thinking, global social responsibility, cross-cultural competence, global innovative capability, and global strategy implementation. Reliability was strong (alpha = 0.908-0.944), and heterotrait-monotrait values (0.130-0.690) supported discriminant validity. The findings suggest that GLC is a multidimensional, educationally embedded construct. Because development and validation relied on one Beijing dataset, the scale remains a preliminary diagnostic tool requiring independent validation across regions, institutions, and student populations.

TI Using intelligent personal assistants as conversational partners in
   informal digital learning of English: revisiting EFL learners'
   willingness to communicate
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Willingness to communicate; intelligent personal assistants; informal
   digital learning of english; Google Assistant; interaction modality;
   Social Sciences; Education; Education Policy & Politics; Education
   Policy; Pedagogy; Arts & Humanities; Humanities; Philosophy;
   Phenomenology; Religion
ID 2ND-LANGUAGE; L2; TEACHER; GENDER; MODEL
AB The integration of Intelligent Personal Assistants (IPAs) into informal digital learning environments has opened new avenues for enhancing L2 learners' spoken language engagement. This mixed-methods study explores the impact of interaction modality-Human-Human Interaction (HHI) versus Human-Google Assistant Interaction (HGI)-on Iranian adult EFL learners' Willingness to Communicate (WTC) in English within an Informal Digital Learning of English (IDLE) context. Sixty pre-intermediate learners were randomly assigned to either group and participated in eight structured, task-based online speaking sessions over three weeks. The HGI group completed the tasks through voice interaction with Google Assistant, while the HHI group performed comparable tasks with human partners. ANCOVA results revealed significantly greater WTC gains in the HGI group, with no significant gender effects. Thematic analysis of post-intervention interviews indicated that learners in the HGI group perceived Google Assistant as a low-stakes, responsive, and nonjudgmental conversational partner that enhanced motivation, reduced anxiety, and supported self-regulation. These findings, interpreted through interactionist, sociocultural, and affective-motivational lenses, underscore the pedagogical value of IPA-mediated interaction in promoting oral language use in informal digital contexts. Nonetheless, learners reported occasional speech recognition errors and technical limitations, highlighting the need to address such challenges for more effective implementation.

TI The impact of Pi application as an AI-assisted speaking assessment tool
   on EFL learners' overall speaking perceptions, foreign language anxiety,
   speaking self-efficacy, and speaking satisfaction
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Overall speaking perception; speaking self-efficacy; foreign language
   anxiety; Pi Application; speaking satisfaction
ID 2ND-LANGUAGE; WILLINGNESS; COMMUNICATE; SKILLS
AB This study examined whether Pi Application (PiApp), an AI-assisted speaking assessment and practice tool, was associated with short-term changes in EFL learners' overall speaking perceptions (OSP), foreign language anxiety (FLA), speaking self-efficacy (SSE), and speaking satisfaction (SS). Using a randomized pretest-posttest control-group design, 30 intermediate EFL learners in Iran were assigned to either a PiApp-supported experimental group or a conventional classroom control group (n = 15 each). During the eight-week intervention, both groups completed comparable speaking tasks, but the experimental group received PiApp-generated formative feedback, whereas the control group received teacher-mediated feedback. TI Schools as galleries: displays of student work
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student work; display; project-based learning (PBL); curation; visual
   ethnography; photos; school spaces; materials; process; collaboration;
   interdisciplinarity; identity; public audience
AB This study investigates how student work is displayed and curated in nine schools that use project-based learning (PBL). In these settings, displays are an integral part of the learning process and help make students' thinking, choices, and collaboration visible. The analysis draws on in-situ photos and walking interviews with teachers. In the article, a purposive sample of ten photos illustrates how work appears across classrooms, hallways, stairwells, ceilings, railings, and outdoor areas, using materials such as drawings, paintings, woodwork, mixed-media pieces, and 3D-printed models. These PBL structures appeared to support deeper learning and gave students some opportunities to shape school spaces. Overall, the findings suggest that displaying project-based student work across school spaces may contribute to a shared culture of knowledge. Purposeful curation helps students make sense of their work's meaning and development while supporting communication and reflection.

TI Graduate employability strategies in Rwanda and Tunisia: a comparative
   study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Employability; youth unemployment; Rwanda; Tunisia; graduates; job
   seeking strategies
ID SKILLS DEVELOPMENT; HIGHER-EDUCATION; BANGLADESH; EMPLOYMENT
AB Graduate employability in African nations has become a critical concern for policymakers seeking to invest in human capital for sustainable development. Rwanda and Tunisia underwent significant changes in the 1990s that affected their labour markets and graduates' transition to employment. Both countries introduced strategies to reduce public sector dominance and promote private sector growth and entrepreneurship. However, graduates continued to face mismatches between their skills and labour market demands. This article presents findings from a study investigating the job search strategies of higher education graduates in Rwanda and Tunisia to enhance employability. Data were collected from 165 graduates in Tunisia and 147 in Rwanda through closed-ended surveys, complemented by thematic analysis of open-ended responses. Networking, including social and professional connections, and online platforms were effective job search methods in both countries. However, Rwandan graduates relied on job portals, whereas Tunisians preferred traditional and systematic recruitment procedures. The study offers insights for policy interventions and educational reforms aimed at improving graduate employability and addressing unemployment in both countries and beyond.

TI Project-based learning as a transformative strategy in professional
   education: a contextualized and competency-based methodological proposal
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Project-Based learning; professional pedagogy; methodological framework;
   competence development; educational innovation
AB Project-Based Learning (PBL) integrates learning and project execution to cultivate knowledge, skills, and professional values through interdisciplinary, contextualized, and collaborative experiences. This article proposes a competency-based methodological model for professional education structured into four stages: problematic situation, research, product development, and evaluation. The model is operationalized through 18 guided activities, a shared analytic rubric with fixed descriptors and levels, standardized process indicators, and lightweight scaffolds. It also includes modular adaptations across disciplines, a digital-first workflow with offline-first options and responsible AI guardrails, a teacher-training framework, a minimal low-tech resource kit, and a stage-based stakeholder engagement protocol to support fidelity and comparability. A preliminary classroom try-out under routine instruction indicated feasibility and acceptance: teams met milestones, produced planned outputs, and reported positive perceptions of clarity, collaboration, and relevance. Formative analysis prompted refinements, including micro-milestones, role-assignment templates, concept-map exemplars with minimum-quality criteria, and explicit peer/self-assessment weighting, without altering the four-stage sequence. Evidence remains preliminary and descriptive, based on a small convenience sample in a single context and lacking counterfactual designs, thereby limiting generalizability. Future work will use quasi-experimental and longitudinal evaluations to estimate effects on competence development across diverse institutional and cultural settings, strengthen assessment reliability, and support scalable implementation in international professional education.

TI "We wrote through the storm": Latinx doctoral student survivance and
   resistance during COVID-19

AB This narrative analysis draws on oral histories to examine how seven Latinx doctoral students navigated doctoral education during the COVID-19 pandemic. TI Retention of fellows to the faculty at a research-intensive academic
   medical center: a mixed-methods study
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical education; graduate medical education; fellowship training;
   faculty recruitment; mixed methods
ID NATIONAL COHORT; RESPONSE RATES; SCHOOL; CONSTRUCTIVISM; PRODUCTIVITY;
   PERCEPTIONS; RESIDENCY; PROGRAMS; CAREER; JOB
AB Background As clinical practice provides >50% of medical schools' revenue, research-intensive medical schools often seek to retain fellows with clinical-care interests. Fellows' considerations when deciding whether to stay at research-intensive institutions where they trained remain understudied. We sought to identify experiential factors associated with faculty-position offers and decisions of fellows in training. Methods We conducted a mixed-methods study using a survey and semi-structured interview. We invited 471 fellows training in all clinical departments at our institution to complete an anonymous survey between April and June 2021 to examine their level of agreement (strongly disagree [1] to strongly agree [7]) with positive training and mentoring experiences and their academic-medicine career goals in association with being offered a position and, if offered, accepting or declining. Fellows described institutional opportunities for intervention, especially enhanced communication about institutional priorities and potential positions. Conclusions Clear communication with clinical fellows about their academic-medicine career goals and fellowship-training and mentoring experiences can inform decision-making about faculty offers and better equip institutional leaders to retain fellows who align with institutional needs.

TI Large language model use in dental education: a cross-sectional
   multi-country study
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic Integrity; Artificial Intelligence; ChatGPT; dental education;
   large language models
AB Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in higher education, but multi-country evidence on dental students' use, verification, and integrity practices is limited.Objective To compare senior dental students' LLM use, perceived time and academic impact, reliability judgements, verification practices, and integrity safeguards across five countries.Methods An anonymous cross-sectional online survey was administered to final-year dental students in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Jordan, Malaysia, Oman, and Brazil. Measures included tools used, frequency and motivations, learning activities, perceived time and academic impact, verification frequency and strategies, guideline awareness, and integrity safeguards. Analyses used Kruskal-Wallis and chi-square tests with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment, effect sizes, Spearman correlations, and ordinal logistic models.Results In total, 454 students participated (UAE 160, Jordan 101, Malaysia 75, Oman 62, Brazil 56; mean age 22.9; 74.9% female). ChatGPT predominated (95.9%), followed by Gemini, formerly Bard (18.0%), DeepSeek (16.4%), and Claude (7.4%). Tool diversity varied across country-based cohorts, with Oman showing greater multi-tool uptake. Use was frequent (several times/week 39.2%, daily 28.6%). Key motivations were saving time (73.0%), clarifying concepts (56.9%), and summarising (54.1%). Common activities included understanding complex concepts (75.3%), summarising lecture notes (70.0%), exam preparation (61.5%), and assignment research (53.2%); exam-time assistance was reported by 25.6%. Verification was 'always' 20.0% and 'often' 34.1%, varying across country-based cohorts, with Oman verifying less frequently than other cohorts. Guideline awareness was 40.3% overall (UAE 61.3% vs Brazil 8.3%). Integrity safeguards commonly involved paraphrasing (69.6%), citations (39.2%), and plagiarism checks (38.0%); disclaimers were uncommon (9.2%). LLM-use frequency correlated with broader academic use (rho = 0.289) but not with integrity concern (OR = 0.963).Conclusions LLM use is widespread and heterogeneous across settings, including non-trivial higher-stakes use. Dental programmes should implement explicit training in verification, evidence traceability, and disclosure, supported by clear, enforceable guidance and assessment designs aligned with real-world LLM practices.

TI From curriculum to career: a grounded theory of AI-driven employability
   in higher education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Employability skills; higher education; human capital theory; social
   capital theory; AI-driven employability; grounded theory
AB This study examines how undergraduate students navigate employability within an AI-driven labor market, highlighting the role of digital social capital, personal branding, and multicultural identity management in a rapidly modernizing, culturally diverse setting. Employing a constructivist grounded theory approach, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 12 undergraduates across STEM and humanities disciplines. Data were coded iteratively using constant comparative methods until theoretical saturation. Five major categories emerged: experiential learning, professional networking, digital self-promotion, cultural identity tensions, and technological adaptability. The study proposes an 'AI-Driven Employability Framework' that integrates Human, Social, and Cultural Capital theories and develops two context-specific extensions: digital social capital, referring to the platform-mediated conversion of professional visibility and relationships into career opportunities, and multicultural capital, referring to the capacity to navigate global professional demands while maintaining and strategically mobilizing cultural and linguistic identity. The findings recommend that higher education institutions integrate digital branding and intercultural competence training into their curricula, align career services with AI literacy goals, and support bilingual identity development to enhance graduate readiness for AI-mediated careers.

TI Determinants of educational attainment in Ghana: ordered probit versus
   generalized ordered logit approach
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Education; educational attainment; Ghana Living Standards Survey; Ghana;
   human capital
ID PARENTAL EDUCATION; INVESTMENT; GENDER; INCOME
AB This study investigates the determinants of educational attainment in Ghana, with a focus on disparities across educational levels, using data from the Ghana Living Standards Survey (GLSS) Round 7. Employing ordered probit, generalized ordered logit, and multinomial logit models, the analysis examines how individual and household factors influence progression through four ordered educational categories: no formal education, primary/Junior High School (JHS), secondary/Senior High School (SHS), and tertiary education (including vocational/technical/commercial, undergraduate, and postgraduate levels). The results identify several significant predictors of educational attainment, including gender, marital status, disability, region, place of residence, parental education, labor force status, age, income, and household size. Specifically, males, individuals who have never married, persons without disabilities, urban residents, those with highly educated parents, individuals who are not in the labor force, persons from high-income households, and those from smaller households are more likely to attain higher levels of education compared to their respective counterparts. Additionally, the study finds a quadratic relationship between age and educational attainment, whereby increasing age is associated with a higher probability of achieving advanced education among younger individuals, but beyond a certain age threshold, this probability declines. The proportional odds assumption is rejected, supporting the generalized ordered logit as the preferred specification, while multinomial logit results confirm robustness. These findings underscore the need for equity-focused interventions to address structural and socio-economic barriers in Ghana's education system, offering evidence for policy alignment with Sustainable Development Goal 4.

   Chinese international doctoral students

DT Article

AB Chinese international doctoral students (CIDS) increasingly navigate legal precarity as U.S.-China geopolitical tensions reshape international education. This study investigates how CIDS experience and respond to legal and institutional challenges while constructing strategies for academic success. Drawing on critical migration studies, this study examines the lived experiences of two Chinese international doctoral students in STEM fields. Using testimonio-inspired storytelling, the study highlights how participants navigate authorized yet precarious legal status. Findings reveal three key dynamics. TI Gamification's impact on vocabulary acquisition in intermediate-level
   English learners: case study, National University of Science and
   Technology, Oman
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gamification; vocabulary acquisition; intermediate learners;
   self-determination theory; higher education; Oman
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION
AB Gamification research in language learning has often prioritised platform-level comparisons over the specific mechanics that support vocabulary acquisition, particularly among intermediate learners. This quasi-experimental study examined -level effects in Omani higher education, an underexplored context in which vocabulary instruction often remains shaped by rote-learning practices. Over 12 weeks, traditional vocabulary instruction (n = 26) was compared with gamified instruction using Nearpod, Pear Deck, and NoRedInk (n = 28). Data were collected through pre- and post-vocabulary tests, motivation surveys, and structured classroom observations. Quantitative analysis employed independent-samples t-tests and Hedges' g effect sizes. Similarly, qualitative classroom data were analysed thematically, with inter-rater agreement reported at Cohen's kappa = 0.87. The gamification group demonstrated significantly larger vocabulary gains (M = +2.79, SD = 1.64) than the control group (M = +1.00, SD = 1.12), t(52) = 4.68, p < 0.001, Hedges' g = 0.90 [95% CI: 0.34, 1.46], indicating a large effect. Notably, 82% of experimental participants showed meaningful improvement, whereas 7% exhibited no gain, revealing important boundary conditions for gamified vocabulary instruction. Thematic analysis indicated that challenges, matching games, immediate feedback, and collaborative tasks were stronger drivers of engagement than points or leaderboards, suggesting that meaningful interaction outweighed the appeal of superficial reward structures. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory, the findings show how autonomy, competence, and relatedness may operate through specific gamification mechanics. The study, therefore, shifts the agenda from asking which digital tool works to examining which mechanisms support which learners under which conditions across culturally situated higher-education language classrooms.

TI Rethinking teacher adoption categories in mandated curriculum reform:
   the role of innovativeness and resistance to change
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mandated curriculum reform; curriculum adopter categories;
   innovativeness; resistance to change; configurational approach;
   secondary school teachers; Tanzania; Arts & Humanities; Arts; Media
   Communication; Humanities; Cultural Studies; Media & Film Studies;
   Communication Studies
AB The successful implementation of mandated curriculum reforms is partly influenced by teachers' psychological dispositions. This study examined how teachers' innovativeness and resistance to change interacted to produce distinct patterns of engagement with mandated reform, moving beyond the assumption that innovativeness and resistance represent opposite ends of a single adoption continuum. Using Tanzania's Competence-Based Curriculum (CBC) as an empirical context, the study collected data from 263 secondary education teachers through an online 5-point Likert scaled questionnaires, conducted cluster analysis to derive teacher profiles based on these dispositions, and examined profile differences in CBC responsiveness. The study advances diffusion of innovations theory by reconceptualising resistance as a co-constitutive dimension of innovation adoption, proposing a framework that captures the simultaneous presence and interaction of these dispositions. Practically, it advocates for a more nuanced understanding of adopter categories, allowing for interventions that address their distinct dispositions.

DT Article

   Educational Psychology
ID SCIENCE; FRAMEWORK
AB The increasingly important role of technology underscores the need for students to acquire 21st-century skills, including a deep understanding of science. As teaching with technology can be highly effective in promoting students' learning processes, it is important for physics teachers to properly leverage technology in the classroom. We examine physics teachers' intentions to use technology-enhanced strategies for cognitive engagement (CE). TI Pedagogical reasons for teachers' engagement or non-engagement with
   learner errors and misconceptions in Measurement in Grade 12
   Mathematical Literacy
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Errors; Mathematical Literacy; misconceptions; Measurement; teacher
   engagement
AB This empirical paper explores the pedagogical reasons for teachers' engagement or non-engagement with learner errors and misconceptions in Measurement in Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy. Although the South African curriculum promotes learner-centred teaching, many teachers still use surface-level practices that overlook learners' conceptual difficulties. The study is grounded in Vygotsky's Social Development Theory and adopts an interpretivist paradigm with a qualitative, exploratory case study design. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with six Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy teachers in the Motheo District, selected through convenience and purposive sampling. Braun and Clarke's six-step thematic analysis was used to interpret the data. The findings reveal three key pedagogical reasons that shape teachers' engagement with learner errors and misconceptions: teachers' pedagogical beliefs and motivations, contextual and institutional constraints that affect daily practice, and the use of reflective practice and feedback. The study argues that improving teachers' engagement with misconceptions requires structural support, including sufficient instructional time, manageable class sizes, and appropriate teaching resources. It recommends that schools institutionalise manageable reflective practices, such as brief reflection sessions in departmental meetings, peer discussions on learner misconceptions, and voluntary reflective journaling supported by subject heads.

TI Balancing cooperation and power: politeness strategies in parent-teacher
   interactions
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher-parent interaction; teacher parent cooperation; teacher parent
   conferences; parent involvement; politeness strategies
ID FAMILY INVOLVEMENT; ELEMENTARY-SCHOOL; EDUCATION; SELF; COMMUNICATION;
   ADOLESCENTS; ACHIEVEMENT; COMPETENCES; PERCEPTIONS; AMERICAN
AB Analysing parent-teacher interactions from a linguistic perspective is crucial because revealing the underlying patterns of language choices provides significant insights into parent-teacher interactions by testing educational ideals against realities. The study investigates the perceived nature of parent-teacher interaction in Turkiye by analysing politeness strategies through teachers' and parents' written responses to interactional scenarios. Brown and Levinson's politeness theory was adopted to investigate interactional dynamics including self-positioning, social power and face-management strategies. To gain a comprehensive understanding of parent-teacher interaction, two different Written Discourse Completion Tasks for parents and teachers were designed. Each task included ten scenarios reflecting topics that could arise in these interactions. WDCTs were applied to 80 parents and 80 teachers. A total of 1,786 politeness strategies were identified, showing that both parties are willing to collaborate even in the most face-threatening situations. Teachers, who use more direct strategies, prioritize their professional roles and position themselves as the more powerful actors. Although they experience greater face loss, parents, who mostly use indirect strategies, acknowledge teachers' power. They also employ pseudo-agreements and use politeness strategies manipulatively to satisfy teachers' face needs. Lastly, both parties focus more on presenting themselves as 'good parents' and 'good teachers' than on issues concerning students.

TI Swedish teachers' perceptions and intended responses to bias-based
   bullying: variations across identity domains and school levels
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teachers; school bullying; bias-based bullying; teachers' bullying
   perceptions; teachers' bullying responses; Social Sciences; Education;
   Primary/Elementary Education
ID INTERVENTION; PRESERVICE; ATTITUDES; EFFICACY
AB Drawing on Swedish data (N = 184) from an international vignette study, this study examines teachers' reported exposure to bias-based bullying as well as their perceptions and intended responses across four identity domains (ethnicity, academic ability, weight, and gender/sexuality) and school levels (elementary and secondary school). Across most outcomes, teachers' perceptions were largely consistent, with two exceptions. Victim blaming was higher for academic ability-related exclusion than for exclusion based on gender/sexuality, and elementary teachers reported higher self-efficacy to intervene in bias-based bullying. Furthermore, elementary teachers were more likely to endorse inclusion and victim support, whereas secondary teachers were more likely to endorse formal escalation and separation response strategies. These contrasts point to the need for professional development that accounts for both the specific nature of bias-based incidents and the structural conditions of different school levels. The findings add to the growing evidence that teachers' responses to bias-based bullying are shaped by educational context, but that many perceptions and intended responses are consistent across identity domains.

ID RACISM
AB In the context of an enhanced focus on racial inequalities in higher education, growing attention has been paid to the role of race and ethnicity as a specific theme in the university curriculum. However, few existing studies have engaged with a broad sample of views from educators about their experiences of teaching in this area. This article aims to address the gap by investigating UK university educators' perspectives on teaching race and ethnicity and exploring this contested aspect of the curriculum with their students. TI Bridging gaps in second language English teaching through collaborative
   evaluation and continuous professional development: a systematic review
   with global scope and focus on Uzbekistan's educational context
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Second language acquisition; teacher professional development;
   collaborative evaluation; educational reform; Uzbekistan education;
   systematic review; Social Sciences; Education; Adult Education and
   Lifelong Learning; Work-based Learning; Philosophy of Education;
   Research Methods in Education
AB This systematic review synthesizes international research on the persistent disconnect between second-language English teaching practices and actual learning outcomes and its implications and applications in the educational setting of Uzbekistan. Although the evidence base is international, the analysis focuses specifically on the implications of these findings for post-Soviet and resource-constrained educational contexts such as Uzbekistan. A review of 127 peer-reviewed articles published in the years 2015-2025 identified four dimensions of practice-performance incongruence that are critical: pedagogical alignment, assessment authenticity, teacher preparedness and institutional support structures. Based on the PRISMA 2020 protocols and the activity theory as an interpretive framework, this review explores the ways collaborative evaluation mechanisms and continuous professional development programs can fill these gaps. Interventions grounded in sociocultural collaboration, contextual adaptation and technology-supported professional learning were consistently associated with stronger outcomes. This paper suggests a Collaborative Professional Development Framework (CPDF), a theoretically-based model that is adjusted to the post-Soviet educational environment. In a meta-analysis of 42 intervention studies, it was found that meaningful improvements in student engagement (d = 0.78, 95% CI: 0.65-0.91) and communicative competence (d = 0.82, 95% CI: 0.71-0.93) were found when collaborative evaluation was systematically applied. The review has a wider applicability to educational policy change in Central Asia and resource-constrained developing contexts in general.

TI The hidden patterns of alignment: exploring variability between
   generative AI and human
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Alignment; accuracy; artificial intelligence; consistency; curriculum
   mapping; curricular Human-AI Teaming; curricular HAT; generative AI;
   GenAI; pharmacology; USMLE
ID PHARMACOLOGY
AB Objective Aligning medical education curricula with standardized competency-based assessments is a multifaceted task that requires accuracy and consistency. While generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) models offer potential assistance, their performance compared to that of human subject matter experts remains unclear. This study investigates the consistency, accuracy, and strategies of human- and AI-generated alignments of pharmacological topics with the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE) Step 1 content.Methods A comparative case study examined curricular alignment results produced by GenAI models and human experts. Agreement percentages and pairwise correlation coefficients were calculated to assess consistency and consensus within and between the two groups, highlighting similarities and differences in alignments. We also examined challenges, strategies, and the impact of time constraints on the alignment task.Results GenAIs exhibited higher inter-rater reliability in within-group comparisons, with exact agreement percentages ranging from 60% to 79% and stronger correlations. In contrast, human raters demonstrated greater variability, with exact agreement percentages between 14% and 66% and weaker correlations. While partial agreement improved alignment for both groups, GenAIs maintained higher overall consistency and consensus. On the other hand, only two human raters and all GenAI models exhibited high inter-rater reliability in between-group comparisons. GenAIs generated alignments based on contextual analysis and hierarchical mapping, while humans engaged in iterative refinement using their expertise and reflection. Time constraints had a minimal impact on GenAIs, whereas it was acknowledged as a limiting factor for human performance.Conclusion GenAIs can efficiently provide accurate and consistent alignments of pharmacological content in medical curricula but lack the sophisticated decision-making capabilities of human experts. While human alignments show variability due to human experts' diverse perspectives and backgrounds, trained experts make more contextually informed decisions. A conceptual model of Curricular Human-AI Teaming (Curricular HAT) could combine these complementary strengths to enhance the workflow and outcomes of curricular alignment. The model supports the transparency and scalability of human-AI collaboration while maintaining the responsibility of human judgment and ethical use of GenAI.

ID IMPACT
AB This study addresses the limited empirical research on social media use in Afghanistan's higher education system and provides evidence-based insights to inform policy and digital learning strategies in a fragile context. It examines social media use, academic engagement, and social life at Mirwais Khan Nika University, Zabul, using a cross-sectional design with data from 361 students analyzed through SPSS 24. Chi-square goodness-of-fit tests, Pearson correlation analysis, independent samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and simple linear regression were applied to examine usage patterns, differences, associations, and relationships among variables. The findings indicate that WhatsApp, Facebook, and Messenger were the most frequently used social media, while LinkedIn, Snapchat, and Pinterest were less used, with students spending two hours or less per day. Chi-square results showed significant variation in social media use and daily time spent online. Moreover, students reported using social media for academic engagement purposes, including learning from teachers, accessing information, sharing educational materials, and self-directed learning, as well as for social life purposes such as awareness of social issues, community involvement, and peer communication. Pearson correlation showed no significant association with outcomes, whereas regression indicated significant relationships with both domains. The study offers theoretical insights and practical guidance for policymakers, educators, and university administrators.

TI Generative AI literacy in Tanzanian higher education: comparing
   instructors and students practices using the knowledge-skills-attitudes
   framework
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational technology; digital competence; higher education; instructor
   practices; responsible tool use
AB Generative artificial intelligence tools are increasingly shaping teaching and learning in higher education, yet evidence from African contexts remains limited. We examined generative artificial intelligence literacy among 320 instructors and 385 students across 10 higher education institutions in Tanzania. Both groups reported substantial engagement, but the literacy profile was uneven: applied use and self-reported skills were relatively strong, whereas conceptual and ethics-related knowledge were comparatively weaker.    WORK
AB In Higher Education (HE) learning about topics that may be disturbing or upsetting can present risks to student engagement and overall wellbeing. Educators should manage this content thoughtfully but there is little clarity and consistency in terms of best practice. Previous research has overlooked the student voice, focussing on educator experiences. Experiments examining 'trigger' warnings are divorced from the learning experience and produce inconsistent findings. We asked 27 undergraduate Psychology students to define 'sensitive material' and describe their associated learning experiences. Our thematic analysis suggested that, to students, 'sensitive material' is a topic that evokes predominantly negative emotional responses, and advanced previous definitions by acknowledging individual and collective responses. Limitations, and ideas for further work are presented with an aim to continue to collaborate with students regarding the teaching of sensitive materials.

TI A critical analysis of school accreditation policy in Tanzania and its
   implications for access, equity, and efficiency in education provision
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE school accreditation; quality assurance; school registration; government
   school; non-government school; critical discourse analysis
ID SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT; AFRICA
AB This study critically analysed Tanzania's school accreditation policy, which has been in place since independence, to uphold educational standards. Data were collected from policy documents and semi-structured interviews with ministry officials, education officers, school managers or owners, school quality assurance officers, and heads of school. The study revealed that the accreditation policy is constructed through discourses that reinforce centralised control over school registration and establishment. These discourses emphasise regulation, authority, and compliance, significantly restricting local actors' decision-making autonomy and framing the central government as the primary authority. Three dominant discourses were identified: establishment by local authorities, public school registration, and non-government school registration. Collectively, these discourses redefined accreditation as a tool for enforcing uniformity and central control rather than fostering local responsiveness or innovation. The analysis further revealed a biased two-tiered system that advantages public schools with minimal requirements, while subjecting private schools to stringent and multi-layered accreditation procedures. This disparity limits private sector participation, fosters inefficiency, and undermines equity and educational innovation. The study concludes that while the current accreditation policy aims to ensure standards, it inadvertently hinders inclusivity and responsiveness. A more balanced and participatory approach is recommended to create a fair and dynamic education sector in Tanzania.

AB Research on the expectations, values, and costs of studying in situ has been scarce. AB This study evaluates an AI literacy programme implemented in a Malaysian Islamic boarding school involving Indonesian junior high school students using the Ethical-CIPP evaluation framework. The programme integrated AI knowledge, practical application, and ethical reflection on issues such as plagiarism, privacy, and responsible AI use within a faith-based educational setting. Quantitative findings revealed significant improvements across AI literacy dimensions, with mean scores increasing from 45% to 86%, while qualitative reflections indicated stronger ethical awareness and more critical attitudes towards AI-assisted learning. The study extends the traditional Context-Input-Process-Product (CIPP) model by systematically embedding ethical and cultural dimensions throughout programme evaluation. The proposed Ethical-CIPP framework provides a contextually responsive approach for evaluating AI literacy programmes in faith-based and resource-constrained educational environments. The findings demonstrate the short-term potential of integrating ethical reflection with technical competence in AI literacy education and provide a foundation for future longitudinal implementation and curriculum integration to support sustained responsible AI engagement in faith-based educational settings.

ID MATTER
AB This article presents the learning journey of a qualitative researcher navigating into post-qualitative terrain. TI Social justice in legal education: a comparative study of perceptions
   between Hong Kong and the United Kingdom
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Social justice; legal education; black-letter law; comparative study;
   legal activism; Social Sciences; Education; Higher Education; Study of
   Higher Education; Teaching & Learning
ID LAW
AB This study examines and compares how law students and recent graduates in the United Kingdom and Hong Kong conceptualise and perceive social justice within legal education and professional practice. Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, the research combines statistical analysis of 260 survey responses with thematic analysis of 24 in-depth interviews. Findings reveal significant national and professional differences in understandings of social justice. UK students framed it in Rawlsian terms of outcome-based fairness, while Hong Kong participants emphasised equality before the law and procedural fairness. Perceived importance of social justice-more than educational exposure-was identified as the strongest predictor of legal activism, with nationality emerging as the most significant determinant. The study concludes with implications for curriculum reform to better align legal education with local contexts and social justice objectives.

LA English
DT Article
DE Classroom Assessment Scoring System (CLASS); Early years education;
   Giftedness; Teaching; Mixed method; Social Sciences; Education; Early
   Years; Development Studies, Environment, Social Work, Urban Studies
AB This article builds on a study that identified three gifted and talented children in preschool and follows them through preschool class, Year 1, and leisure-time centres within the Swedish educational system. Employing a longitudinal multiple-case study design, it examines how giftedness and talent are recognised and facilitated, focusing on teaching practices, teacher-child interactions, and children's experiences. AB This paper explores the factors affecting the extent of students' behavioral intention to adopt ChatGPT among university students in Mogadishu, Somalia using an extended version of the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The study integrates perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, perceived risk and institutional trust to examine their influence on students' behavioral intention to adopt ChatGPT. TI The influence of in-service computer science teachers' demographic
   characteristics on their self-efficacy
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Computer science; demographic characteristics; Pakistan; self-efficacy;
   teacher education
ID GOAL STRUCTURES; GENDER; EXPERIENCE; TECHNOLOGY; EDUCATION; BELIEFS
AB In the digital age, computer science (CS) has become a vital component of the education system. Grounded in social cognitive theory, this study examines the demographic characteristics of in-service CS teachers. Although teacher self-efficacy has garnered increasing scholarly attention, the influence of demographic variables on CS teachers' self-efficacy remains underexplored, particularly in Pakistan. A quantitative research design was adopted for this study. Data were collected from 325 in-service CS teachers through a standardized questionnaire adapted from the Teaching and Learning International Survey (TALIS, 2018), which was distributed electronically using Google Forms. Descriptive statistics, independent-sample t-test, and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) were used for data analysis. The findings revealed no significant differences in teacher self-efficacy based on gender, teaching experience, teaching level, and educational qualification. However, significant differences were observed in age, and school location. Younger CS teachers demonstrated higher self-efficacy than older ones, urban CS teachers reported greater confidence than rural ones, and those who viewed their profession as more important exhibited stronger self-efficacy. The results suggest that educational stakeholders should design professional development programs that support older and rural CS teachers, strengthen teachers' professional identity, and promote equitable access to resources so as to build a confident, motivated, and capable teaching workforce for the digital age.
