TI Investigating the intent of nursing faculty to integrate collaborative
   learning: exploratory research study in a collectivistic culture
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Attitude; collaborative learning; culture; education; faculty; nursing;
   health knowledge
ID TEACHERS
AB Although collaborative learning (CL) is widely recognized as an effective pedagogical approach in health professions education, little is known about the factors influencing nursing faculty intentions to implement CL in collectivistic cultural contexts. Most existing research has been conducted in individualistic, Western contexts, resulting in limited understanding of how cultural expectations and social norms influence faculty adoption of collaborative learning. To address this gap, this study employed the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) to examine the relationships among faculty beliefs, attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and intentions to implement CL in teaching. A cross-sectional study using an exploratory correlational design was conducted across nine branches of the Oman College of Health Sciences. Nursing faculty members (n = 96) completed a 69-item TPB-based questionnaire measuring intention, attitudes, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and associated behavioral, normative, and control beliefs. Hierarchical multiple regression, and Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests were used to analyze the data. The findings indicated that attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control were included in the model explaining variance in faculty intention to implement CL; however, only subjective norms emerged as a significant independent predictor of intention. Previous experience implementing CL was significantly associated with higher intention, stronger subjective norms, and greater perceived behavioral control, whereas nationality and academic qualification were not associated with differences in intention. These findings highlight the importance of social expectations and prior experience in shaping faculty behavior, underscoring the need for institutional support to promote CL in nursing education.

TI How organizations learn: investigating boundary crossing activities for
   redesigning equity-oriented principal preparation programs
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Organizational learning; boundary crossing; partnership; principal
   preparation program (PPP); equity
AB This paper examines how multi-institutional partnerships drive systemic changes in equity-centered principal preparation programs (PPPs). Using a district partnership team (DPT) within the Equity Leadership Pathway (ELP, pseudonym) initiative in the United States as the case study, we apply a multilevel boundary-crossing framework to analyze how organizations learn as universities, districts, and state agencies navigate bureaucratic and cultural friction. Our findings reveal that these discontinuities were not mere barriers, but vital catalysts for ideological negotiation and institutional reforms. Through identification, coordination, reflection, and transformation mechanisms, the stakeholders co-governed the leadership development program to bridge the theory-practice gap. Future research should include longitudinal data to explore how this equity-centered training could impact leadership practices, school environments, and long-term student learning outcomes.

TI The impact of moral education on student virtue in higher education:
   evidence from Jiangxi Province, China
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Moral education; student virtue; teacher behaviors; teaching
   effectiveness; Social Sciences; Education; Teachers & Teacher Education;
   Higher Education; Assessment; Multicultural Education
AB Against the construction requirements of high-level talent cultivation systems, curriculum-based moral education has been comprehensively promoted in Chinese higher education institutions. However, empirical research on the relationship between such moral education initiatives and student virtue development remains markedly scarce. Therefore, examining the relationship is essential for advancing and refining current moral education practices. A random survey was conducted among 318 undergraduate students from eight universities in Jiangxi province. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was employed, given its suitability for predictive, multidimensional and complex models, to develop a factorial model that elucidates the determinants influencing student virtue cultivation. Meanwhile, the independent samples T-test was applied to analyze the perceptions of students of different genders regarding moral education, teaching effectiveness, teacher behavior, and student virtue. The findings reveal that moral education significantly enhances both teaching effectiveness and teacher behaviors. Moreover, teaching effectiveness and teacher behaviors positively influence student virtue, with teaching effectiveness exerting a stronger impact. Additionally, teacher behaviors were found to positively affect teaching effectiveness. Gender differences also emerged, indicating that male participants demonstrating a deeper understanding of both teaching effectiveness and student virtue. This research contributes both theoretical and practical contributions it advances the understanding of moral education mechanisms and offering strategies to enhance virtue cultivation in higher education institutions.

TI Pragmatic failures in L2 English learners: a cross-cultural
   mixed-methods study of implicature and presupposition
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pragmatic failure; implicature; presupposition; L2 learners; second
   language acquisition; Social Sciences; Sports and Leisure; Physical
   Education; Education; Secondary Education; By Subject;
   Primary/Elementary Education; Curriculum Studies
ID TEACHING PRAGMATICS; SPEECH-ACT
AB This paper explores the pragmatic failure in L2 English learners and its implicature and presupposition in cross-cultural communication. A convergent mixed-method design was employed, and 120 Arabic- and Japanese-speaking learners were requested to complete Discourse Completion Tasks (DCTs), questionnaires, and semi-structured interviews. The results indicate systematic group differences in pragmalinguistic and sociopragmatic failures which are influenced by cultural norms and L1 transfer. The quantitative findings indicate that the implicature processing is more difficult than presupposition and that affective variables (especially anxiety and confidence) have a strong impact on pragmatic accuracy. Qualitative analysis brings out roles of cultural expectations, emotional constraints and minimal exposure to authentic discourse. The intercultural-relevance model of pragmatic failure, the combination of cognitive, sociocultural, and affective levels, is suggested in the study. The pedagogical implications of the findings are explicit pragmatic teaching and affect-sensitive teaching to improve L2 communicative competence.

   in EFL students across islamic and general universities in Indonesia
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Perceived learning outcome; student engagement; teacher support; peer
   support; foreign language anxiety; demotivation
ID TEACHER SUPPORT; ENGAGEMENT; SCHOOL; CLASSROOM
AB Language learning is not merely a cognitive endeavor; it is shaped by students' emotional experiences and social environment. This study investigates how teacher support, peer support, foreign language anxiety, and demotivation in EFL associate with student engagement and perceived learning outcomes in English language education. A total of 511 university students from 9 Indonesian higher education institutions located in 5 provinces in Indonesia participated in the research. TI Comparative study of school caste in Japan and Indonesia 2: unraveling
   occurrence triggers and influencing factors
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE School caste; peer hierarchy; institutional arrangement; comparative
   analysis; Indonesia
AB This study examines the formation of school caste, or informal peer hierarchies, in Indonesian schools. Using anonymous questionnaire data, correlation and logistic regression analyses were conducted and compared with findings from Japan. The results revealed three characteristics: (1) clear hierarchical classification among peer groups; (2) a stronger tendency toward hierarchical structuring among female students; and (3) a more pronounced manifestation of school caste in senior high school than in middle school. Unlike Japan, where peer hierarchies become institutionalized relatively early, Indonesian peer dynamics are marked by high boundary permeability and social intimacy, delaying the consolidation of hierarchical recognition until later educational stages. Although the term school caste is not widely used in Indonesia, similar structural mechanisms were identified. By clarifying these "double-edged" peer structures, which involve both risks of exclusion and opportunities for social development, this study provides a foundation for structure-aware approaches to communication-based bullying in Indonesian secondary education.

TI Framework for Islamic education in Muslim minority countries:
   experiences from Finland
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Islamic education; Finland; religious minorities; religious communities;
   national education systems
ID RELIGIOUS-EDUCATION; DIVERSITY; PERSPECTIVES; GOVERNANCE
AB Finland has garnered considerable global attention for having one of the world's best education systems. As a secular Nordic country, Finland has seen the number of Muslim students interested in Islamic education (IE) almost triple over the past few decades. This article examines IE within the Finnish National Education System (FNES), focusing on the construction of IE in Finland and its curriculum. Examining IE as a form of minority education, this study also explores Finnish IE teachers' perceptions of religious moderation in heterogeneous Muslim classrooms. The findings show that IE is allocated the same curricular weight as majority religious education; designing such curricula-with varying emphases on "introduction" and "understanding" content across different levels of comprehensive schooling-requires close collaboration with religious communities and municipal governments. Furthermore, teachers addressed debates over Islamic denominational differences among students by fostering a consensus-based, non-denominational approach to Islam. These findings carry theoretical implications for developing a representative model of IE. The study further contributes to IE policy discussions by emphasizing student development over administrative concerns.

TI Constructing excellence? The role of Academic Reputation in University
   rankings
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE University rankings; academic reputation; QS methodology; indicator
   weighting; variance decomposition; methodological sensitivity;
   comparative evaluation
ID QUALITY; POLICY
AB This study examines whether Academic Reputation is structurally privileged within the QS World University Rankings and whether its influence reflects institutional performance or the ranking model's weighting design. Using the full 2026 QS dataset covering 1,501 universities and 10 indicators, the paper applies variance decomposition to estimate the net and joint contribution of each indicator to overall-score variance and compares the official weighted model with an unweighted counterfactual. Academic Reputation makes the largest net contribution to overall-score variance (13.6%); with its strongest joint effects involving Employer Reputation (12.2%) and Citations per Faculty (10.6%). This dominance is driven primarily by its high assigned weight rather than by empirical dispersion alone. When weights are removed , its net contribution falls to 1.5%. Although weighted and unweighted scores remain highly correlated, only eight universities retain the same rank, indicating substantial positional sensitivity. The results show that QS rankings are shaped by weighting design rather than serving as neutral measures of institutional performance. Universities should therefore avoid treating rankings as self-evident measures of quality, providers should justify indicator weights transparently , and policymakers should use rankings cautiously as proxies for excellence, or performance.

TI Effectiveness of virtual biology experiments developed by Rwanda Quality
   Basic Education in enhancing students' understanding and engagement in
   genetics
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Virtual Biology Laboratories; genetics; dominance; codominance; biology
   education; students' engagement
ID REMOTE
AB Teaching and learning genetics remain challenging because of the abstractness of key concepts, inherent complexity of genetic processes, and the extensive time often needed for experimental investigations. To address this issue, virtual biology laboratory tools (VBLs) for genetics aligned with the lower secondary Rwandan curriculum were developed and their effectiveness was assessed. Data were collected from 120 students and 16 biology teachers selected from 4 districts in Rwanda. 97.8% of students and 95% of teachers revealed that these VBLs were interactive, engaging, and effective in developing critical thinking and analytical skills as well as offering flexibility in learning. Additionally, students reported high motivation when using the developed VBLs, and students' motivation correlated positively (r=0.67) with pedagogical effectiveness of the tools. Furthermore, students improved their performance (t(119) = 29.30, p < 0.05) after interacting with the VBLs, reflecting the contribution of these tools on genetics conceptual understanding. However, limited computer availability, technical difficulties and inadequate digital skills were identified as factors limiting the use of these tools to teach and learn genetics in Rwandan lower secondary schools. Strengthening ICT infrastructure, providing technical teachers' training and the development of VBLs mobile-compatible versions were recommended to increase accessibility and use of VBLs.

TI Enhancing synchronous online mathematics instruction using the visual
   learning analytics-supported ADDIE approach: implications from two
   post-pandemic studies
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Online instruction; mathematics teaching; learning analytics; secondary
   education; ADDIE; Mathematics education; Technology-enhanced learning
ID ENGAGEMENT; TEACHERS
AB Synchronous online instruction eliminates geographical constraints, ensuring students' access to education (Sustainable Development Goal 4) even in unforeseen circumstances. This study explored the potential of this instructional environment in the post-pandemic world. Using the analysis, design, development, implementation and evaluation (ADDIE) approach, it began with an analysis to identify instructional challenges from the literature and a pilot study. Subsequently, instructional materials for an enrichment programme for high-ability students (Study 1) and a remedial programme for underperforming students (Study 2) were designed and developed, both informed by variation theory. After implementing these synchronous online programmes, the study examined teacher instruction through the lens of visual learning analytics (VLA) and students' mathematics achievement and engagement. The VLA results revealed that the teacher used fewer types of mathematics instruction related to naming (e.g. referencing mathematical terminology) and tasks (e.g. asking students to undertake specific steps) in the remedial programme, and that student participation in class discussions increased when the teacher provided feedback on their classwork. The test results indicated that the mathematics achievement of the students in Study 1 was significantly improved, whereas the learning recovery of the students in Study 2 was not statistically significant. Nevertheless, the students in both groups demonstrated high levels of engagement in their survey and attendance rate. This study provides methodological implications for facilitating research and improvements in synchronous online mathematics instruction through VLA. It also provides pedagogical and policy-related implications for addressing challenges associated with this instructional environment to create additional, sustainable learning opportunities.

LA English
DT Article
DE Big data; online teaching; teaching quality monitoring; monitoring mode;
   educational data mining
AB Direct transplantation of traditional classroom monitoring modes to online teaching scenarios leads to inherent incompatibility, as such modes fail to adapt to data-intensive nature of virtual instruction. Given the innate big data attributes of online teaching, big data technology emerges as an ideal solution to this problem. TI "From Exhaustion to Invigoration": a mixed-methods study exploring the

LA English
DT Article
DE Medical education; medical students; physician burnout; physician
   wellness; resilience
ID BURNOUT
AB Objectives It is critical to identify factors in the work environment that contribute to physician burnout to foster a professional culture that nurtures wellness. This study examined the prevalence of burnout symptoms among a group of Canadian pediatric undergraduate education leaders and explored how membership in a national community (Paediatric Undergraduate Program Directors of Canada, PUPDOC) may serve as a potential mitigating factor.Methods This mixed-methods study involved a survey and subsequent focus groups of PUPDOC members. TI Student perceptions of generative AI in built environment education:
   Evidence from a mixed-methods study and a five-pillar integration
   framework
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; AI chatbots; built environment
   education; student perceptions; personalised learning and digital
   literacy
ID USER ACCEPTANCE
AB This study critically examines students' perceptions and experiences of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in built environment education. Employing a mixed-methods (pragmatist approach), we surveyed 277 undergraduates and postgraduates in Nigeria and Namibia, complemented by thematic analysis of open-ended responses. TI SAFE-CBL: a Legitimation Code Theory-informed framework for large-cohort
   practice-based teaching
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Legitimation Code Theory LCT; Competition-Based learning; student
   engagement; accelerated development; active learning
AB Massification has intensified tensions between authentic, feedback-rich learning and the practical constraints of large-cohort practice-based higher education. While competition-based learning (CBL) has demonstrated potential to enhance engagement and skill development, concerns regarding scalability, workload, and assessment design have limited its wider adoption. This study examines how CBL can be structured as a scalable curriculum architecture rather than a discrete pedagogical intervention. Drawing on an eight-year programme of longitudinal action research (2018-2025), the paper develops SAFE-CBL (Scalable, Authentic, Feedback-Embedded Competition-Based Learning) through iterative framework refinement informed by performance data, learning analytics, student and educator reflections, and implementation evidence. Legitimation Code Theory (LCT), specifically the Semantics dimension, is employed to examine how recurring challenge-feedback-reattempt cycles support movement between abstract disciplinary knowledge and contextualised professional practice. Findings suggest that scalable implementation depends on the alignment of authentic challenge tasks, structured feedback, reattempt opportunities, and psychologically safe learning conditions. SAFE-CBL contributes a theoretically informed and empirically grounded curriculum architecture that reframes competition as a mechanism for feedback, progression, and learner agency, offering a transferable approach to assessment design in massified higher education.

ID SELF-EFFICACY; IDENTITY; STUDENT; BURNOUT; STRESS
AB Critical incidents (CIs) experienced by university faculty represent key moments that reveal not only pedagogical challenges but also underlying sociocultural tensions within the classroom. The study highlights a gap between managing critical incidents and understanding their sociocultural dimensions, emphasizing the need to strengthen culturally responsive competencies in teacher professional development. TI The intersection of internet epistemic beliefs and perception of writing
   in shaping students' views of ChatGPT's feedback
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT feedback; internet epistemic beliefs; academic writing;
   AI-assisted learning; Language Teaching & Learning; Education; Classroom
   Practice; Assessment; Education & Training; Teacher Education & Training
ID INFORMATION; CHALLENGES
AB This study addresses the limited research on how students' internet epistemic beliefs (IEB) and perceptions of writing (PoW) jointly influence their engagement with AI-generated feedback, particularly across English as a Foreign Language (EFL) and English as a Second Language (ESL) contexts. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was adopted, involving 235 undergraduate students from Indonesia (EFL) and Malaysia (ESL). Data were collected through a structured questionnaire measuring IEB, PoW and perception of ChatGPT (PoC), followed by semi-structured interviews that explored students' epistemic stance and experiences with ChatGPT in writing tasks. Structural equation modeling (SEM) showed that IEB strongly predicted PoC (beta = 0.827, t = 15.5, p < 0.001), whereas PoW had no significant effect (beta = -0.0658, t = 1.23, p = 0.219). The model explained 61.8% of the variance in PoC. Thematic analysis further revealed students' epistemic vigilance, pragmatic reliance on ChatGPT for linguistic and organizational support, and their consistent preference for human feedback in evaluating content quality. This finding suggests that while students' beliefs about online knowledge critically shape their evaluation of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated feedback, their writing-related motivation and self-efficacy may not directly determine whether they perceive such feedback as useful. Pedagogically, this highlights the need to integrate epistemic literacy into writing instruction through practical strategies such as source triangulation, peer-AI feedback comparison, and reflective tasks on the reliability of AI outputs.

TI Training of trainers on medical education reforms: a prospective
   multicenter French survey among intensivists
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical education; competency-based medical education; teacher training;
   objective structured clinical examination; simulation-based teaching
ID SIMULATION; PROGRAM; OSCE; TOOL
AB Background The recent reform of the second cycle of medical education in France introduced competency-based medical education (CBME) with the incorporation of several pedagogical modalities into undergraduate training and assessment, including objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs), simulation-based teaching (SBT), and clinical reasoning (CR) instruction throughout the academic year. While these tools are central to preparing competent practitioners, their effective implementation depends on adequately trained educators. We hypothesized that training would be insufficient, notably in the recently introduced pedagogical modalities.Methods We conducted a national, cross-sectional survey (June-September 2023) to assess the level and adequacy of training of board-certified physicians practicing in critical care and involved in undergraduate teaching. An anonymous online questionnaire collected demographic data, teaching frequency, training characteristics, perceived adequacy and usefulness of training, preparedness, and barriers. The responses were analyzed descriptively and comparatively.Results Among the 151 eligible respondents (72% male, median age 41 years, 70% working in teaching hospitals, and 44% holding an academic position), lectures remained the most common teaching modality despite CBME implementation. Only 60% of the respondents reported involvement in OSCEs. Teachers' training rates across pedagogical modalities were low and heterogeneous: 32% for OSCEs, 30% for SBT, 29% for written assessment design, 24% for lectures, and 12% for CR. Training in the SBT was more often practical, longer in duration, and rated as more useful and adequate than training in other modalities. Overall, the respondents reported moderate preparedness and frequent teaching difficulties. Prior training was associated with higher perceived preparedness and fewer difficulties when teaching students. Lack of dedicated time was the most frequently reported barrier to training (69%).Conclusion This national survey revealed insufficient and heterogeneous training of intensivist educators in all pedagogical modalities of the undergraduate curriculum. Trainers report limited preparedness and frequent challenges. Standardized, accessible, and time-protected faculty development programs are urgently needed to support CBME education.

AB The study looks into the challenges to Institutional External Evaluation (IEE) of higher education in T & uuml;rkiye. TI Construction and practical implications of an interdisciplinary teaching
   path for DNA diffraction patterns-from the perspective of scientific
   history and principle visualization
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE DNA diffraction patterns; interdisciplinary teaching; scientific history
   education; principle visualization; scientific practice; senior high
   school biology
AB DNA diffraction patterns are critical evidence for the DNA double helix and an interdisciplinary bridge linking biology, chemistry and physics. To address gaps in high school biology teaching including ambiguous pattern-structure reasoning and fragmented cross-disciplinary learning, this research builds a three-stage teaching path guided by situated cognition, constructivism and NGSS. It traces the historical discovery of DNA diffraction from Astbury to Franklin, clarifies mappings between X-ray diffraction rules, diffraction images and DNA structures, and develops history-based inquiry, visual experiment and interdisciplinary teaching strategies. TI Provision of teaching and learning resources in schools as a
   prerequisite for high-quality social sciences education: an analysis of
   Lithuanian general education schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Competence-based education; teaching and learning materials; social
   studies education, educational resources; curriculum implementation
ID HISTORY
AB The implementation of competence-based curricula requires not only methodological change but also adequate material conditions that enable meaningful learning experiences. This study examines the availability and use of teaching and learning materials as a structural precondition for high-quality social studies education in Lithuanian general education schools. Using a mixed-methods design, the research combines national quantitative data from 1,315 schools with qualitative interviews conducted with 32 school principals. The findings indicate a systemic shortage of teaching materials in history, geography, and primary social studies. Schools often possess only part of the required resources, with particularly limited access to interactive and inquiry-based tools that support analytical, spatial, and historical thinking. While traditional visual materials are more common, modern and subject-specific resources remain insufficient. School leaders report prioritizing materials necessary for formal curriculum implementation, especially textbooks, while innovative tools are frequently postponed due to financial constraints. Although many schools aim for equal distribution across subjects, social studies are often perceived as relatively under-resourced. The findings suggest that teaching materials function as an important mediating factor between intended curriculum and classroom practice. A more strategic, subject-sensitive approach to resource provision is needed to ensure equitable and high-quality competence-based social studies education.

TI Preferred sources of meaning in life amongst preservice teachers from
   Generation Z: an exploratory qualitative study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Q-methodology; LeBe/SoMe; university students; existential meaning;
   existential concerns
ID CARE
AB In emerging adulthood, especially among university students, the search for meaning in life is a significant existential concern. This study investigates whether there are differences in preferences for sources of life meaning between preservice teachers and students in other disciplines. Grounded in Schnell's theory of sources of meaning, the study utilises Q-methodology, employing 26 statements describing sources of life meaning, with participants (n = 351) ranking them through forced sorting. Q-methodology was selected for its ability to capture subjective perspectives while allowing systematic statistical analysis. Although some statistically significant differences emerge regarding challenge, success, freedom, knowledge, love, comfort, care, and harmony, the core finding applies across Generation Z. Love, health, and freedom consistently rank highest among all groups of university students, whereas explicit religiosity, spirituality, and tradition rank lowest. These patterns reveal a distinctive value profile of young adults in a post-secular context, characterised by a strong focus on relational and autonomy-based values rather than traditional religious frameworks. This insight has important implications for teacher development and values education. Comparing results from an explicitly secular country with findings from culturally and religiously diverse nations, including traditional Catholic countries, could provide further insights into the meaning of life among younger generations.

TI Corporate governance as a driver of university sustainability: a PLS-SEM
   analysis in public higher education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Corporate governance; university sustainability; public higher
   education; new institutionalism; structural equations; reflective
   measurement; Social Sciences; Education; Higher Education; Study of
   Higher Education; Teaching & Learning
ID DIMENSIONS
AB Corporate governance is a key determinant of university sustainability. Although theoretical work describes the interaction between these constructs, there is a lack of empirical studies assessing their causal relationship. To address this knowledge gap, this study assessed the impact of corporate governance on university sustainability in an accredited public institution in Colombia. The novelty lies in presenting corporate governance as the primary construct that affects university sustainability from a management perspective. In contrast, in the reported studies, it appears only as an isolated indicator in evaluating sustainability. The new institutionalism, the resource-based view, and the new stakeholder theory underpinned the theoretical model. The research was developed using deductive reasoning. It applied a structural equation model using least squares in Smart PLS 4.1.0.9 based on a sample of 398 respondents (professors and administrative staff) to evaluate the reflective measurement model and the structural model. The empirical analysis found that corporate governance, comprising the administrative process, university autonomy, stakeholders and the accountability system, positively affects university sustainability, which includes education for sustainable development and a sustainable campus. The study provides valuable recommendations for assessing university sustainability, highlighting the strategic significance of corporate governance for self-regulation and continuous improvement.

TI What do young people's menstruation stories do?
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Menstruation; stigma; agency; education
ID GIRLS EXPERIENCES
AB The menstruation stories of young people have been part of research that draws attention to youth experiences of menstrual stigma. Young people's menstruation stories are not, however, part of education policies in England that the Government says are crucial to addressing menstrual stigma. Relationships, Sex and Health Education (DfE 2025a) and the free period products policy (DfE 2025b) focus on teachers instructing pupils about menstruation and providing them with products. This paper considers what young people's menstruation stories do and what they could do as part of such initiatives. Drawing on the Deleuze-Guattarian (1987) notion of the assemblage, it analyses the menstruation stories of 21 young people aged 15 years old. It suggests that such young people's stories contributed to, but also helped to disrupt, three types of menstruation narrative (or narrative-assemblage): the gender division narrative-assemblage; the personal struggle narrative-assemblage and the spectator narrative-assemblage. The paper then considers what such an analysis implies about possibilities for reforming menstruation education policy and practice. To do so, it draws on Karen Barad's () practice of diffractive reading and reads young people's stories though education policies to present proposals for reforming menstruation education.

TI Research interest in nursing undergraduate students: an exploration of
   research-linked courses
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing students; research interest; higher education; research
   training; educational innovation
ID RESEARCH OUTCOME EXPECTATIONS; SOCIAL COGNITIVE THEORY; SELF-EFFICACY
   BELIEFS; R PACKAGE; CAREER
AB Background Among Hispanic undergraduate students, the association between research-related coursework and research interest remains largely underexplored. This exploratory study examined differences in research interest among undergraduate nursing students according to their exposure to research-related coursework, drawing on Social Cognitive Career Theory. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted with 106 nursing students from a Peruvian university. Participants completed the Interest in Research Questionnaire (IRQ), which demonstrated excellent internal consistency (alpha = 0.98). Research interest was compared across four academic-semester groupings reflecting proximal and distal exposure to research-related coursework using rank-based nonparametric methods. Results Significant differences in research interest were observed across groups (Anderson-Darling test = 9.41, p = 0.001), indicating a curvilinear pattern. Students currently or recently exposed to research-related coursework (levels 2 and 4) reported significantly higher research interest than those with more distal exposure (level 3; p < 0.05; medium effect sizes). First-semester students showed research interest levels comparable to those of the proximally exposed groups. Conclusion Research interest may decline in the absence of sustained engagement in research activities, underscoring the importance of early and continuous integration of research experiences throughout undergraduate nursing curricula. The findings also provide initial evidence supporting the use of the IRQ in Spanish-speaking undergraduate contexts.

TI Bending the rules in favor of the child in socioeconomically
   disadvantaged areas: principals as street-level bureaucrats
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Street-level bureaucracy; School-Age Educare (SAEC); school principals;
   socioeconomic disadvantage; discretion; Social Sciences; Education;
   Early Years; Development Studies, Environment, Social Work, Urban
   Studies; Sociology
ID HEALTH; POLICY
AB The aim of this study is to examine school principals' work-related considerations and decisions, and how they navigate tensions between state policy and children's needs, while leading School-Age Educare Centers (SAECs) in Swedish socioeconomically disadvantaged areas. Drawing on interviews with principals, the framework of street-level bureaucracy, in addition to vertical and horizontal governance, is applied. The results extend the theoretical understanding of street-level bureaucracy by demonstrating the interplay between vertical governance, horizontal contextual culture and a socially just leadership, underscoring the critical importance of contextually responsive, socially responsible decision-making in education.

TI Pedagogical Symbiosis: conceptualizing the Post-Human Learner in the age
   of cognitive AI
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pedagogical symbiosis; Post-human learner; Generative AI in education;
   Extended mind thesis; Critical posthumanism; Distributed cognition;
   Cognitive choreographer
AB The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into educational settings exposes a fundamental inadequacy in existing pedagogical frameworks, which typically treat technology as a mere instrument rather than a constitutive cognitive partner. This paper introduces Pedagogical Symbiosis, a conceptual framework redefining the learner as a Post-Human entity whose cognitive processes are genuinely hybrid and distributed across biological and artificial systems. Grounded in Vygotskian mediation, the extended mind thesis, critical posthumanism, and distributed cognition, the framework proposes four principles: Cognitive Offloading and Augmentation, Epistemic Co-construction, Metacognitive Symbiosis, and Dynamic Identity Formation. A developmental progression informed by Piagetian, Vygotskyan, and Eriksonian stage theories supports these principles. Unlike TPACK and SAM, which retain instrumentalist limitations, Pedagogical Symbiosis offers an ontological reorientation. The paper details practical K-16 operationalization through subject-specific curriculum applications, a Symbiotic Portfolio Assessment Rubric, and a five-module professional development structure for the "Cognitive Choreographer" teacher role. Institutional policy pathways and direct engagements with counterarguments regarding autonomy, techno-determinism, and epistemic opacity further contextualize the model. Ultimately, this paper makes a threefold contribution through ontological reorientation, an integrative framework, and practical operationalization, providing curriculum designers, teacher educators, classroom teachers, and policymakers with a robust paradigm for navigating human-AI partnerships in modern educational systems.

TI The impact of teacher corrective feedback on students' sense of
   belonging, academic vitality, and engagement: a multidimensional
   exploration
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher corrective feedback; sense of belonging; academic vitality;
   engagement
ID SCHOOL CONNECTEDNESS
AB This study explores the multidimensional impact of teacher corrective feedback (CF) on students' sense of belonging, academic vitality, and engagement in secondary school settings. While CF is a well-established pedagogical tool for improving academic skills, its psychological effects remain underexplored. Drawing on self-determination theory, school connectedness theory, and feedback literacy frameworks, this mixed-methods investigation examined how CF influences these constructs and their implications for teaching practice. Participants included 320 students and 18 teachers from five urban secondary schools, assessed via pre- and post-intervention surveys (Psychological Sense of School Membership Scale, Subjective Vitality Scale, Student Engagement Instrument), classroom observations, and semi-structured interviews. A repeated-measures MANOVA revealed significant post-intervention increases in the experimental group, with CF explaining 51% of variance in belonging, 49% in vitality, and 56% in engagement, compared to minimal changes in the control group. Qualitative findings highlighted the importance of feedback variety, immediacy, and supportiveness, with students reporting enhanced motivation and connection when CF was constructive. Results align with theoretical predictions that autonomy-supportive, relational CF fosters psychological well-being and academic investment. Cultural and individual variability, such as proficiency and feedback tone preferences, moderated outcomes, suggesting the need for tailored approaches.

TI Technology transfer practices and curriculum-integrated utilisation of
   Open Educational Resources by secondary school teachers
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Technology transfer; Open Educational Resources; curriculum integration;
   secondary Education; digital infrastructure
ID ACCEPTANCE
AB Open Educational Resources (OERs) are increasingly recognised as mechanisms for enhancing curriculum quality and expanding equitable access to educational resources; however, empirical evidence on their adoption in sub-Saharan African secondary education remains limited. This study investigated technology transfer practices and OER utilisation among secondary school teachers, guided by the Technology Acceptance Model and Diffusion of Innovations theory. Adopting a post-positivist research paradigm, the study employed an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. Data were collected from 70 participants (56 teachers and 14 administrators) across 10 stratified-randomly selected secondary schools in Kigamboni District, Tanzania. Findings reveal that 87.5% of teachers were aware of OERs and 71.4% frequently integrated them into curriculum delivery through AI tools, educational videos, and curriculum-aligned lesson plans, mainly accessed via mobile devices. Nevertheless, poor internet connectivity, fragmented training, and absent curriculum policies constrained sustained integration. The findings indicate that the perceived usefulness of OERs was high, while perceived ease of use was limited by infrastructure deficits. The study highlights the need for OER-aligned policies, digital infrastructure investment, and structured professional development to support effective and sustainable OER adoption in Tanzania across similar contexts.

TI Discovering old values: a professional trajectory story of a mid-career
   English teacher
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE English teacher; higher education; life course approach; mid-career;
   narrative inquiry
ID QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; CAREER STORIES; LIFE-COURSE; LANGUAGE;
   PERSPECTIVE; MOTIVATION; COMMITMENT; IDENTITIES; EDUCATION; CONTEXT
AB The career of English teachers has attracted significant attention from scholars worldwide. With the introduction of the life course approach, a new stream of research on teacher career trajectories has emerged to explore their complexity and the forces that shape them. This study, following this approach, aimed to investigate how a university English teacher shaped her mid-career trajectory. TI A system dynamics analysis of higher education admission policy:
   evidence from highly selective degree programs in Iran
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE System dynamics; higher education policy; University admission; labor
   market balance; admission capacity policy
ID DEMAND
AB The balance between the supply and demand of university graduates is crucial for preventing professional shortages, graduate unemployment, and labor market mismatches. This study examines Iran as a case of a centralized higher education admission system in which national entrance examination results and state-regulated admission capacities strongly shape access to selective degree programs. Focusing on medicine, engineering, and law, the study uses system dynamics modeling to analyze how admission capacity policies influence student choices, graduate supply, professional income, and labor market balance over time. The simulation results show that coordinated adjustments across fields are more effective than isolated policy changes. Extending medical admission expansion can increase physicians per capita and improve healthcare access, while reducing engineering admissions can help mitigate graduate oversupply and underemployment. Increasing law admissions can expand access to legal services, although a 5% increase appears insufficient to generate substantial system-level change. The findings suggest that proportional and coordinated admission policies can support national development goals, including improved healthcare access, better employment outcomes, and stronger access to justice. Although the model is based on Iran, its implications are relevant for countries with centralized or highly competitive admission systems facing similar challenges in aligning higher education capacity with labor market demand .

TI Digital infrastructure and educational gender parity in the Western
   Balkans: a multilevel analysis of regional patterns and technology
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Educational gender parity; multilevel modelling; Western Balkans;
   digital infrastructure; feminisation of higher education; post-socialist
   education
ID SELF-EFFICACY; INTERNET; COMPUTER; ICT; KNOWLEDGE; BELIEFS; SCIENCE;
   DIVIDE; SKILLS; WOMEN
AB This study examines educational gender parity across six Western Balkan countries-Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Serbia-between 2018 and 2023, against a background of uneven digital infrastructure development. Drawing on integrated World Bank and Eurostat indicators, we estimate cross-classified multilevel models that partition variance simultaneously across countries and educational levels. Primary and secondary education are at parity throughout the region, while tertiary education shows a substantial and durable female advantage. Educational level accounts for approximately five times more systematic variance than country context, indicating that supranational educational expansion processes outweigh national digital infrastructure differences in shaping contemporary gender outcomes. The article treats digital infrastructure as a contextual rather than causal determinant of educational gender parity, and demonstrates the value of cross-classified multilevel modelling for comparative regional research where individual-level longitudinal data are unavailable. Findings imply that gender-equity policy should shift from access-oriented interventions towards addressing horizontal field segregation at tertiary level.

TI Multi-sited ethnography: investigating inherent racism in education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Multi-sited ethnography; racialised discourse; inherent racism; widening
   participation
ID CRITICAL RACE THEORY; WIDENING PARTICIPATION; DISCOURSE; WHITENESS;
   POLICY; ISSUE
AB Multi-sited ethnography has been adopted in different national contexts to shed light on the dynamics of race, ethnicity and racism in education. This includes research that favours a "travelling" or "following" design as proposed by the anthropologist George Marcus. This paper extends this scholarship by exploring the potential of a multi-sited approach to engage with racism as inherent in education systems. It explores this by reflecting on a multi-sited study to "follow" widening participation policy in UK higher education. Of significance to the discussion is an engagement with David Theo Goldberg's excavation of racialised discourse to address the clarity of racial definition in multi-sited research. The paper argues that multi-sited research that avoids falling into the "trap" of what has been described as "tacit holism" in the multi-sited imaginary, offers possibilities for signalling the pervasiveness of racist "common sense" in education systems without claiming to represent those racist structures.

TI Navigating the ethical landscape of educational research: a systematic
   scoping review
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Research ethics; educational research; social science research; scoping
   review; systematic review; Research Ethics; Educational Sciences;
   Research Methods
ID QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; NURSING-EDUCATION; INFORMED-CONSENT; 12 TIPS;
   CHILDREN; HEALTH; STUDENTS; ISSUES; REPRESENTATION; PARTICIPATION
AB Research ethics is at the core of responsible and trustworthy scientific practice. This scoping review maps how peer-reviewed, English-language studies published between 2000 and 2022 have addressed research ethics within educational research, broadly defined to include preschool to higher education and the perspectives of learners, educators, policymakers, and the public. As a transdisciplinary field with relational and normative aims, educational research often seeks to enhance teaching and promote fairness and justice, thereby generating distinctive ethical challenges. Growing expectations for research-informed educational practice and the formalization of ethics through international, national, and institutional guidelines further underscore the importance of ethical competence at individual, collective, and organizational levels. Despite this, existing reviews indicate that ethical debates remain dominated by medical paradigms, with limited attention to the situated dilemmas common in educational settings, particularly for researchers studying their own professional contexts. This review examines (1) the characteristics of studies addressing research ethics, (2) the ethical principles they engage, and (3) how ethics is approached contextually, theoretically and methodologically. Findings show broad yet uneven engagement: participant protection is prioritized, while ethical dimensions of research quality and societal relevance are underexplored. The discussion points to a conceptual imbalance and the need for clearer definitions, context-sensitive approaches, stronger theoretical grounding, and improved dialogue with ethics committees.

TI Muslim parental school choice and the negotiation of religious identity
   and social belonging in Muslim-minority societies: narratives from
   suburban Maryland, the United States
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Islamic school; parental school choice; American Muslim; Social
   Ecological Model
AB Previous literature on Muslim parents' school choice has highlighted the challenge of balancing secular and religious education in Muslim-minority contexts. However, little attention has been paid to understanding these dynamics through the lens of school-choice systems themselves. This study examined factors influencing Muslim parents' school choices in suburban Maryland. Interviews with 14 participants from a private Islamic school were analysed using the Social Ecological Model and thematic analysis. Twelve themes emerged, illustrating how choices were shaped by school characteristics, reputations, the pursuit of religious and social identity, and temporal contexts. Results demonstrated that school-choice decisions are better understood as contextually embedded navigational strategies, in which school characteristics are evaluated through the lens of macrosystemic values around religious identity and social belonging. Parents sought schools balancing Islamic and secular education, yet divergent visions of what Islamic education should represent-particularly around de-ethnicised versus culturally particularistic interpretations-may also generate divisions among Islamic schools, suggesting that school-choice systems have the potential to reconfigure boundaries not only between Muslims and secular society, but also within the Muslim community itself.

TI Determinants of ChatGPT adoption in underdeveloped academic settings: a
   case study of Somalia using an extended TAM approach
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT adoption; technology acceptance model; higher education in
   Somalia; AI in education; social influence; facilitating conditions
ID PLS-SEM; INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; STUDENTS ACCEPTANCE; SOCIAL-INFLUENCE;
   USER ACCEPTANCE; BUSINESS; TRUST
AB Artificial Intelligence (AI) has revolutionized various domains, including higher education, particularly through generative tools like ChatGPT. To date, only one study has used the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to examine students' intention to use ChatGPT in Somalia, focusing mainly on core constructs like perceived usefulness and ease of use. This study extends previous work by introducing additional constructs, including awareness of ChatGPT, facilitating conditions, and the moderating effects of trust and gender, uncovering more meaningful, localized determinants of ChatGPT adoption among university students in Mogadishu. A self-administered, cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 468 students from five universities in Mogadishu. Data were analyzed using SmartPLS 4. Results indicate that awareness alone does not directly impact adoption intention; however, perceived usefulness fully mediates this relationship. Further, social influence and facilitating conditions emerged as strong predictors of adoption intention, while perceived ease of use, trust, and gender differences showed weaker effects. The findings highlight the importance of peer influence, resource availability, institutional support, and perceived benefits in driving AI adoption in low-income settings. The study recommends that universities should clearly communicate ChatGPT's practical benefits and promote peer-driven learning environments. The Somali higher education sector should establish and implement guidelines to ensure ethical and effective integration of AI tools like ChatGPT.

TI Extra-CURRICULAR activity participation at an English post-92
   university: an exploration of student drivers and barriers through the
   lens of Possible Selves Theory
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Engagement; employability; experience; extra-curricular activities;
   Possible Selves; identity transformation; widening participation
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; EMPLOYABILITY; EXPERIENCES; COLLEGE
AB This study explores student engagement with university-led extracurricular activities (ECAs) through the lens of Possible Selves Theory (PST) (individuals' ideas about what they might become, what they would like to become and what they are afraid of becoming) to understand motivations and barriers around ECAs. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 students (12 ECA participants, 8 NON-ECA participants) from diverse academic backgrounds at an English post-92 university. Thematic analysis revealed distinct patterns in how students constructed their possible future selves in relation to the idea of ECAs. ECA engaged participants articulated hoped-for selves centred on professional confidence, university integration and authentic identity development, while non-participants expressed feared selves around competency anxiety, time management overwhelm and financial vulnerability. Linguistic analysis indicated ECA participants used significantly more agentic language, future-oriented temporal markers and transformation narratives compared to NON-ECA participants' constraint-focused and present-anchored language patterns. We suggest that ECAs function as 'identity laboratories' where students safely experiment with future professional selves while developing confidence and capabilities. These insights have important implications for ECA design, recruitment strategies, and supporting diverse student populations in higher education. The research extends PST by showing how institutional programs can facilitate identity transformation beyond traditional academic learning.

TI Pre-service English teachers' perceptions of artificial intelligence as
   pedagogical support during teaching practicum across educational level
   and frequency of AI use
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Perception; AI as pedagogical support; teaching practicum; educational
   level; frequency of AI use
AB Pre-service English teachers (PSETs) perceive artificial intelligence (AI) as pedagogical support potentially helping them manage cognitive load during teaching practicum. However, differences in their perceptions of AI use based on educational level and frequency of use remain understudied. Guided by Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) as theoretical lens, this comparative quantitative study involved 105 PSETs completing two months of teaching practicum in Indonesia. Data were collected using a four-point Likert-scale questionnaire with four dimensions: Perceived Utility and Effectiveness in Classroom Practice (PUECP), Readiness and Confidence in Practical Use (RCPU), Role of AI in Student Engagement and Inclusivity (RASEI), and Concerns and Challenges Experienced in Practicum (CCEP). These findings suggest that higher frequencies of AI use are associated with positive perceptions regarding the usefulness of AI, readiness and confidence in using AI, and role of AI in enhancing student engagement and inclusivity. The findings highlight the importance of integrating AI literacy into teacher education programs.

TI Optimizing job resources to foster innovative work behaviour:
   psychological well-being as a mediator among Indonesian educators
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Job resources; innovative work behaviour; psychological wellbeing;

   SCIENCE; MODEL; ENGAGEMENT; TEACHERS; SUPPORT
AB Although job resources are widely recognised as important drivers of employee innovation, limited research has explained how such resources translate into innovative work behaviour through educators' internal psychological conditions. Grounded in the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework, this study investigates the effect of job resources on innovative work behaviour and examines the mediating role of psychological wellbeing among Indonesian educators. TI An integrated AI literacy framework for higher-education teachers: a
   critical review and conceptual synthesis
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; educator; teacher; higher education; AI competency;
   framework
ID INTELLIGENT TUTORING SYSTEMS; AUTOTUTOR
AB The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education necessitates a comprehensive understanding of AI literacy among educators. This critical interpretive synthesis aimed to identify emerging themes in teacher AI literacy and to synthesise those themes into an integrated framework. Guided by PRISMA principles, a systematic search yielded 23 peer-reviewed studies. These articles were subjected to critical interpretive synthesis to resolve conceptual conflicts and include competencies overlooked in existing frameworks. The study identified significant gaps in ethical understanding, innovative use of AI and institutional support among faculty. Conceptualised as a holistic competency model, the framework extends beyond core foundational knowledge and pedagogical application to encompass advanced capabilities in evaluating, creating and deploying AI tools. Eight core dimensions were identified: foundational knowledge and understanding, application and pedagogical integration, critical evaluation, innovation, ethical, epistemic, legal and institutional governance and emotional and professional wellbeing. By incorporating epistemic, legal governance and emotional dimensions, the integrated eight-dimension framework provides educators with human-centred oversight of responsible and ethical AI pedagogy. The study underscores the necessity for higher education institutions to adopt tiered, long-term GenAI literacy training that integrates foundational knowledge with advanced AI competencies, thereby fostering responsible GenAI adoption that enhances student learning.

TI The predicament of saying: Writing the unsayable in interpretivist
   qualitative educational research
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Interpretivist qualitative research; educational research; academic
   writing; phenomenology; post-qualitative inquiry
AB Critiques of methodology-as-technique within qualitative educational research have produced a generative turn toward inner stances-lyricism, meditative thinking, experiential attunement, reflexive sincerity-as routes to experience that resists technical capture. This paper argues that within interpretivist qualitative inquiry, which retains commitments to representation as scholarly currency, these inner-stance turns generate a writing predicament. The fluid, anti-analytical qualities they seek to honour must travel through the analytical, objectifying, procedurally visible medium of academic prose. The paper diagnoses three structural sources of the predicament and traces three consequences for educational research practice: dilemmas of doctoral training that risk methodological elitism; peer-review and examination deadlocks that incentivise performances of sincerity; and communicative breakdowns that produce structural misreading. The paper then engages post-qualitative responses to ask whether they dissolve the predicament or relocate it, and closes with implications for doctoral training, peer review, and dissemination in educational research.

TI Agreement, calibration, and failure of three large language models as
   high-stakes multimodal ospe graders: a comparative psychometric analysis
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Large language models; OSPE; automated grading; multimodal assessment;
   inter- responsible AI
ID LOW KAPPA; RELIABILITY; BIAS
AB Background Medical education faces increasing demand for scalable grading solutions. Large language models have been proposed as automated graders for high-stakes assessments, but evidence for their reliability in multimodal practical examinations remains limited.Methods This retrospective inter-rater reliability study compared three LLMs: ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Claude 3.5 Haiku with original human reference scores on 19 integrated anatomy, histology, and physiology objective structured practical examination items completed by 309 pre-medical students. Human reference scores were assigned during live summative grading by two content experts who divided items, with each item marked by one expert across all students; no human inter-rater reliability estimate was available. Items required simultaneous image interpretation and short-answer responses. Models were evaluated using zero-shot prompting reflecting deployment-realistic conditions. Agreement was assessed using Spearman's rho, Cohen's kappa, intraclass correlation coefficients, and Bland-Altman analysis. Item-level gap analysis compared student success rates with LLM performance across items.Results Rank-order correlations were strong across all models (rho = 0.784-0.921), but categorical agreement diverged substantially. Pass/fail agreement ranged from 52.1% (ChatGPT; kappa = 0.067, slight) to 84.1% (Claude; kappa = 0.680, substantial). Bland-Altman analysis showed inconsistent systematic bias: Claude over-scored by +2.5 points, Gemini under-scored by -5.0 points, and ChatGPT by -10.0 points. Item-level gap analysis highlighted three recurring divergence patterns: non-standard histological staining, three-dimensional spatial reasoning from two-dimensional images, and semantic inflexibility in short-answer evaluation. The most extreme case was a pelvic three-dimensional model item on which 93.3% of students succeeded by human grading but all three LLMs assigned a mean score of zero.Conclusions Strong rank-order correlation alone does not support LLM grading for categorical decisions in high-stakes assessment contexts. LLMs may serve as assessment assistants for first-pass ranking and discrepancy flagging, but item-level human review of flagged discordances, error-profile monitoring, and preserved human authority over pass/fail decisions are required before high-stakes deployment.

TI Impact of faculty and resident gender on milestone evaluations in
   anesthesiology residency: a retrospective analysis
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Gender bias; anesthesiology; residency; qualitative; evaluation
AB Background: Anesthesia-specific milestone evaluations are intended to objectively assess performance in ACGME core competencies for anesthesiology residents. Recent reports in several medical specialties have documented differences in resident evaluations based on gender. Objective: We studied the impact of faculty and resident gender on milestone evaluations during Anesthesiology residency. Design: This was a retrospective analysis of 20,570 anesthesiology resident milestone evaluations from a single institution over a 7-year period during the ACGME milestones 1.0 time frame. Standardized scores were analyzed using a linear mixed model. Results: 170 anesthesiology residents were evaluated by 194 faculty. For CA1 evaluations, mean standardized milestone scores for the core competencies of professionalism (p = 0.002) and interpersonal/communication (p < 0.001) and for overall assessment (p = 0.009) were dependent on faculty gender. For CA2 evaluations, regardless of the evaluator gender, the mean standardized milestone scores for many individual core competencies were significantly higher for female residents compared to male residents. For CA3 evaluations, mean standardized milestone scores did not differ significantly between male residents and female residents for any core competency, however overall assessment scores were dependent on faculty gender with male faculty scoring male residents more highly and female faculty scoring female residents more highly (p < 0.001). Conclusions: We observed an association between faculty gender and milestone evaluation scores of residents that was most evident for CA1 residents. We also observed the overall assessment scores for male and female residents were significantly influenced by the gender of the faculty evaluator. Further work is required to better understand and mitigate gender bias to promote equity in resident assessment.

TI Screen time and physical activity in schoolchildren

DT Article

AB The rural world is not exempt from sedentary lifestyles and the globalization of screen use. TI 'Igniting the spark': the path to sustainable professional development
   for teachers in small-scale rural schools in China
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE small-scale rural schools; sustainable professional development;
   pathway; rural teacher; irrational beliefs
AB This study examines sustainable professional development for teachers in small-scale rural schools, where challenges include geographic isolation, heavy workloads, high turnover, inadequate mentoring, and limited advancement. Using a qualitative approach grounded in relational ontology, semi-structured and focus group interviews with 62 principals, teaching-research directors, and teachers from Jiangsu Province were analysed through classical grounded theory. Three pathways emerged: (1) teachers restoring the essence of education by reconnecting with teaching's intrinsic value; (2) school leaders and policymakers instilling hope through supportive conditions, recognition, and positive cultures; and (3) teachers transforming irrational beliefs, such as the irrelevance of professional development to rural contexts. Addressing these three dimensions is essential for sustainable professional development in these settings.

TI Developing an instrument to measure the perceived impact of moral
   education teaching practices on university students' behavioral changes
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Moral education; teaching practices; behavioral change; pro-social
   behavior; pro-environmental behavior; university students; instrument
   development
AB This study aims to develop and validate a questionnaire instrument to measure the perceived impact of moral education teaching practices on university students' behavioral changes, particularly in the domains of pro-social and pro-environmental behavior. Grounded in Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory, the research conceptualizes teaching practices as environmental factors influencing behavior through dynamic interaction with students' cognition and values. The study addresses a significant gap in existing literature by focusing on university-level moral education and integrating the measurement of both pro-social and pro-environmental behavioral outcomes, which have rarely been examined together in previous research. All behavioral outcomes measured in this study were based on students' self-reports. Following Borg and Gall's research and development model, the study employed a systematic four-stage design. The results demonstrate strong psychometric properties, with clear factor structures emerging for both teaching methods (three factors) and behavioral changes (two factors). The instruments showed high reliability, with Cronbach's alpha values of 0.870 for teaching methods and 0.941 for behavioral changes. Theoretically, the findings provide empirical support for Bandura's model in the moral education context and extend its application to environmental ethics. Practically, the validated instrument offers a tool for educators to assess and optimize teaching strategies, fostering students' moral development.

TI Reflections on teaching practice: a study with pre-service mathematics
   teachers
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mathematics education; pre-service mathematics teachers; action
   research; knowledge; curriculum
ID EDUCATION; KNOWLEDGE
AB Changes in certain educational practices may be influenced by the initiative of pre-service teachers and by processes arising from their professional practice. This article aims to identify and characterize a problem related to teaching practices aimed at fostering critical citizenship in students through school mathematics, working with a group of pre-service mathematics teachers. The research was conducted using a qualitative approach, employing a diagnostic action research method, with five pre-service mathematics teachers who voluntarily participated from a Mathematics Education Bachelor's program at a university in Colombia. The reflections generated by the participants revealed two main issues in their teaching practice. These findings underscore the need to promote reflection during initial teacher education so that future teachers can begin their professional development in an appropriate manner and critically examine their teaching practice.

TI Gifted education in Indonesia: reframing gifted education through the
   lens of the Actiotope Model of Giftedness
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gifted education; Actiotope Model of Giftedness; Indonesia; Merdeka
   Belajar; learning capital; educational capital; talent development
ID RETHINKING
AB Gifted and talented education (GATE) in Indonesia has gained renewed attention under the Merdeka Belajar policy, yet scholarship remain fragmented, with weak alignment between national policy, school practice and learning resources. This study examines Indonesia's gifted education landscape by reframing it through the Actiotope Model of Giftedness (AMG) and its Education and Learning Capital Model, a systemic framework emphasizing individual-environment interaction. Using a qualitative multi-source design, data were drawn from document analysis of 16 policy texts, content analysis of 15 peer-reviewed publications (PRISMA-guided) and semi-structured interviews with 20 educators, policymakers, university experts and parents. The AMG framework maps both endogenous learning capitals (actional, organismic, telic, attentional, episodic) and exogenous educational capitals (economic, social, cultural, infrastructural, didactic). Findings reveal a system that is fragmented but evolving. Strengths include strong parental involvement and a cultural emphasis on achievement. Key constraints are limited dedicated funding, uneven infrastructure, narrow conceptions of giftedness and inadequate teacher preparation. Gifted learners were described as highly motivated and agentic, yet with underdeveloped reflective and socioemotional capacities. The study proposes an AMG-aligned reconceptualization of GATE in Indonesia centered on ecological support, systemic collaboration and sustainable enrichment.

TI Leveraging arts-based methodologies to critically examine monoracism in
   higher education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Monoracism; arts-based research methods; ontoepistemology; liminality
ID IDENTITY
AB While arts-based methods have been used in higher education research broadly, few studies have employed such methods to examine the racialized experiences of multiracial college students. Critical and creative pedagogy that integrates the arts can support multiracial college students in navigating monoracism, a system of power that privileges rigid racial categories. We consider how the integration of arts-based methods might strengthen critical approaches to research on multiraciality in higher education. First, we highlight a study that explored liminal identity experiences, including participants' visual representations of what their multiracial identity means to them. We conclude with recommendations for future methodological applications.

TI Operationalizing critical consciousness: a transformative framework for
   educational praxis
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Critical consciousness; transformative potential; feminist pedagogy;
   intersectionality; collective action; social justice
ID TEACHER-EDUCATION; PEDAGOGY; SELF
AB This conceptual article reimagines critical consciousness (CC) for teacher education and educator praxis, shifting it from an under-operationalized idea to a practice-oriented framework that institutions can engage with meaningfully. Drawing from an integrative review of theoretical, empirical, and practitioner scholarship, often rich in theory yet limited in actionable guidance, it builds upon Freirean pedagogy, feminist and intersectional critiques, and Jemal's transformative potential (TP) to elaborate five actionable tenets: critical praxis, collective identity and political efficacy, dialogic engagement, systemic interconnectedness, and intersectional awareness. It includes illustrative tools such as justice journals, counter-narrative circles, equity audits, and intersectional curriculum reviews, which demonstrate how reflection and collective action become mutually reinforcing. Because the article is conceptual, it provides a transferable and context-responsive model that scholars and practitioners can adapt to their contexts and empirically test. In doing so, the framework provides educators and researchers with conceptually grounded and implementation-oriented guidance for mobilizing CC as a sustained force for social justice and systemic transformation.

TI Culturally disruptive qualitative research: troubling whiteness in
   research cultures
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Culturally responsive research; culturally disruptive research;
   whitestream
ID SCIENCE
AB Culturally responsive research (CRR) posits that culture is always present and should thus be a fundamental organizing principle in all facets of inquiry. However, within whitestream research cultures this work can be assimilated into the white, colonial logics it seeks to resist. In this paper, I offer a loving critique and critical reimagining of CRR by tracing its genealogy, situating contemporary research within whiteness and coloniality, and identifying three contraindications for researching while white-defining cultures, engaging in reflexivity, and employing cultural competence. Drawing from my experiences in Aotearoa New Zealand and Cambodia, I discuss culturally disruptive research as one method to dismantle the cultural foundations of research that perpetuate white supremacy. Cultural disruption invites researchers into spaces of desire, dynamic dissonance, and relational negotiations to foreground creative, critical, and capacious knowledge generation.

AB The world and learning sciences are at a critical point in history, especially in the US. Recent political fascism and discriminations are rooted in the Trump administration's governance. AB This paper examines the cultural foundations of resilience among Latinas in STEM through the case of Chilean women teaching in Vocational Education and Training (VET) programs linked to male-dominated skilled trades. AB This study examines barriers to parental involvement in Indigenous children's education from the perspectives of school authorities and parents. Using Indigenous Standpoint Theory, semi-structured interviews and focus groups were conducted with 102 Australian Aboriginal students and parents, along with teachers and principals from six New South Wales high schools.
