TI Identity without milestones: a narrative inquiry into the rites of
   passage shaping professional identity formation in health professions
   educators
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Professional identity formation; educator identity; health professions
   education; medical educator; narrative inquiry
ID MEDICAL-EDUCATION; FEEDBACK; FRAMEWORK; STUDENTS; FACULTY
AB Introduction Professional Identity Formation (PIF) in medicine is typically supported by certain milestones and well-researched rites of passage. In contrast, educators who enter Health Professions Education (HPE) often do so without such signposts, inhabiting a liminal space where identity is constantly negotiated. Despite the growing availability of HPE academic programs, little is known about how these programs shape educators' identities or which experiences serve as significant identity-forming moments. Our study aims to identify the transformative 'aha' moments, which can serve as rites of passage, helping to strengthen the health professions educators' identity.Methods Guided by a social constructionist stance, we employed narrative inquiry to explore the stories of 16 healthcare professionals enrolled in, or recently graduated from HPE academic programs. Semi-structured interviews were conducted and analysed using a re-storying technique. Transformative Learning Theory (TLT) informed the understanding of cognitive, emotive, and affective dimensions of identity shifts, which were captured through the lens of epiphanies.Results Through the analytical interpretation of these stories, we identified four epiphanies. The 'power of people' in the form of competent faculty to develop educational alliances, which influenced all dimensions of TLT. The 'Language of HPE', articulated through paradigmatic orientations and vocabulary, instilled cognitive shifts. The 'burden of tasks', reflecting the distinct nature of the HPE-related assignments, exerted emotional weight. Finally, the 'sense of belonging' through live social interactions between faculty and peers, strengthened the modes of belonging.Conclusion Identification of these transformative 'aha' moments provides clear, measurable steps into how educator identity formation can be fostered and strengthened in the context of HPE academic programs. Such insights call for thoughtful faculty selection, improved curriculum structuring, and scheduling practices. By honoring the educators' stories, we give voice to their lived realities and recognize the significance of HPE academic programs as beautiful avenues for identity formation.

   interactive simulation for first-grade addition learning
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital simulation; learning addition; creative mathematical reasoning;
   primary school students; play based learning
ID EDUCATION
AB This study aimed to (1) design and implement web-based digital interactive simulations to support first-grade students in learning addition, and (2) examine the effects of these simulations on students' mathematical creative reasoning. The research employed a Design Learning approach grounded in the design experiment framework proposed by Paul Cobb, emphasizing iterative cycles of design, classroom implementation, analysis, and refinement to develop both practical learning solutions and theoretical insights. TI Mapping the deterministic path from teaching passion to instructional
   effectiveness: a soft determinism framework for teacher behaviour
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Curriculum implementation; expanded reciprocal determinism; professional
   knowledge; student engagement; teaching passion; teaching self-efficacy
ID SELF-EFFICACY BELIEFS; STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; SCHOOL ENGAGEMENT;
   PERFORMANCE; QUALITY
AB Teacher education programmes, particularly in developing contexts, often emphasise cognitive competencies while giving limited attention to teaching passion (TP), an important affective driver of instructional effectiveness. Although previous studies have established the individual importance of TP, professional knowledge (PK), and self-efficacy, the mechanisms through which TP contributes to instructional effectiveness remain underexplored, and its integration into teacher education frameworks lacks adequate theoretical attention. This study examines how TP functions within a structured yet adaptable system to influence instructional effectiveness skills (IES) among preservice business teachers (N = 210). Using an explanatory correlational design, data were collected through validated instruments and analysed using mediation models. The findings reveal that TP does not directly enhance IES but instead operates through indirect pathways. Specifically, TP positively influences IES through PK (TP -> PK -> IES), while its strongest effect occurs through a sequential mediation pathway where PK and student engagement efficacy (SEE) jointly mediate the relationship (TP -> PK -> SEE -> IES), explaining 89.72% of the variance in instructional effectiveness (R & sup2; = 89.72%). Furthermore, SEE serves as the critical mechanism through which professional knowledge translates into effective instructional practice, demonstrating that knowledge alone is insufficient without confidence in engaging students. These findings extend teacher education research by revealing the conditional influence of TP and illustrating how affective and cognitive resources interact to strengthen teaching effectiveness. Grounded in a soft determinism framework, the study highlights the importance of integrating TP, PK, and SEE within teacher education programmes to enhance future teachers' instructional effectiveness.

LA English
DT Article
DE Educational cash transfers; child labor; school participation;

ID POVERTY; WORK
AB This study assesses the association between educational cash transfers on child labor and school participation in Indonesia. Using This study examines the association between educational cash transfers and children's labor and schooling outcomes in Indonesia using nationally representative microdata from National Socioeconomic Survey (Susenas) 2023, covering 161,651 children aged 10-17. It compares conditional transfers (PKH) and labeled unconditional transfers (PIP) across four activity categories: only working, only schooling, dual activity, and neither working nor schooling. TI Passports, power, and exclusion in TESOL: a critical narrative inquiry
   into legitimacy, symbolic capital, and resistance
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Native-speakerism; passports; raciolinguistics; intersectionality;
   narrative inquiry
ID IDENTITIES; CONSTRUCTION; TEACHERS
AB This article explores the experiences of eight highly qualified South Asian non-native English-speaking teachers (NNESTs) who face systemic exclusion in Gulf and European hiring practices. Using critical narrative inquiry, it contrasts the frequent rejections of five participants with the significantly increased employability of three who gained Western citizenship, despite having the same qualifications. Drawing on the concepts of native-speakerism, Bourdieu's ideas of capital and field, raciolinguistics, intersectionality, and counter-storytelling, the study identifies six narrative patterns: identity reconstruction, informal leadership, institutional and visa obstacles, emotional exhaustion, community support, and the "passport pivot." These counter-stories challenge assumptions of neutrality and meritocracy, showing that TESOL's global labor market is influenced more by geopolitics, race, and citizenship than by expertise. The article advocates for skills-based hiring, blind shortlisting, and greater recognition of NNEST leadership to foster ethical and equitable recruitment. An urgent rethinking of legitimacy in international English language education is essential.

AB Inclusive education remains an important yet underdeveloped goal in post-conflict higher education systems, where psychological and institutional barriers hinder implementation. Grounded in Expectation-Disconfirmation Theory (EDT), Social Cognitive Theory and Organizational Support Theory, this study examines the roles of teacher psychological readiness and perceived institutional support in shaping inclusive education implementation for students with special needs in post-conflict Somali higher education. Using a quantitative cross-sectional design, data were collected from 296 university lecturers in Mogadishu and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that teacher psychological readiness and perceived institutional support significantly predict teacher self-efficacy for inclusive practices and inclusive teaching practices. Inclusive teaching practices emerged as the strongest direct predictor of inclusive education implementation, while teacher self-efficacy functioned as a key psychological mechanism linking readiness and institutional conditions to practice. Mediation analysis further revealed both direct and indirect pathways, with inclusive teaching practices playing a central mediating role. The model demonstrated substantial explanatory power, accounting for over half of the variance in inclusive education implementation. The study contributes theoretically by integrating psychological and institutional perspectives within a unified SEM framework and empirically by extending inclusive education research to a post-conflict higher education context. The findings offer practical implications for policymakers and universities seeking to promote inclusive education through psychologically informed and institutionally responsive strategies.

TI A comparative study of content areas in education for sustainability in
   eco- and non-eco-certified preschools in Sweden
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Sustainable development; content areas; early childhood education;
   preschool teacher; Social Sciences; Education; Early Years; Development
   Studies, Environment, Social Work, Urban Studies; Sociology;
   SDG4-Quality education
ID EARLY-CHILDHOOD EDUCATION
AB Content areas in education for sustainability can be defined as the domain of knowledge and skills that are crucial for laying the foundation for children's understanding of sustainability practices. This study explored and compared the integration of sustainability-related content areas in the teaching practices of 25 eco-certified and 25 non-eco-certified preschools across 25 municipalities in Sweden. Cross-sectional data on sustainability-related teaching practices were collected from 322 teachers using an open-ended questionnaire. An interpretative content analysis was used. Qualitative responses were analyzed using the OMEP ESD Rating Scale, while quantitative data were processed with IBM SPSS Statistics. The study was approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority. Commonly used content areas in education for sustainability were waste sorting and recycling, guardianship (nature stewardship), cultivation, social and cultural diversity, and equity and equality. Statistical analysis revealed no significant differences between eco- and non-eco-certified preschools in terms of the number of content areas addressed. However, teachers from eco-certified preschools demonstrated higher-quality responses in one of the 12 content areas: waste sorting and recycling. The findings indicate that teachers engage more strongly with the economic and social dimensions of sustainability. These findings of this study differ from previous research, likely because the present study classifies waste sorting and recycling as economic sustainability rather than environmental sustainability.

TI Exploring students' acceptance of ChatGPT in higher education:
   application of the extended UTAUT2 model approach
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT; UTAUT2 model; institutional policy; student perception; student
   awareness; artificial intelligence in education; technology acceptance
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; UNIFIED THEORY;
   PERCEPTIONS
AB This study investigates students' acceptance of ChatGPT in higher education through the lens of the extended Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2) model, incorporating institutional policy as a mediating variable and students' perception and awareness as moderators. Despite growing interest in the academic potential of ChatGPT, limited empirical research has examined the interaction of institutional frameworks and student-related factors in shaping AI adoption. Drawing on survey data from 11,675 Nigerian students, the study tested both direct and moderated-mediation effects. Findings reveal that performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, facilitating conditions, and hedonic motivation significantly influence institutional policy. These results suggest that students have largely embraced ChatGPT, and institutional policies must evolve to guide its ethical and equitable use. Theoretically, the study contributes by extending UTAUT2 with mediating and moderating variables, while practically, it underscores the importance of policies, infrastructures, and training to ensure responsible AI adoption in higher education.

TI Do public education platforms increase online course participation?
   Evidence from a difference-in-differences study of German adult
   education centres
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Platforms; online education; online courses; participation; adult and
   continuing education; Social Sciences; Education; Adult Education and
   Lifelong Learning; Research Methods in Education
ID BARRIERS; RISE
AB Following the sharp increase in online courses during the COVID-19 pandemic, online education platforms have gained growing relevance. While research has investigated effects of platforms on learning outcomes, this study is the first to empirically evaluate adult education platforms with respect to online course participation. Three of Germany's sixteen federal state associations of public 'adult education centres' (Volkshochschulen, VHS) have implemented online platforms called 'onlinevhs'. We use this case to employ a heterogeneous difference-in-differences estimator, accounting for staggered implementation across federal states and time. The results indicate that the platforms themselves have no causal effect on online course participation. Although a model without covariates suggests a positive effect, this is explained by pre-existing regional and organisational differences between VHS with and without platform adoption. Overall, the platforms reproduce existing disparities in online participation rather than reducing them. The results indicate that the implementation of a platform alone is insufficient to increase online course participation. Therefore, careful consideration should be given to how a platform is designed and what additional measures are required. Additionally, the study contributes to the theoretical discourse on the efficiency of public platforms, as it shows that an imitation of commercial platforms might not lead to the desired results.

   secondary school curriculum
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article

   Humanities; Arts; Media Communication; Humanities; Cultural Studies;
   Media & Film Studies; Media & Communications; Communication Studies
ID EDUCATION
AB Education is recognised as a catalyst for social and developmental transformation, and its efficiency is dependent on a curriculum that reflects and empowers its students. The study argues that the curricula fall short of reflecting West Africa to its students, thus hindering education's true purpose of providing "worthy objectives". The paper concludes by advocating urgent decolonising reforms to empower a new generation of leaders capable of driving the continent's development.

TI Environmental sustainability implementation in primary and secondary
   schools: evidence from the UAE

LA English
DT Article

   management; operations; schools; UAE
ID HUMAN-RESOURCE MANAGEMENT; EDUCATION; COMMUNITIES; HRM
AB This paper examines environmental sustainability (ES) implementation in United Arab Emirates (UAE) primary and secondary schools. Our objectives were to examine to which extent ES was 1) considered a strategic initiative and was integrated into their 2) human resource management, 3) operations, and 4) curricular and extra-curricular practices. We adopted a quantitative, descriptive research approach using a self-administrated questionnaire from 85 school teachers and staff representing 52 UAE schools. The majority of our responding schools include ES in their vision, mission, and strategic objectives, but only 38% of the schools had a formal ES management plan. More than 50% of schools implemented sustainable transportation, waste separation, or waste reduction practices into their daily operations, and integrated ES into their basic courses and offered relevant extra-curricular activities. However, the majority of schools did not integrate ES in their human resources management practices. This paper highlights the progress that has been made in integrating ES into UAE schools and suggests areas for improvement. It contributes to a gap in literature on sustainability and EaS implementation in schools and discuss the limitations of this study and possible future avenues of research.

TI How universities become ready for AI-supported crisis intervention: a
   hierarchical model of psychological and institutional readiness
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-enabled crisis intervention; technological pedagogical readiness
   (TPR); higher education mental health; human-centered artificial
   intelligence; Perceived readiness; Social Sciences; Education; Higher
   Education; Technology
ID MENTAL-HEALTH; TECHNOLOGY
AB The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has expanded possibilities for data-informed psychological crisis intervention. Grounded in the Technological Pedagogical Readiness (TPR) framework and crisis-intervention theory, this study develops and validates a hierarchical model of perceived AI-supported crisis-intervention readiness. Here, perceived readiness refers to university staff members' self-reported preparedness to interpret AI-generated information and make ethically responsible crisis-intervention judgments. Using survey data from 906 university staff members in China, partial least squares structural equation modeling was employed to test a reflective-reflective second-order model linking external (professional development, contextual conditions, student technological literacy, parent/community involvement) and internal (AI-TPACK, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, ethical competence) readiness factors to three domains of crisis readiness: developmental, situational, and existential. External readiness was positively associated with all crisis domains and substantial indirect effects through internal readiness, supporting a statistical dual-pathway pattern. Internal readiness emerged as the core psychological correlate of AI-supported judgment and ethical decision-making. The findings extend TPR research beyond instructional contexts into mental-health governance and position AI as supporting, rather than replacing, professional judgment in higher education crisis intervention.

TI Modalities for the provision of community education in preparing women
   to implement community development initiatives in Tanzania: reflection
   from the field
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Community education and community development initiatives; women; and
   community educators; Social Sciences; Education; Adult Education and
   Lifelong Learning; Work-based Learning; Philosophy of Research Methods
   in Education
AB This paper is based on a study that examined how community education was provided to women as a means of preparing them to implement Community Development Initiatives (Community development initiative). The study intended to find out whether these modalities adequately prepare them to implement Community development initiatives successfully, as their income-generating activities fail. The study employed a case study design and used purposive and convenience sampling techniques to select 30 participants. Data were generated through semi-structured interviews, observation and focus group discussion and analysed thematically. The study contributes to a three-stage model of community education as a framework for strengthening women's implementation of Community development initiatives. It highlights the need for tailored approaches that integrate adult learning principles and responsive facilitation, with implications for policy and practice in designing community education programmes that genuinely empower women and sustain income-generating activities.

TI Generative AI and media literacy: how AI tools reshape students' skills
   of searching, verifying, and interpreting information
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; media and information literacy; verification; lateral
   reading; civic online reasoning; pre-service teacher education;
   performance-based assessment; Social Sciences; Education; Higher
   Education; Study of Higher Education; Teaching & Learning
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used as an "answer engine" in higher education, raising risks of plausibility replacing verifiability. This study tested whether a semester-long GenAI media literacy module improves undergraduates' procedural skills of searching, verifying, and interpreting AI-mediated information. Using a quasi-experimental non-equivalent groups pretest-posttest design (T0-T1), we compared two cohorts from L.N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University and Astana International University in Astana, Kazakhstan (N = 135; EG n = 70; CG n = 65). ANCOVA models adjusted for baseline scores and covariates (age, gender, language of instruction, GPA, baseline GenAI-use frequency) showed a post-test advantage for the experimental group: adjusted EG-CG differences were +0.63 on GMLQ total and +4.67 on performance. Positive effects were consistent across GMLQ subscales and performance components (Search, Verify, Interpret). The findings support embedding sustained, procedure-focused GenAI media literacy instruction in pre-service teacher education to strengthen evidence-based practices.

   relational pedagogy; interior architecture education
AB Design studio education relies not only on project production but also on peer-mediated and relational forms of learning. Although near-peer mentoring is widely discussed in higher education, there is limited mixed-methods evidence combining mentee perceptions with mentor accounts of how support is enacted in studio-based contexts. This study examines a structured near-peer mentoring model embedded in a vertical studio in an undergraduate interior architecture program. A convergent mixed-methods case study was conducted with 48 second-year mentees and 12 fourth-year mentors at one institution. Quantitative data came from a 15-item evaluative questionnaire, while qualitative data came from mentee written responses and mentor reflective reports. Findings showed consistently positive mentee perceptions across mentoring support, perceived learning gains, and satisfaction/belonging. Cross-perspective analysis identified psychological safety, feedback-based scaffolding, prioritization, and encouragement as enabling mechanisms, while unplanned contact, unequal access, noisy studio conditions, and ambiguity around mentoring boundaries emerged as key constraints. Rather than demonstrating general effects of near-peer mentoring, the study offers a context-bound account of how one vertical studio implementation was experienced by mentees and enacted by mentors.

   inclusive education; DisCrit classroom ecology
ID PRESCHOOL INCLUSION; CHILDREN; EDUCATION; ETHNOGRAPHY; CHALLENGES;
   DISABILITY; PARENTS
AB The increasing number of students with disabilities in general education settings signifies progress in inclusion; however, it does not alleviate the challenges faced by parents, particularly mothers, who often serve as primary caregivers. This article foregrounds the voices of mothers of multiply-marginalized children to explore their values regarding early childhood inclusion. By utilizing a method of narrative inquiry and Video-Cued Ethnography (VCE), five mothers of children with disabilities-four African-American mothers and one Turkish immigrant mother-were interviewed. They also highlighted the significance of authentic teacher-student relationships in building a caring classroom community within inclusion spaces.

TI From classrooms to chaos: racialized institutional environments,
   anti-black misogyny, and racial battle fatigue across the life course
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Anti-black misogyny; Racial Battle Fatigue; black girls and women; life
   course racism; historically White institutions; racialized gender

AB This study examines how anti-Black misogyny shapes Black women's life course experiences and contributes to gendered Racial Battle Fatigue. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with twenty-five Black women across multiple U.S. regions, the analysis traces how racialized gender regulation emerges in childhood, intensifies through adolescence and postsecondary schooling, and evolves within professional environments in historically White institutions. Anti-Black misogyny is defined as the structural system through which people, institutions, and environments interpret and regulate Black women's bodies, emotions, and intellectual contributions across a continuum ranging from apathy and indifference to hostility and overt hatred. The study extends Racial Battle Fatigue by identifying two mechanisms that shape these trajectories: the Conditional Inclusion Threshold and White Racial Homeostasis Threat. Together, the findings demonstrate how anti-Black misogyny produces a systemic racism-related repetitive stress injury across the life course.

LA English
DT Article
DE Critical Race Theory; Islamophobia; racism; Muslim students; formal

ID ISLAMOPHOBIA; IDENTITIES; POLITICS; RACISM
AB Recently, there has been an increase in anti-Muslim sentiment in Western societies which permeates educational systems and classrooms. Muslim migrant students face discrimination, racism and Islamophobia in their schools, which affects them negatively and discourages their involvement. This study aims to analyse Moroccan Muslim migrant mothers' perceptions of the discrimination experiences of their children in their Spanish schools; and identify the protection strategies these mothers and their children use against discrimination. There is still a need for interventions and the development of specific policies that build more inclusive educational settings.

TI Professional identity formation among participants in a longitudinal
   pediatric program for final year medical students: a qualitative case
   study
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Transition to residency; professional identity formation; fourth-year
   medical student; pediatric community; pediatric residency preparation
ID PREPARATORY COURSE; BOOT CAMP; 4TH YEAR; FRAMEWORK; RESIDENCY
AB Objective To explore aspects of professional identity formation in participants of a longitudinal pediatric program for final-year medical students in the US.Introduction Many institutions have specialty-specific courses focused on the transition to residency, typically at the end of medical school. This study examines professional identity formation among participants of a longitudinal fourth-year Pediatric Concentration.Methods Authors used a case study design for this qualitative research study using semi-structured interview questions based on a conceptual model of professional identity formation. Authors used purposeful sampling to identify study participants who were randomly selected from former students who completed the program between 2019 and 2021. Three interviewers independently conducted interviews with individual program participants. Thematic analysis with coder reliability was utilized for data analysis; two investigators independently coded and performed inter-rater reliability (IRR) on three sets of questions from transcriptions. After ensuring acceptable IRR, investigators coded the remaining questions and subsequently identified themes and sub-themes.Findings Eleven former students completed interviews. Following initial independent coding, IRR for three questions was 80%. After coding the 11 interviews, investigators determined that code saturation was achieved. They subsequently identified six main themes: career development, interpersonal connection, personal growth, positive role models, skill-building, and supportive learning environment. Two cross-cutting themes were recognized throughout the data: sense of belonging and gaining confidence toward starting residency.Conclusions Participants in a longitudinal specialty-specific program in the final year of medical school experienced professional identity formation through a supportive learning environment fostering connection and personal growth while building skills, surrounded by positive role models. This community of practice cultivated a sense of belonging and helped participants gain confidence toward their residency and career. This longitudinal, specialty-specific approach to the final year of medical school may enhance professional identity formation for students entering all specialties and could facilitate transition to internship.

TI Exploring medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness among Korean medical
   students: a cross-sectional study
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; medical AI readiness; AI curriculum; MAIRS-MS;
   medical students
AB Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming healthcare systems and clinical practice, increasing the need to prepare future physicians to work effectively with AI technologies in clinical contexts. Despite growing interest in integrating AI into medical education, empirical evidence regarding medical students' readiness to use AI remains limited. This study aimed to assess medical AI readiness among Korean medical students and explore factors associated with their readiness.Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among medical students enrolled in a six-year medical program at a university in Korea. A total of 204 students participated in the study. Medical AI readiness was measured using the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students (MAIRS-MS), which assesses four domains: cognition, ability, vision, and ethics. Descriptive statistics, independent t-tests, and Pearson's correlation analyses were performed using SPSS version 27.Results The overall mean score of medical AI readiness was 4.19 on a 7-point Likert scale, indicating a moderate level of medical AI readiness. Among the subscales, ethics showed the highest mean score (4.69), followed by vision (4.44), ability (4.18), and cognition (3.92). The frequency of AI use was significantly associated with medical AI readiness, whereas the daily duration of AI use was not. No significant gender differences were observed. When students were divided into the low (pre-medical years 1-2) and high (medical years 1-4) groups, the high group showed significantly higher scores only in the ability subscale.Conclusions The findings suggest that medical students are not yet sufficiently prepared to utilize AI technologies in clinical practice, particularly in terms of knowledge and practical competencies related to AI. These results highlight the need for structured and longitudinal AI education in medical curricula to better prepare future physicians for AI-integrated healthcare environments.

TI Consensus and learning climate in temporary versus permanent teams in
   team-based learning
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Active learning; discordant decision; medical students; team
   familiarity; learning climate
ID HIGH-QUALITY RELATIONSHIPS; INTRINSIC MOTIVATION; WORK; PERFORMANCE
AB Background In team-based learning, students are typically placed in fixed teams based on the idea that stable group membership fosters collaboration: as teammates get to know each other, they share more information, resolve differences and feel motivated to contribute. This rationale had not been tested in a randomized controlled trial.Objective The study compares team-based learning in temporary teams with the default permanent teams regarding individual and team readiness assurance test performance (iRAT, tRAT), reaching team consensus, the learning climate, and intrinsic motivation.Design In a randomized controlled trial, first-year medical students were assigned either to permanent TBL teams or to teams that were re-assigned for each problem. The team readiness assurance test (tRAT) votes, submitted individually and covertly, served as an indirect indicator for team consensus (concordant versus discordant tRAT vote).Results Discordant tRATs (n = 268, 11.8% of all votes) were submitted more frequently in temporary than in permanent teams, both for correct and incorrect majority decisions. The self-rated learning climate was more cooperative in permanent than in temporary teams, while intrinsic motivation and tRAT scores were similar for both types of teams. A poorer learning climate was associated with a higher proportion of discordant tRATs.Conclusion Working in temporary teams does not lead to inferior intrinsic motivation; this was previously also shown for knowledge gain. However, the poorer learning climate, together with reaching a consensus less often, might indicate that at least some members of temporary teams feel not adequately appreciated in the discussion and do not accept the majority decision. With instructional strategies promoting a cooperative learning climate in temporary teams, preclinical TBL courses might serve as an early promoter of the relational team competencies required for subsequent clinical workplace learning in temporary teams.

TI Integrating sustainable development topics into tertiary-level EFL
   education in Yemen: faculty attitudes, challenges, and strategies
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Sustainable development (SD); education for sustainable development
   (ESD); global citizenship; EFL education; tertiary education; Yemen;
   Social Sciences; Education; Curriculum and Teaching Studies; EFL /
   Language Education; Higher Education; Teacher Education and Development
AB With sustainable development (SD) as a global priority, education is required to equip learners with knowledge and skills necessary to contribute to global SD. In tertiary-level EFL education, SD integration is critical for enabling students to develop language skills while engaging with global issues. This study investigates the integration of SD into EFL education at Yemeni universities, focusing on faculty attitudes, challenges, and strategies for integration. Data were collected from 106 faculty members using an online questionnaire. The results showed that, although faculty hold positive attitudes toward integrating SD into EFL education, SD topics are rarely incorporated in practice. This limited integration is attributed to teaching and curriculum, educational culture and environment, and resources and funding constraints. Interestingly, no significant differences were found in faculty ratings of attitudes, perceived challenges, or suggested strategies based on gender, university type, college, experience, specialization, or academic rank variables. This suggests a broad consensus among faculty. The study also identified strategies for integrating SD into EFL education, including curriculum reform, faculty professional development, technology-enhanced learning tools, appropriate instructional materials, effective pedagogical methods, and alignment of assessment with SD goals. The study proposes practical recommendations to strengthen SD integration and highlights directions for future research.

TI Integrating experiential learning and JD-R model in entrepreneurship
   education: evidence from Indonesian Islamic boarding schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Entrepreneurship education; experiential learning theory; JD-R model;
   Islamic values; digital marketing literacy; business success; Islamic
   boarding schools
ID BUSINESS; PASSION
AB Responding to the global call for sustainable and ethical entrepreneurship education aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals, this study examines how entrepreneurship learning, entrepreneurial passion, and digital marketing literacy are associated with business success in value-based educational settings. Drawing on experiential learning theory and the job demands-resources framework, it investigates the mediating role of Islamic values. Data were collected from 638 students enrolled in entrepreneurship programs at Islamic boarding schools across Java, Indonesia, through a hybrid survey conducted between May and September 2024. PLS-SEM results show that entrepreneurship learning, entrepreneurial passion, and digital marketing literacy are positively associated with business success, both directly and indirectly through Islamic values. Islamic values, comprising shiddiq (honesty), amanah (trustworthiness), and 'adl (fairness), function as a normative conversion mechanism through which competencies and motivation are translated into ethically grounded entrepreneurial behavior and sustainable performance. The study contributes to value-based entrepreneurship education by clarifying the role of ethical mediation in linking learning, motivation, and business outcomes. It also highlights Islamic boarding schools as platforms for developing digitally capable and ethically grounded entrepreneurs in emerging economies.

TI Inclusive learning practices based on local cultural values in the
   context of four ethnic groups in South Sulawesi
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Inclusive learning practices; local cultural values; multicultural
   education; ethnic diversity; inclusive pedagogy; Social Sciences;
   Education; Behavioral Sciences; Educational Psychology; Cognitive
   Psychology; Motivation
ID EDUCATION
AB This study examines inclusive learning practices grounded in local cultural values among four major ethnic groups in South Sulawesi Bugis, Makassar, Toraja, and Mandar. Using a comparative quantitative design, data were collected from 354 teachers across diverse educational settings through a validated and reliable inclusive learning practices instrument. The instrument demonstrated acceptable internal consistency across all six dimensions , supporting the reliability of the measurement model. The data were analyzed using the General Linear Model (GLM) with multivariate and univariate procedures. Descriptive results indicate relatively consistent patterns across six dimensions of inclusive learning: inclusive pedagogical orientation, responsiveness to learner diversity, adaptive instructional practices, inclusive classroom interaction, integration of local cultural values, and professional commitment. Multivariate analysis revealed no statistically significant overall effect of ethnic background on inclusive learning practices. After applying Bonferroni correction to control for alpha inflation across six dimensions, no individual dimension reached statistical significance at the univariate level. These patterns were largely consistent across all four ethnic groups, suggesting a broadly shared orientation toward inclusive pedagogical practice. Local cultural values may thus function as a common contextual foundation that reinforces inclusive practices, with implications for the development of culturally responsive inclusive education in non-Western multicultural settings.

TI A teacher-facing method for interpreting bilateral handgrip in Year 5-6
   Primary PE: writing-hand-coded percentage difference and decision bands
   (9-11 years)
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Physical and health education; Primary PE; assessment for learning;
   formative assessment; teacher decision-making; handgrip strength
AB Primary teachers need lesson-feasible ways to interpret bilateral handgrip so feedback, grouping, and task design in primary physical education (PE) can be adjusted fairly within lessons. This study presents and validates a teacher-facing interpretation routine for Year 5-6 pupils (9-11 years) using two trials per hand (best of two) and a writing-hand-coded asymmetry percentage. Data from 18 schools (n = 568; 10.3 +/- 0.7 years) showed good within-session reliability, with more stable classification when best-of-two scores were used compared with a single trial. Writing-hand preference matched the stronger hand in only 54.8% of cases, cautioning against assuming the writing hand is stronger. Mean signed asymmetry was small (1.36%), indicating minimal group-level advantage. Using absolute asymmetry, 38.4% exceeded 10% and 7.5% exceeded 20%, supporting pragmatic decision bands (<= 10%, >10-20%, >20%) linked to proportionate classroom actions. The routine is presented as assessment for learning rather than ranking or diagnosis to support inclusive, fair decision-making in primary PE.

TI Teacher powerlessness in curriculum management for educational quality
   at traditional Islamic boarding schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher powerlessness; curriculum management; traditional Islamic
   boarding schools; Educational Studies; Islamic Educational Management;
   Islamic Boarding School; Islamic Education; Curriculum Management
AB Traditional Islamic boarding schools (pesantren) have long prioritized moral and spiritual values. Yet in recent decades, modernization pressures have threatened the sustainability of these traditions. The challenges are both structural and psychological, especially for teachers who face limited autonomy in decision-making and remain vulnerable to external policy pressures. This study examines the roots of teacher powerlessness and its consequences for the quality of education in pesantren. Using a qualitative descriptive approach, it relies on observation, interviews, and analysis of policy documents available online. The findings show that teacher powerlessness is primarily a product of hierarchical managerial structures and the dominance of kiai (authority figure) charisma. As earlier research has observed, curriculum management within pesantren often sidelines teachers' capacity to innovate in adapting to modernization and digitalization. The absence of sustained professional training and the consistent exclusion of teachers from decision-making processes deepen this disempowerment. Given these findings, the study stresses the need to strengthen teacher agency through training opportunities and greater autonomy. Equally important is the call for closer collaboration among government, educational institutions, and teachers themselves to secure and improve the quality of education in traditional pesantren.

AB This study examined relationships between digital distress (DD), social development (SD), identity formation (IF), and religiosity (RE) among Religious Studies students at the University of Cape Coast (UCC).    students and teachers
SO COGENT EDUCATION

DT Article
DE Digital transformation; metaverse; teachers; students; educational
   institutions
ID PARTIAL LEAST-SQUARES; ACCEPTANCE; TECHNOLOGY; VARIABLES; DRIVERS; SEM
AB The study aims to investigate the adoption of the metaverse among students and teachers at schools and learning institutions from the perspective of how determinants of adopting technologies affect their intentions on the use of immersive learning environments. TI Internal and external factors shaping STEM teachers' professional
   development: evidence from Vietnam's secondary education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Continuing professional development; secondary education; STEM teachers;
   professional learning community; educational reform; Vietnam; Social
   Sciences; Education
ID LEARNING COMMUNITIES; ONLINE COMMUNITIES; KNOWLEDGE; NETWORKS; INQUIRY;
   LESSONS; MEDIA
AB The rapidly evolving science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) education landscape requires teachers to continually update their knowledge and skills, making continuing professional development (CPD) essential for effective instruction. This study investigates the complex interplay of internal and external factors influencing STEM teachers' engagement with professional development in the context of Vietnam's recent curriculum reforms. Using structural equation modeling (SEM), we analyzed survey data from 393 secondary school STEM teachers across six provinces representing diverse geographical regions of Vietnam. Our findings reveal that external factors, including institutional support and resource availability, have a significantly stronger influence on teachers' CPD participation than internal school-based factors. Additionally, teachers demonstrate comparable motivation to both share knowledge and learn from colleagues, supporting the viability of collaborative professional learning communities (PLCs). The study identified notable differences in CPD engagement patterns between public and private school teachers, with private school teachers showing higher participation in school-based professional development activities. Teacher self-efficacy emerged as a significant predictor of willingness to support colleagues, aligning with theoretical frameworks on communities of practice (CoPs). These findings contribute to understanding the dynamics of teacher professional development during educational reform and provide an empirical foundation for policy recommendations to enhance STEM teacher preparation in Vietnam and similar contexts. The study offers implications for structuring professional development opportunities that leverage both internal motivation and external support systems to maximize teacher engagement and effectiveness.

TI Pre-qualifications, learning strategies, and study satisfaction among
   medical students: insights from a multicenter German study
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical students; study satisfaction; learning strategies; part-time
   employment; prior qualifications
ID ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; EDUCATION; MOTIVATION; PREDICTORS
AB Introduction Although medical students with pre-medical qualifications (e.g., paramedic training) may enhance diversity within the student body, they have received little attention in international research. Their prior experience may influence study satisfaction through different learning strategies or working alongside their studies. This study investigates how pre-qualifications relate to three dimensions of study satisfaction (content, conditions, and coping with study load) and examines whether deep-processing learning strategies (elaboration and critical thinking) and part-time employment help explain these associations.Method The authors conducted a cross-sectional survey at five German medical schools across different stages of study (3rd, 6th and 10th semester, final year). A structural equation model tested (a) whether pre-qualifications (i.e., academic degree, vocational training in the medical field) moderated the relationship between deep-processing strategies and study satisfaction and (b) whether part-time employment mediated the relationship between pre-qualifications and study satisfaction, controlling for age, gender, undergraduate GPA, semester, and medical school.Results Associations between deep-processing strategies and satisfaction did not differ by pre-qualifications. Regardless of students' pre-qualifications, elaboration was positively (ss = .51) and critical thinking negatively (ss = -.31) associated with satisfaction with study contents. Students with vocational training or prior academic degree more often worked part-time to finance studies; part-time employment was associated with lower satisfaction with study conditions (ss = -.07) but higher satisfaction with coping with study load (ss = .08). Indirect effects via part-time employment were significant but small.Discussion The findings suggest that elaboration may be a particularly relevant learning strategy for satisfaction with study contents, regardless of students' prior professional or academic qualifications. The negative association between critical thinking and satisfaction highlights the complexity of students' perceptions of study contents. Although associations involving part-time employment were small, the findings contribute to a better understanding of students with professional and academic pre-qualifications and may inform efforts to support increasingly diverse medical student populations.

TI Associations among positive childhood experiences, resilience, and
   psychological distress in health professions students
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Positive childhood experiences; health professions students; resilience;
   psychological distress; mediation analysis
ID MISSING DATA; EDUCATION
AB Objective To assess the mediating role of psychological resilience in the negative association between positive childhood experiences (PCEs) and psychological distress in health professions students (HPS). Methods The authors obtained cross-sectional data, including demographic information, the Brief Resilience Scale, and Medical Student Well-Being Index, from a longitudinal survey with circannual waves of data collection in medical, advanced practice provider, (i.e., nursing and physician assistant), and veterinary students at a single institution. The confidential, web-based survey included seven questions about PCEs. The authors conducted a mediation analysis of wave 3 of the data (N = 181) using structural equation modeling, which adjusted for age, gender, underrepresented in medicine (URM) status, and first-generation status. Bootstrap confidence intervals modeled and tested the total and indirect pathways. Results The path model demonstrated an excellent fit with the data (CFI/TLI = 1.00; RMSEA < .001; SRMR < .001). As hypothesized, PCEs were positively associated with resilience (b = 0.020; p = .049), and resilience was negatively associated with psychological distress (b = -0.815; p = .003). Although PCEs were negatively associated with psychological distress (b = -0.061; p = .003), the indirect path between PCEs and psychological distress through resilience was not significant (b = -0.016; p = .114). Conclusion To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine PCES and resilience in HPS. PCEs and resilience may represent independent predictors of mental well-being in HPS. Our findings underscore the significance of identifying students with fewer PCEs and adopting interventions that support the psychological well-being of HPS, especially those who might be at a higher risk of distress.

TI Analysing the pedagogical potential of ChatGPT: a usability testing with
   educators
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ChatGPT; Artificial Intelligence; usability testing; university
   teachers; benefits
ID ENGLISH
AB The integration of artificial intelligence into education has transformed language learning and teaching, with tools such as ChatGPT offering new avenues for interaction, feedback, and learner autonomy. Despite the growing use of such technologies, limited research has explored how educators themselves perceive and utilize AI tools in their pedagogical practice. This study examines the usability and pedagogical potential of ChatGPT for teaching English as a foreign language at the university level. Twelve educators from universities in the Czech Republic and Norway participated in structured usability testing, engaging with ChatGPT across diverse language-learning tasks, including conversation, writing, grammar correction, and vocabulary development. The results reveal that teachers perceived ChatGPT as an accessible and adaptable tool that enhances self-paced learning, supports personalized instruction, and provides instant feedback. Younger educators and those more familiar with digital tools rated its usability and usefulness particularly high, indicating a generational influence on technology acceptance. Moreover, the study highlights ChatGPT's flexibility across linguistic and cultural contexts, reinforcing its potential for global educational settings. Nonetheless, participants emphasized the importance of addressing ethical challenges, including data privacy and the need for teacher training to ensure responsible use. Overall, the findings underscore ChatGPT's promise as a supportive pedagogical tool while calling for longitudinal and large-scale studies to assess its long-term impact on language learning outcomes.

TI Enhancing teacher well-being and SEL through social-emotional game-based
   learning: a study on the SEGBL program
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Developing social-emotional learning; teacher well-being; teachers'
   professional development; game based learning; social-emotional
   competencies; Teacher Professionalization; Educational Research; Teacher
   Education and Training
ID COMPETENCE
AB Developing social-emotional learning (SEL) skills enables teachers to embed SEL principles effectively into their interactions with students, thereby supporting SEL practices across formal and informal educational settings. This study addresses the gap between the expectation that teachers foster their students' SEL and the limited SEL training available for teachers themselves. It examines the effect of a newly developed Social-Emotional Game-Based Learning (SEGBL) program for teachers, validated by experts, which uses experiential, game-based activities to promote teachers' personal, emotional, and social skill development. Using a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design, 71 elementary school teachers were assigned to intervention and control groups. SEL was assessed using the EduSEL Questionnaire, and teachers' well-being was measured using the TSWQ. Results indicated significant improvements in overall SEL and selected SEL components, as well as substantial improvements in teachers' well-being for the intervention group, while no significant changes were observed in the control group. No differences were found based on teaching experience. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of the SEGBL program in enhancing teachers' social-emotional competencies (SEC) and well-being and highlight the importance of teacher-centered SEL professional development in supporting sustainable teaching practice. Further research should examine the long-term effects and applicability of SEGBL across diverse educational contexts.

DT Article

   Media Education; Social Sciences; Behavioral Sciences; Educational
   Psychology
ID LANGUAGE; ONLINE
AB This study examines English as a foreign language (EFL) students' perceptions of ChatGPT-assisted learning in relation to self-directed learning (SDL) practices at two Palestinian higher education institutions, An-Najah National University and Al-Quds Open University. TI Trends in mathematics achievement among Ghanaian senior high school
   students: an analysis of performance patterns and contributing factors
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Curriculum reforms; digital learning platform; socio-economic status;
   students' mathematics achievement; senior high school (SHS)
AB Mathematics performance among Ghanaian senior high school (SHS) students has been inconsistent, with empirical evidence showing periods of improvement and decline. In addressing the fluctuations in mathematics achievement of SHS students in Ghana, this study examined the effects of curriculum reform, digital learning platforms, and socio-economic status on Ghanaian senior high school students' mathematics achievement. The population size was 785 students, and a sample of 265 was drawn for analytical purposes. Data was collected through systematic questionnaires and analyzed by SPSS and AMOS to verify structural equation modeling. The statistically non-significant socio-economic status findings suggest that equity-increasing policies, such as Ghana's Free Senior High School policy, can reduce achievement gaps typically associated with home background. Ultimately, this study contributes to the literature by demonstrating how the collective interplay of systemic reforms and technology can neutralize traditional socio-economic predictors of achievement.

TI Micro-credentials as a pathway to higher learning: the case of an MSc in
   data science and artificial intelligence degree
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Micro-credential; short courses; lifelong learning; adaptable industrial
   capacity building; emerging technologies
AB Micro-credentials (M-Cs) are gaining prominence as credible and flexible options that support lifelong learning. Increasing acceptance by business for capacity building is pressuring higher education institutions to recognize and integrate these certifications. Pioneered by universities like MIT and Deakin, M-Cs must yet be scaled for parity with traditional degree programs. The primary challenges to integration include non-standardized quality assurance, difficulties in credit mapping, and institutional governance barriers. This gap is critical in emerging technology fields, including data science and artificial intelligence, where industry needs outpace university curriculum accreditation, new staff appointments for course delivery, and degree completion times. Consequently, industry's increasing use of M-Cs for skilling staff in new technologies creates a disconnect between professional and academic recognition. This study investigates this challenge by comparatively analyzing a conventional MSc in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence and industry-recognized M-Cs. Furthermore, it explores using M-Cs as a pathway toward a Master of Science degree in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence. The research compares the skills and competencies provided by M-Cs to those of the traditional degree program, identifies gaps, and proposes a mechanism for their formal recognition and integration into an MSc degree in Data Science and Artificial Intelligence.

TI Evaluating practical methodologies in Scottish certificate level
   physics: electrical circuits
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Electrical circuits; participatory action research; physics; practical
   work; secondary schools; teaching; Social Sciences; Education; Physics;
   Science
AB Electrical circuits are central to high-school physics courses globally. However, it is commonly stated that there are challenges both for educators and students with the abstract nature of the concepts. This action research examines the practical methods used by a group of five teachers when teaching electrical circuits at the National 5 level. Participants attended a workshop to test and evaluate these methods, while group discussions allowed consideration of alternatives. The Current Test Evaluate Ideal Reality (C-TEIR) framework was developed during this research to analyse the workshop notes and conversations and give structure to the findings. The main outcomes were that equipment is sufficient though not ideal, a similar teaching pattern is followed by all participants, and there are concerns over the introduction of electrical circuits at earlier stages of students' education. Although schools have the components required, there was concern over the quality and cost of replacements, and the lack of technical support for repairs. Teaching of the concepts tends to begin with building circuits, series before parallel. Voltage and current rules were considered before resistance, which followed alongside Ohm's law. These concepts are core to the understanding of the topic, and this research highlights a need for consideration of when they are introduced, how and by whom.

TI Decoding undergraduates' English reading proficiency: EEG evidence and
   GPA-SES effects in a computerised English assessment
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Computer-based testing (CBT); English reading comprehension; English
   reading proficiency; electroencephalography (EEG); neurocognitive
   evidence; academic achievement (GPA); socioeconomic status (SES)
ID PERFORMANCE; METAANALYSIS; OSCILLATIONS; IMPACT; ALPHA
AB This study investigates undergraduate students' English reading proficiency through a sequential mixed-methods design that integrates neurocognitive evidence, behavioural performance, learner perceptions, and background characteristics within a computerised assessment context. In Phase 1, paper-based testing (PBT) and computer-based testing (CBT) were compared using electroencephalography (EEG) and qualitative inquiry. Five Thai EFL undergraduates completed parallel Thai Reading Evaluation and Decoding System (Thai-READS) tasks in both formats while EEG data were recorded using a single-channel MindWave Mobile 2 device. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests indicated no significant differences in Thai-READS scores between PBT and CBT (Z = -1.633, p = 0.102). EEG analyses revealed largely comparable cognitive processing across test modes; however, a significant difference in alpha frequency emerged for difficult items answered incorrectly (Z = -2.023, p = 0.043), with higher alpha frequency observed in the CBT condition, suggesting differential neural engagement under increased task difficulty. Semi-structured interviews further indicated that students generally perceived CBT as convenient, organised, and supportive of focus, while also expressing concerns related to technical reliability, digital navigation, and limited opportunities for annotation. Phase 2 analysed Thai-READS performance data from 3,274 undergraduates using a two-way analysis of variance to examine the effects of academic achievement (GPA) and socioeconomic status (SES). Results revealed significant main effects of both GPA and SES on reading proficiency (p < 0.05), with GPA demonstrating a larger effect size (eta(2) = 0.06). The findings support the feasibility of CBT while highlighting the importance of considering cognitive processing and learner background to ensure valid and equitable assessment practices in Thai higher education.

TI Understanding beginner Korean language learners' motivation and cultural
   learning orientations
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Beginner Korean language learners; cultural learning; learner
   motivation; cultural topic preferences; authenticity
AB The global proliferation of Hallyu (the Korean Wave) and widespread access to Korean media have changed the profiles and expectations of Korean language learners; however, prevailing instructional practices often remained anchored in traditional, grammar-centered approaches. In this mixed-methods study, we investigated how beginner Korean learners' motivations and cultural preferences changed over time and varied by cultural background, using survey data from 246 students at an Australian university (2019 and 2023 cohorts) and interviews with 15 participants. Results showed a shift from passive media consumption to active, integrative language use, with 'gaining new language knowledge' moving to first place in motivational rankings. However, learners reconceptualized this as integrated communicative competence that combines linguistic knowledge with cultural understanding. Despite elementary language proficiency, learners demonstrated sophisticated cultural aspirations and complex expectations. Cultural background analysis showed that non-Asian learners acted as 'cultural interpreters,' showing significantly higher preferences for systematic understanding of Korean culture, whereas Asian learners acted as 'cultural participants,' leveraging cultural familiarity for direct engagement. These findings highlight the importance of culturally responsive and flexible curricula that treat learner diversity as a pedagogical resource. They also point to the potential of personalized instructional approaches, including adaptive learning environments, to support diverse cultural learning pathways by drawing on learners' varied cultural backgrounds as complementary scaffolding rather than obstacles.

TI Navigating cross-cultural learning: a case study of international
   occupational therapy students' reflection on their clinical placement in
   India using the Kawa Model
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Social Sciences; Behavioral Sciences; Work & Organizational Psychology;
   Leadership; Education; Higher Education; Globalization
ID COMPETENCE
AB Background: International clinical placements provide occupational therapy students with opportunities to develop cultural competence, adaptability, and reflective practice. Culturally responsive reflective frameworks may support students in interpreting cross-cultural experiences more meaningfully. Objective: This study explored the reflective experiences of international occupational therapy students during a 12-week clinical internship in India using the Kawa Model. Methods: A qualitative descriptive case study was conducted with two Norwegian occupational therapy (OT) students who completed a clinical internship in India. Data were collected through Kawa River drawings and Kawa-guided semi-structured interviews conducted after completion of the placement. Data were analyzed thematically, with visual and narrative data interpreted through the core constructs of the Kawa Model. Results: Seven themes emerged: cultural adaptation and identity exploration; language and communication barriers; self-awareness and personal growth; environmental support; physical environment challenges; development of cultural competence; and the Kawa Model as a facilitator of meaningful reflection. Participants described challenges related to communication, climate, fatigue, and adjustment to unfamiliar clinical and social environments. Peer support, supervisory guidance, family contact, local relationships, and personal coping strategies supported adaptation. The Kawa Model enabled participants to organize and externalize their experiences by identifying barriers, support, personal resources, and opportunities for reflective growth. Conclusion: The Kawa Model supported structured reflection and meaning-making among international OT students undertaking clinical placement in India. The findings suggest that culturally responsive reflective tools may help students develop selfawareness, adaptive capacity, and cultural competence.

DT Article
DE Education; history; history education; scientification; historical
   thinking; By Subject; Education - Social Sciences; Subject
AB The scientification of history education refers to the ongoing process of transforming history teaching and learning into a scientific discipline. This shift marks a paradigm change, viewing history not just as a narrative of the past, but as a field of scientific inquiry. This article analyzes the process of scientification in history education in Indonesia from the early years of independence to the post-Reformation era (1957-2013). The central question explores how this transformation influenced the theory and practice of history teaching in the country. Using content analysis, the study examines curriculum documents and history textbooks from 1957 to 2013. The findings indicate that the early stages of scientification began with the Indonesian History Seminar in December 1957 and continued through Curriculum 1964 to Curriculum 1995. The process reached its peak with Curriculum 2004, which introduced detailed descriptions of historical research methods in textbooks, signaling a commitment to scientific approaches in understanding and reconstructing history. Additionally, Curriculum 2013 formally mandated the use of a scientific approach in history education, influencing teaching methods, textbooks, and assessment models.

AB Digital transformation in vocational education has intensified the need to understand how students engage with technology and regulate their own learning. TI Cross-cultural adaptation and psychometric evaluation of the artificial
   intelligence learning intention scale (AILIS) among medical sciences
   students: a methodological study
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Instrument validation; medical education; technology acceptance; student
   motivation; psychometric assessment
ID OF-FIT INDEXES; CONTENT VALIDITY; MEASUREMENT INVARIANCE;
   RECOMMENDATIONS; RELIABILITY; TECHNOLOGY; ACCEPTANCE; GUIDELINE; VALUES;
   COSMIN
AB Background This study aimed to adapt and psychometrically evaluate the Artificial Intelligence Learning Intention Scale (AILIS) among Iranian medical sciences students.Methods This methodological psychometric study was conducted among 800 medical sciences students at Babol University of Medical Sciences, Iran. The AILIS was translated and culturally adapted into Persian using a standardized cross-cultural adaptation process. Construct validity was examined through exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Reliability was assessed using Cronbach's alpha, McDonald's omega, and the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Convergent and discriminant validity were evaluated using composite reliability (CR) and average variance extracted (AVE). Measurement invariance across gender and structural stability were assessed using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis and exploratory graph analysis (EGA).Results EFA supported a four-factor structure consisting of Epistemic Capacity, Psychological Attitudes, Facilitating Environments, and Psychological and Behavioral Outcomes, explaining 44.55% of the total variance, with factor loadings greater than 0.40. Confirmatory factor analysis indicated an acceptable model fit, supporting the proposed factor structure (chi & sup2;/df = 3.42, RMSEA = 0.078, CFI = 0.932). Internal consistency and test-retest reliability were satisfactory, with Cronbach's alpha ranging from 0.854 to 0.904, McDonald's omega from 0.854 to 0.899, and ICC from 0.750 to 0.860. Composite reliability values were adequate, while AVE values indicated acceptable but partially limited evidence of convergent validity. Discriminant validity was generally supported. In addition, multi-group analysis demonstrated measurement invariance across gender, and exploratory graph analysis confirmed the structural stability of the four-factor model.Conclusion The Persian AILIS is a valid and reliable instrument for assessing AI learning intention among medical sciences students. Beyond its psychometric robustness, the instrument may support curriculum planning, evaluation of AI-related educational interventions, and evidence-based decision-making in medical sciences education by providing a standardized measure of students' intentions to engage with AI learning.

TI Relative achievement rank, gender and school-related stress: a
   multilevel study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pupils; students; gender; performance; pressure; well-being
ID SELF-WORTH; BIG-FISH; PERFECTIONISM; PERFORMANCE
AB While academic achievement is often regarded as positive, emerging research has highlighted high levels of stress among high-achieving pupils. However, it remains unclear whether school-related stress is driven by pupils' absolute achievement or by their rank within their peer group. The aim of this study was to examine the association between pupils' achievement rank in class and school-related stress, with a particular focus on gender differences. The study utilised longitudinal survey data from 1691 Swedish pupils, collected in grade 6 (age 13) and grade 9 (age 16), analysed through multilevel and fixed-effects models. There was a positive association between class rank and school-related stress among female pupils, with high-ranking girls exhibiting significantly elevated stress levels also after adjusting for absolute achievement. No association was found among boys. Class rank was not associated with more severe forms of stress or mental health problems. The study suggests that girls may be particularly susceptible to performance pressures and identity formation tied to academic achievement. One interpretation is that there may be a trade-off between short-term stress and long-term educational and labour market success. Schools and educators should acknowledge that high-achieving girls may experience stress despite - or because of - their success.

TI Navigating ethical ambiguity without institutional guidance: generative
   AI decision-making among students in Zimbabwean higher education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; academic integrity; ethical decision
   making; peer norms; institutional governance; African higher education
ID OPTIMAL NUMBER; DISHONESTY
AB Generative artificial intelligence tools have fundamentally altered the landscape of higher education. Students make daily decisions about appropriate AI use without meaningful institutional support. This study investigated how undergraduate learners reason about generative AI ethics in Zimbabwe, where two universities with no formal AI governance policies provided the research environment. A sequential mixed methods design combined qualitative interviews with quantitative vignette surveys across three phases. Phase one comprised semi structured interviews with 22 students across both institutions. Four critical findings emerged from integrated analysis. The study contributes empirical evidence from sub-Saharan Africa and advances the institutional responsibility literature by reframing the ethical ambiguity problem as a governance concern with distributive justice implications.

TI The interplay between gestures and analytical questioning in mathematics
   group discussion: a case study of a blended learning context
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gestures; analytical questions; LMS; group discussion; university
   student; embodied cognition; Gestures; analytical questions; LMS; group
   discussion; university student; embodied cognition
ID HAND GESTURES; SPEECH; RESOURCES; LEARNERS
AB The interplay between gestural communication and analytical questioning in Learning Management System (LMS) assisted group discussions remains an under explored area in educational literature. Gestures serve as critical markers of cognitive developmental levels and provide a window into the human understanding of the thinking process. However, their contribution as a link between non-verbal communication and students' analytical thinking in classroom interactions has often been overlooked. This study examined the types of gestures employed by presenters and non-presenters in an LMS supported collaborative setting and explored how these bodily expressions operate in tandem with analytical inquiry. In this framework, the LMS served as a preparatory platform for asynchronous material sharing, while face-to-face interaction acted as the synchronous space for discourse. Adopting a qualitative case study design, this research observed 18 second-year Mathematics Education students in a Number Theory course through video recordings and interactional analysis. Data were analyzed using gesture coding (deictic, iconic, metaphorical, and beat) alongside a taxonomy of analytical questioning. The findings demonstrate that gestures play a substantial co-expressive role alongside analytical questions. Specifically, presenters' representational gestures, including iconic and metaphoric movements, frequently co-occurred with deeper inquiry, while non-presenters' regulatory gestures accompanied the flow of academic conversation. These multimodal interactions enriched the collective cognitive process through varied and complex questioning. While limited by its specific context and sample size, this study underscores the importance of embodied cognition in blended learning environments. Further research with larger cohorts is recommended to enhance transferability.

TI Inaugural year of preference signaling in im subspecialty fellowships:
   multi-institutional survey about program director perceptions, benefits,

DT Article
DE Preference signalling; fellowship applications; internal medicine;
   medicine subspecialty fellowship; graduate medical education; medical

ID RESIDENCY
AB BackgroundPreference signalling was introduced into internal medicine subspecialty fellowship recruitment in the 2025-2026 cycle, adding a new consideration for applicants, mentors, and fellowship programs. We sought to characterize program director (PD) perceptions of signalling during this inaugural cycle and identify implications for advising.MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional anonymous survey of PDs in five internal medicine subspecialties at three West Coast academic institutions (University of Washington, Oregon Health & Science University, and University of California, San Francisco) from December 2025 to January 2026. DT Article
DE Digital competence; MOOCs; scaffolding; application-oriented learning;
   marketing content design board
AB Although massive open online courses (MOOCs) have expanded access to learning, many learners still struggle to translate knowledge into practical digital competence. This study examined whether a MOOC supported by a marketing content design (MCD) board could strengthen digital competence and perceived application outcomes among Thai university students. Quantitative data measured their perceptions of the MOOC learning environment (MOOCLE), the utility of the MCD board, digital competence and perceived application outcomes, while qualitative interviews and learner-generated artefacts provided explanatory depth. The findings showed that both the MOOCLE and the perceived utility of the MCD board were strongly associated with digital competence, which in turn explained a substantial share of variation in perceived application outcomes. Digital competence also functioned as a mediator linking learning conditions to learners' reported ability to apply what they had learned. The qualitative findings further indicated that the MCD board helped learners organise ideas, analyse audiences and translate local cultural content into more structured digital communication plans. The results highlight the value of embedding structured design scaffolds in MOOCs to support competence-orientated and application-orientated learning.
