TI Training climate matters: programmatic openness, individual belonging,
   and trainee mistreatment in graduate medical education
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Wellbeing; burnout; mistreatment; programmatic openness; belonging
ID SOCIAL-SUPPORT; INCLUSION; DIVERSITY; EQUITY; DISCRIMINATION; BURNOUT;
   ABUSE
AB BackgroundMedical trainee mistreatment remains a widespread challenge in graduate medical education, contributing to burnout, depression, and workforce attrition. Graduate medical education programs have sought to create safer learning environments by fostering programmatic openness-climates perceived as transparent, welcoming, and supportive. Yet it remains unclear how such programmatic conditions interact with individual experiences of belonging to shape wellbeing. Drawing on ecological systems theory, we examine how programmatic openness and trainee belonging interact to mitigate trainee mistreatment during residency.MethodsWe conducted an anonymous online survey (Dec 2023-Jan 2024) at three large US teaching sites with 62 GME programs. Scales with robust validity evidence measured perceived programmatic openness, individual belonging, perceived mistreatment, burnout, and social support. We built a latent moderation model, encompassing both confirmatory factor analysis and latent interaction effects. We examined how programmatic openness moderated trainee perceived mistreatment while controlling for social support and trainee demographics.ResultsOf 675 eligible trainees, 266 responded (39.4%). Measurement models demonstrated good fit, supporting construct validity. Both programmatic openness and belonging were protective against perceived mistreatment, which was strongly associated with burnout. Residents' belonging to the training program was significantly associated with low burnout, even after accounting for social support. Moderation analyses revealed that programmatic openness most strongly buffered mistreatment among trainees who experienced low belonging, with diminished effects at higher belonging levels.ConclusionFindings revealed a compensatory effect, suggesting the beneficial effects of programmatic openness were especially crucial among trainees who experienced low individual belonging. This finding aligns with the ecological system theory, which posits that supportive environments may mitigate individual-level vulnerabilities. Both burnout and perceived mistreatment were at its lowest when programmatic openness and individual belonging were both present. This underscores the need for residency programs to foster both openness and belonging as core strategies to support trainee wellbeing.

TI Cognitive and non-cognitive efficiency gaps between private and public
   schools and their determinants in the Latin America region-a hybrid data
   envelopment analysis and interpretable machine learning approach based
   on PISA 2022
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE School efficiency; private and public schools; DEA; explainable machine
   learning; Latin America; PISA 2022
AB Latin America's education systems are fragmented by school type. Knowing whether private and public schools are making an efficient use of resources is critical, even more so after the post-pandemic learning crisis. In this paper, relying on data of 2,034 schools and nine Latin American countries from PISA 2022, I offer new evidence on school efficiency (both on cognitive and non-cognitive dimensions) using Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) by school type and, then, I estimate efficiency determinants through interpretable machine learning methods (IML). This hybrid DEA-IML approach allows to accommodate the issue of big data, assessing several determinants of school efficiency. I find a cognitive efficiency gap of nearly 0.10 favouring private schools and of 0.045 for non-cognitive outcomes, and with a lower heterogeneity in private than public schools. For cognitive efficiency, leading determinants for the chance of a private school of being highly efficient are a higher stock of books and computers at home, a lack of engagement in paid work and higher school autonomy; whereas low-efficient public schools are shaped by poor school climate, large rates of repetition, truancy and intensity of paid work, fewer books at home and increasing barriers for homework during the pandemic.

TI Developing grammar lessons: a flipped learning approach to elevate Thai
   EFL learners' grammatical competence and writing performance
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Flipped learning; grammar instruction; writing performance; grammatical
   competence; learner satisfaction; Education; Language Teaching &
   Learning; Educational Technology; Higher Education; Applied Linguistics;
   Curriculum & Instruction
ID CLASSROOM; SATISFACTION
AB This embedded mixed-methods study developed flipped grammar lessons and assessed their effects on learners' grammatical competence, writing performance, and satisfaction. During an eight-week intervention, 31 Thai undergraduates majoring in English engaged in the flipped grammar lessons. To evaluate the effects of the intervention, data were generated from grammar tests, writing tests, a satisfaction questionnaire, and student logs. The paired-samples t-test results revealed significant improvements in learners' grammatical competence and writing performance following the exposure to flipped grammar lessons. In terms of learner satisfaction, the questionnaire results revealed a high level of satisfaction with the lessons across three domains, particularly with their usefulness, design, and ease of use. The thematic analysis of student logs corroborated these findings, highlighting several favorable aspects of the lessons, namely learning flexibility, useful video functions, comprehensive content, enhanced grammatical knowledge, and improved writing performance. Nevertheless, unfavorable aspects were also reported concerning limited synchronous interaction, unstable internet connectivity, and self-regulation difficulties. This study extends flipped learning research by connecting the effects of flipped grammar instruction to writing development, an area that remains underexplored in existing flipped learning studies. The study provides empirical evidence and practical pedagogical implications supporting the potential effectiveness of flipped learning in grammar instruction.

TI What are the benefits of the funds of knowledge approach? A qualitative
   study on teachers' and families' perceptions
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Funds of knowledge; teachers' beliefs; families' beliefs; family-school
   relationships; family engagement
ID HOME VISITS
AB Previous studies suggest distinct benefits of the funds of knowledge approach, such as enhancing curriculum relevance by connecting it to students' lives and strengthening family-school relationships. However, the impact of this approach is unknown from the point of view of the families that have been visited by the teachers. In order to remedy this shortcoming in the literature, this study aims to both identify the perceptions of families after teachers' household visits and to analyse the perception that the participating teachers had of the experience of the program on the families visited. The novelty of these findings is the analysis of the families' perceptions following teacher home visits, which have not been previously documented in the literature.

TI Renewable Rangers as a maternal autoethnographic innovation in
   early childhood STEM education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Maternal autoethnographic innovation; self-directed learning; ecological
   literacy; early childhood STEM; digital game-based learning; Social
   Sciences; Education; Early Years; Development Studies, Environment,
   Social Work, Urban Studies; Sociology
AB Renewable Rangers is a digital educational game designed to foster early childhood learning in renewable energy, environmental awareness, and problem-solving. My paper explores the creation of the game as an example of maternal autoethnographic innovation, highlighting how pedagogical tools can emerge from every day, domestic spaces. Employing a maternal autoethnographic methodology, data were collected through reflective journaling, narrative reconstruction, and dialogic engagement with my children. The game integrates Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, Self-Directed Learning, Ecological Literacy, and Culturally Responsive Education for Sustainability within a South African context. Players, guided by the character 'Dr Mummy Ranger', engage in culturally grounded, play-based missions that explore renewable energy concepts while connecting emotionally with the environment and developing agency and problem-solving skills. Findings demonstrate that the home can function as a dynamic site of curriculum innovation, where maternal knowledge, cultural experience, and emotional engagement generate meaningful, inclusive, and contextually relevant learning experiences. This paper underscores the potential of maternal-led educational interventions to expand notions of who produces knowledge, how learning tools are developed, and how early childhood education can be enriched by play, culture, and lived experience. Renewable Rangers illustrates the intersection of theory, practice, and care, positioning mothers as theorists, designers, and co-educators in shaping children's learning and environmental stewardship.

TI The identity trajectory of an international junior female faculty: an
   autoethnography study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Identity trajectory; international faculty; junior faculty; female
   faculty; Japan
AB To more effectively advance diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) efforts in Japan, greater scholarly attention should be directed toward those underrepresented groups directly. Adopting autoethnography as an analytical methodology, this study examines the identity trajectory of an international junior female faculty. Drawing on Identity Trajectory Theory and an intersectional perspective, the study analyzes the author's diary entries from August 2022 to July 2025. Theoretical and practical implications, therefore, are provided to better support these groups and to advance DEI efforts in Japanese higher education contexts.

TI Determinants of the fee-based education structure in public English
   medium primary schools in Tanzania
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Public education; public-English medium primary school; school fees;
   educational equity; education financing; Public education;
   public-English medium primary school; school fees; educational equity;
   education financing
ID MEDIUM INSTRUCTION; LANGUAGE; INEQUALITIES; QUALITY; PRIVATE; POLICY
AB Tanzania's primary schools have both public and private systems. Private primary schools use English as the medium of instruction, while public primary schools, which are officially fee-free, use Swahili. Recently, the government has introduced a fee-based model for public English-medium schools. The present study explores factors influencing the increase of fee-based model in public English-medium schools. This study, grounded in Linguistic Capital and Human Capital theory, employed a qualitative case study design. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with purposively selected educational officers, head teachers, and parents, and were analysed thematically. The results point to four primary determinants of the fee-based system in public primary English-medium schools:high operational costs, the growing demand from parents, the shift in policy towards cost-sharing between the state and households, and attempts to control enrollment demand and sustain the quality of education. The study concludes cost-sharing arrangements in public primary schools create disparities between fee-based and fee-free schools, as well as between households that can afford the fee and those that cannot. The study suggests that the government should formulate a standalone policy that regulates school expenses and parental contributions, thereby expanding access for many.

TI Teachers' instructional practices reflecting Mathematics for Sustainable
   Development implementation in secondary schools in Uganda
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mathematics for Sustainable Development; Instructional practices;
   Uganda; secondary schools; competence based curriculum
ID EDUCATION
AB This paper explores the mathematics teachers' practices during the implementation of Mathematics for Sustainable Development (Math4SD) in lower secondary schools in Uganda. The study used a qualitative case study research design with an embedded professional development intervention. Data was collected using lesson observation field notes, interviews, and students' focus group discussions. The study adopted the theory of learning levels of accommodation, reformation, and transformation to evaluate teachers' knowledge of SDGs integration in modelling Math4SD tasks when teaching business mathematics. The study therefore recommends further research on integrating the SDGS in Mathematics at the secondary school level, using topics unrelated to business mathematics.

AB This study explores how indigenous Ugandan basketry can be integrated into lower secondary school mathematics instruction as a culturally responsive pedagogical resource. Using a qualitative multi-case ethnographic approach, data were collected from indigenous basket weavers, secondary school mathematics teachers, and mathematics teacher educators across four regions of Uganda through interviews, focus group discussions, observations, and document analysis. The analysis identified mathematical concepts embedded in basketry, including geometry, measurement, ratio and proportion, symmetry, and pattern. The findings indicate that basketry can serve as a meaningful context for teaching and learning mathematics by connecting abstract concepts to learners' cultural experiences. A prototype lesson plan is presented to illustrate how this approach may be implemented in classroom practice. Overall, the study suggests that integrating basketry into mathematics instruction offers a promising pathway for supporting culturally responsive pedagogy and enhancing conceptual understanding.

AB This study evaluated the use of video vignettes to teach cultural competence in non-verbal, cross-cultural simulated healthcare situations to Master of Pharmacy (MPharm) students at a pharmacy school in the UK. An online survey was conducted between May and June 2025 among Year 3 and Year 4 pharmacy students at the Reading School of Pharmacy using Online Surveys (R). Ethical clearance was obtained. Student feedback was collected following a teaching session that incorporated video vignettes. The questionnaire included demographic items and Likert-scale questions exploring satisfaction with the vignettes, perceived learning impact, representation of diversity, and technical and acting quality. Regression analysis showed that White ethnicity was a negative predictor of positive feedback, while preference for working with diverse people was a positive predictor. Overall, students responded positively to video vignettes, and further avenues for this work have been identified.

TI Embedding multidisciplinary learning into sport and exercise science
   degree provision
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Higher education; multidisciplinary; knowledge; sports students;
   undergraduate
ID EDUCATION
AB The purpose of this study was to understand the student experience on multidisciplinary modules combining biomechanics, physiology and psychology rather than these disciplines being taught separately. Using a mixed-methods cross sectional study design, thirty-nine students completed a questionnaire at the end of two 12-week modules. In the section of the survey exploring module belonging, engagement and self-confidence, over 70% of students reported positive perceptions of motivation, learning expectations, and staff relationships, and 20% agreed with having some concerns about the module related to difficulty and their own ability. In conclusion, our findings suggest there may be a place in undergraduate sport degrees for the inclusion of such multidisciplinary modules, but students require guidance to recognise the relevance to their development and applied practice.

TI The development of project management competence indicators through

SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Project-based learning; personal competence; peer review; higher
   education institution; project management
AB Project-Based Learning (PjBL) is recognized for its ability to enhance 21st-century soft skills but the existing assessment methods often lack comprehensive indicators and do not integrate cooperative learning (CL) principles. Therefore, this study aimed to develop and validate personal competence indicators of project management derived from PjBL activities in a university internship class. TI The impact of artificial intelligence software on the
   supervisor-graduate student relationships
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence software; supervisor-graduate student
   relationships; graduate students; supervisors
ID USER ACCEPTANCE; TECHNOLOGY
AB This theoretical paper systematically investigates the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) software on supervisor-graduate student relationships (SGSR) from a socio-technical systems perspective. It proposes the concept of 'technology acceptance alignment' across three dimensions-capability, purpose, and pacing-to explain how the match between supervisors and students determines whether AI functions as a 'relationship optimizer' or a 'defect amplifier'. The core mechanism lies in reshaping the dimensions of 'influence' and 'intimacy' through empowering supervisors, regulating students, setting rules, and mediating interactions. Applying the influence-intimacy typology across eight relationship types, the analysis reveals that under appropriate use, AI helps each type overcome inherent limitations; under misaligned use, it exacerbates existing vulnerabilities. The study proposes a multi-level strategy involving relational contracts, differentiated interventions, and institutional support, emphasizing the principle of 'prioritizing the relationship while leveraging technology' to ensure AI serves human development and the academic community.

TI Development and evaluation of a station rotation blended learning model
   to enhance creative thinking and poetry writing skills
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Linguistic creativity; online-teacher-collaboration model; poetry
   writing; station rotation
ID EXPERIENCES; ONLINE
AB Poetry writing reflects ideas, wisdom, and culture while supporting the development of analytical, synthetic, and evaluative skills essential for holistic thinking and creative expression. Despite these benefits, poetry instruction in Thai lower secondary classrooms remains predominantly lecture-based with limited activity diversity, reducing student engagement with composition. However, poetry writing offers substantial potential for creative thinking, a key 21st-century competency. This study developed and evaluated a blended learning model based on the Online-Teacher-Collaboration (OTC) Rotation Model to strengthen linguistic creative thinking and poetry-writing skills. The research involved two phases: model development through theoretical synthesis and expert validation by 7 specialists, followed by effectiveness testing using a quasi-experimental posttest-only control-group design with cluster random sampling. Participants included 78 Secondary 2 students, equally divided into experimental and control groups. Assessment data on linguistic creative thinking and poetry-writing skills were analyzed using MANOVA. Results indicated that students taught with the OTC Rotation Model scored significantly higher both in poetry writing and creative thinking than the control group. These findings carry meaningful implications for language educators and curriculum designers: the OTC Rotation Model offers a structured, evidence-based instructional framework that integrates creative thinking directly into literary composition, making it readily applicable to Thai-language classrooms without requiring extensive institutional resources. Teachers are encouraged to adopt its three-station structure online, teacher-led, and collaborative as a replicable format for designing active learning environments. Beyond Thai education, the model can be adapted across other educational levels and linguistic contexts where poetry instruction and creative thinking development are curricular priorities.

TI Procrastination in practice: examining impacts and interventions for
   community development students in Thailand
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Behavioral strategies in fieldwork; Community-Based learning; stress
   management in higher Education; student procrastination; work efficiency
   and quality
ID HEALTH
AB Academic procrastination remains a widespread challenge in higher education, often reflecting predictable lapses in self-regulation that undermine learning, performance, and well-being. Addressing that issue, the study examined procrastination in a Community Development program where delays affect grades, report quality, and community relationships. A mixed-methods approach, a questionnaire with 80 students and interviews and observations of 17 key informants, integrating descriptive statistics, inferential statistics with qualitative content analysis to generate a comprehensive, context-sensitive understanding. Findings revealed moderate overall impacts, with stress highest, accompanied by moderate declines in work quality and efficiency, and interpersonal effects that, whereas lower, remained meaningful. Interviews showed that accumulated tasks, last-minute starts, and deadline pressure created cycles of rushed work, reduced concentration, superficial analysis, and disrupted collaboration, sometimes affecting academic progression. Student-endorsed strategies included identifying causes, prioritizing tasks by urgency and difficulty, setting short-term goals, segmenting work, scheduling balanced routines, and seeking support politely and clearly after demonstrating effort. These components informed a NO-DEIAY framework linking consequences, origins, task decomposition, prioritized execution, goal setting, help-seeking, and disciplined routines, providing practical guidance for instructors, supervisors, and program leaders in field-based community courses.

TI Temporal trends and moderating effects of sex, curriculum revisions and

DE Assessment; physical Education; longitudinal; population; lower
   secondary school
ID SPORT; ACHIEVEMENT; TEACHERS
AB Examined how PE grades developed over time and whether structural breaks were associated with curriculum reforms and the COVID-19 pandemic. The results showed a marked upward shift in grades, with the proportion receiving Grade 6 increasing from approximately 5% in 2002 to over 20% in 2023, while lower and mid-range grades declined. These findings suggest substantial changes in grading patterns in Norwegian PE, potentially reflecting both curriculum-related shifts and broader changes in assessment practice. While the trends may indicate movement toward more inclusive assessment, they also raise concerns about grade inflation and the validity of grades as indicators of competence. The study highlights the need for transparent and coherent assessment frameworks and for continued research on grading practices in PE.

TI The impact of extrinsic rewards on organisational performance and
   turnover intentions among academic staff at a selected higher education
   institution
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Effectiveness and efficiency; extrinsic rewards; higher education
   institution; turnover intentions; organisational performance; Social
   Sciences; Education; Higher Education; Study of Higher Education;
   Teaching and Learning
ID MOTIVATION
AB The study investigated the impact of extrinsic rewards on organisational performance and turnover intentions among academic staff. The primary objective was to assess how extrinsic rewards influence both the effectiveness and efficiency of the HEI and the turnover intentions of the academic staff. The study was guided by positivist research paradigm, which emphasises objectivity, measurement, and statistical analysis. Furthermore, the study adopted a quantitative research approach and descriptive research design. the data was collected using structured and adapted questionnaire which was administered online through Google Forms. The target population comprised of permanent academic staff members at the selected HEI, and a total of 400 completed questionnaires were obtained. The collected data were analysed using IBM statistical package for social sciences (SPSS) version 30 for Microsoft Windows. Both descriptive and inferential statistical techniques were used to determine the nature and strength of the relationships between extrinsic rewards, organisational performance, and turnover intentions. The findings revealed that extrinsic rewards have a low but significant positive influence on turnover intentions and a moderate positive influence on organisational performance. Moreover, turnover intentions showed a strong positive relationship with organisational performance indicators such as effectiveness and efficiency. The study concludes that extrinsic reward practices play a critical role in shaping both employee retention and institutional outcomes. These results align with Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory and Equity Theory, highlighting the importance of fair and adequate rewards in promoting satisfaction, commitment, and organisational success. The study recommends that policymakers implement transparent and equitable reward structures to reduce turnover intentions and enhance overall institutional performance.

TI Artificial intelligence readiness in Pakistan's medical and dental
   education: training-phase decline, a knowledge-practice paradox, and the
   role of digital determinants of health
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; cross-sectional survey, clinical training,
   barriers; Pakistan; digital equity, professional identity formation;
   digital determinants of health
ID IDENTITY
AB Background: We assessed AI knowledge, attitudes, and use among medical and dental students in Pakistan, a lower-middle-income country (LMIC), and identified predictors of low AI use within Digital Determinants of Health (DDoH) and Professional Identity Formation (PIF) frameworks. Methods: A cross-sectional survey of 501 medical and dental students in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa assessed knowledge, attitudes, practices, and barriers related to AI. Analyses used ANOVA and logistic regression for low AI use (score <= 15; 7-35 scale, higher = greater use), with sensitivity models adjusted for age, knowledge, attitude scores, and selected barriers. Results: Mean (SD) scores were 4.23 (1.71) for knowledge (0-7), 32.72 (6.64) for attitude (10-50), and 15.85 (6.32) for practice (7-35); higher scores indicated greater knowledge, more favorable attitudes, and greater AI use. Practice differed across years [F(4,496) = 4.025, p = 0.003, eta & sup2;p = 0.031], with Year 2 scoring higher than Year 4 and the final year. This exploratory model (AUC = 0.618) identified only associations. Fourth-year (OR = 2.02, 95% CI: 1.11-3.70; p = 0.022), female (OR = 1.51, 95% CI: 1.05-2.17; p = 0.025), and dental students (OR = 1.58, 95% CI: 1.01-2.50; p = 0.046) had higher odds of low AI use. The Year 4 association strengthened in sensitivity analyses (OR = 3.83, 95% CI: 1.66-8.85; p = 0.002), and higher knowledge paradoxically predicted lower use (OR = 1.52, 95% CI: 1.34-1.72; p < 0.001). The most significant barriers were a lack of training (71.7%) and limited technical access (69.7%). Conclusions: AI use was lower in later training years and differed by gender and specialty. The inverse knowledge-practice association contradicts standard adoption models and warrants longitudinal investigation; one PIF-based hypothesis is that higher-knowledge students exercise professional restraint, although cross-sectional data cannot confirm it. The clinical-phase decline implicates ward-based norms as independent barriers. Competency-based training with structured access provisions and faculty development, particularly in clinical phase education, is needed.

TI Dual vocational education and training: Self-reported perception of
   teachers in Ethiopia
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Dual vocational education; perception; TVET; Ethiopian TVET; teachers'
   perception; Social Sciences; Education; Curriculum Studies; Science
   Education; Higher Education
ID WORK
AB The purpose of this study was to trace the perceived attitudes of trainers about the perception of dual vocational education and training (VET) in Ethiopia by using a survey and Nominal Group Technique (NGT) research design. Data collected from 148 trainers from four Colleges in Addis Ababa were analysed via thematic and descriptive statistical analysis techniques. The findings indicated that vocational trainers positively perceive that dual VET was understood as a model that leads to better training outcomes in the labour market by exposing learners to the real world of work. Nonetheless, trainers perceived that graduates and employers believe that industries were not willing to accept learners for practice in their companies due to the overwhelming number of practitioners and do not use VET to anticipate their current and future skilled human power demands. Lack of industry-supervisors, uncertainty about the future of dual VET, lack of financial resources, and lack of consent between partners in the dual VET system were the most perceived barriers in the implementation of dual VET. The findings of the study call for strong collaboration between partners to establish effective dual VET. Moreover, the study will be motivational for further study since studies around the issue remain scarce.

TI Digital storytelling in economics education: the use of analogy-based
   cartoons to improve student performance
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital storytelling; cartoons; collaborative analogies; economics;
   conceptual understanding
ID TOOL
AB Digital Storytelling (DS) has been a popular instructional tool since the 1990s, with its effectiveness lying in that stories function as narrative analogies, bridging abstract concepts to familiar experiences and prior learning. This educational role of DS (EDS) can be reinforced through collaborative analogy generation and enhanced with cartoon co-design rendering these analogies in accessible, engaging, and memorable forms. Research has consistently shown that EDS and cartoons can have a positive impact on student engagement and learning outcomes. In higher education subjects such as economics, however, most studies remain opinion-based and descriptive, with claims about the value and role of EDS and cartoons being essentially views and ideas on integrating them as pedagogical tools rather than empirical evidence on their effectiveness in facilitating understanding economic concepts and student engagement. This study examines the relationship between exposure to EDS co-designed cartoons that embed co-generated analogies and students' conceptual understanding by surveying 60 undergraduate students on their performance through an ordinary least squares estimation technique. The findings suggest that exposure to EDS cartoons may be associated with improvements in students' understanding and point to the need for future research on the underlying mechanism in promoting conceptual understanding of economic concepts.

TI An empirical study on factors contributing to limited oral English
   proficiency among English majors in an under-resourced context
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE EFL; speaking; limited proficiency; anxiety; L1; EFL; speaking; limited
   proficiency; anxiety; L1
ID ANXIETY; STUDENTS
AB Despite a burgeoning body of research on oral English proficiency among English majors, this issue is largely unexplored in under-resourced contexts. Therefore, this study examined the factors influencing the proficiency of English majors. Using a convergent parallel mixed-methods design, 120 English majors completed a survey, and qualitative data were also collected from students (N = 8) and teachers (N = 6) through group discussions and interviews. Descriptive analysis revealed that students perceive a compensatory linguistic gap, avoidance-driven L1 use, and speaking anxiety as the most salient barriers. Pearson correlation analysis indicated a significant negative relationship between oral proficiency and avoidance-driven L1 use, but speaking anxiety indicated only a marginal negative correlation. At the same time, other factors showed no significant direct correlations. However, a multiple regression analysis controlling for all variables simultaneously identified two significant predictors: avoidance-driven L1 use negatively predicted proficiency, and the compensatory linguistic gap emerged as a positive predictor-a relationship not apparent in the bivariate analysis. Moreover, the qualitative data analysis revealed the following factors that impeded the development of oral proficiency: Speaking anxiety, instructors' behavior, limited linguistic competence, use of L1, and speaking-curriculum-related issues. A series of instructional strategies is recommended to mitigate the factors. The study provides implications for teachers and students regarding the development of oral proficiency and its contributing factors.

TI Integrating cultural dimensions into English language teaching: evidence
   from IPDN students in Indonesia
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Sustainable education; cultural factors; teaching methods; student
   engagement; English learning outcomes
ID BIAS; SELF
AB This research investigates how cultural factors influence English learning outcomes among 901 students at the Institut Pemerintahan Dalam Negeri (IPDN) in Indonesia. Utilizing partial least squares structural equation modelling through SmartPLS, the study identifies cultural elements as key determinants in shaping instructional approaches and student engagement. Both of these mediating variables significantly impact English language proficiency. Teaching methods are shown to directly improve language skills while also boosting student involvement, which plays a pivotal role in learning success. Furthermore, the research underscores the indirect contribution of cultural factors, demonstrating that culturally attuned teaching strategies enhance student engagement and, consequently, learning outcomes. These findings underline the importance of adopting pedagogical practices that are both culturally relevant and sustainable within higher education settings. By embedding cultural awareness into instructional design, institutions can foster more inclusive educational environments that promote enduring academic achievement and sustainable learning development.

TI Toward ethical governance of generative artificial intelligence in
   higher education: a Delphi study of key dimensions and priorities
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative artificial intelligence; Delphi method; higher education; AI
   ethics; governance; education policy; Generative artificial
   intelligence; Delphi method; higher education; AI ethics; governance;
   education policy
AB The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) into higher education has introduced significant opportunities alongside complex ethical challenges. While existing research has largely focused on specific tools such as large language models, there remains limited consensus on the broader dimensions that shape the ethical use of GAI across institutional, pedagogical, and technological contexts. This study addresses the gap by identifying and prioritizing key dimensions that influence the ethical use of GAI in higher education. A three-round Delphi method was employed, involving 31 experts from higher education institutions across China and Malaysia. In Round 1, qualitative responses were analyzed using an inductive approach to derive six overarching dimensions. In Round 2, experts ranked these dimensions based on perceived importance. A third round was conducted to refine consensus, resulting in a statistically significant level of agreement (Kendall's W = 0.248, p = .001), indicating moderate convergence of expert opinion. The findings revealed six key dimensions, ranked in order of importance: (1) Institutional Governance and Policy Frameworks, (2) Academic Integrity and Ethical Accountability, (3) GAI Literacy, Training, and Capacity Building, (4) Technical Safeguards, Data Privacy, and Fairness, (5) Transparency, Critical Thinking, and Responsible Use Culture, and (6) Pedagogical Adaptation and Teacher Roles. Among these, institutional governance emerged as the foundational dimension. The study contributes to the literature by proposing a structured, multi-dimensional framework for ethical governance of GAI in higher education. The findings highlight the need for coordinated institutional strategies to ensure the responsible, sustainable integration of GAI into academic environments.

TI Understanding learners' intentions and learning outcomes in ICT
   education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ICT education; UTAUT model; behavioral intention; digital literacy;
   Lesotho secondary education; Educational Technology; Information and
   Communication Technology Education; Technology Acceptance Model; Digital
   Literacy; Secondary Education; Structural Equation Modeling
ID TECHNOLOGY ACCEPTANCE MODEL; INFORMATION-TECHNOLOGY; USER ACCEPTANCE;
   UNIFIED THEORY; UTAUT; STUDENTS; BEHAVIOR; ADOPTION
AB The integration of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) into secondary education is crucial for equipping students with the necessary digital skills for the modern economy. However, in Lesotho, ICT education faces substantial challenges, including inadequate infrastructure, limited teacher training, and disparities in student engagement. This study investigated the factors influencing students' behavioral intention and actual learning of ICT education using the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) model. These insights provide a foundation for educational policies aimed at improving digital literacy in resource-constrained environments. The study conclude that targeted interventions such as improved infrastructure, teacher training, and curriculum development are necessary to enhance ICT education. The study calls on policymakers to prioritize ICT integration to ensure equitable digital education access.

TI Aligning educational and learning capitals for gifted and talented
   students in the Indian context: a collaborative autoethnographic study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gifted education; ELCM; Panchakosha; guru shishya parampara; Ecosystem
   model of giftedness development; NEP 2020
ID ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT; ACTIOTOPE MODEL; PREDICTORS; PERFECTIONISM;
   PERFORMANCE; ATTAINMENT; FRAMEWORK; CHILDREN; ANXIETY; ABILITY
AB Gifted education in India is shaped by the interplay of cultural traditions, socio-economic conditions, and institutional frameworks. This article examines that landscape through the Educational and Learning Capital Model (ELCM) and indigenous frameworks and proposes an Ecosystem Model of Giftedness Development reflecting Indian parallels from the findings. Using collaborative autoethnography and document analysis, the study explores how five educational capitals and five learning capitals are shaped in Indian contexts. Findings reveal strong reservoirs of cultural, social and didactic capital, rooted in family expectations, community networks and mentoring traditions, alongside fragile economic and infrastructural supports that limit access for many high-potential learners, particularly girls, rural youth and students outside English-medium systems. With this backdrop, recent policy reforms, notably the National Education Policy 2020 (Ministry of Education, 2020), advocate for differentiated curricula, teacher training, and equitable access within an ELCM-informed, culturally grounded framework. Harnessing India's indigenous traditions alongside contemporary pedagogical approaches can better support gifted learners to realize their potential and contribute creatively, ethically, and meaningfully to society.

   ethical knowledge; International education standards (IES); professional
   values ethics and attitudes (PVEA); responsive institutions
ID BUSINESS ETHICS; GENDER-DIFFERENCES; DECISION-MAKING; CONSUMER ETHICS;
   STUDENTS; PERCEPTIONS; RELIGIOSITY; UNIVERSITY; ATTITUDES; BEHAVIOR
AB This study examined ethical knowledge of accounting faculty in Ghanaian tertiary institutions and assessed the extent to which accounting curricula align with the Professional Values, Ethics, and Attitudes (PVEA) requirements of International Education Standard 4 (IES 4). Motivated by persistent ethical failures within the accounting profession and limited empirical evidence from developing economies, the study adopted a positivist paradigm and cross-sectional survey design. Data were collected from accounting faculty across public tertiary institutions in Ghana during the 2023-2024 academic year, yielding 69 usable responses through a census approach. Descriptive statistics and multiple linear regression were employed for data analysis. The findings revealed that accounting curricula demonstrated approximately 70% alignment with IES 4 requirements and that faculty members possessed high levels of ethical knowledge. Regression results further indicated that religiosity significantly influenced ethical knowledge, whereas sex and age showed no statistically significant effects. The study contributes to accounting education literature by providing one of the first empirical evaluations of faculty ethical knowledge and curriculum alignment with international ethics standards in Ghana. The findings emphasize the importance of value-based orientations, faculty development initiatives, and stronger ethics integration within accounting curricula. These measures can enhance ethical preparedness among future accounting professionals worldwide.

TI Constructivist-teaching and learning practice implementation among
   middle-level school social studies teachers in West Gojjam, Northwest
   Ethiopia
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Constructivist teaching and learning approach; social studies education;
   middle-level schools; teachers' practices; teachers' perceptions
ID ASSIMILATION; EXPERIENCE; EDUCATION; GENDER
AB This study examined social studies teachers' implementation of Constructivist Teaching and Learning Approaches (CTLA) in middle school classrooms in West Gojjam, Northwest Ethiopia. A descriptive survey design was employed, and data were collected from 178 teachers selected through multistage sampling. The data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistical methods. The findings revealed that CTLA implementation was below the expected level (M = 2.90), indicating limited application of CTLA in instruction. Independent samples t-tests showed no statistically significant differences in CTLA practices based on gender, t(176) = 0.712, p > 0.05, d = 0.11 and school location, t(176) = 0.436, p > 0.05, d = 0.05, suggesting these factors did not significantly influence implementation. However, rural teachers showed slightly higher scores in the personal relevance dimension (M = 3.03, SD = 0.56) than urban teachers (M = 2.85, SD = 0.67), t(176) = 1.886, p < 0.05, d = 0.29. Furthermore, a one-way ANOVA revealed a statistically significant difference in the critical voice component across teaching experience levels, F(4, 173) = 3.24, p = 0.010, eta(2) = 0.069, indicating a moderate effect of experience. The study concludes that CTLA implementation is inadequate and recommends strengthening professional development and targeted training to improve teachers' use of constructivist approaches.

TI The role of affective factors in language proficiency: a structural
   equation modeling approach
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Affective factors in language learning; language proficiency; Structural
   Equation Modeling; Anxiety; Motivation; Social Sciences; Education;
   Theory of Education; Educational Psychology; Education - Social
   Sciences; Theories of Learning; Higher Education
ID ANXIETY; MOTIVATION; ENJOYMENT; LEARNERS; SPANISH
AB The procedure of learning a language individually differs, akin to the interfering emotional factors; These interventionist elements may hinder or facilitate learning. Krashen (1982) asserted that language could be acquired through comprehensible input and low affective factors. The main purpose of this paper is to propose a model on the procrastinating relationship between affective factors on one hand and language proficiency on the other, using structural equation modeling. The study was performed on one hundred and fifty university students. The study findings revealed an excellent match between the data and the model, as the Chi-square (CMIN/DF) value is 0.410. Furthermore, the study's Goodness of fit (GFI) value reached 0.995, indicating an excellent fit. The Baseline Comparison revealed a comparative fit index (CFI) 1, surpassing the threshold of 0.95 for an excellent fit. More specifically, the current study has sought to develop and validate a structural equation model explaining the relationship between the affective factors of motivation, anxiety, self-confidence, and attitude in terms of language proficiency among EFL learners. Results indicate that while anxiety negatively impacts proficiency, motivation, and attitude have a positive effect on learners' grammatical knowledge and reading comprehension. It also allows a glimpse into how these emotional variables can be managed to facilitate improvement in language learning outcomes, consequently contributing to both theoretical and pedagogical practices in the EFL context.

TI The correlation of vocabulary size and anxiety on students' foreign
   language speaking proficiency
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Vocabulary size; foreign language anxiety; speaking ability; high
   school; Arts & Humanities; Humanities; Media & Film Studies; Journalism
   & Professional Media; Publishing; Arts; Music; Music & Education; Early
   Years; Social Sciences; Education
AB Effective spoken communication in a foreign language requires both linguistic competence and psychological readiness. However, many high school students struggle with limited vocabulary and anxiety, which may hinder their speaking proficiency. This study aimed to examine the relationship between vocabulary size, foreign language anxiety, and students' speaking ability in English. The participants consisted of 100 tenth-grade students from a senior high school in North Sumatera, Indonesia, selected using the Isaac and Michael table for sampling. The research employed a correlational design, using three instruments: a foreign language classroom anxiety questionnaire, a vocabulary size test, and a speaking performance assessment. Data were analysed using SPSS version 20 for correlation and regression analysis. The findings revealed statistically significant but weak to moderate positive correlations between vocabulary size and speaking ability, and between foreign language anxiety and speaking ability. Additionally, vocabulary size and foreign language anxiety together accounted for approximately 15% of the variance in speaking proficiency. These results suggest that while both vocabulary and anxiety influence speaking performance, other contributing factors should also be explored. The study underscores the importance of vocabulary development and anxiety reduction strategies in enhancing students' oral proficiency in English.

AB BackgroundClinical education occurs formally during educational rounds across various departments and through discussions in small groups within clinical settings. TI The construct validity of the Achievement Emotions Questionnaire and the
   associations of demographic and contextual factors with achievement
   emotions in South African Grade 9 and 10 learners
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Control-value theory; English; high school; learners; mathematics;
   positive and negative achievement emotions; South Africa
ID MEASUREMENT INVARIANCE; ACADEMIC EMOTIONS; STUDENTS EMOTIONS; LEISURE
   BOREDOM; SUBSTANCE USE; ADOLESCENTS; PERFORMANCE; ENJOYMENT; CLASSROOM;

AB This study examined the construct validity of the Achievement Emotions Questionnaire and the associations of demographic and contextual factors with achievement emotions in English and mathematics among Grade 9 and 10 learners. A cross-sectional survey design was used with a sample of 547 learners (n(Grade 9) = 258; n(Grade10) = 226, and n(missing) = 63) in public secondary schools in the Sedibeng District of the Gauteng Province in South Africa. The Achievement Emotions Questionnaire - Language and Achievement Emotions Questionnaire - Mathematics were administered together with a biographical questionnaire containing various socio-demographic questions. Latent variable modelling was used to test the measurement model and the measurement invariance of the questionnaire for Grade 9 and Grade 10 learners. Standard multiple regression analyses were used to investigate the associations between demographic and contextual variables and achievement emotions among these subjects. Confirmatory factor analyses supported a six-factor model of achievement emotions consisting of enjoyment, pride, anger, anxiety, shame, and boredom for mathematics and English. a good fit to the data. Multiple regression analyses showed that language, the ability to focus on schoolwork at home, liking or disliking the mathematics and English teachers, and finding mathematics and English interesting were statistically significantly associated with these positive or negative achievement emotions.

TI Integrating eye-tracking, emotional engagement, and reflection in
   experiential manufacturing systems learning
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Eye-tracking; STEM; undergraduate
ID SCIENCE; ACHIEVEMENT; PERFORMANCE; BOREDOM; IDENTITY; OUTCOMES; PROGRAM
AB Experiential learning can strengthen STEM students' ability to connect theory to practice, yet students vary in how they allocate attention and experience emotions during authentic evaluation tasks. This embedded case study examined cognitive and affective engagement during a manufacturing systems learning sequence grounded in the 5E instructional model and the 5S methodology. Twenty-two engineering technology students completed (1) an observational walk-through of a campus Smart Factory (authentic environment) and (2) an eye-tracking-supported visual simulation using industrial workstation images. We analyzed ocular indicators of visual attention (fixations, saccades, pupil diameter) alongside self-reported achievement emotions (AEQ) and post-activity reflections. Ward's hierarchical clustering (Euclidean distance on standardized features) suggested a two-profile solution, interpreted as a heuristic grouping supported by dendrogram structure and instructional interpretability. Students in Cluster 1 showed shorter completion times, fewer fixations, and larger pupil diameters, paired with higher hope/pride/enjoyment and lower frustration/anxiety. Their reflections emphasized confidence from prior knowledge and interest in applying advanced analytic tools. Cluster 2 showed longer task durations, higher fixation counts, smaller pupil diameters, and lower pride with moderate frustration/anxiety; reflections highlighted uncertainty due to limited exposure time and the need for stronger scaffolding. Findings showcase that experiential designs benefit from aligning cognitive load supports with achievement emotions through pre-briefing, structured prompts, and differentiated guidance, and illustrate how eye-tracking plus reflection can provide actionable feedback for learning design.

TI Sentence complexity in Arab EFL learners' academic writing: a
   qualitative case study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE EFL writing; corrective feedback; syntactic complexity; process
   approach; qualitative case study; EFL writing; corrective feedback;
   syntactic complexity; process approach; qualitative case study
ID WRITTEN CORRECTIVE FEEDBACK; SYNTACTIC COMPLEXITY; 2ND-LANGUAGE;
   ACCURACY; STUDENTS; FLUENCY; SLA
AB This study investigates the syntactic challenges faced by B1-B2 level EFL learners in the Preparatory Year Program (PYP) at a public university in Muscat, Oman. Using a qualitative case study within the process approach to writing, this research examines how students use sentence complexity, clause subordination, clause integration, and text cohesion across multiple drafts of academic essays. The students' perceptions of their syntactic difficulties were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, while a syntactic framework was applied to manually code sentence types, clause integration, and cohesive devices across multiple drafts. Findings indicate that EFL learners primarily rely on simple sentence structures, as complex clauses are challenging to implement, and they often feel anxious and unprepared to respond to feedback from their peers and teachers. The findings also suggest the importance of explicit grammar instruction and metalinguistic awareness in the EFL context. The pedagogical implications are particularly useful in enhancing writing instruction in similar educational settings in the Gulf region.

TI AI-assisted case-based learning and flipped classroom to improve
   clinical decision-making: a randomized controlled trial in reproductive
   medicine
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Assisted reproductive medicine; artificial intelligence; case-based
   learning; flipped classroom; clinical decision-making; resident training
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; EDUCATION
AB BackgroundEfficient training of reproductive medicine clinicians is critical in the context of declining global fertility and increasing infertility. Traditional lecture-based instruction often fails to sufficiently develop clinical decision-making skills within limited residency rotations. Innovative strategies that integrate artificial intelligence (AI) with case-based learning (CBL) and flipped classroom (FC) formats may enhance clinical reasoning, however rigorous evidence in reproductive medicine education remains limited.MethodsWe conducted a randomized controlled trial involving 50 obstetrics and gynecology residents at the First Hospital of Jilin University. Participants were randomly assigned to an AI-assisted CBL+FC group or a traditional lecture control group. The AI-assisted CBL+FC group completed pre-class interactive case work with virtual standardized patients on the DoctorU platform and case analyses on the Superstar Learning platform, followed by interactive in-class discussions. Primary outcomes included post-course theoretical knowledge tests, Mini-Clinical Evaluation Exercise (Mini-CEX), and Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) scores. Secondary outcomes assessed learner motivation, clinical thinking, self-directed learning, and perceived course effectiveness using a 5-point Likert scale.ResultsBaseline characteristics were comparable between groups. After the intervention, the AI-assisted CBL+FC group achieved significantly higher theoretical test scores than the control group. The AI-assisted CBL+FC group also demonstrated superior overall clinical competence in Mini-CEX assessments and higher OSCE total scores. Participants in the AI-assisted CBL+FC group reported greater improvements in learning motivation, clinical reasoning, self-directed learning, and perceived course effectiveness.ConclusionsThe AI-assisted CBL+FC instructional model significantly enhances theoretical knowledge, clinical decision-making skills, and learner engagement among reproductive medicine residents. This blended learning model offers an efficacious and generalizable methodology for training practitioners to address the evolving clinical requirements within contemporary fertility care.

TI Discursive colonialism in Nigeria's environmental education: a critical
   discourse analysis
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Environmental education; critical discourse analysis; postcolonial
   theory; Indigenous knowledges; curriculum reform; decolonising pedagogy;
   Social Sciences; Education; Classroom Practice; Assessment & Testing;
   Teaching & Learning
AB This study investigates how colonial discourses persist in environmental education in Nigeria through the marginalisation of Indigenous knowledge systems. Drawing on postcolonial theory, particularly orientalism, subalternity and epistemic violence, the study employs a qualitative design integrating critical discourse analysis (CDA), interpretive phenomenological analysis (IPA) and participatory action research (PAR). CDA, guided by Fairclough's framework, was used to analyse curriculum documents, textbooks and lesson plans, while IPA informed the interpretation of teachers' experiences derived from interviews, classroom observations and PAR focus group discussions. The findings reveal that environmental education content remains dominated by Western epistemologies, with limited representation of Nigerian environments and Indigenous knowledge. Pedagogical practices further reinforce passive learning, privileging rote memorisation over critical engagement and action. These dynamics sustain discursive colonialism by positioning Western knowledge as authoritative and Indigenous perspectives as peripheral or absent. The study concludes that meaningful transformation requires the integration of Indigenous knowledge systems and critical, context-responsive pedagogies. Implications include the need for curriculum reform, teacher professional development, and policy shifts that support place-based, participatory and critically engaged environmental education.

TI Teachers' perceptions of the use of authentic materials in English as a
   foreign language classrooms
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Authentic materials; teachers' perception; ELT; EFL; secondary school;
   Education; Secondary Education; By Subject; English; Arts & Humanities;
   Language & Literature; Language Teaching & Learning; Languages of
   Western Europe
ID IMPACT; TASKS
AB The use of authentic materials increases exposure for target learners in foreign-language classroom contexts. However, little is known about how teachers perceive the use of authentic materials in English as a foreign language (EFL) context, such as classrooms in Tanzanian secondary schools. This qualitative case study research explored teachers' perceptions of the use of authentic materials in EFL. The study was conducted in the Kilimanjaro region of Tanzania, specifically in the Moshi District Council. It involved five public lower secondary schools to represent the context in which most secondary school students in Tanzania learn EFL. Specifically, the study involved 20 teachers teaching the English language subject, from Form One to Four. Data were generated through in-depth semi-structured interviews. The findings revealed that teachers had positive perceptions of the use of authentic materials, as they enhance students' understanding of the subject matter, long-term memory retention, linking the classroom to the real world, and motivation to learn. It also reports on challenges such as a lack of institutional support and inadequate training for EFL teachers. The findings have implications for improving English language teaching, teacher training and instructional practices in the country.

TI Divergent assessment practices in international joint education
   programmes in higher education: a case study of cross-cultural
   challenges
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Transnational education; higher education; joint degree; cultural
   difference; assessment
ID EXPERIENCE; CHINA
AB This study examines divergent assessment practices in international joint higher education programmes (IJEPs) through a case study of a collaborative initiative between universities in the UK and China. While IJEPs offer significant benefits, including enriched cross-cultural learning experiences, they also pose unique challenges, particularly in aligning assessment frameworks across institutions. This case study reports the content of two university meetings concerning differing cultural expectations in assessment practices. It highlights an issue: students assessed in China consistently receive higher marks than their United Kingdom (UK)-based counterparts, raising questions about grade inflation and cultural differences. The findings suggest that these discrepancies are influenced by cultural and institutional factors, including China's emphasis on developing self-efficacy and recognising effort, rooted in Confucian educational values. Contrastingly, UK institutions often prioritise performance-based evaluations. This misalignment reflects broader systemic differences in pedagogical and policy approaches between the two countries. Addressing these challenges requires developing co-designed assessment frameworks that respect cultural nuances while ensuring fairness and consistency across partner institutions. By examining the underlying causes of these assessment disparities, this research contributes to the limited literature on cross-cultural pedagogical challenges in IJEPs. It calls for greater collaboration and mutual understanding to enhance the operational integrity of such programmes. Impact statement This study reveals significant grading disparities in UK-China international joint higher education programmes, where students assessed in China consistently receive higher marks due to cultural differences rooted in Confucian emphasis on effort and self-efficacy versus UK performance-based standards. By highlighting these challenges, the research underscores the need for co-designed assessment frameworks that respect cultural nuances while ensuring fairness, consistency, and academic integrity in transnational education.

TI Gender inequality in Italian higher education: a comparative analysis of
   two Italian universities
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gender inequality; higher education; Italy; regional disparities;
   critical discourse analysis; feminist institutionalism; Gender Equality
   Plans
ID EQUALITY; RACE; END
AB This article examines how Italian universities conceptualise and address gender inequality, focusing on regional disparities and institutional discourse. Addressing a gap in the literature on how gender equality policies are discursively constructed and operationalised within national contexts, the study compares the University of Turin and the University of Palermo, selected as contrasting cases within Italy's North-South divide. Using Fairclough's model of Critical Discourse Analysis, integrated with MacKinnon's feminist theory of the state and feminist institutionalism, the article analyses institutional policy documents, including Gender Equality Plans and Codes of Conduct, alongside quantitative indicators of gender inequality (2021-2025). Institutional documents are treated as primary empirical material, enabling an examination of how gender equality is constructed at the discursive level and how these constructions relate to observable patterns of inequality. The findings show that both universities frame gender equality through predominantly symbolic and compliance-driven approaches, but with distinct patterns: Palermo's discourse reflects a legalistic and reactive model shaped by weaker institutional and regional infrastructures, while Turin exhibits a form of managerial formalism characterised by procedural commitment but limited structural engagement at the departmental level. Overall, gender policies remain largely performative rather than transformative, revealing a misalignment between discursive commitments and persistent patterns of horizontal and vertical segregation. The analysis demonstrates that institutional discourse not only reflects but contributes to the reproduction of gendered power relations in higher education, highlighting the limits of current policy approaches and the importance of context-sensitive, structurally oriented interventions.

TI Digital literacy and learning motivation as determinants of ICT
   integration: challenges and opportunities for university students in
   Pakistan
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital literacy; learning motivation; ICT integration; academic
   performance; Pakistan higher education; Digital literacy; learning
   motivation; ICT integration; academic performance; Pakistan higher
   education
ID ADOPTION; INFORMATION; TECHNOLOGY; ACCEPTANCE
AB In Pakistan's evolving higher education landscape, the integration of information and communication technology (ICT) plays a vital role in promoting student engagement and academic success. However, the extent to which students' digital literacy and learning motivation shape this integration remains underexplored. This study investigates how digital literacy and learning motivation influence ICT integration, adopting the technology acceptance model and self-determination theory as the guiding framework. Using a cross-sectional survey of 450 undergraduate students from nine campuses of a public university, data were analyzed through partial least squares-structural equation modeling with 5,000 bootstrapped resamples. The results revealed that ICT use significantly enhances students' academic performance, learning motivation, and digital literacy (beta = 0.335, p < .001). Both learning motivation (beta = 0.208, p < .001) and digital literacy (beta = 0.211, p < .001) were strong predictors of academic performance, while their indirect effects (beta = 0.071 and beta = 0.113,) confirmed their mediating roles. These findings highlight that the effective integration of ICT extends beyond technological access, requiring pedagogical support and motivational engagement. The study contributes to the growing body of evidence from developing contexts by emphasizing that equitable ICT integration depends on addressing digital inequities, fostering digital competence, and embedding motivation-oriented learning practices within higher education curricula.

TI Relationships and predictive roles of self-regulated learning strategy
   use and grit in vocabulary learning among EFL learners
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE EFL learners; grit; self-regulated learning strategy use; vocabulary
   learning; predictive relationships; EFL learners; grit; self-regulated
   learning strategy use; vocabulary learning; predictive relationships
ID ENGLISH; KNOWLEDGE; EDUCATION; POLICY; TASK
AB EFL learners often face challenges in acquiring vocabulary both in the short and long term. To address this issue, the present study examined the relationships among self-regulated learning strategy use, grit, and vocabulary learning in a sample of Iranian EFL learners. A correlational research design was employed with 147 undergraduate English majors from several universities in Semnan Province, Iran, selected via convenience sampling. The Oxford Quick Placement Test ensured participant homogeneity. Three additional instruments were utilized: the Self-Regulation Capacity in Vocabulary Learning Scale, the Language-Domain-Specific Grit Scale, and the academic section of the Vocabulary Levels Test. Results revealed a strong association between the use of self-regulated learning strategies and vocabulary learning success. Moreover, a strong correlation was found between self-regulated learning strategies and grit, while grit demonstrated a moderate correlation with vocabulary learning. Further analyses indicated that self-regulated learning strategy use is a significant predictor of vocabulary acquisition. These findings offer important implications for curriculum developers, policymakers, educators, and EFL learners.

TI Educational inequality in fragile states: tackling barriers to SDG 4 in
   Somalia
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Somalia; school participation; education inequality; food insecurity;
   remittances; fragile states; Social Sciences; Education; Education
   Policy & Politics; Education Policy; Curriculum; Philosophy of
   Education; Moral & Values Education; Primary/Elementary Education; By
   Subject; Geography; SDG 4: Quality education
AB This study examines the determinants of school participation among 18,212 children aged 6-18 years using nationally representative microdata from the 2022 Somalia Integrated Household Budget Survey (SIHBS). Guided by human capital and capability perspectives and a resilience lens on fragility, we estimate linear probability models and logit models for the full sample and for subgroups defined by gender, age cohort, settlement type, displacement status, food security, remittance receipt, and federal member state of residence. The results show that girls, nomadic children, internally displaced children, and those in food-insecure households face pronounced attendance penalties, with the largest gaps in Hirshabelle, Jubaland, and Southwest states. Remittances are positively associated with participation and partially buffer the negative effects of food insecurity and displacement but do not fully offset structural exclusion. These findings highlight the intersecting nature of educational disadvantage in fragile settings and demonstrate how household resilience factors interact with institutional constraints. The paper concludes with concrete policy priorities for SDG 4 in Somalia, including gender-responsive interventions, targeted support for displaced and nomadic children, and integration of education, social protection, and food assistance in the most deprived regions.

TI Do student and tutor expectations align? Comparing perceptions of
   undergraduate students and tutors
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Ideal student; ideal tutor; professional qualities; teaching style;
   personal qualities
AB How do HE tutors and students perceive what an 'ideal' student or tutor is? Their perceptions feed into and are indicative of expectations, experiences and, ultimately, outcomes in HE. Guided by Weber's theory of ideal types, this explorative study utilised surveys and focus group discussions to gather insights from 69 students and eight tutors, drawn from the same department within a UK HE institution. All participants were asked about their understanding of 'ideal' students and tutors. Comparative analysis revealed that students held higher expectations of themselves than did tutors. These 'ideal' aspirations pertained both in and outside the classroom and were expressed through general characteristics as well as academic prowess. Tutors perceived that an ideal tutor strongly related to their professional qualities and teaching styles, although students laid more emphasis on tutors' personal qualities rather than professional. Awareness of both alignments and mismatches in student and tutor perceptions of the 'ideal' helps to bring greater understanding to the teaching/learning relationship.

TI Perspectives of Taiwanese high school physical Education teachers and
   scholars on the integration of physical literacy into physical Education
   curriculum
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teaching practices; teacher perception; differences in understanding;
   continuous professional development; teaching practice
AB This exploratory qualitative study investigates how Taiwanese senior high school physical education (PE) teachers and university-based scholars conceptualize and enact physical literacy within the context of competency-based curriculum reform. Adopting a single-case embedded design, the study involved semi-structured interviews with seven high school PE teachers and three teacher-educators purposively selected for their involvement in curriculum reform. Follow-up interviews were conducted with selected participants to clarify analytically significant areas of convergence and divergence. Data were analyzed through iterative thematic analysis, incorporating both inductive coding and theoretically sensitized interpretation. Findings reveal shared endorsement of competency-based and student-centered approaches, yet persistent tensions regarding the role of foundational motor skills, student autonomy, and assessment reform. Teachers tended to prioritize skill competence and pragmatic feasibility under structural constraints, whereas scholars foregrounded holistic development, motivation, and lifelong engagement. Interpreted through curriculum implementation theory and professional knowledge frameworks, these divergences appear less as ideological opposition and more as layered interpretations shaped by positional responsibility and institutional context. Given the small, purposively selected sample within a specific reform setting, the findings provide exploratory insight into mechanisms shaping physical literacy integration in Taiwan, rather than evidence of national implementation patterns.

TI Exploring the relations between higher education teachers' state and
   trait emotions - a multi-method approach
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Higher education; teacher emotions; longitudinal study; experience
   sampling
ID ACHIEVEMENT; ANXIETY
AB This study examines the relationship between trait-level teaching emotions and state-level emotional experiences of higher education (HE) teachers before and after teaching situations. Data from 59 teachers across seven Finnish research and applied universities were collected using: 1) experience sampling via a smartphone app to assess momentary emotional valence and arousal before and after teaching (185 teaching situations), and 2) an online survey measuring trait-level enjoyment, anger, and anxiety. Results showed that teachers reported more positive state emotions than negative ones both before and after teaching situations. Emotional arousal shifted from predominantly activating emotions before teaching to deactivating emotions afterwards. Trait-level teaching enjoyment was positively associated with state-level emotional valence before teaching situations and with emotional arousal after teaching situations. Trait-level teaching-related anxiety showed a negative relationship with state-level emotional valence before teaching situations, while trait-level teaching-related anger was not related to state-level emotional valence or arousal. This study adds to the expanding research on HE teachers' emotions by emphasising the intricate relationship between trait emotions and state emotions. The results highlight the need to account for both the stability and variability of emotional experiences in HE teaching environments.

TI Development of an online sleep education program for university
   students: a Co-design approach
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Higher education; health education; participatory research; co-design;
   sleep health
ID COLLEGE-STUDENTS; QUALITY
AB Poor sleep is common among university students, with substantial implications for health, well-being, and academic performance. While digital health interventions show promise, many are insufficiently tailored to the students' specific needs and preferences. This study describes the multistage development and feasibility testing of an online sleep education program for university students using a participatory co-design approach. The development process comprised six stages across pre-design, co-design and post-design phases, combining qualitative interviews, World Caf & eacute; workshops, iterative feedback loops, and feasibility testing. Students, researchers, and teaching experts were actively involved to ensure content relevance, usability, and acceptability. Interviews revealed a demand for practical, actionable strategies to improve sleep and highlighted barriers such as time constraints and irregular routines. World Caf & eacute; workshops emphasized concise and engaging formats, leading to the integration of podcasts, videos, and interactive elements. The core development team iteratively structured modules and refined content. Feasibility testing showed high acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility of the program. The program offers a scalable, user-centred approach to promote sleep health among university students. This study advances the evidence on participatory design in sleep health education by identifying key design principles and student perspectives that can inform the development of a student-centered sleep education program in higher education.
