TI Measuring AI literacy in medical students: scale development and
   validation within a self-determination theory framework
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; literacy; medical education; self-determination
   theory (SDT); structural equation modeling (SEM)
ID MISSING DATA; SAMPLE-SIZE; MOTIVATION; AUTONOMY; GUIDE
AB Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly important in healthcare. It is therefore crucial that today's medical students have certain basic AI skills that enable them to use AI applications successfully. These basic skills are often referred to as "AI literacy". Previous research projects that aimed to investigate medical students' AI literacy and attitudes towards AI have not used reliable and validated assessment instruments. Methods We used two validated self-assessment scales to measure AI literacy (31 Likert-type items) and attitudes towards AI (5 Likert-type items) at two German medical schools. The scales were distributed to the medical students through an online questionnaire. The final sample consisted of a total of 377 medical students. We conducted a confirmatory factor analysis and calculated the internal consistency of the scales to check whether the scales were sufficiently reliable to be used in our sample. In addition, we calculated t-tests to determine group differences and Pearson's and Kendall's correlation coefficients to examine associations between individual variables. Results The model fit and internal consistency of the scales were satisfactory. Within the concept of AI literacy, we found that medical students at both medical schools rated their technical understanding of AI significantly lower (M-MS1 = 2.85 and M-MS2 = 2.50) than their ability to critically appraise (M-MS1 = 4.99 and M-MS2 = 4.83) or practically use AI (M-MS1 = 4.52 and M-MS2 = 4.32), which reveals a discrepancy of skills. In addition, female medical students rated their overall AI literacy significantly lower than male medical students, t(217.96) = -3.65, p <.001. Students in both samples seemed to be more accepting of AI than fearful of the technology, t(745.42) = 11.72, p <.001. Furthermore, we discovered a strong positive correlation between AI literacy and positive attitudes towards AI and a weak negative correlation between AI literacy and negative attitudes. Finally, we found that prior AI education and interest in AI is positively correlated with medical students' AI literacy. Conclusions Courses to increase the AI literacy of medical students should focus more on technical aspects. There also appears to be a correlation between AI literacy and attitudes towards AI, which should be considered when planning AI courses.

TI Leveraging near-peer teaching: the impact of cognitive and social
   congruence on naloxone training
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Naloxone; opioids; near-peer teaching; cognitive congruence; social
   congruence
ID INTERPROFESSIONAL EDUCATION
AB Background: Equipping future clinicians to recognize and reverse opioid overdoses requires experiential training and access to naloxone. Near-peer instruction may leverage cognitive and social congruence to enhance learning compared with traditional faculty-led models. This study evaluated whether near-peer teaching yields superior knowledge gains and attitudes in a naloxone training workshop. Methods: Preclinical medical students completed a 60-minute session comprising a high-fidelity inpatient opioid overdose simulation and hands-on naloxone administration practice. Immediately pre-and post-workshop, participants completed the Opioid Overdose Knowledge Scale (OOKS) and Opioid Overdose Attitudes Scale (OOAS). We compared near-peer-led versus faculty-led sessions using descriptive statistics and independent t-tests. Using an explanatory sequential design, 10 students completed semi-structured interviews exploring preferences for near-peer teaching. Interviews were transcribed and analyzed using grounded theory, applying the concepts of cognitive and social congruence as an analytical lens. Results: From 2019 to 2022, 537 students attended the workshop, and 288 students provided complete survey data. Near-peer facilitation was associated with higher OOKS scores (84.5% +/- 0.09 vs 80.2% +/- 0.10 correct; p < 0.001) and more favorable OOAS totals (105.5 +/- 8.4 vs 102.4 +/- 13.7; p = 0.02) compared with faculty-led sessions. Interviewees highlighted a shared knowledge framework, familiar language/explanations, and understanding of learning challenges. Additionally, interviewees noted informal communication, reduced anxiety, and interest in near-peer students' experiences. Conclusion: A brief, near-peer-led overdose simulation and naloxone skills workshop was associated with an improvement in medical students' knowledge and attitudes compared to faculty-led delivery. Integrating trained near-peer educators into pre-clinical curricula may accelerate acquisition of overdose recognition and response skills while promoting clinical readiness. Programs seeking scalable strategies to expand skill-based, practical competencies should consider near-peer models that benefit from students' diverse prior experiences.

TI Mind the gap: pre-service elementary teachers' application of
   mathematics error analysis
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pre-service elementary teachers; mathematical errors; error analysis
ID CONTENT KNOWLEDGE
AB This mixed-methods study examines how pre-service teachers in a dual certification elementary and special education program apply error analysis in mathematics. Guided by Shulman's pedagogical content knowledge (PCK) framework, researchers examined strengths and challenges in participants' ability to identify, categorize, and describe mathematical errors and determine appropriate instructional supports for remediation. Participants (N = 32) in the third and fourth year of their program examined work samples in two rounds of data collection: a survey, and focus group interviews. Results show participants recognized the value of error analysis as a means of supporting student learning. However, survey results showed they had difficulty describing errors, highlighting challenges in applying their mathematical content knowledge. Findings suggest the need for teacher preparation programs to explicitly focus on error analysis, building both conceptual and pedagogical understandings to foster the ability to recognize the instructional needs of teacher candidates' future students. Specific recommendations include designing coursework that connects pedagogical and content knowledge, directly teaching an error analysis protocol, and providing explicit opportunities for practice, including discussion and reflection to build pre-service teacher competencies and confidence.

TI The role of self-efficacy dimensions on organisational commitment: a
   study of academic staff in Ugandan universities
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-efficacy; organisational commitment; academic staff; universities;
   Uganda
AB While self-efficacy is widely recognized as a predictor of organizational commitment (OC), existing literature mainly treats it as a single-dimensional construct, which conceals the specific roles of its underlying sources. Drawing on Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), this study fills this gap by breaking down self-efficacy into four theoretically based dimensions of enactive mastery, vicarious experiences, verbal persuasion, and physiological arousal. The study investigates how each dimension independently affects OC among academic staff in Ugandan public and private universities. Using a cross-sectional survey, data were gathered from 574 faculty members and analyzed through hierarchical regression in SPSS v27. Results show that all four self-efficacy dimensions significantly influence OC, collectively accounting for 14.6% of its variance. Although the modest explanatory power reflects the complex nature of OC, the findings provide a detailed, contextually relevant advancement beyond global self-efficacy models. This research extends SCT by validating its dimensional structure in a non-Western higher education setting. Practically, it provides practical levers for university leaders in resource-limited settings to increase staff retention through targeted interventions in mentoring, feedback, professional development, and well-being support. Finally, the findings of this study helps develop more accurate, culturally responsive strategies for improving OC in African higher education.

TI A quasi-experimental study of lab rotation integrated with generative AI
   and peer code review model to enhance students' critical thinking and
   academic resilience in introductory programming
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Lab rotation; generative artificial intelligent; peer code review;
   critical thinking; academic resilience; introductory programming
AB Lab rotation provides a dynamic and interactive learning environment; generative artificial intelligence can help novices overcome learning challenges; and peer code review offers a collaborative learning environment. This study investigates how incorporating these designs into a new instructional model can enhance students' critical thinking and academic resilience. A total of 83 first-year college students participated in the experiment, which lasted 6 weeks. The students were from two classes, majored in Educational Technology, and were enrolled in an introductory programming course titled 'C Programming'. Class 1 was randomly selected as the control group and Class 2 as the experimental group. The experimental group and the control group were taught by the same teacher. The control group employed the traditional programming teaching method, whereas the experimental group utilized a new instructional model comprising four learning stations: instruction, lab, teacher-led, and review stations. All participants took a critical thinking test and an academic resilience questionnaire before and after the experiment. The results showed no significant difference in critical thinking and academic resilience between the pretest groups. In contrast, the post-test results showed that the experimental group's critical thinking and academic resilience significantly outperformed those of the control group. The findings highlight the effectiveness of the instructional model on students' critical thinking and academic resilience. This study is the first to integrate lab rotation, generative artificial intelligence, and peer code review into the design of a new instructional model for introductory programming and to demonstrate its effectiveness in enhancing students' critical thinking and academic resilience. This study can serve as a reference for future studies.

TI Cognitive engagement with feedback in L2 writing: Interactions with
   diverse feedback sources among Chinese undergraduate English majors
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AWE feedback; peer feedback; teacher feedback; cognitive engagement with
   feedback; L2 writing
ID WRITTEN-CORRECTIVE-FEEDBACK; STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; TEACHER
AB Undeniably, feedback can improve second language (L2) writing among undergraduate learners. It is cognitive engagement that leads learners to actively understand and internalize feedback, which is crucial to learners' writing development. Yet, studies focusing on cognitive engagement with feedback alone remain relatively scarce. It is important to determine how learners cognitively engage with diverse feedback sources, including automated writing evaluation (AWE), peer and teacher feedback, to better support them in writing. Therefore, this study has explored the cognitive engagement of three participants with these three feedback sources in a writing task. However, the uniqueness of this study was also the use of multiple data sources, including writing texts, received feedback, interviews, and reflective journals, all of which were thematically analyzed and integrated to determine the results. The results revealed that participants showed significant individual differences throughout the three rounds of feedback revisions and that their cognitive engagement increased progressively with each additional round. While teacher feedback facilitated deep cognitive processing, participants used meta-cognitive strategies more frequently in AWE and peer feedback. More importantly, AWE feedback seems to be more effective when combined with peer and teacher feedback, not only in addressing surface-level concerns, but also in promoting deeper cognitive engagement. In conclusion, aside from enriching the research on feedback effects on L2 writing, the study has provided support that the use of AWE and peer feedback together with teacher feedback improves learners' cognitive engagement with feedback.

AB This paper examines secondary school students' experiences with Team-Based Learning (TBL) in Ireland, Spain, and the UK. In TBL, an active learning method, students work in small teams on collaborative, applied exercises. The Erasmus-funded TALENT Project trained 23 secondary teachers in Fundamentals of TBL. Two hundred forty-seven of their students completed a survey about their TBL experiences. Most (71%) preferred TBL to traditional lectures, though some disliked how others' performance could affect individual grades. Positive responses indicate benefits of TBL in secondary education including: (1) increased student engagement and active participation; (2) enhanced quality of learning, including critical thinking and content comprehension; and (3) increased skills development through collaborative learning activities. These findings align with existing research on TBL in higher education and early studies in secondary education. The authors recommend further research and promotion of TBL in secondary education due to its benefits for student engagement, learning quality, and skills development.

TI Patterson and Kehoe's historical case for understanding
   science-technology-society and social Justice
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Education; controversies; justice; technology; socio-scientific issues
ID NATURAL LEAD ENVIRONMENTS; POLLUTION
AB This paper presents a didactic proposal focused on a possibility for critically understanding the relationships between Science, Technology, and Society (STS) from a Social Justice perspective. The study was implemented in secondary school chemistry with 10th-grade students (13-14 years old) in the Colombian context. The topic addressed the historical controversy between Calir Patterson and Robert Kehoe regarding the distinction between Natural and Typical regarding lead concentrations in the environment. This controversy highlighted fundamental questions about how science defines environmental safety standards and whose interests those definitions serve. Methodologically, we resorted to Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) and the qualitative tool called 'Epistemic Networks (ENA)', using content analysis techniques and semi-structured interviews. From the evaluation of the didactic proposal, the pedagogical value of the historical case analyzed was highlighted, emphasizing the importance of recognizing the political dimension of science education. The purpose of this work is to demonstrate how the explicit and reflexive use of the history of science shows that it puts students in a participatory attitude, since it involves knowledge of history, sociology and philosophy of science and technology in the analysis of phenomena and their implications and applications both social and personal in students.

TI Smartwatches as tools for emotion regulation in higher education:
   evidence from an action research project
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Smartwatches; emotion regulation; self-regulated learning; bio-feedback
ID MOTIVATION; BEHAVIOR
AB Digital technologies are increasingly integrated into higher education, yet the role of wearable devices in supporting learning remains underexplored. This study investigates how students in higher education use smartwatches as tools for emotion regulation in their study practices. Drawing on Gross's model of emotion regulation, we conducted an action research study with a group of nine university students combining smartwatch biofeedback with reflective diaries to examine how they interpreted and applied physiological data in their study practices. We found that smartwatch feedback acted as a real-time cue for reflection enabling students to implement both proactive and reactive strategies. Three themes emerged: (1) using smartwatches to promote general well-being, (2) organizing study sessions, and (3) maintaining focus during study sessions. While the students found that strategies aimed at promoting wellbeing and organizing study sessions were relatively straightforward, and yielded immediate benefits, focus-oriented strategies such as distraction management and mindfulness proved more challenging and elicited complex emotions. The study contributes to higher education research by highlighting the potential of smartwatches as scaffolds for emotion regulation and self-regulated learning, while also addressing the limitations of purely data-driven approaches in understanding students' behaviour.

TI Assessing the efficacy of the direct method against the
   grammar-translation method of language teaching in interdisciplinary
   contexts through a sociolinguistic lens
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Direct/natural method; interdisciplinary context; oral communication
   skill; sociolinguistic lens; Language Teaching Methodologies
AB Language-teaching methodologies have always posed a significant challenge for teachers and learners, particularly in teaching a second language. The interdisciplinary context provided to students in academic institutions has created a methodological issue in the pedagogy of both content subjects and language subjects. In interdisciplinary contexts, stimulating the Direct/Natural Method of language teaching as an appropriate teaching methodology for language learners can be a stepping stone, because several studies in this regard have produced very fruitful results in adopting this method in the said context, identifying the reliable measures against other methods, especially the GT method, in a quantifiable way. The sociolinguistic background of learners provides a strong indicator for adopting the direct method in language classrooms, as it can serve as a research tool for their socio-demographic identity. This study employs the Direct/Natural Method as an appropriate approach to develop oral communication skills by measuring the inclination of responses from 113 students across 26 departments of study at the faculties of Aligarh Muslim University, and by comparing the key characteristic features of the Direct method with those of the GT method. Comparing the two methods suggested a preference for the Direct method over the GT method. Impact statement This study is significant because it contributes to the growing body of research on effective language-teaching methodologies, particularly in the context of English as a second language in higher education. By comparing the Direct Method with the Grammar-Translation Method, the study provides empirical evidence that communicative and interaction-based teaching approaches are more effective in developing oral communication skills among undergraduate learners. The study is especially important in interdisciplinary academic contexts, where students require strong English communication skills for academic, professional, and social purposes. Its findings highlight the importance of intensive oral interaction, conversational practice, and target-language use in enhancing communicative competence. Another major contribution of this study lies in its sociolinguistic perspective. By examining factors such as gender and place of residence (urban/rural), the research demonstrates that students' positive attitudes toward the Direct Method are consistent across different socio-demographic groups. This suggests that the Direct Method can be effectively applied in diverse educational settings. Furthermore, the study offers practical implications for teachers, curriculum designers, and policymakers. It supports the integration of communicative and learner-centered methodologies into English language classrooms, particularly in Indian universities where traditional Grammar-Translation practices still dominate. The findings may also encourage institutions to adopt teaching strategies that promote fluency, confidence, and willingness to communicate in English. Finally, the study fills an important research gap by providing context-specific evidence from Aligarh Muslim University and contributes to contemporary discussions in Second Language Acquisition, communicative language teaching, and sociolinguistics.

SO COGENT EDUCATION

AB This study investigates stakeholders' perceptions of the role of secondary school agriculture students in enhancing household food security. Despite extensive research on agricultural education and skills development, limited studies have explored how stakeholders perceive students' specific roles as learners, innovators, trainers, informants and implementers of food security policy. Using descriptive and correlational designs, data were collected from 376 students, 111 agriculture teachers and 323 parents. TI 'Individual strengths, collective power!', a teacher-driven proof of
   concept for strengths-based education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Proof of concept; positive interdependence; classroom climate; character
   strengths; strengths-based program
AB This proof-of-concept study evaluated the relevance and applicability of 'Individual Strengths, Collective Power!', a character strengths-based program designed to improve classroom climate in inclusive Swiss schools. Inspired by the 'Awesome Us!' program, it incorporates five key steps: building shared language, recognizing others' strengths, identifying own strengths, practicing strengths, and recognizing collective strengths. A simplified version was implemented in three classes of 9-12-year-olds over five weeks, with teachers using it thrice weekly. Students were assessed using the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) and a questionnaire survey, while teachers participated in a focus group. Results showed high interest in character strengths among students and teachers. Students' positive affect increased significantly throughout the program. Both students and teachers provided positive feedback on the activities' pedagogical quality, with students finding them engaging. Suggestions for improvement included clearer instructions and visual supports. The material proved relevant and applicable to the Swiss school context, indicating potential for larger-scale implementation. The study highlights the promise of strengths-based interventions in Swiss inclusive education and emphasizes the need for cultural and contextual adaptability. Limitations include a small sample size and potential subjectivity in data interpretation. Future research should evaluate the program's efficacy on classroom climate and student relationships.

AB In an era of overlapping environmental, social, economic, and political crises, a proliferation of food-related programs has emerged at universities across the globe. TI Evaluating a targeted educational intervention to promote high-value,
   cost-conscious care among medical students
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE High-value care; cost-conscious care; value-based care; medical
   education; curriculum development
AB Rising healthcare costs in the United States, with estimates suggesting up to 25% of spending is wasteful, have created an urgent need for cost-conscious, value-based care (VBC). VBC aims to improve patient outcomes relative to costs, yet its integration into medical education remains inconsistent, leaving future physicians underprepared for cost-sensitive practice. Early exposure to VBC principles can promote resource stewardship and reduce unnecessary interventions, yet few studies have rigorously evaluated structured educational interventions for medical students. This study examined the effectiveness of a single one-hour educational intervention on high-value, cost-conscious care (HVCCC) in improving pre-clerkship students' attitudes, confidence, and preparedness to apply VBC concepts in clinical practice. Pre-clerkship students (Class of 2027, Medical College of Georgia) completed pre- and post-lecture surveys using the validated Maastricht HVCCC Attitude Questionnaire (MHAQ), which measures three domains: Provision of High-Value Care, Integration of Costs, and Perceived Drawbacks. Additional items assessed self-efficacy and communication confidence regarding cost-related discussions. Paired t-tests compared pre- and post-intervention responses. Of the 85 students who participated, 78 provided paired responses for MHAQ items, while all 85 completed the additional non-MHAQ survey items. Following the lecture, total MHAQ scores increased significantly (mean 70.48 to 72.31; p < 0.001), indicating a more favorable overall attitude toward HVCCC. Both the Provision of High-Value Care and Integration of Costs domains improved significantly (p < 0.001 for each), while Perceived Drawbacks decreased (p = 0.019), suggesting reduced concerns about the negative consequences of HVCCC. Students also demonstrated gains in self-efficacy: confidence discussing cost-conscious care increased by 28-30 percentage points across communication settings, and 90.6% agreed they felt better equipped to initiate VBC conversations. A brief, structured HVCCC lecture improved medical students' attitudes, confidence, and preparedness for value-based practice. Integrating targeted VBC education early in training may foster sustainable, cost-conscious, and patient-centered care.

TI How do college students weigh the reliability of AI in academic writing?
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-assisted writing; article summarisation; AI-based proofreading;
   citation management; AI plagiarism; digital lingua franca
AB This study examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in academic writing - with particular attention to article summarisation, proofreading, citation management and plagiarism detection - and explores how AI can enhance reading comprehension as well as future trends in AI-assisted writing in higher education. A mixed-methods approach was used with a survey of 405 participants from higher education institutions in the Gulf region. The quantitative data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. AI-assisted summarisation was found to significantly enhance reading comprehension, and AI-driven proofreading was found to enhance the quality of paraphrasing. Effective paraphrasing also contributed to robust plagiarism detection mechanisms, thus strengthening academic integrity. However, AI citation management had a limited influence on writing development, reflecting continued reliance on conventional tools, but AI-powered presentation design appears to be exerting an effect on future writing trends by improving data visualisation and knowledge dissemination. We propose a solution-oriented algorithm for AI integration based on academic level, technical proficiency, learning style, institution type, AI policy orientation and teaching assessment methodologies.

TI Exploring linguistic inequalities through Global Englishes in US higher
   education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Global Englishes; higher education; linguistic inequalities; United
   States; language ideologies; African American
ID WORLD ENGLISHES; LANGUAGE; IDEOLOGIES; ATTITUDES; DIVERSITY
AB US higher education has been through a long-standing dominance of white mainstream English (WME), creating systematic linguistic inequalities for students who do not use WME, such as African American students (AAS). This demands an inclusive instructional approach. While Global Englishes (GE) embraces diversity in instructional policies and practices and acknowledges GE in language education, it may offer inclusive pedagogical practices in US higher education. Although GE-informed teacher-student research has gained a momentum in language education, there is a lack of research on exploring the ideologies of African American students, a marginalized population, in US. However, participants reported that "standard" English ideology that advocates for WME over other varieties of English, is predominantly used for instruction. Such "standard" English ideologies create linguistic inequalities by granting greater power and prestige to one language variety compared to others within the classroom. Thus, findings suggest that educational policymakers, materials designers, and teachers need to develop educational policies and practices in such a way that embraces linguistic diversity and inclusivity.

   South African instructional designers

   visual design; higher education; Global South
ID EMOTIONAL DESIGN; ACCESSIBILITY; QUALITY; IMPACT
AB Higher education institutions in South Africa are adopting online learning systems, providing learning material in electronic format to a growing number of students. Online learning material is a crucial component of the learning experience, demanding considerable attention and ample time for its development. While much of the existing literature stems from the Global North, recent work has begun to examine diverse educational contexts, including those in the Global South. This study aimed to explore the perspectives of South African instructional designers regarding quality indicators of effective visual design of the online learning material they develop. Findings underscore the significance of considering and implementing effective visual design principles in online learning material to enhance the overall learning experience for students.

   the valuable life concept

DT Article

   Thailand
AB In today's educational landscape, many Thai teachers face burnout. Teacher development must therefore move beyond technical training to embrace the "valuable life" concept, emphasizing positive attitudes, meaningful experiences, and societal contributions. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study aimed to: (1) examine the developmental needs of teachers under Thailand's Office of the Basic Education Commission (OBEC) regarding this concept, and (2) propose relevant development approaches. Consequently, development approaches focusing on fostering professional attitudes, enriching lived experiences, and enhancing societal contributions were proposed to sustain teachers' professional growth.

TI Enhancing motivation in gamified learning: how relatedness moderates the
   ARCS model
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Gamification; ARCS model; relatedness; motivation; higher education;
   PLS-SEM
ID SELF-DETERMINATION; DISCRIMINANT VALIDITY; SEM
AB Gamification is widely adopted to enhance student motivation, yet its effectiveness remains context-dependent and theoretically fragmented. This study examines how the ARCS motivational model (Attention, Relevance, Confidence, and Satisfaction) influences motivation in gamified learning environments, and whether Relatedness, drawn from Self-Determination Theory, moderates these relationships. It also investigates the role of control variables (gender, academic major, and institutional affiliation) in predicting motivation. A quantitative survey was administered to 453 business students from two Malaysian universities following gamified activities implemented through the Socrative platform. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings reveal that Relevance and Satisfaction significantly predicted motivation, whereas Attention and Confidence did not. Relatedness moderated the effects of Satisfaction (positive) and Confidence (negative), suggesting its dual role in shaping social and psychological engagement. Control variables were non-significant. Theoretically, this study extends the ARCS framework by incorporating relatedness as a social moderator, advancing understanding of motivational processes in gamified learning. Empirically, it contributes evidence from a non-Western higher education context. Practically, the results highlight the need for educators to design gamified learning that prioritizes relevance, satisfaction, and social connectedness rather than demographic tailoring. Despite demonstrating moderate explanatory power (R-2 = 0.557), the model's predictive performance was low, indicating limited forecasting ability. This limitation suggests the importance of testing more diverse samples and additional moderators in future research to strengthen predictive generalizability.

TI Impact of longitudinal integrated clerkships on national medical
   licensing examination (Japan) performance
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Community-based medical education; longitudinal integrated clerkship;
   national examination; summative assessment; undergraduate medical
   education
ID STUDENTS; OUTCOMES
AB Introduction: Longitudinal integrated clerkship (LIC) represents an innovative clinical education model emphasizing continuity of patient care, supervision, and interdisciplinary learning. Previous studies have demonstrated educational advantages of LIC and its stable performance in institutional assessments; however, its impact on high-stakes national licensing examinations remains to be elucidated. In Japan, where the National Medical Examination is a critical summative assessment, evidence regarding the influence of clerkship type on examination outcomes is lacking. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of LIC participation on academic performance, compared with the traditional block rotation (TBR) model. Materials and methods: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at the University of Toyama. Medical students completed a mandatory 50-week TBR followed by a 24-week optional clerkship, during which up to 12 weeks could be taken as LIC across seven affiliated community hospitals. Students with missing examination data or who withdrew consent were excluded. Data collected included Computer-Based Test Item Response Theory (CBT-IRT) scores and results from the 118th and 119th National Medical Licensing Examinations. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was used to assess the association between LIC participation and total, essential, and specific examination scores, adjusting for age, sex, and CBT-IRT performance. Results: A total of 119 students were included. In the 118th cohort, LIC students had significantly higher CBT scores, while in the 119th cohort, a greater proportion had repeated a year (both p < 0.05). After adjustment, no significant differences were observed between LIC and TBR students in total or component National Examination scores in either cohort. Discussion: The findings indicated that LIC participation was not associated with inferior outcomes on the National Examination after adjusting for baseline academic performance. These results suggest that LIC may be implemented without apparent detriment to academic outcomes in the context of Japanese medical education.

TI Learning planetary health through international & interprofessional
   education: a qualitative study of student reflections
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Planetary health education; interprofessional education; international
   collaboration; global health; environmental health; health education and
   promotion; interdisciplinary research; qualitative study
ID CLIMATE
AB Background: Planetary health, defined as the interdependence of human and ecological systems, is recognised as an urgent concern for health professional education. Most reported interventions have been developed within single institutions, and empirical evidence examining international and interdisciplinary approaches remains limited. Methods: Reflective writings from 25 medical, nursing, and pharmacy students who participated in a one-week in-person international summer school on planetary health, delivered across seven universities in the Global Alliance of Medical Excellence consortium, were thematically analysed. The curriculum, co-designed by 11 faculty and planetary health experts, combined lectures, simulations, and group projects to foster intercultural and interprofessional collaboration. Reflections were collected using structured prompts based on Gibbs' reflective cycle and analysed using Braun and Clarke's approach. Rigour was supported through independent coding, team consensus, adhering to COREQ guidelines. Results: Three themes with seven subthemes were identified. First, students articulated their understanding of planetary health, including reflections on advocacy and systems thinking as relevant professional frameworks. Second, they valued interprofessional and intercultural collaboration, recognising opportunities of diverse perspectives and challenges of communication across contexts. Third, students expressed considerations regarding potential advocacy at individual, institutional, and societal levels, ranging from personal practice to curricular reform and stakeholder engagement. While mostly aspirational, these comments reflected early awareness of sustainability as a professional responsibility and represent immediate, self-reported perceptions rather than evidence of behavioural change. Conclusions: This study provides exploratory empirical insights into how students perceive and reflect on planetary health learning. The findings extend beyond the scope of single-institution interventions by suggesting that cross-border programmes may add distinctive value. Given the short duration, self-selected sample, and reliance on self-report, outcomes should be interpreted cautiously. Future research should examine longitudinal learning processes, scalability through virtual or regional models, and inclusion of perspectives from low- and middle-income countries to strengthen equity and sustainability.

TI Explore bilingual education and STEAM integration in science curriculum:
   a case study on electric circuit learning in fourth-grade elementary

DT Article

   Yunlin County; Taiwan
AB This study investigates the integration of bilingual instruction and STEAM education in an elementary science curriculum, focusing on how learners with differing levels of prior knowledge engage with electricity concepts. Guided by Taiwan's Bilingual Nation 2030 policy and the emphasis on interdisciplinary learning, the research examines whether bilingual STEAM instruction can support science understanding, English use and learning attitudes in a rural context. ID ANXIETY
AB Previous Medium of instruction (PMoI) and Gender as structural determinants of glossophobia have been understudied in the multilingual educational setting where language proficiency overlaps with identity construction. To explore the relationship between PMoI, gender, and glossophobia among higher education students of Pakistan, we surveyed 246 undergraduates from six Pakistani universities using the Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale (FLCAS), adapted to capture phenomenological experiences, and conducted semi-structured interviews to analyze their experiences (n = 30). Chi-square tests were used to test the relationship between PMoI/gender and anxiety dimensions (communication apprehension, fear of negative evaluation, and test anxiety). However, in contrast to proficiency suppositions, English-PMoI students reported 1.6 & times; greater anxiety than Urdu-PMoI students, which was due to the identity preservation pressures instead of language shortcomings. Female participants realized as 2.3 times more afraid of negative evaluation, and this tendency was associated with the patriarchal surveillance relationships. The results of the qualitative analysis demonstrated that the intersection of PMoI-gender conditions four different types of anxiety. The study proposes new theoretical frameworks, such as attentional hierarchies, which provide evidence for educational socialization rewiring the threat perception, and presents the first population-scale study of the so-called English-medium anxiety paradox in South Asia. The results require PMoI-specific pedagogical interventions and policy changes to address linguistic hegemony in plurilingual classes and its use in other contexts of plurilingual education worldwide.

SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Eco-cultural values; sustainability education; culturally responsive
   pedagogy; environmental literacy; local knowledge systems
ID TEACHERS
AB This study examines how eco-cultural values in local communities can inform culturally responsive and sustainability-oriented education in Indonesia. It focuses on how traditions, communal practices, and human-nature relationships shape environmental understanding and responsibility. Using a qualitative exploratory design, the research was conducted in eight eco-cultural communities in East Java, representing coastal, highland, agrarian, and mixed forest-agricultural settings. A total of 48 participants were purposively selected, including community elders, cultural practitioners, farmers, artisans, and local leaders with recognized ecological knowledge. The study highlights the potential of integrating eco-cultural perspectives into education to strengthen environmental literacy, cultural awareness, and responsible behavior. However, the research is limited to a single regional context and relies on qualitative interpretation, which may limit generalizability. Future research should include more diverse communities and examine how these values can be systematically integrated into curriculum and pedagogy.

TI Internal auditing of hands-on teaching events improves learning among
   students in the clinical phase of the university level medical school
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teaching event; auditing; feedback; medical student; hands-on; learning
ID EXPERIENCES; EDUCATION; FEEDBACK; SKILLS
AB The purpose of auditing teaching is to develop teaching through observation, feed-back, and reflection. There is a limited literature on auditing individual teacher-led teaching events in medical schools. The Musculoskeletal and Plastic Surgery course in University of Helsinki is held four times a year and consists of 13 teacher-led teaching events comprising Examination of the patient and Procedures. The auditing process included formal evaluation and feedback of each of these teaching events, collection of student feedback, and exam results before and after the audit, resulting in over 3500 feedback responses from 467 students. TI Beyond technical skills: the critical role of mindset in language
   assessment literacy development
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Language assessment literacy; mindset; formative assessment;
   professional development; high-stakes contexts
AB This study investigates the interplay between teachers' mindsets and language assessment literacy (LAL) in high-stakes EFL contexts, with a focus on Iranian educators operating under extreme exam pressures. Grounded in Dweck's mindset theory, the research employs a convergent parallel mixed-methods design combining questionnaires (n = 110) and in-depth interviews (n = 20) to analyze assessment beliefs and practices among 120 EFL teachers. The study proposes a novel conceptual model (Figure 1) that demonstrates how mindset mediates between teaching experience and assessment practices. This framework advances beyond traditional competency-based LAL models by explicitly positioning teachers' beliefs about learning malleability as a foundational component intersecting three domains: technical knowledge, pedagogical skills and socio-cultural awareness. Findings reveal that growth-mindset teachers exhibit significantly higher LAL (M = 4.1, d = 1.71), particularly in implementing formative assessments and adaptive feedback, whereas fixed-mindset teachers rely predominantly on summative methods. Teaching experience enhances assessment flexibility, with mindset mediating 45% of this relationship (p = 0.002). The research underscores the critical need to integrate mindset training into professional development programs. Practical recommendations include adaptable protocols for large-class constraints, mindset-focused workshops and peer mentorship initiatives. These evidence-based insights offer actionable strategies for reforming teacher education in exam-dominated systems like Iran, China and Saudi Arabia, while advancing theoretical understanding of affective factors in LAL.

TI Leadership under informal coercion: Unpacking the emotional costs of
   principals' roles in Indonesian schools
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Leadership; principal role; emotional cost; informal coercion;
   Indonesian schools; Leadership; principal role; emotional cost; informal
   coercion; Indonesian schools
AB This study explores how Indonesian public senior and vocational high school principals (SMAN/SMK) experience and interpret informal coercion in their everyday leadership. Using a phenomenological design with semi-structured interviews and field observations, the research indicates that coercion is not an isolated incident but a systemic emotional condition embedded within bureaucratic, community, and institutional relations. Three interrelated forms of coercion emerged: bureaucratic intimidation, community interference, and institutionalised reciprocity. These pressures generate persistent fear, moral dissonance, and emotional withdrawal, transforming leadership into an act of emotional survival. Drawing upon Role Conflict Theory, Emotional Labour Theory, and Riley's Wellbeing Framework, the study demonstrates that principals' emotional strain arises from structural contradictions demanding simultaneous compliance, harmony, and integrity. Informal coercion thus functions as a form of emotional governance-maintaining bureaucratic stability through moral sentiment and affective conformity rather than formal sanction. By conceptualising informal coercion as a locally embedded form of emotional governance, this study offers a novel framework for understanding leadership under systemic ambiguity and highlights the need for policy and professional support to mitigate emotional strain.

TI Exploring EFL learners' switching intention to AI-assisted learning
   through Push-Pull-Mooring framework: a SEM analysis
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; EFL learners; higher education; PPM; learners'
   switching intention
ID USER ACCEPTANCE; ADOPTION; TECHNOLOGY; STUDENTS; MODEL
AB Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education through personalized learning, yet factors driving students' switching intentions (SWI) from traditional methods remain underexplored in Global South contexts. This study offers the first comprehensive analysis of AI adoption among Pakistani EFL learners using the Push-Pull-Mooring (PPM) framework. Data from 435 students across twelve public universities were analyzed via PLS-SEM. Five significant predictors of SWI emerged: student innovativeness (beta = 0.274), perceived enjoyment (beta = 0.187), threats to AI (beta = 0.152), learning autonomy (beta = 0.143), and perceived boredom (beta = 0.122). Notably, dissatisfaction, learning convenience, and network externalities showed no significant influence. These findings underscore the primacy of internal motivators over external factors and challenge the assumption that dissatisfaction is a primary push factor in developing countries. Contextually, realistic threats to AI significantly shape switching intentions despite technological normalization. In practice, the study advocates for AI curricula that promote autonomy, ethical risk awareness, and innovation-focused training, alongside national policy guidelines. Theoretically, it validates PPM's applicability in non-Western EFL settings and introduces a novel framework that integrates realistic threats and boredom constructs, thereby advancing predictive models for educational technology adoption in resource-constrained environments.

SO COGENT EDUCATION

DT Article

   self-esteem

   ADOLESCENTS; CHILDREN; YOUTH; ACHIEVEMENT; PERFORMANCE; PREVALENCE
AB The use of online social networks takes up a large amount of students' time, increasing the risk of cyber victimization that have adverse educational consequences. The present study aimed to investigate the relationship between cyber victimization and academic well-being with a focus on the mediating role of self-esteem and perceived social sup-port in high school students. The participants in this study were 400 high school stu-dents in Kermanshah, Iran who were selected in 2023 using multi-stage cluster random sampling. Using data from 400 Iranian adolescents, the findings reveal that cyber victimization dir-ectly and negatively predicts academic well-being. Importantly, both self-esteem and perceived social support act as significant mediators, buffering the adverse effects of cyber victimization. These results highlight the need for school based interventions that strengthen students' self worth and social support networks-particularly from family, friends, and teachers to protect academic engagement and well being in the face of online harassment.

TI Using randomization to compare AI and expert-generated formative
   assessment questions in medical education
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; medical education; formative assessment; multiple-choice
   questions; randomized study
AB Background: AI-generated content is being used across the education spectrum and is beneficial for creating complex multiple-choice questions, such as those used in medical education. However, evaluating AI-generated content is challenging, and existing testing and evaluation methods are falling short. This study uses randomization to compare medical students' performance on and subjective evaluation of AI versus expert-generated questions. We hypothesized that there would be no difference in student performance or subjective evaluation of AI vs expert-generated questions. Methods: We designed a single-center, randomized study where medical student participants received either one AI- or expert-generated question per day over four weeks. Results: Our study showed that participants had similar perceptions of AI versus expert-generated questions (p = 0.18), with no significant difference between the distributions of the proportion of correct responses. The cumulative proportion of questions answered correctly over 28 days was consistent across the two question sets. However, participants rated 53% of AI-generated questions as very easy or easy compared with only 31% of the expert-generated questions. Discussion: Randomization was crucial to show that AI-generated questions were nearly imperceptible from expert-generated questions, demonstrating the need for additional evaluation methods to compare AI- and expert-generated medical education content.

TI The impact of supervisor support on academic adaptation of medical
   research postgraduates: a serial mediation model of research
   self-efficacy and psychological resilience
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Supervisor support; research self-efficacy; psychological resilience;
   academic adaptation; medical postgraduate education
ID STUDENTS; STRESS
AB Supervisor support (SS) constitutes a core element in cultivating academic Master of Medical Science (MMS) students, yet the psychological mechanisms associated with academic adaptation (AA) remain insufficiently elucidated. This study investigates the pathways through which supervisor support influences academic adaptation via research self-efficacy (RSE) and psychological resilience (PsyRes). Employing a cross-sectional design, 1,486 academic MMS students from two medical universities in Xinjiang were surveyed through cluster sampling. Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) validated variable associations, while Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) tested chain mediation effects. Results indicated significant positive correlations between supervisor support and research self-efficacy (r = 0.411, P < 0.001), psychological resilience (r = 0.379, P < 0.001), and academic adaptation (r = 0.623, P < 0.001). Research self-efficacy strongly correlated with psychological resilience (r = 0.760, P < 0.001) and academic adaptation (r = 0.619, P < 0.001), while psychological resilience positively was positively associated with academic adaptation (r = 0.634, P < 0.001). Redundancy analysis revealed the first canonical variable (U-1 = -0.643X(1) - 0.374X(2)) explained 96.3% of supervisor support variance, with the second (U-2 = -2.654X(1) + 2.705X(2)) explaining 3.7%. Further mediation analysis revealed a significant direct effect of supervisor support on academic adaptation was 0.377 (95% CI:0.346,0.408), accounting for 67.20% of the total effect. The total indirect effect through research self-efficacy and psychological resilience was 0.184 (95% CI:0.159,0.210), representing 32.80% of the total effect, confirming significant chain mediation (P < 0.001). The findings suggest that to enhance academic adaptation, we recommend strategically leveraging supervisor support, cultivating positive research mindsets, proactively tracking motivation and efficacy, and facilitating deep scientific engagement.

TI Perceptions and practices of sustainability education among university
   lecturers in Somalia
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Education for sustainable development; higher education; SEM; Somali
   universities; ESD; SDGs
AB Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) plays a critical role in addressing environmental, social, and economic challenges, particularly in post-conflict regions such as Somalia. This study evaluates the integration of ESD within Somali universities, aiming to assess educators' knowledge, attitudes, practices, and perceived barriers. A quantitative methodology was employed, utilizing structured questionnaires administered to 247 university lecturers across five universities. Data analysis was conducted using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) software, complemented by Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) and regression analysis to identify relationships between variables. The results revealed a strong consensus on the importance of ESD, with a mean score of 4.25 for the statement "ESD is crucial for Somalia's development." Teaching practices emerged as the most critical factor for ESD integration, with the inclusion of sustainability topics achieving the highest factor loading of 0.79. Correlation analysis indicated a positive relationship between confidence in teaching sustainability and the inclusion of ESD topics r = 0.238. These findings highlight the urgent need for targeted interventions, such as curriculum reform and professional development programs, to overcome barriers and foster sustainable development in Somali universities.

TI Exploring Portuguese teachers' understanding of differentiated
   instruction through Q-methodology
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Differentiated instruction; teachers perceptions; inclusive education;
   Q-methodology; equity
ID EDUCATION
AB In contemporary educational settings, marked by diverse student populations, the effective implementation and understanding of DI remain complex and multifaceted. By employing Q-sort methodology, we identified four distinct groups of teachers, each with unique interpretations of DI, ranging from a one-size-fits-all approach to more competency-based adaptive methods. These perceptions include: (1) Egalitarian DI Practices - Student Needs Unresponsive, focusing on participation without individual tailoring; (2) Competence Adaptive - Grouping Struggling Pupils Unfavorable, emphasizing adaptive teaching while resisting segregation of struggling learners; (3) One-Size-Fits-Most - Student Voice Unfavorable, limiting DI to students with significant challenges; and (4) One-Size-Fits-All - High-performing Inattentive, neglecting the needs of high-performing students. No differences were found in teachers' perceptions of DI across different grade levels or years of experience. Based on these results, particularly in Portugal, genuine practices of DI are not a commonplace but rather an exception. These findings underscore the imperative for targeted professional development to address misperceptions and enhance teachers' comprehension of DI as an inclusive methodology.

TI Synergy of public spending on health and education and human development
   in the WAEMU countries
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Human development; public spending on health and education; life
   expectancy; IV-2sls; WAEMU; Human development; public spending on health
   and education; life expectancy; IV-2sls; WAEMU
ID ECONOMIC-GROWTH; EXPENDITURES; INVESTMENT; INCOME
AB In the context of a major societal preoccupation with improving economic and human development, governments are likely to rely heavily on public spending on health and education as key instruments and fundamental support for improving the quality of life of their citizens. This study examines the synergistic effects of public expenditures on health and education on human development in seven (7) countries of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU) between 1999 and 2022. Information on the variables is drawn from three major institutional sources (UNDP, WDI and WGI), ensuring their reliability and international comparability. This study is limited by the quality and irregularity of the panel data in the WAEMU. A risk of residual endogeneity (omitted variable bias) remains, despite modeling efforts. The results of the panel-corrected standard error (PCSE) and Driscoll-Kraay methods indicate that spending in these two sectors significantly improves the human development index, life expectancy and primary school enrollment rates while reducing infant mortality. The analysis reveals that complementary investments in health and education generate greater effects on human development than isolated investments do. This finding underlines the importance of a balanced policy approach that simultaneously promotes both sectors, a result confirmed by the IV-2SLS method, which corrects for potential endogeneity. These findings call on WAEMU governments to adopt coordinated budgetary policies to harness the health-Education synergy. The implication is to move away from silo management towards joint budgeting. It is crucial to increase expenditure efficiency by focusing on primary healthcare and the quality of education.

TI What shapes AI learning outcomes? Investigating the role of
   self-efficacy, institutional support and gender
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI self-efficacy; AI learning outcomes; institutional support; social
   cognitive theory; Social Sciences; Education; Educational Technology;
   Teacher Education & Training; Education & Training
ID SOCIAL COGNITIVE THEORY; ACHIEVEMENT GOALS; SAMPLE-SIZE; STUDENTS;
   PREDICTORS; MODELS; POWER; PEER
AB Artificial Intelligence (AI) education has become a critical component of modern curricula worldwide, aiming to equip students with the necessary skills to thrive in an AI-driven future. Despite numerous initiatives, students often struggle to master fundamental AI concepts, highlighting the need to explore factors influencing AI learning outcomes. This study investigates the relationship between students' AI self-efficacy and their AI learning outcomes, with a focus on the mediating role of institutional support and the moderating effect of gender. Drawing on Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory, the research employs a two-phase sequential design with multi-wave data collection, involving 743 high school students enrolled in AI-related courses. The findings reveal a significant positive relationship between AI self-efficacy and AI learning outcomes, with institutional support partially mediating this relationship. Gender disparities were also observed, with male students benefiting more from AI self-efficacy and institutional support compared to female students. The study underscores the importance of fostering AI self-efficacy and providing equitable institutional support to enhance AI learning outcomes, particularly for female students. These insights offer actionable recommendations for educators, policymakers, and curriculum developers to design more effective and inclusive AI education strategies.

TI Academic resilience assessment program for pharmacy students: a
   cross-sectional study
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic resilience; pharmacy students; ARS-30; India; education; Social
   Sciences; Education
ID EDUCATION; INDIA
AB Academic stress and burnout are common among pharmacy students, yet the factors influencing their resilience remain unclear. We aimed to assess the factors contributing to academic resilience among pharmacy students and accordingly, a cross-sectional study was conducted among 423 pharmacy students in Karnataka, India. The participants demonstrated high academic resilience (median Academic Resilience Scale-30 [ARS-30] score = 112 [IQR = 19]). Their resilience was associated with stronger academic performance (beta = 0.300, p < 0.001), higher social support (beta = 0.158, p < 0.001), and effective coping strategies (beta = 0.135, p = 0.002). The implementation of an effective peer mentorship, nutrition counselling, digital literacy, and gender-sensitive support in schools may strengthen academic resilience.

TI Innovative thinking and application skills-oriented pedagogy in
   mechanics education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Application skills; innovative thinking; mechanics education;
   engineering education reform; adaptive learning
AB This study introduces a Three-Phase Pedagogical Model (TPM) for foundational mechanics education to better cultivate students' innovative application competencies. The TPM comprises three temporal phases-Phase 1 Experiential Foundations, Phase 2 Scaffolded Application, and Phase 3 Innovation & Industry Integration-supported by cross-cutting Micro (real-time analytics and adaptive feedback), Meso (cognitive apprenticeship and collaborative design cycles), and Macro (PDCA-driven curriculum and industry alignment) Operational Layers. A longitudinal mixed-methods, quasi-experimental design followed 2,100 students (2020-2024), integrating learning analytics, expert-rated performance rubrics, and qualitative triangulation (surveys, reflective artifacts, instructor debriefs). Multi-source evidence indicates consistent gains across composite competency indices and performance metrics after adjustment and sensitivity analyses, suggesting that coupling phased experiential progression with layer-based adaptive supports can accelerate foundational-to-innovative skill transfer. The model yields actionable design principles for globally scaling adaptive, Industry 4.0-aligned reform in mechanics curricula. However, causal inference remains limited by the non-randomized, single-system context; future work should employ multi-site randomized or stepped-wedge trials, test cross-institutional measurement invariance of competency indices, and evaluate cost, equity, and VR-integrated adaptive cycle scalability in resource-constrained settings. These findings position the TPM as a structured, evidence-informed architecture advancing outcome-focused engineering education reform.

TI A pedagogical framework to enhance students' perception of mathematics
   relevance in Information Technology education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pedagogy; Information Technology; perception shift; mathematics; student
   engagement
AB Mathematics is fundamental to Information Technology (IT), supporting areas such as programming, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and networking. However, many IT students perceive mathematics as abstract and disconnected from computing practice, resulting in low engagement and weak competency. This study proposes the IT Mathematics Relevance and Perception Framework (ITM-RPF), a structured pedagogical model designed to improve students' perceptions of mathematics by linking it to real-world IT tasks. The framework comprises four phases: Perception Analysis and Diagnostic, Contextualized Integration and Applied Learning, Experiential Simulation and Performance Enhancement, and Perception Shift Evaluation and Continuous Learning. Using a quasi-experimental design, the study involved 152 undergraduate IT students at AAMUSTED, Ghana, and examined mathematical competency and perceptions before and after a 12-week intervention. Results showed that average test scores improved from 41% pre-intervention to 64% post-intervention, indicating a substantial increase in competency. While 52% of students initially fell within the weak proficiency category, none remained in this group after the intervention. Perceptions of mathematics relevance also improved significantly, with mean agreement rising from 2.3 to 4.1 out of 5. Paired samples t-tests confirmed statistically significant improvements (p < 0.001).

TI Encouraging peer interaction through fishbowl learning and student
   seminar during small group teaching in medical undergraduate students
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Fish bowl; interaction; seminar; active learning; peer; undergraduate;
   Arts & Humanities; Arts; Media Communication; Humanities; Cultural
   Studies; Media & Film Studies; Communication Studies
ID EDUCATION; KNOWLEDGE
AB Modern medical education stresses upon the use of active learning and peer interaction, which improve communication skills, motivation, and acquisition of knowledge. This study aimed to compare the efficacy of fishbowls and student seminars in medical undergraduate students and assess students' perceptions of them. The study was conducted on 92 undergraduate students of year 2 divided into two groups, with half assigned to the fishbowl method and the remaining to the student seminar. TI Job sharing practices and organisational performance in higher
   education: a Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling
   (PLS-SEM) approach in Tanzanian universities
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Job-sharing; shared responsibility; divided responsibility; unequal
   ratio splits; perceived organisational performance
ID HUMAN-RESOURCE MANAGEMENT; SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; WORK; MOTIVATION;
   EMPLOYMENT; IMPACT
AB The study investigates how job-sharing practices influence academic staff's perceived organisational performance of universities in Tanzania. Guided by Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, the study conceptualises job sharing through three responsibility configurations; shared responsibility, divided responsibility, and unequal ratio splits, and tests their effects on perceived organisational performance. A positivist cross-sectional survey design was employed. The institutional study frame comprised operational universities in Tanzania, while the analytical unit was academic staff; usable data were obtained from 306 academic staff drawn from 11 public and 17 private universities. Data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory indicator reliability, internal consistency, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. The structural model showed that shared responsibility, divided responsibility, and unequal ratio splits all had positive and significant effects on perceived organisational performance. A substantial proportion of the variance in perceived organisational performance was explained by the model, and blindfolding results showed adequate predictive relevance. The findings indicate that collaboration in accountability, clear division of tasks, and transparent workload allocation are performance-supportive ways of organising shared academic work. The study adds to job sharing theory by modelling job sharing in the form of a multidimensional responsibility structure as opposed to a generic flexible work strategy and demonstrating that unequal ratio divisions are not always performance destructive. The study recommends that universities establish formalised job-sharing structures that align work distribution with expertise, transparency, and coordination in shared academic work.

AB Research in written feedback (WF) engagement has proliferated in the recent decade. However, most studies are centred around learners' engagement on the feedback, rather than with feedback. TI Closing the achievement gap? Financial aid and academic performance in
   higher education
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Higher education; scholarships; propensity score matching; causal
   impact; Morocco
ID STUDENT AID; COLLEGE; IMPACT
AB This paper evaluates the impact of scholarship aid on higher education outcomes in Morocco, examining whether financial support improves academic performance and progression. Using a sample of 13,300 graduate and undergraduate students observed between 2010 and 2023, the study applies Propensity Score Matching (PSM) with nearest-neighbor, radius, and kernel matching algorithms to compare scholarship recipients with similar non-recipients while controlling for observable characteristics. The results indicate that scholarships significantly improve academic outcomes. In particular, receiving a scholarship reduces the average time required to obtain a diploma by approximately five months and increases the likelihood of graduating with academic distinction. Balance diagnostics and sensitivity analyses confirm the robustness of these estimates. By providing new evidence from a developing-country context, this study contributes to the literature on financial aid, which has largely focused on access or evidence from high-income countries. The findings suggest that scholarship programs in Morocco could be further strengthened by combining financial aid with complementary academic support mechanisms.

TI Prioritising teaching and learning for quality instruction: school
   leadership practices of public primary headteachers in Gasabo District,
   Rwanda
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Prioritising teaching and learning; quality instruction; school
   leadership; public primary headteachers; Gasabo District; Rwanda;
   Teacher Professional Development; Quality Education; School Leadership;
   Primary Education
AB This study investigated how headteachers in Gasabo District prioritise teaching and learning through coordinating instructional activities, motivating teaching-learning, and monitoring assessment. The study's novelty lies in its integrative analysis of relational and technical leadership practices, offering empirical insights into the mechanisms through which learning-centered and transformational leadership theories translate into tangible instructional outcomes. A mixed-methods design was adopted, combining quantitative questionnaires administered to purposively selected 99 teachers, 37 Directors of Studies, and 37 headteachers, with semi-structured interview to 15 headteachers. Qualitative findings from headteachers highlight variability in leadership practice, compounded by structural challenges such as overcrowding, limited resources, and administrative workload. This study advances knowledge by providing empirical evidence on the nuanced ways leadership practices interact with school context, offering practical guidance for policy-makers, headteachers, and researchers seeking to strengthen primary education leadership in Rwanda and similar settings.

TI A study on the Dilemmas faced by Chinese clinical medicine interns
   preparing for postgraduate entrance examinations: a grounded theory
   approach
SO MEDICAL EDUCATION ONLINE
LA English
DT Article
DE Grounded theory; conflict between internship and postgraduate entrance
   examinations preparation; weak enforcement of regulations; teaching
   incentive mechanism; clinical skill evaluation system
AB IntroductionClinical internship is a critical stage for cultivating clinical competence among medical undergraduates. However, Chinese clinical medicine interns (CMI) often face intense conflicts between completing internships and preparing for the postgraduate entrance examination (PEE), which severely affects the quality of clinical internship and professional development.MethodsAdopting a grounded theory approach, this study conducted in-depth interviews with CMI who had experienced an internship and PEE preparation. Data were analyzed using open coding, axial coding, and selective coding to explore the dilemmas and corresponding solutions.ResultsThree levels of dilemmas were identified: (1) Student-level dilemmas: limited learning outcomes from internships, pressure for postgraduate advancement, and aspiration-reality gaps. (2) Teaching-level dilemmas: low sense of teaching accomplishment and low teaching efficacy. (3) Institutional-level dilemmas: weak regulation enforcement and misalignment of institutional orientation.ConclusionTo alleviate these conflicts, this study proposes optimizing the internship model, strengthening teaching incentives, redesigning the clinical skill evaluation system, and tightening regulation enforcement. These strategies are expected to foster a supportive clinical learning environment and strengthen the development of competent medical professionals.

AB This study explores the lived experiences of first-generation graduate students in Israel, highlighting the socio-psychological complexities of academic identity formation. As the first in their families to pursue higher education at the graduate level, these students face intersecting social, cultural, and class-based challenges, often accompanied by feelings of alienation and partial belonging. TI Exploring the role of active learning in developing student competencies
   for a knowledge-based economy
SO COGENT EDUCATION

DT Article

   thinking; knowledge-based economy; lifelong learning
ID CRITICAL THINKING; SCIENCE
AB This study examines how Activity-Based Learning (ABL) relates to competencies for a knowledge-based economy (KBE) and addresses limited evidence from non-Western higher education contexts. A cross-sectional survey of 481 undergraduates at Sultan Qaboos University measured seven validated Likert constructs: perceived relevance, ABL engagement, lifelong learning, critical thinking, skills development, knowledge creation, and contribution/preparedness for KBE. Analyses used descriptive statistics, reliability testing, and multiple regression; internal consistency was strong (Cronbach's alpha space=space0.81-0.90) with no missing data and no multicollinearity. TI Between didactic formalisms and didactic excellence: multiple-case study
   revealing quality of content transformation in the classroom
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Content transformation; case studies; quality improvement trajectory;
   teaching and learning quality
ID CONTENT KNOWLEDGE PCK; TEACHERS; CONCEPTUALIZATION; SCIENCE; MATTER;
   CORE
AB The transformation of content lies at the core of teaching and learning. However, content remains a neglected topic in educational research, and our understanding of how improvement processes unfold is limited. This paper aims to elucidate the nature of quality improvement trajectories that describe the progression from relatively poorer ways of mastering the content transformation (didactic formalisms) to their relatively better counterparts (didactic excellence). Drawing on the Deep Structure of Teaching and Learning Model, which underpins the 3A Methodology, we conducted a multiple-case study that revealed the following improvement trajectories: (a) from stolen representation toward closeness of representation, (b) from distortion of representation toward interconnection of empirical and instrumental experience, (c) from instrumental ineffectiveness to instrumental aptness, (d) from instrumental obscurity to instrumental clarity, and (e) from untapped to constructive handling of mistakes. Through concise examples, the paper offers a framework to help researchers and practitioners in evaluating and improving teaching and learning practices in the classroom.

It also reveals that excessive social media use may lead to internalizing behavioral issues, highlighting the need for parental supervision. The findings offer important guidance for developing balanced, AI-driven educational strategies that support both learning outcomes and student well-being.

TI Teachers' adaptation and implementation of the common core mathematics
   curriculum for junior high schools in Ghana: insight from private school
   teachers
SO COGENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Curriculum adaptation; mathematics; private school; Ghana; Common Core
   Programme
ID POLICY; SENSEMAKING
AB The purpose of the study is to examine how private school mathematics teachers adapt and implement Ghana's Common Core Programme (CCP) mathematics curriculum. The study adopted a phenomenological inquiry approach. Four teachers consented to participate in the study, and data was collected through interviews and lesson observations. Data analysis was carried out using inductive content analysis. The study revealed that teachers' patterns of adaptation were related to three areas: content, instructional expectations, and assessment. In relation to content adaptation, teachers make adaptations such as modifying content and curriculum activities based on learners' assimilation level. In terms of instructional expectations (for example, teaching and learning resources), it was established that teachers improvise using videos and cut-out shapes to facilitate teaching and learning. The study also found that teachers' assessment adaptation is based on the purpose for which they are assessing. It was also established that the lack of adequate resources, such as essential instructional materials and insufficient professional development opportunities, hinder participating teachers' operations as they adapt the CCP curriculum. The study highlights the critical need for provision of resources by the Ghana education sector authorities and collaborative professional development to enhance successful implementation of the CCP curriculum.
